title: Core features to build
text: 1. **Topic-based modules** - Each unit as a standalone “chapter” (Concept → Animation → Practice). - Example: “What is an OS?” → short animated intro → interactive diagram of user/kernel mode. 2. **Animated concept explainers** - Use simple SVG/Canvas animations for: - Process lifecycle (new → ready → running → waiting → terminated) - CPU scheduling (FCFS, SJF, RR, priority) - Synchronization (semaphores, producer-consumer, dining philosophers) - Deadlock (resource allocation graph, cycle detection) - Memory management (paging, segmentation, page faults) - Page replacement (FIFO, LRU, Optimal) - File systems (inode, directory tree, disk allocation) 3. **Interactive simulators** - Let the user input values and watch the algorithm run step by step: - Round-robin with custom time quantum and arrival times - Page-reference string + page frames - Banker’s algorithm with custom allocation/need matrices - Disk scheduling (SSTF, SCAN, C-LOOK) 4. **Mini coding labs** - Browser-based C/Python code exercises: - fork/exec/wait - thread creation (pthreads or Python threads) - IPC (pipes, shared memory) - simple shell - implementation of a page-replacement algorithm 5. **Quizzes & flashcards** - MCQs, drag-and-drop matchings (e.g., match algorithms to characteristics), fill-in-the-blanks after each concept. 6. **Progress dashboard** - Track completed topics, quiz scores, time spent.

Here is a concrete blueprint for achieving that level of quality.

title: 1. Visual design language
text: - **Design system first** - Use a strong color palette (e.g., dark slate + electric blue + neon purple for OS kernel, green for user space). - Consistent typography (Inter / Satoshi / Geist for UI; JetBrains Mono for code). - Glassmorphism panels, subtle gradients, rounded corners, and soft shadows. - A fixed 8-point spacing grid and reusable component tokens. - **Immersive “OS Command Center” theme** - Think dashboard for an OS: process tables, memory banks, CPU meter, I/O lanes. - Animated background grid, particle effects, glowing “active process” orbs. - Dark mode by default with a high-contrast light mode.

title: 2. Animation & graphics stack
text: | Goal | Best tool / approach | |---|---| | UI micro-interactions (hover, transitions, page loads) | **GSAP + Framer Motion** | | 2D animated explainers (process lifecycle, scheduling) | **SVG/Canvas + GSAP**, or **Rive** for state-machine animations | | Algorithm visualizations (page replacement, disk scheduling) | **D3.js**, **p5.js**, or custom Canvas renderer | | 3D / spatial concepts (memory hierarchy, disk platters, file system tree) | **Three.js / React Three Fiber** | | Real-time, game-like simulations | **HTML5 Canvas or PixiJS** with a requestAnimationFrame loop | | Pre-rendered cinematic clips | **Manim** exported as Lottie / MP4 / WebM |

title: 3. Interaction depth
text: - **Live simulators, not just videos** - Drag-and-drop processes into a CPU queue. - Click a process to inspect its PCB (registers, state, burst time). - Pause / step / rewind / speed-control every animation. - Editable input tables for processes, page frames, resource matrices, etc. - **Smart visual feedback** - State changes emit particles or color flashes. - Tooltips, mini-cards, and popovers appear contextually. - Sound effects for context switches, page faults, and deadlocks (optional, togglable). - **Interactive code labs** - Monaco editor (VS Code editor in the browser) for C/Python code. - One-click run in a container or Pyodide/WebAssembly sandbox. - Split view: code on the left, OS visualization on the right updating live. - **AI / helper bot** - Ask the user to input a confusing concept; explain with an on-the-fly diagram. - Could use a local LLM or an API.

title: 4. Architecture for real “production-grade” performance
text: ``` Next.js 14 (App Router) ├── Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui ├── GSAP / Framer Motion ├── React Three Fiber (3D scenes) ├── Zustand / Redux Toolkit (simulator state) ├── Web Workers (heavy algorithm runs) ├── Canvas/WebGL layer (PixiJS/Three.js) ├── Monaco Editor (code labs) └── Supabase (auth, progress, comments) ``` - Use **Web Workers** so heavy simulations do not freeze the UI. - Use a **central animation loop** to sync all components to a global “OS clock”.

title: 5. Content structure per topic
text: For every topic, follow this consistent flow: 1. **Hook** — 5-second motion intro (e.g., a process wakes up and enters the queue). 2. **Concept** — Animated explainer with narration or text. 3. **Playground** — Interactive simulator with user input. 4. **Quiz** — Instant, animated feedback. 5. **Lab** — Code it yourself, with a visual trace.

title: 6. “Wow” features
text: - **3D OS world**: a memory manager room, disk arm that physically moves, a CPU that “executes” instructions. - **Replay & share**: export a GIF/MP4 of a simulation; share a URL with pre-filled inputs. - **Gamification**: XP, badges, streaks, leaderboards for fastest scheduler or fewest page faults. - **Mobile app feel**: PWA, offline cache, smooth gestures, swipeable cards. - **Accessibility**: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, reduced-motion mode.

title: 7. Realistic path to “best”
text: Because “best graphics and fully working” is a lot, build in tiers: | Phase | Deliverable | |---|---| | Phase 1 | 1 beautiful, fully working simulator (e.g., Round-Robin) + 1 concept animation | | Phase 2 | 6 core OS topics with matching simulators | | Phase 3 | 3D scenes, code labs, auth, progress tracking | | Phase 4 | AI tutor, PWA, mobile polish, social sharing |

text: **Objective**: Expand NetPulse from 4 scenarios into a comprehensive sandbox — 4 new attack/recon scenarios, a WAF mitigation toggle, manual IP blocking, deep upgrades to every existing pane (filters/export in Packet Analyzer, extended metrics + incident timeline in Telemetry, pan/zoom + world map + firewall node in Topology, autocomplete + new commands in Terminal), an in-app Guide panel, a theme switcher, fullscreen mode, and an onboarding tour — plus Vitest tests, code-splitting, and mobile responsiveness. Explicitly **excludes** auto-play/cinematic sequencing, sound, and persistence/URL deep-links per your answers. **Key architectural decisions:** 1. Replace the flat `phase` union with a **scenario registry** (`src/lib/scenarios/`) — each scenario is a self-contained module (telemetry curve, packet generator, terminal command, description) so adding scenarios doesn't multiply if/else branches across 6+ files. 2. Switch theming to **CSS variables via Tailwind v4 `@theme inline`** so palettes can swap at runtime without touching component code (flagged as a risk to spike-test early). 3. New depth goes **inside** existing panes via tabs/drawers (not new grid cells), preserving the original 4-pane layout. 4. WAF mitigation and manual IP blocking are **orthogonal toggles/actions**, not scenarios — they modulate whichever attack is active. 5. Anti-cheat ban is **generalized** to work from any attack scenario, funneling into one shared recovery ramp. The plan file has full detail on all 9 scenarios' exact behavior, every new/modified file, acceptance criteria, and a suggested (non-user-facing) implementation sequence. title: 1. Tool Description
text: **The Network Mapper** The Network Mapper Nmap is a utility for network exploration or security auditing. It supports ping scanning (determine which hosts are up), many port scanning techniques, version detection (determine service protocols and application versions listening behind ports), and TCP/IP fingerprinting (remote host OS or device identification). Nmap also offers flexible target and port specification, decoy/stealth scanning, sunRPC scanning, and more. Most Unix and Windows platforms are supported in both GUI and commandline modes. Several popular handheld devices are also supported, including the Sharp Zaurus and the iPAQ. ---

title: 2. What This Tool Is Used For
text: - **Category:** Information Gathering - **Learn priority:** Essential (in Kali's official top-10 — learn it early) - **Main use:** Scan in verbose mode (-v), enable OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute (-A), with version detection (-sV) against the target IP (192.168.1.1): - **Sub-tools included:** `nmap`, `ncat`, `ndiff`, `nmap-common`, `zenmap` ---

title: 3. How To Install
text: Already installed on standard Kali. Otherwise: ``` sudo apt install nmap ``` ---

title: 4. How To Use It — Step By Step
text: **1. nmap** Scan in verbose mode (-v), enable OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute (-A), with version detection (-sV) against the target IP (192.168.1.1): ``` $ nmap -v -A -sV 192.168.1.1 ``` Output you'll see: ``` Starting Nmap 6.45 ( http://nmap.org ) at 2014-05-13 18:40 MDT NSE: Loaded 118 scripts for scanning. NSE: Script Pre-scanning. Initiating ARP Ping Scan at 18:40 Scanning 192.168.1.1 [1 port] Completed ARP Ping Scan at 18:40, 0.06s elapsed (1 total hosts) ``` **2. nping** Using TCP mode (–tcp) to probe port 22 (-p 22) using the SYN flag (–flags syn) with a TTL of 2 (–ttl 2) on the remote host (192.168.1.1): ``` $ nping --tcp -p 22 --flags syn --ttl 2 192.168.1.1 ``` Output you'll see: ``` Starting Nping 0.6.45 ( http://nmap.org/nping ) at 2014-05-13 18:43 MDT SENT (0.0673s) TCP 192.168.1.15:60125 > 192.168.1.1:22 S ttl=2 id=54240 iplen=40 seq=1720523417 win=1480 RCVD (0.0677s) TCP 192.168.1.1:22 > 192.168.1.15:60125 SA ttl=64 id=0 iplen=44 seq=3377886789 win=5840 <mss 1460> SENT (1.0678s) TCP 192.168.1.15:60125 > 192.168.1.1:22 S ttl=2 id=54240 iplen=40 seq=1720523417 win=1480 RCVD (1.0682s) TCP 192.168.1.1:22 > 192.168.1.15:60125 SA ttl=64 id=0 iplen=44 seq=3393519366 win=5840 <mss 1460> SENT (2.0693s) TCP 192.168.1.15:60125 > 192.168.1.1:22 S ttl=2 id=54240 iplen=40 seq=1720523417 win=1480 ``` **3. ndiff** Compare yesterday’s port scan (yesterday.xml) with the scan from today (today.xml): ``` $ ndiff yesterday.xml today.xml ``` Output you'll see: ``` -Nmap 6.45 scan initiated Tue May 13 18:46:43 2014 as: nmap -v -F -oX yesterday.xml 192.168.1.1 +Nmap 6.45 scan initiated Tue May 13 18:47:58 2014 as: nmap -v -F -oX today.xml 192.168.1.1 endian.localdomain (192.168.1.1, 00:01:6C:6F:DD:D1): -Not shown: 96 filtered ports +Not shown: 97

title: Overall objective
text: The enduring goal is to transform the ESP-Linux ESP32 web interface into a polished, reliable browser-based operating system branded **Icy OS**. The original motivation was to make the ESP32 feel like a complete operating system rather than a simple control panel, with a realistic desktop UI, file management, terminal tools, built-in applications, networking, Wi-Fi utilities, and stable firmware behavior. The intended end state includes: - Branded Icy OS desktop UI. - Responsive support for mobile phones and touch devices. - Reliable file upload and SD-card-backed web assets. - File manager, terminal, settings, Wi-Fi tools, attacks, captive portal, and built-in utility apps. - Games and productivity applications. - STA internet connectivity for the ESP32. - NTP synchronization, OTA, security hardening, logs, backups, and production-readiness improvements. - Stable AP behavior that does not repeatedly disconnect clients. - A polished, smooth, realistic, and bug-free user experience. The user’s enduring instruction has been to implement the complete feature set and make the project “fully working,” “reliable,” “production ready,” and free of UI and firmware problems.

title: Firmware fixes
text: I improved `main.cpp` to keep the AP from dropping: - `restoreAP()` now only reconfigures if the IP or mode actually changed. - `connectSTA()` no longer calls `WiFi.disconnect()` (which was resetting the AP and could crash the radio). - `connectSTA()` now checks if STA is already connected to the same SSID and does nothing. - `connectSTA()` still has a 30-second timeout: if the router password is wrong, it gives up and keeps AP-only. - `setup()` now uses `restoreAP()` instead of separate `softAPConfig`/`softAP` calls. - Auto Wi-Fi rescan loop is still removed.

title: Why you cannot connect now
text: The ESP32 is not showing up as a USB serial device anymore: ```text /dev/cu.usbserial-5B150435941 ``` is missing from the system. This means either: - The USB cable is loose or unplugged. - The ESP32 is not getting power. - The CH340 USB-serial chip needs a re-plug after the hard reset.

title: How to avoid this next time
text: After any `pio run -t upload`, the board may need a manual **reset**: - Press the `RST` button on the ESP32, **or** - Unplug and replug the USB cable. This is a common CH340/CP2102 issue on macOS where the upload leaves the reset line asserted.

In the DMS sheet, row 96 shows: - **CO1**: B, C, I, J - **CO2**: D, E, K, L - **CO3**: F, G, H, M, N, O - Student CO totals are computed: - CO1 total = `B + C + I + J` - CO2 total = `D + E + K + L` - CO3 total = `F + G + H + M + N + O` ### 4. CO Attainment percentage There are **two methods** visible in the sheets: **Method A: % of students reaching a target score** - `DMS_2324` rows 94–95: - Count how many students scored ≥ target in each CO (e.g. `COUNTIF(CO1_total, ">=7")`). - Divide by total number of students and multiply by 100. **Method B: Average marks percentage (used in the “graph” and `attainment.xlsx`)** - For each CO: - Total marks actually scored by all students in that CO - ÷ Total marks possible for that CO - × 100 - Example in DMS rows 97–105: - `CO1 PERCENTAGE = (CO1 student marks / CO1 total possible marks) × 100` - Final CO attainment = `AVERAGE` of the percentages for all sub-parts mapped to that CO. ### 5. title: What was wrong
text: The parser expected the first row of the Excel to contain `Roll No`. Your DMS file has metadata rows first, and the real header row is **row 3**: - Row 1: `Q.`, `Q.1`, `Q.2` - Row 3: `Roll No`, `a`, `b`, `c`, ..., `g`, `a`, `b`, ..., `g` So the app was reading the wrong row. ---

title: What I fixed
text: 1. **Smart header detection** — the parser now scans for the row that actually contains `Roll No`. 2. **Sub-part label normalization** — original files use `a, b, c...` instead of `Q1a, Q1b...`. The parser now auto-converts them. 3. **Two-block detection** — when the letter sequence restarts (`a-g` then `a-g`), it starts a new block (`Q2`). 4. **Footer row filtering** — rows like `Mrs.S.S.Jogdand` or `(Course Coordinator)` are skipped. 5. **Added DMS subject** — `Database Management System (313302)` is now in the subject dropdown. ---

title: Project Workflow
text: ### 1. Setup Phase - Flash ESP32 with dashboard firmware - Connect to `FaultDetect-ESP32` Wi-Fi - Open `192.168.4.1` on phone/laptop ### 2. Machine Selection - Select machine type: **DC Motor / House Fan / Pump** - Each machine loads its own trained model profile ### 3. Data Collection Mode - Select machine + label (healthy / unbalance / misalignment / bearing / overheat) - Press **RECORD 2s SAMPLE** - ESP32 captures audio + vibration + temperature - Saves to flash as WAV + logs to CSV ### 4. Health Check Mode - Press **START HEALTH CHECK** - ESP32 captures 2 seconds of sensor data - Runs TinyML inference on-device - Shows result: **Healthy / Fault Type + Confidence %** - OLED displays status, buzzer alerts on fault ### 5. Model Training (on PC) - Download WAV samples from ESP32 - Train model in Python (`model_training/` folder) - Convert to C header (`model.h`) - Flash back to ESP32 for real inference

title: Bad USB / remote device control
text: **No — not with this board.** The current ESP32 is an `ESP32-D0WD-V3` (ESP32-DevKit). Its USB port goes through a **USB-to-UART chip** (CP2102/CH340). That means: - It can receive serial data from your laptop. - It **cannot** pretend to be a USB keyboard/mouse to another device. - It cannot control the laptop or phone it is plugged into. To do Bad USB / DuckyScript / HID attacks you need an **ESP32-S3** with a native USB-OTG port, wired to a target computer's **USB D+/D- lines** (not the same serial cable). If you switch to that hardware, I can add: - A **Bad USB** module that runs DuckyScript payloads from SD. - A **HID Replay** tool. - Keystroke injection from the web app. For the current board, the closest you can get is the **Sniffer** and **Wardrive** (network recon), but not HID or host control. === MESSAGE 316 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. title: 2. Different Wi-Fi scanning behavior on ESP-IDF 4.4.5 and ESP-IDF 5.1.1 (IDFGH-11150) · Issue #12317 · espressif/esp-idf
text: URL: https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf/issues/12317 I have a project in which the ESP32 must be connected to some access point and periodically scanning the other access points. It means that ESP32 works in STA mode and sometimes uses a scan procedure. When scanning, it is very important that the microcontroller remains connected to the access point. To achieve this goal, I use breaks between channel scans so that packets over Wi-Fi have time to be transmitted. This algorithm works fine on ESP-IDF 4.4.5. Some time ago it became necessary to upgrade to version ESP-IDF 5.1.1 (I need the specific Ethernet chip support). On the new version, my scanning algorithm stopped working correctly. On the new version my scanning algorithm stopped working correctly because when the scanning function is called, the event of disconnection from the access point immediately occurs. title: The core architecture — `cliMode` state machine
text: One mechanism unlocks all interactivity: `cliMode` in the linuxMaster store. When set, the terminal routes input to a mode handler instead of the command dispatcher: - `ssh user@host` → `password` mode → real "user@host's password:" prompt → typed input IS the password - `msfconsole` → `msf` mode → `use`/`set`/`exploit` REPL → matching vuln → `meterpreter` mode (`meterpreter >` shell with `hashdump`, `getuid`, `shell`, `download`) - `nc -lvnp 4444` → `nc-listen` mode → catches remote `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/...` callbacks → reverse-shell session - `ftp <ip>` → `ftp>` REPL with `get`/`put`/`ls` on the real target fs

title: The real "nothing works" bug — FIXED
text: Found it in `WiFiAttack::baseSetup`: when your phone is connected to `Icy-OS` (always true — it IS the screen), the code refused to move the radio off the AP channel. **So a deauth aimed at an AP on ch6 transmitted on ch1 and hit nothing — every targeted attack was a no-op.** Now the softAP **moves to the target channel with the radio** — your phone loses the link ~3–10s while it roams to the new channel, then the UI comes right back and the attack is actually transmitting where the target lives. On stop, the AP returns to its home channel. Honest limits that remain: - **`-hop` still can't move while a client is connected** — a phone can't follow a hopping AP; the start message now says so plainly. - **PMF/802.11w-protected networks ignore deauth** — that's protocol, not a bug. - **BadUSB** only does anything when the board's native USB port is plugged into a *host* (laptop), not just power — check `badusb status` says "HID armed", run `badusb run /payloads/demo.txt` with it connected to a test machine. - **BLE spam** TX counter increments in its app — popups only appear on vulnerable phones in range (modern iOS shows the AirPods-style card; unpatched Androids show Fast Pair). Also fixed while in there: corrupted icons are gone everywhere, `modules.json` is now the icon source of truth, and the deauth description warns about the ~5s channel hop. **Test it**: Wi-Fi Scanner → scan → click your lab AP → ⚡ Attack → deauth → Start. text: **Desktop icons** — the actual bug: `dblclick` doesn't fire reliably on touch, and your phone is the display. Now: **tap = open** on touch devices; on mouse, first click selects, second click (or dblclick) opens. **Cascading module failure** — real bug in `loadModules`: one module script error would `reject` and **kill every module after it**. Each module now fails independently — one bad script can't take down the desktop. **Dead-app crashes** — `openWindow` used to throw on a missing app (e.g., module not loaded yet), killing the click handler entirely. Now guards with a toast instead. **Lock screen logic** — dismissing the lock used to force re-login even when authed. title: A. Critical real-time/coverage gaps (things that silently leak today)
text: 1. **`all_frames: true` missing in manifest.** Content scripts only run in the top frame. Embedded iframes — payment widgets, Docs embeds, chat panels, internal dashboards — are completely unprotected. Also add `match_about_blank` / `match_origin_as_fallback` for sandboxed/blank frames. 2. **Inner scroll containers desync overlays.** `overlay_manager.js` listens to `scroll` on `window` without `capture` — scroll events don't bubble, so scrolling inside `overflow: auto` divs (Gmail panels, chat sidebars, code viewers) leaves overlays behind while real text scrolls. Fix: `window.addEventListener('scroll', sync, { capture: true, passive: true })` + `visualViewport` resize/scroll listeners. 3. **Shadow DOM of the host page is never scanned.** Enterprise apps (Salesforce, anything using web components) hide text in open shadow roots. TreeWalker must recursively descend into `el.shadowRoot` and `slot.assignedNodes()`. Same for the MutationObserver — it won't fire inside shadow roots unless observed separately. 4. **Top-layer elements render above everything — including our `z-index: 2147483647` overlays.** `<dialog>` with `showModal()`, fullscreen video, and popovers paint above all non-top-layer content. While screen sharing a Meet call in fullscreen or a modal containing PII, secrets are fully visible. Fix: listen to `fullscreenchange`/`popover` events and remount the overlay container inside the active top-layer element. 5. **Form field values aren't scanned.** `input.value` / `textarea.value` aren't text nodes, so credentials typed into login fields, secret values in dev-tool inputs, etc., are invisible to the scanner. Also `title`/`alt`/`aria-label`/`placeholder` attributes. For inputs, blur the whole field box (sub-range masking inside an input needs a mirror-div trick

text: 20. **Scan only mutated subtrees.** Currently every mutation triggers a full `document.body` TreeWalker pass + `getComputedStyle` per text node — painful on Gmail/Jira-scale DOMs. Collect `addedNodes`/`characterData` targets and scan only those subtrees; keep full scan for init/navigation. 21. **Batch layout reads.** `syncOverlayPositions()` calls `getBoundingClientRect()` per overlay then writes styles per overlay — layout thrash each frame. Read all rects first, then write all styles. 22. **Cap/coalesce overlays.** Merge adjacent boxes on the same line, cap overlay count (e.g., 300) with a "count exceeded" summary badge — each `backdrop-filter` div is a compositing layer, and screen-share encoders amplify every dropped frame. 23. **Regex consolidation.** Combine all rules into one alternation pass (named groups) or pre-filter text nodes by cheap heuristics (`\d` present → only digit rules) before running the full set. title: 3. Suggested demonstration flow
text: ### A. Open the core panes Click these desktop icons to open the windows: 1. **Terminal** — command console. 2. **Packet Analyzer** — Wireshark-style packet list with filters. 3. **Match Server** — BGMI-style lobby/HUD. 4. **Network Topology** — abstract + world map views. 5. **Telemetry** — live ping, tick rate, packet loss, player count. ### B. Baseline (idle state) - In the **Terminal**, type `status` and press Enter. - You see nominal UDP game-tick traffic. - Watch **Telemetry** show low ping, high tick rate, 0% packet loss. - **Packet Analyzer** shows benign game-tick UDP packets. - **Match Server** shows matchmaking → connecting → in-match. ### C. Recon phase In the **Terminal**: ```text sniff ``` - **Packet Analyzer** fills with captured packets flagged as malicious. - **Telemetry** may twitch slightly. - **Match Server** continues normally. ```text nmap -sS 192.168.1.10 ``` - Simulates a TCP SYN port sweep. - Packets appear in **Packet Analyzer**. ### D. Attack phase Pick one attack: ```text arpspoof -t 192.168.1.1 -r 192.168.1.50 ``` - MITM/ARP spoof scenario. - **Topology** highlights the attacker and rerouted path. - **Telemetry** shows a ping spike. - **Match Server** starts rubber-banding. ```text hping3 -S --flood -p 7777 104.22.15.89 ``` - SYN flood DDoS. - **Telemetry** shows high packet loss and ping. - **Packet Analyzer** floods with spoofed-source TCP SYN packets. - **Match Server** drops players. ```text hping3 --amplify -p 123 104.22.15.89 ``` - UDP reflection/amplification attack. - **Packet Analyzer** shows oversized UDP packets. ```text slowloris 104.22.15.89 ``` - Low-and-slow connection exhaustion. - **Telemetry** gradually degrades. ### E. Defend / mitigate While an attack is running: ```text waf on ``` - Dampens the attack impact in telemetry

title: Overall objective
text: The project is transforming the ESP-Linux ESP32 web interface into a polished, real-feeling operating system branded **Icy OS**. The enduring goal is to provide a reliable browser-based OS with file management, terminal functionality, Wi-Fi tools, applications, responsive UI, and stable firmware behavior on ESP32 hardware. The original motivation was to make the ESP32 system feel more like a complete operating system rather than a basic control panel. The intended end state includes: - A branded “Icy OS” interface. - Reliable file management and terminal tools. - Multiple built-in applications. - A mobile-friendly virtual keyboard. - A polished window manager. - Wi-Fi scanning and authorized attack/testing tools. - Stable AP behavior during scans and attacks. - Optional internet connectivity through STA mode. - NTP synchronization, OTA, settings management, security features, and extensible apps.

title: AP stability fixes
text: I found the likely cause of the AP reconnecting/disconnecting repeatedly and fixed it in `main.cpp`: 1. **Removed the 30-second auto-scan loop** — the Wi-Fi Scanner was triggering a scan every 30s, which forced `WIFI_AP` mode and kicked clients. 2. **`finishWiFiScan()` now calls `restoreAP()`** instead of dropping to `WIFI_AP` mode, so the AP stays up after a scan. 3. **`restoreAP()` only changes `WiFi.mode()` if needed** — no more unnecessary AP restarts. 4. **`connectSTA()` has a 30-second timeout** — if the STA password is wrong or the router is unreachable, it gives up and keeps the AP stable instead of endlessly retrying and switching channels. 5. **STA no longer auto-reconnects on its own** — the firmware manages it manually so the AP channel stays fixed.

title: Power rails (do this first)
text: - **3.3V rail** — powers: TFT, NRF24, IR receiver, joystick, IR LED - **5V rail** — powers: SD card adapter, PN532 - **GND** — every module's GND goes to a common ground with the ESP32

title: The shared SPI bus
text: Three modules share the same 3 wires — connect all of them to the same pins: | Signal | ESP32-S3 GPIO | Goes to | |---|---|---| | SCK (clock) | **GPIO 12** | TFT SCK + SD SCK + NRF24 SCK | | MOSI | **GPIO 11** | TFT SDA + SD MOSI + NRF24 MOSI | | MISO | **GPIO 13** | SD MISO + NRF24 MISO *(TFT has no MISO — skip it)* | Each module then gets its **own separate CS pin** (that's what tells them apart on the bus). ---

title: 1. TFT Display (1.8" ST7735, red board)
text: | TFT pin label | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | VCC | 3.3V | | GND | GND | | SCK | GPIO 12 | | SDA | GPIO 11 *(this is MOSI — the label is confusing)* | | AO (or DC) | GPIO 14 | | RESET (or RES) | GPIO 15 | | CS | GPIO 10 | | LED (or BL) | GPIO 16 |

title: 2. Micro SD Card Adapter (blue board)
text: | SD pin | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | VCC | **5V** (this blue module has a regulator — needs 5V in) | | GND | GND | | CS | GPIO 17 | | MOSI | GPIO 11 | | MISO | GPIO 13 | | SCK | GPIO 12 |

title: 3. NRF24L01+ (with antenna)
text: | NRF24 pin | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | VCC | **3.3V — never 5V, it will burn** | | GND | GND | | CE | GPIO 18 | | CSN | GPIO 21 | | SCK | GPIO 12 | | MOSI | GPIO 11 | | MISO | GPIO 13 | | IRQ | not connected | Tip: NRF24s are picky about power — if it acts flaky, solder a 10µF capacitor across its VCC/GND pins.

title: 4. PN532 NFC Module (red Elechouse board)
text: First: **set the two DIP switches to I2C mode** — SW1 = ON, SW2 = OFF. | PN532 pin | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | VCC | 5V (or 3.3V — module accepts both) | | GND | GND | | SDA | GPIO 8 | | SCL | GPIO 9 |

title: 5. IR Receiver (3-pin metal can)
text: | Receiver pin | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | OUT (usually left/middle per datasheet — check markings) | GPIO 46 | | GND | GND | | VCC | 3.3V | If unsure of pinout: facing the dome/bump toward you, most VS1838 types are **OUT–GND–VCC** left to right.

title: 6. IR Transmitter LED (clear LED)
text: - **Long leg (anode)** → 100Ω resistor → **GPIO 38** - **Short leg (cathode)** → **GND** (The resistor is required — without it you'll fry the LED or the GPIO.)

title: 7. Joystick Module
text: | Joystick pin | ESP32-S3 GPIO | |---|---| | +5V | **3.3V** *(feed it 3.3V, NOT 5V — the ESP32 ADC can't read above 3.3V)* | | GND | GND | | VRx | GPIO 4 | | VRy | GPIO 5 | | SW | GPIO 7 | **Controls:** push up/down = scroll menus, click (or push right) = select, push left = back/escape. ---

title: 1. Request and Intent

title: Root cause
text: **The product PDFs never made it into the download function on Vercel.** Vercel's serverless bundler only ships files it can *see* in the code — `readFile` with a dynamic filename (`private/` + `product.fileName`) isn't traced, so the lambda deployed **without the PDFs**. Buyer pays → link generates fine → download API tries to read a file that doesn't exist → `File unavailable`. That's why *every* test we ran (forge attempts → 403) looked healthy — we never did a real end-to-end download in production.

title: The three fixes
text: | Fix | What it does | |---|---| | `outputFileTracingIncludes` | Forces `private/*.pdf` into the download lambda — **the actual root cause fix** | | Resilient watermark | If PDF stamping ever fails, serves the file anyway — watermark must never block delivery | | Resend sender fix | Default sender changed to `onboarding@resend.dev` — `store@icywall.tech` gets rejected by Resend unless the domain is verified, which silently killed buyer emails |

title: 2. What will actually break in real labs (and how to fix it)
text: ### Apps getting killed by anti-cheat / block - **Problem**: Windows `notepad.exe`, `calc.exe`, `explorer.exe`, `msedge.exe`, and Linux `gnome-terminal`, `nautilus`, etc. may be killed or blocked. - **Fix before staging**: - Start with an **allowlist-only** exam policy: put the exact exam app name in `Allowed processes` and test. - Add `AppName.exe` **without** `.exe` to block lists; the agent already strips `.exe`. - Keep the base `alwaysAllowed` list conservative; for a real pilot, add `msedge`, `firefox`, `chrome`, and the chosen terminal/shell to the admin-configured allowlist. ### Full reset on Windows - **Problem**: `os.RemoveAll` on `C:\Users\student` will fail if the user is logged in or files are locked. It also cannot delete an *in-use* profile. - **Fix**: - Schedule the reset from the admin console **before the user logs in** or use the agent service to delete the profile at the next logoff/shutdown. - Alternatively, use a *new-account* golden profile: create a dedicated `examuser`, copy a clean skeleton into `C:\Users\Default`, and let Windows build the profile on next login. - On Linux, the reset works as long as the `student` user is logged out; enforce this with `power.Lock()` before reset. ### USB blocking on Windows - **Problem**: `devcon.exe` is not on most Windows images. The registry method requires a reboot, so USB works until the next restart. - **Fix**: - Use `pnputil.exe` (built-in since Windows 10) for immediate disable/enable of the `USBSTOR` class. - I can add a `pnputil` fallback to `security_windows.go` now. ### Auto-enroll security - **Problem**: With `LABDESK_AUTO_ENROLL=true`, any rogue machine on the lab subnet can get a certificate. - **Fix**: - Keep auto-enroll **only for the initial rollout window**, then disable it. - Better: add a o

title: 3. Security hardening for real production
text: - **TLS**: Replace the self-signed cert with an internal CA cert or a public cert for `8443` and `8444`. - **Firewall**: Allow `8443`/`8444` only from lab/admin subnets; do not expose to the internet. - **Auto-enroll**: Disable after the first day, or use the pairing-key model. - **Audit**: Keep `audit_log` append-only and back it up. - **CA backup**: Back up `/var/lib/labdesk-admin/data` or `C:\ProgramData\labdesk-admin\data` offline; losing it requires re-enrolling every machine. - **Agent updates**: Sign Windows binaries and submit to Microsoft/AV vendors before mass rollout.

title: Overview
text: The project involves enhancing the ESP32 Marauder firmware for the Super Mini S3 board and its web application. The primary goal is to implement additional advanced WiFi attacks, verify their functionality, and refine the web user interface for a more polished and user-friendly experience, while ensuring stability and robustness. In this session, the agent focused on implementing and verifying several new attacks, updating the web interface, and debugging issues that arose during compilation and testing.

title: Guide
text: Quick start & safety How to use this webapp 1. **Connect** — plug the S3 into your Android/Windows/macOS/Linux device, then tap *Connect S3* (Chrome/Edge only). 2. **Scan targets** — tap *Scan APs*, wait for it to finish, then *List APs* to see results. 3. **Run an attack** — select one or more APs if an attack needs them, tap the attack, then *Stop Scan* when done. 4. **Portal** — paste your landing page HTML (max 10 KB) and tap *Set HTML*. Form submissions log only client IP/MAC, never credentials. 5. **Wardrive** — tap *Wardrive* and let it run. On stop it saves the log to `/wardrive.csv` on the S3. 6. **Terminal** — type any command, e.g. `help`, `scanall`, `stopscan`. Attack / command reference `scanall` — discover APs and stations `list -a` — show discovered APs `select -a all` — select every AP `attack -t deauthall` — deauth all scanned APs + channel hop `attack -t pmkid` — capture EAPOL for all APs `attack -t authflood` / `assocflood` — 802.11 auth/assoc floods `attack -t sae` / `badmsg` / `sleep` / `csa` / `quiet` — advanced attacks `wardrive` — log APs to SPIFFS `arpscan` / `pingscan` / `portscan -a <index>` — network tools `evilportal -c start` — start the benign portal Safety rules * Only use on networks and devices you own or have written permission to test. * The portal is **benign** by design: it logs client IP/MAC only and does not store credentials. * Do not store credentials, real AP names, or scanned data in public places. * `stopscan` returns the S3 to a clean state after any attack.

title: Overview
text: The project transitioned from a web AP-controlled ESP32 Marauder firmware to a USB-serial controlled firmware for the ESP32 Super Mini S3. The primary goal was to enable control of the Marauder device via USB serial from various platforms (macOS, Android, iOS) and to fully remove the web UI components. After successfully implementing and verifying the USB-serial control, the focus shifted to creating a web-based application utilizing the Web Serial API for cross-platform control (excluding iOS).

text: - **Shift to USB-serial control:** The user decided to abandon the web AP approach due to persistent connection issues and hardware limitations of the ESP32-S3 (single radio). title: 1. Request and Intent
text: ### Enduring objective The user is building a portable machine-behavior and fault-monitoring device using: - ESP32 - ADXL345 3-axis accelerometer - INMP441 I2S microphone - SH1106 OLED - Active buzzer - GPIO33 Learn button The original motivation was: > “if we place this device on any of the Machine motor or electronic then will press the button Learn then the Device will learn the behaviour of the machine and then the Devce will detect the fault and if the machine is vibrating more that the device learned or change its position or etc then it will mark as faulty” The intended product is a universal, portable monitor that: - Learns healthy behavior for each machine or installation. - Continuously monitors vibration, audio, and mounting/orientation. - Detects sustained deviations rather than transient noise. - Detects stopped machines, abnormal vibration, abnormal sound, mounting changes, and movement. - Uses vibration and audio together. - Displays health and diagnostics on the OLED and local web dashboard. - Sounds a buzzer on confirmed faults. - Works across motors, fans, coolers, pumps, traction motors, drive motors, and other rotating equipment through per-installation learning. - Produces evidence suitable for sponsorship, technical publication, copyright registration, and possible patent filing. - Avoids unsupported claims of perfect universal diagnosis. The system is an anomaly detector with learned-normal behavior and indicative fault signatures. It should not be represented as a guaranteed universal root-cause classifier or “100% accurate” device without controlled validation. ### Evolution of requests The project has gone through these major phases: 1. text: The KY-012 Module will be our main component for this tutorial. This module has an active piezoelectric buzzer mounted on a breakout board. Figure 1 shows the module as seen in fritzing. The seal is only part of the packaging, remove it prior to using the module. Figure 1: KY-012 Active Buzzer Module ... Figure 2 shows the connection between the Arduino Uno and the KY-012 Active Buzzer Module.

title: 5. Pinouts:
text: URL: https://dynamic.me/index.php?document_id=2233&pdf=227&route=product%2Fproduct%2Fdownload ActiveBuzzerModule5VFeatures: The Active Buzzer Module 5V KY-012 provides a ready-to-use sound output solution for embedded systems. Unlike passive buzzers, this active buzzer integrates an internal oscillator, allowing it to generate sound simply by applying a DC supply without requiring an external signal. With a stable 5V operating voltage, it offers high reliability and ease of use, making it suitable for Arduino UNO R3 and other 5V logic microcontrollers. Its compact PCB design allows easy integration in constrained spaces. Typical use cases include audio alerts, fault alarms, interactive projects, and robotics. Download the rpi logo and resize it to fit the 128x64 oled display resolution: ```bash # see https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Raspberry_Pi_logos wget -qO rpi-logo-big.png https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/RPi-Logo-White-SCREEN.png python3 <<'EOF' from PIL import Image image = Image.open('rpi-logo-big.png') image.thumbnail((128, 64), Image.BICUBIC) image.save('rpi-logo.png', 'PNG') EOF ... luma.core.interface.serial ... i2c from luma.oled.device import ssd1306 from luma.core. ... import canvas ... # NB ssd1306 devices are monochromatic; a pixel is enabled with ... white and disabled with black. # NB the ssd1306 class has no way of knowing the device resolution/size. device = ssd1306(i2c(port=1, address=0x3c), width=128, height=64, rotate=0) ... # load the rpi logo. logo = Image.open('rpi-logo.png')

title: Software-only upgrades that matter
text: ### 1. Welch spectral averaging — *biggest free win* Right now each window is one raw 256-pt FFT → noisy spectra → wider learned envelopes → less sensitive detection. **Change:** split the 256 samples into 4 overlapping 128-pt segments (or upgrade to 512-pt buffer), average the periodograms. **Effect:** spectrum noise drops ~50% → envelopes tighten → smaller real deviations cross the fault threshold. Works on all 3 machines. ### 2. True Hilbert-transform envelope demodulation — *bearing faults* Current envelope uses a one-pole rectifier approximation. **Change:** FFT → zero negative frequencies → IFFT → take magnitude → FFT again. You have all the FFT machinery already. **Effect:** much cleaner bearing-modulation signal on the CG motor — the 74 Hz / 120 Hz bearing tones become *measurable* instead of marginal. ### 3. Harmonic-ratio features — *pseudo order analysis, no RPM sensor needed* You already track dominant frequency. The dominant peak on these machines **is** the shaft speed (24 Hz / 47.5 Hz). **Add as features:** - ratio of 2×/1× harmonic energy → **misalignment signature** - ratio of 3×/1× → looseness indicator - sideband energy around 1× (modulation) → bearing/gear wear This gets you 70% of what an RPM sensor gives — free. ### 4. Time-domain RPM estimation — *fixes the gearmotor* At 88 RPM the shaft turns at 1.5 Hz — below FFT resolution. But the **time between acceleration peaks** directly measures rotation. **Add:** peak-interval detector on the vibration waveform → RPM estimate + regularity score. Suddenly M3 is a valid monitoring target with zero hardware cost. ### 5. Long-window mode for slow machines Bump the vibration buffer 256→512 or 1024 samples @ 400 Hz (ESP32 RAM can afford ~8 KB more). **Effect:** frequency resolution improves 1.56 → 0.39 Hz/bin

If the user exits fullscreen (e.g., via `Esc`), instantly pause the test, trigger a full-screen warning modal, and log a violation event. - *Mobile Fallback:* For iOS Safari, implement a fixed-position lockdown overlay (`fixed inset-0 z-50`) to handle non-supported fullscreen APIs. - **Tab Switch & Focus Detection:** - Listen to `visibilitychange` (detect tab switching/minimizing) and `blur` events (detect clicking on second screens or side drawers). - Track violation durations. A focus loss > 10 seconds auto-submits the test immediately. - **Input & Keyboard Lockdown:** - Prevent `copy`, `paste`, `cut`, `contextmenu`, and `selectstart`. - Intercept and disable hotkeys: `Ctrl+C`, `Ctrl+V`, `Ctrl+Shift+I`, `F12`, `Alt+Tab`, `Cmd+Tab`. - **Proctor Video Stream & Snapshots:** - Capture media stream via `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true })`. - Stream camera feed into a PIP window. - Automatically render a frame to HTML5 Canvas and upload an image snapshot to S3/Cloudinary upon every recorded violation + every 60 seconds at random intervals. ### 2. title: 1. Tool Description
text: **Fast web fuzzer written in Go (program)** ffuf is a fast web fuzzer written in Go that allows typical directory discovery, virtual host discovery (without DNS records) and GET and POST parameter fuzzing. This program is useful for pentesters, ethical hackers and forensics experts. It also can be used for security tests. ---

title: 2. What This Tool Is Used For
text: - **Category:** Web Applications, Information Gathering - **Learn priority:** High (installed by default in Kali) - **Main use:** Fuzz directories on a web server by replacing the FUZZ keyword with each wordlist entry. ---

title: 3. How To Install
text: Already installed on standard Kali. Otherwise: ``` sudo apt install ffuf ``` ---

title: ffuf — fast web fuzzer written in Go
text: **Category:** Web Applications, Information Gathering | **Docs:** https://www.kali.org/tools/ffuf/ ### What it does / when to use it ffuf replaces the keyword `FUZZ` anywhere in a request — URL path, vhost header, GET/POST params — with every line of a wordlist, at high speed. Reach for it over gobuster/dirb when you need parameter fuzzing, vhost discovery, or fine-grained response filtering. ### Install ```bash sudo apt install ffuf # preinstalled on standard Kali ``` ### Step-by-step 1. Pick a wordlist — good defaults on Kali: - `/usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt` (~4.6k entries, quick) - `/usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt` (thorough) 2. Basic directory fuzz — put `FUZZ` where you want words injected: ```bash ffuf -u http://target.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt ``` 3. You'll get noise — e.g., everything returns the same 200/42-byte "not found" page. Filter it out: ```bash ffuf -u http://target.com/FUZZ -w wordlist.txt -fs 42 ``` Or let ffuf calibrate automatically with `-ac` (sends junk requests first, learns what to ignore). ### Key flags / cheat sheet | Flag | Meaning | |---|---| | `-u` | Target URL — put `FUZZ` anywhere in it | | `-w` | Wordlist path (or `list.txt:KEYWORD` for a second FUZZ point) | | `-e` | Extensions: `-e .php,.txt` → tries `FUZZ.php`, `FUZZ.txt` | | `-mc` | Match status codes (`-mc 200,301`) | | `-fs`/`-fw`/`-fl` | Filter by response size / words / lines | | `-fc` | Filter status codes (`-fc 404`) | | `-ac` | Auto-calibrate filters (use this first on unknown sites) | | `-H` | Custom header: `-H "Host: FUZZ.target.com"` for vhosts, `-H "Cookie: session=..."` for auth'd fuzzing | | `-X`, `-d` | Method + POST body (`-X POST -d "user=FUZZ&pass=x"`) | | `-t` | Threads (default 40; lower it on r

title: How it works (the flow)
text: ``` 1. Buyer clicks "Buy" on your page 2. Your API route creates a Razorpay Order (server-side, uses key_secret) 3. Razorpay checkout popup opens → buyer pays (UPI/cards/etc.) 4. Razorpay returns payment_id + signature to your page 5. Your API route VERIFIES the signature server-side (this is the security step) 6. If valid → issue a signed one-time/expiring download token 7. /api/download?token=... streams the PDF (file lives OUTSIDE /public, never directly reachable) ``` **Critical rules:** `key_secret` never touches the frontend; the PDF never goes in `/public`; no verification = people sharing the download URL for free.

title: Copilot prompt — paste this in your icywall repo
text: ``` Build a Razorpay digital-download checkout for selling a PDF on this Next.js site. Requirements: 1. `POST /api/create-order` — uses the `razorpay` npm package to create an order: amount = PRICE_IN_PAISE from env (e.g. 4900 = ₹49), currency "INR", receipt = `pdf_${Date.now()}`. Uses env vars RAZORPAY_KEY_ID and RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET (server-side only). Returns { order_id, amount, key_id }. 2. A sales page/component `/pdf` (or a BuyButton component fitting existing site style): - Shows the product (kali-tools-reference.pdf), price, and a "Buy Now" button - Loads Razorpay checkout.js dynamically (https://checkout.razorpay.com/v1/checkout.js) - Calls /api/create-order, then opens Razorpay checkout with order_id, key_id, site name/logo, prefill email field - On payment success (handler callback), POSTs { razorpay_order_id, razorpay_payment_id, razorpay_signature } to /api/verify-payment - On verified: shows a download link/button pointing to the returned download URL. On failure: shows error. 3. `POST /api/verify-payment` — verifies Razorpay signature: expected = HMAC_SHA256(order_id + "|" + payment_id, RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET), compare with razorpay_signature using timing-safe compare. If valid: generate a signed download token = HMAC_SHA256(`${payment_id}.${expiry}`, DOWNLOAD_TOKEN_SECRET) where expiry = now + 24h. Return { download_url: `/api/download?pid=${payment_id}&exp=${expiry}&sig=${token}` }. If invalid: 400. 4. `GET /api/download` — validates sig + expiry (recompute HMAC, timing-safe compare, reject expired). If valid: stream the PDF from `private/kali-tools-reference.pdf` (fs.readFile / createReadStream, path OUTSIDE public/) with headers Content-Type: application/pdf and Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="kali-tools-reference.pdf". If invalid/expired: 403.

title: Two real gaps worth knowing about
text: 1. **No webhook.** If a buyer pays then instantly closes the tab before the success callback fires, Razorpay captures the money but they never see the download link. Rare, but it'll happen eventually. Fix: a `/api/webhook` route handling `payment_link.paid`/`payment.captured` → emails the download link via Resend/SES. 2. **24h link is reusable** — anyone the buyer shares it with can download during that window. Acceptable for a ₹99 PDF; if you want stricter, tokens need a DB (one-time use or bound to email). Also minor: `payment.failed` events aren't handled (modal retries internally, so it's cosmetic). title: Fix steps
text: ### 1. Use a proper USB data cable Many USB cables are **charge-only**. Try a different cable that you know carries data. ### 2. title: Correct wiring with external power
text: ```text External 5V Supply Arduino Uno R3 MG995 Servo + ------------------- +-------------+ +-----------+ | | | | | +-------------------------+ | | VCC (R) +----+ | | | | | - -------------------+ | Pin 9 +------> Signal(O) | | | | | | | +---> GND | | GND(Bk) +----+ | | | | +-------------+ +-----------+ ``` **Key point:** The servo's VCC (red) and GND (brown/black) go to the **external 5V supply**. Only the signal wire (orange/yellow) goes to the Arduino Pin 9. The Arduino and external supply must share **GND**.

title: On "real Metasploitable"
text: You can't put a real Metasploitable *inside* the browser app — it's a full 800MB VM, needs VirtualBox/VMware. But there are three levels of "more real": ### Option A — "Go Real" mission mode (recommended, most impactful) NetPulse becomes the **mission controller for a real lab the student runs locally**: - New "Real Lab" tab per module: guided setup (download VirtualBox + Kali + Metasploitable2, step-by-step) - NetPulse gives the real mission: *"Run `nmap -sV 192.168.56.101` on your Kali — paste the output"* - Student pastes real output → NetPulse's validator (already exists — `matchesOutput` regex) parses it → flag awarded, progress saved - The book's Module 1 (lab setup) already teaches this exact VM build — perfect cross-sell **Effort:** medium. **Realism:** actual Metasploitable, actual commands. **Cost:** ₹0. ### Option B — Hosted vulnerable target Spin up a containerized vuln app (DVWA / Juice Shop / a Metasploitable-like Docker image) on a cheap VPS, students connect over the internet. More "real" than sims but: ~₹500/mo infra + you must isolate it hard (a publicly reachable vuln target will get scanned/abused by others). Worth it later, not now. ### Option C — Sharper simulation (no infra) Make the fake terminal *behave* more like real tools: - Strict command parser — only real flags work, wrong syntax gets real error output - Real captured output (not simplified) — actual nmap/msfconsole transcripts - Tab-completion, history (`↑` key), `man` pages — muscle memory transfers to real Kali

title: Module improvements for better understanding
text: Looking at the actual mission structure, these fit the codebase cleanly: | Improvement | What it does | Why it works | |---|---|---| | **Command anatomy** | Click any command → flag-by-flag breakdown (`-sV` = service detection) | Students copy commands without understanding them | | **Output annotation** | After each step, highlight the lines that matter — "this port = your way in" | Raw output overwhelms beginners | | **3-level hint ladder** | Nudge → direction → exact command | Current model probably jumps to answer too fast | | **"Predict the output"** | Before running, ask "what will you see?" — free-text or MCQ | Active recall beats passive typing | | **Persistent engagement state** | Ports found in the Scanning module become targets in Exploitation | Makes it feel like ONE engagement, not isolated drills | | **Attack → defend flip** | After attacking, "now write the firewall rule that blocks this" | Defenders corner → understanding, not just hacking | | **Wrong-path demo** | Show what happens if you skip recon (you miss the open port, exploit fails) | Teaches methodology, not just commands |

title: esptool-js
text: # [Javascript implementation of esptool][2] This repository contains a Javascript implementation of [esptool][3], a serial flasher utility for Espressif chips. `esptool-js` is based on [Web Serial API][4] and works in Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge [version 89 or later][5] browsers and Google Chrome on Android [version 61 or later][6] via the [web-serial-polyfill][7] compatibility layer. **NOTE:** Unlike the Python-based esptool, `esptool-js` doesn't implement generation of binary images out of ELF files, and doesn't include companion tools similar to [espefuse.py][8] and [espsecure.py][9]. **📚 [API Documentation][10]** - Complete API reference with detailed class and method documentation.

title: [Installation][11]
text: **CDN** `https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/lib/index.js` or `https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/bundle.js` to use the single bundle JavaScript file. **NPM** `npm install --save esptool-js `Copy **Yarn** `yarn add --save esptool-js `Copy **Nightly builds** for [ESPTOOL-JS][12]

title: [How to Use][13]
text: ### [Basic Setup][14] First, import the necessary classes and types: `import { ESPLoader, Transport, LoaderOptions, FlashOptions, FlashModeValues, FlashFreqValues, FlashSizeValues, IEspLoaderTerminal, } from "esptool-js"; `Copy ### [1. Request Serial Port Access][15] Request access to a serial port using the Web Serial API: `// Request port access (user will be prompted to select a device) const port = await navigator.serial.requestPort(); // Optionally, filter by USB vendor/product IDs const portFilters = [ { usbVendorId: 0x10c4, usbProductId: 0xea60 } // Example: Silicon Labs CP210x ]; const port = await navigator.serial.requestPort({ filters: portFilters }); `Copy ### [2. Create Transport and ESPLoader][16] Create a `Transport` instance and configure the `ESPLoader`: `// Create transport instance const transport = new Transport(port, true); // Optional: Create a terminal interface for logging const terminal: IEspLoaderTerminal = { clean() { console.clear(); }, writeLine(data: string) { console.log(data); }, write(data: string) { console.log(data); }, }; // Configure loader options const loaderOptions: LoaderOptions = { transport: transport, baudrate: 115200, // Communication baud rate terminal: terminal, // Optional terminal for logging debugLogging: false, // Optional debug logging }; // Create ESPLoader instance const esploader = new ESPLoader(loaderOptions); `Copy ### [3. Connect to Device][17] Connect to the ESP device and detect the chip: `try { // Connect and detect chip (this will reset the device) const chipName = await esploader.main(); console.log(`Connected to: ${chipName}`); } catch (error) { console.error("Failed to connect:", error); } `Copy ### [4. title: What was added
text: - **Flash GhostNet panel** in the webapp with: - Promo code input. The correct code is `Ghost10` (SHA-256 hashed in `app.js`). - `Unlock` button validates the promo code before enabling the flash button. - `Flash GhostNet` button fetches `firmware.bin`, verifies its SHA-256, then uses `esptool-js` to flash a fresh S3. - Cancel button, progress bar, and status text. - **Bundled `firmware.bin`** at `webapp/firmware.bin` — a full merged image (bootloader + partitions + app) generated at offset `0x0`. - **Bundled `webapp/esptool-js.js`** — the `esptool-js` ESM bundle from `unpkg.com`. - **SHA-256 integrity check** — `FIRMWARE_SHA256` is hard-coded; the webapp refuses to flash a `.bin` that does not match. - **Security hardening**: - CSP, `Referrer-Policy`, and `Permissions-Policy` in `index.html`. - `vercel.json` headers for `nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, and `serial=(self)`. - `.gitignore` excludes `build_output/` and `webapp/firmware.bin` so the binary is not committed. - README explains how to rebuild `firmware.bin` and keep `esptool-js.js` out of public repos. - **Promo code gate** — prevents accidental or unauthorized flashes through the UI.

title: How to use the web flasher
text: 1. Put the ESP32-S3 into bootloader mode (usually hold **BOOT** and press **RESET**). 2. Open the webapp, scroll to **Flash GhostNet**. 3. Enter promo code `Ghost10` and tap **Unlock**. 4. Tap **Flash GhostNet**, select the S3 in the Web Serial picker. 5. Wait for the progress bar; the S3 will reset when done.

title: Production notes
text: - `firmware.bin` is ~900 KB. It is not cached by the PWA service worker; the browser downloads it each time. - The promo code is a **UI gate**, not encryption. If you need stronger protection, host the webapp behind HTTP auth or a paywall. - The hard-coded `FIRMWARE_SHA256` in `app.js` must be updated every time `firmware.bin` is rebuilt (see `README` for the one-liner). - Verified `node -c` passes and the webapp renders at `http://localhost:8080`. === MESSAGE 98 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. title: 1. Prepare the deployable `webapp/` folder
text: Make sure these files exist inside `webapp/`: ``` webapp/ index.html app.js style.css manifest.json favicon.svg service-worker.js vercel.json esptool-js.js ← from unpkg/esptool-js bundle firmware.bin ← the full merged S3 binary README.md ``` If `firmware.bin` is missing, build it: ```bash # Build the firmware ./flash.sh # Merge bootloader + partition table + app into one file python3 -m esptool --chip esp32s3 merge_bin -o webapp/firmware.bin --flash-size 4MB \ 0x0000 build_output/esp32_marauder.ino.bootloader.bin \ 0x8000 build_output/esp32_marauder.ino.partitions.bin \ 0x10000 build_output/esp32_marauder.ino.bin # Update the SHA-256 in app.js shasum -a 256 webapp/firmware.bin # paste the hex string into FIRMWARE_SHA256 in webapp/app.js ``` Also make sure `esptool-js.js` is present: ```bash curl -fsSL -o webapp/esptool-js.js https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/bundle.js ```

title: 2. Decide how to get it on GitHub
text: Vercel deploys from Git. The main problem earlier was that the whole repo is 1.1 GB, so GitHub push timed out. The easiest fix is to push only the `webapp/` folder as a separate, clean repo. ### Option A — separate `GhostNet-Web` repo (recommended for Vercel) ```bash cd webapp git init git add . git commit -m "GhostNet webapp" git remote add origin https://github.com/abhay-ethically/GhostNet-Web.git git push -u origin main ``` ### Option B — keep it in the main repo If the big history push eventually works, set the **Root Directory** to `webapp` in Vercel. If `firmware.bin` is in `.gitignore`, Vercel may not upload it. Either remove `webapp/firmware.bin` from `.gitignore` and commit it, or deploy from the CLI.

title: 3. Deploy to Vercel
text: ### Using Vercel CLI ```bash cd webapp npx vercel --prod ``` ### Using the Vercel dashboard 1. Go to https://vercel.com/new and import the GitHub repo. 2. **Framework Preset** → `Other` 3. **Root Directory** → `webapp` (if it is in the main repo) or `.` (if it is the repo root) 4. **Build Command** → leave empty 5. **Output Directory** → `.` (or `public` if you move files there) 6. Click **Deploy** You will get a HTTPS URL like `https://ghostnet-s3.vercel.app`.

title: 4. User flow after hosting
text: 1. Open the Vercel URL in **Chrome or Edge**. 2. Plug the ESP32-S3 into the phone/computer. 3. Tap **Connect S3** to use the attacks, dashboard, and terminal. 4. To flash a fresh S3: - Hold **BOOT** and press **RESET** on the S3. - Scroll to **Flash GhostNet**. - Enter promo code `Ghost10`, tap **Unlock**. - Tap **Flash GhostNet** and select the S3 in the picker.

title: 5. Security notes for public hosting
text: - The webapp already has CSP, `X-Frame-Options`, `nosniff`, and `Permissions-Policy: serial=(self)`. - The `firmware.bin` will be downloadable from the Vercel URL. If you want to restrict it, either: - Password-protect the Vercel project, or - Keep `firmware.bin` out of the GitHub repo and deploy only via Vercel CLI from your local machine. - The promo code `Ghost10` is a UI gate, not encryption. It stops accidental flashes but does not hide the `.bin` from someone who knows the URL.

title: How websites get compromised
text: Attackers almost never "hack the website" directly — they abuse one of these classes: **1. Injection flaws (the classics)** - **SQL injection** — app puts your input into a database query without sanitizing. `admin' --` as a username can dump entire databases or bypass login. - **Command injection / RCE** — user input reaches an OS shell. Worst case: full server takeover. - **File upload bypass** — upload a PHP/JS shell disguised as an image → execute commands on the server. **2. Broken authentication & access control** - Weak/default creds, session tokens you can guess or steal, IDOR (change `?user_id=123` to `124` and see someone else's data) - JWT misconfigurations — `alg: none` attacks, weak secrets you can crack **3. Known vulnerabilities in components** - This is the big one nobody talks about: **most real-world breaches aren't clever zero-days, they're unpatched WordPress plugins, old Apache/nginx, exposed admin panels.** Attackers scan the internet for version X and mass-exploit. **4. Misconfiguration** - Exposed `.git` folders, open S3 buckets, debug modes left on, directory listing enabled, admin panels on `/admin` with default passwords. This category causes a shocking percentage of breaches. **5. XSS** — doesn't "hack the site" but hacks its *users*: steal session cookies → log in as admin.

title: How websites get taken down
text: **1. DDoS — the main one.** Three flavors: - **Volumetric**: flood the pipe with junk traffic (botnets like Mirai — armies of hacked IoT devices) - **Protocol**: SYN floods, malformed packets that exhaust connection tables - **Application layer (L7)**: send expensive requests (search queries, login attempts) that exhaust CPU/DB — hardest to stop because traffic looks legit Defense side: Cloudflare/fastly absorb it, rate limiting, anycast. This is why big sites survive. **2. Compromise → destroy.** Take over via the vulns above, then delete files, wipe the DB, or deface the homepage. The takedown is a *consequence* of the compromise. **3. DNS attacks.** Hijack the domain (social-engineering the registrar, or exploiting weak registrar creds) or poison/cache-attack DNS so nobody can resolve the site. Site is fine — nobody can reach it. **4. Resource exhaustion.** Exploit a specific vuln — e.g., a regex that takes exponential time (ReDoS), decompression bombs — to crash the app with a single request.

title: The honest part
text: - The *methodology* is always: **recon → enumerate → find one weak point → exploit → escalate**. Attackers don't need to win everywhere; they need one hole. Defenders need to patch all of them. - DDoS-as-a-service exists ("booter/stresser" services) — and it's unambiguously illegal everywhere, no gray area, people get prosecuted regularly for it. - Everything above is practiceable legally: DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Metasploitable, PortSwigger labs — these are deliberately broken sites built for exactly this. **Your move:** spin up OWASP Juice Shop locally (`docker run -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop`) — it's a broken web app with a built-in scoreboard of ~100 vulns covering every class above. Start with the scoreboard's easy challenges and you'll *feel* every concept on this list within a weekend. Here are the actual techniques, ranked by how much of the real world's bugs they produce:

title: 1. Understand the app better than its developer
text: This is the real secret. Bugs live where the developer's **assumptions don't hold**: - "Users will only send numbers" → send a string, negative number, `0x`, huge value - "This API is only called after step 3" → call it directly, skip steps, replay it - "Only admins see this button" → the API endpoint doesn't check (IDOR/BOLA — the #1 bounty bug class) - "Two requests can't arrive at once" → race condition: withdraw money twice, redeem a coupon 50 times **Business logic flaws** can't be found by scanners — they require a human who mapped the app's workflow. This is where top bounty hunters make their money.

title: 2. Input-point enumeration
text: Every input is a potential bug: URL params, headers, cookies, JSON bodies, file uploads, hidden form fields, API endpoints the frontend never calls. Method: use Burp to crawl/proxy everything → build a map of every parameter → test each systematically against the vuln classes (SQLi, XSS, SSTI, traversal...). PortSwigger Academy teaches exactly this workflow.

title: 3. Fuzzing (how memory bugs get found)
text: For binaries/protocols — feed the program millions of mutated inputs and watch for crashes: - **Coverage-guided fuzzers**: AFL++, libFuzzer, Honggfuzz — they learn which inputs reach new code paths - Build with **sanitizers** (ASan, UBSan) so silent memory bugs become loud crashes - Most browser/kernel/parser CVEs of the last decade came from fuzzing, not human review

title: 4. Static analysis + code review
text: - Read source code hunting **source→sink flows**: user input reaching `exec()`, `eval`, SQL concat, `memcpy` unchecked - **CodeQL** — treat code as a queryable database; write a query like "show me every place user input reaches a command execution" — used to find real CVEs - Semgrep — fast pattern scanning across huge codebases

title: 5. Patch diffing (the clever one)
text: When a vendor releases a security patch, diff old vs new code/binary — the difference literally *points at the bug*. This is how researchers write "1-day exploits" and how they learn to find sibling bugs the patch missed.

title: 6. Dynamic scanning
text: Burp Scanner, nuclei, ZAP — automated tools that hammer endpoints with known-payload lists. Finds the low-hanging fruit; everyone else already scanned there, so it's your baseline, not your edge.

title: 7. Reading prior art (underrated)
text: Hacktivity disclosures, Pentester.land writeups, CVE writeups, CTF solutions. Every writeup teaches a pattern. After ~200 read writeups you'll *see* bugs before you test them — this is literally how "intuition" forms.

title: The real workflow of a bounty hunter
text: ``` Recon (subdomains, JS files, endpoints) → map the app → learn what it does & what it assumes → probe the assumptions → find anomaly → escalate anomaly into impact → write report ``` **Hard truths:** - The money bugs aren't exotic — IDOR, auth bypass, XSS account-takeover chains, and logic flaws pay more consistently than fancy memory corruption. - "Finding bugs" = forming hypotheses and testing them. Not running tools. - Your edge as a beginner: **new attack surface** (fresh features, new subdomains, mobile APIs) that experienced hunters haven't looked at yet. This is Phase 3→5 of your syllabus. title: What it actually is
text: The "dark web" is just **websites that intentionally hide their location**. The technology is mostly **Tor (The Onion Router)**: - Normal web: your browser → ISP → server. Everyone sees the route. - Tor: your traffic bounces through **3 random volunteer relays** around the world, each peeling off one layer of encryption. The destination sees only the last relay, not you. Sites run as **hidden services** with `.onion` addresses (like `facebookcorewwwi.onion` — yes, Facebook has one) that aren't reachable from normal browsers or DNS. Also worth knowing: **deep web ≠ dark web**. Deep web = anything not indexed by Google (your Gmail inbox, bank portal, paywalled pages) — that's 95%+ of the internet and utterly boring. Dark web is the tiny sliver requiring Tor/I2P.

title: How to access it
text: Legitimately and simply: 1. Download **Tor Browser** from torproject.org (it's just hardened Firefox + Tor built in) 2. Open it → it connects to the Tor network 3. Visit `.onion` addresses — which you get from directories like **Ahmia.fi**, the Hidden Wiki (mostly dead links and scam lists, honestly), or sites that publish their own onions (BBC, ProPublica, DuckDuckGo all have them) That's it. There's no secret handshake. I2P and Freenet are alternative networks but Tor is 99% of what people mean.

title: Is it really "dark"?
text: **The unfiltered truth: mostly no — it's mostly boring and scammy.** What you'll actually find: - **Dead links everywhere** — onion sites go up and down constantly - **Scams, on scams** — "hitmen for hire" (all fake, and they take your crypto anyway), fake marketplaces, fake everything. The dominant economic activity on the dark web is **scamming people who came looking for illegal stuff** - **Real criminal markets do exist** — drug markets, stolen data dumps, carding forums. They rotate constantly because they get seized or exit-scam (operators steal everyone's escrow and vanish — happens constantly) - **Legit uses** — journalists & whistleblowers (SecureDrop), activists under censorship, privacy nerds, people reading BBC in countries that block it. Tor was literally funded by the US Navy originally.

title: Real risks (not the movie kind)
text: - **Law enforcement runs honeypots** — a large share of "markets" and forums are monitored or operated by agencies. Silk Road's founder is doing life in prison. Anonymity is not magic — OpSec failures, not Tor breaks, catch people. - **Malware paradise** — downloading random files there is asking for it - **Illegal content exists** — stumbling into it isn't a crime in most places, but engaging/downloading absolutely is - Tor only anonymizes **transport** — log into your real Gmail over Tor and you've deanonymized yourself instantly

title: Bottom line
text: Accessing Tor is legal in most countries (India included) — it's a privacy tool. The "darkness" is 80% media myth, 15% scams, 5% real criminal infrastructure that's heavily watched anyway. title: The anonymity stack (weakest → strongest)
text: **Level 1 — Baseline (what most people do, mostly insufficient)** - Tor Browser, security level set to **"Safest"** (disables JS — JS is how deanonymization attacks run) - Never resize the window (fingerprinting), never go fullscreen **Level 2 — Tails OS (the real answer)** - **Tails** — amnesic live OS on a USB stick. Boots into a clean system, routes *everything* through Tor at the OS level, leaves zero traces on the machine when shut down. This is what Snowden used and what journalists use. - Alternative: **Whonix** — runs Tor in one VM and your work in another VM; even if the work VM is fully compromised by malware, it can't leak your real IP because it physically can't reach the clearnet. Strongest architecture available to civilians. **Level 3 — Compartmentation (where everyone actually fails)** - Separate identity for everything: new handles, new email (via Tor-created accounts only), **never** reuse a username/password/writing style from your real life - Never access personal accounts — one Gmail login over Tor and the whole setup is wasted - Assume stylometry exists: your writing style is a fingerprint **Level 4 — Payments/crypto (if it ever comes to that)** - BTC is **pseudonymous, not anonymous** — blockchain is public forever. Buying BTC with KYC-exchange funds then spending it creates a permanent trail. This is how actual criminals get caught years later.

title: Behavioral rules (the part that matters most)
text: - No downloads, no opening files — a PDF/doc can call home with your real IP when opened offline-from-Tor - No plugins, no JS on untrusted sites - Don't brag, don't post details, don't be consistent enough to pattern-match - VPN + Tor is debated — it shifts trust to the VPN rather than adding real anonymity. Tails/Whonix docs explain this honestly.

title: Where to find .onion links
text: Legitimate, maintained directories (the Hidden Wiki is mostly rotten/scam links): - **tor.taxi** — best current directory, verified links, clean - **dark.fail** — verified onion list, checks for phishing clones - **onion.live** — status monitoring + verified links - **Ahmia.fi** — clearnet-accessible search engine that filters out the worst content - **Daunt.link** — link directory - Sites self-publishing onions: ProPublica, BBC, DuckDuckGo, CIA (yes, really — for anonymous tips) **Critical habit:** phishing clones of onion sites are *everywhere* — identical pages with different addresses harvesting credentials. Only trust links verified across 2+ sources. Never follow onion links from random Reddit/YouTube comments.

title: The truth to end on
text: This stack makes casual browsing genuinely private and safe-ish. But if the threat model is "law enforcement actively hunting you," history shows people get caught through **habits, not tech**: logging into a personal account once, reusing a handle from 2015, slipping a real detail into a post. Dread Pirate Roberts ran Silk Road for years and was caught because he used his real email on a forum in 2011 before going dark. So: Tails USB + tor.taxi directory + Safest mode + zero personal info = browse safely and legally. Anything beyond that — the risk floor never hits zero, and the sites selling otherwise are the same ones running honeypots. === MESSAGE 30 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. There's no single method — it depends on what the app is made of. Here's the real workflow:

title: Step 0 — Identify what you're dealing with
text: Different stacks = totally different difficulty: | App type | Difficulty | Why | |---|---|---| | Java/.NET (JAR, APK Java-layer, C#) | Easiest | Decompiles back to near-original source | | Web/JS (Electron, websites) | Easy | Code ships to you, just obfuscated | | Native C/C++ binaries | Hard | Only machine code survives compilation | | Go/Rust binaries | Hard+ | Huge binaries, mangled names | | Packed/protected (Themida, VMProtect) | Nightmare | Deliberately anti-RE | First move on any binary: check what it is — `file`, `strings`, `Detect It Easy`, check imports/entropy (packed binaries look like noise).

title: The two core techniques
text: **Static analysis** — dissect it without running: - **Disassembler** (Ghidra — free, NSA-built, genuinely excellent; IDA Pro — industry standard; Binary Ninja — nicest UX) - Reads machine code → shows you assembly + a decompiler's best-guess C code - You read functions, follow calls, rename things as you understand them - Quick wins first: `strings` output, imported functions, hardcoded URLs/keys **Dynamic analysis** — run it and watch: - **Debugger** (x64dbg on Windows, gdb+GEF on Linux, Hopper/lldb on macOS) — set breakpoints, step through, inspect registers/memory live - **Frida** — inject JavaScript into a running app to hook functions, log arguments, change return values. Absolute game-changer for mobile apps - Watch behavior: Process Monitor (file/registry access), Wireshark (network calls), strace/ltrace Reality: you alternate — static to form a hypothesis, dynamic to confirm it.

title: Per-platform cheat sheet
text: **Android** (best starting point — easiest real-world RE): ``` APK → jadx (decompiles to readable Java) → read logic → apktool (smali bytecode you can modify + repack) → Frida to bypass cert pinning / hook runtime ``` **iOS**: jailbroken device + class-dump + Frida. Higher barrier to entry. **Windows EXE**: Ghidra/IDA for static, x64dbg for dynamic. **Web/Electron**: `asar` extract → read the JS; websites → DevTools, unminify, read. **Malware**: isolated VM + FlareVM tools, never on your real machine.

title: The actual skill
text: Tools are 20%. The real skill is **pattern recognition**: recognizing a loop, a string comparison, a crypto routine, a license check — then asking "what happens if I patch this jump?" Most entry-level RE is finding the `if (license_valid)` check and flipping a `JE` to `JNE` — that's literally how cracks have worked since the 80s.

title: Legality (briefly)
text: - Your own software, CTF targets, crackmes, malware analysis, security research — fine in most jurisdictions - EULAs often forbid RE contractually; DMCA §1201 has security-research exemptions in the US; India has no direct equivalent but research/interop is generally defensible - Cracking commercial software to pirate it — that's just piracy

title: Where to practice (this is the fun part)
text: - **crackmes.one** — thousands of deliberately-made RE challenges, ranked easy→hard - **pwn.college** — free structured course, assembly → RE → exploitation - **Flare-On** — FireEye's annual RE challenge, the Olympics of this stuff - **LiveOverflow** (YouTube) — binary playlist is the best free intro that exists - **"Practical Reverse Engineering"** book, **Malware Unicorn's RE101/102** workshops (free)

title: Your realistic entry point
text: Week 1: pwn.college's assembly module → learn just enough asm to read functions (you don't need to *write* it). Week 2: 3 easy crackmes on crackmes.one with Ghidra — break them with patching. Week 3: jadx on an APK you built yourself or an open-source app — see how clean managed decompilation feels. This is the Phase 4 "Binary/Pwn" track in your syllabus — hardest track, but the most respected skill in all of security. Nobody accidentally becomes good at RE, which is exactly why it's valuable. title: Tier 1 — Automated static analysis
text: **MobSF (Mobile Security Framework)** — the workhorse. Free, open source, does 80% of this automatically: - Drag in APK → it decompiles, scans for hardcoded secrets, suspicious API calls, permissions abuse, trackers, exported components, weak crypto — gives you a report in minutes - Run it via Docker: `docker pull opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf` Manual alongside it: - **jadx** — decompile → read the Java code yourself - **apktool** — get the manifest + smali; check `AndroidManifest.xml` for permissions, exported activities, services, receivers, deep links

title: What you're actually hunting for (static)
text: The signature of "takes data secretly": **sensitive-data read + network write in the same flow**. - Reads: `getContacts`, `SMS`, `Location`, `MediaStore`, clipboard, `AccessibilityService` (huge red flag — screen/key logging), call logs - Writes: `HttpURLConnection`, OkHttp/Retrofit calls to weird domains, hardcoded IPs, `Socket` - Stealth tricks: `DexClassLoader`/`loadDex` (downloads code at runtime — hides the real payload from scanners), reflection to hide API calls, base64/encrypted strings, native `.so` libraries doing the dirty work - Permissions abuse: `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES`, `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` (overlay attacks), `BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE`, battery-optimization exemption, foreground services that never stop Search jadx for: `http`, `upload`, domain strings, `getDeviceId`, `content://`, `exec(`.

title: Tier 2 — Dynamic analysis (the truth test)
text: Static lies — real malware decrypts its payload at runtime. So run it and watch: **Setup:** - Android emulator (Android Studio's AVD) or a spare/spare-ish device — **never your daily phone** - **PCAPdroid** — on-device VPN that captures ALL the app's network traffic, shows every domain it phones home to. Easiest win in this whole list. - **mitmproxy / Burp** — proxy the traffic, read the actual requests: what data leaves, where it goes **Then escalate if needed:** - HTTPS pinning blocking your proxy? **Frida** + a pinning-bypass script defeats it in minutes - **MobSF dynamic** mode — instruments the app in an emulator, logs API calls live - Watch filesystem: what does it read/write outside its sandbox permissions? **The moment of truth:** capture traffic → find a request carrying your contacts/location/device ID to `random-domain.xyz` → that's your smoking gun, documented.

title: Red flags that scream "malicious"
text: 1. Accessibility service requested by a non-accessibility app (banking trojan classic) 2. Dynamic code loading + heavy obfuscation (why hide, if innocent?) 3. Contacts/SMS/location exfil'd to domains with no relation to the app's function 4. Requests permissions it never functionally uses 5. Runs immediately at boot + persistent foreground service + disables battery optimization 6. Sideloaded-only distribution, or a "modded/premium free" APK from a random site — this category is where actual Android malware lives

title: Your honest starting setup
