title: HT: AF_ALG concurrent-writer scatterlist underflow to kernel write (af-alg-concurrent-writer-scatterlist-oob)
text: # AF_ALG concurrent-writer scatterlist underflow to kernel write {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} An unprivileged process can use an `AF_ALG` `skcipher` operation socket to reach `af_alg_sendmsg()`. On kernels without the concurrent-write fix, two writers sharing that socket can leave its persistent transmit scatterlist in an impossible state: `ctx->merge` is true, but the final `af_alg_tsgl` has `cur == 0`. The next write reads `sg[-1]` and can turn that out-of-bounds metadata read into a kernel write. This is a **writer race in the skcipher input path**, not the AEAD page-cache overwrite described in [Copy Fail](../../linux-hardening/main-system-information/kernel-lpe-cves/copy-fail-af_alg-splice-page-cache-overwrite-cve-2026-31431.md).<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reachability and state (af-alg-concurrent-writer-scatterlist-oob)
text: ## Reachability and state Create an `AF_ALG` `SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket, bind it to `salg_type = "skcipher"` and an available cipher such as `cbc(aes)`, set its key with `setsockopt(SOL_ALG, ALG_SET_KEY, ...)` on the transform FD, and then call `accept()` to obtain the operation FD. `sendmsg()` supplies input and optional operation/IV control messages; `MSG_MORE` keeps the input open across calls. The attack has **both writers use the same operation FD**, not separate accepted sockets. `recvmsg()` consumes the accumulated input and frees send-buffer space.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> `af_alg_ctx` persists across these calls. Its `tsgl_list` holds transmit scatterlist groups, `used` counts queued bytes, and `merge` means a partially filled final page can accept more bytes. Each `af_alg_tsgl` has a flexible `sg[]` array and `cur`, the number of valid entries. For an ordinary write without `MSG_SPLICE_PAGES`, the merge branch assumes `merge => tail->cur > 0` before evaluating `tail->sg + tail->cur - 1`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Break the merge invariant across a wait (af-alg-concurrent-writer-scatterlist-oob)
text: ## Break the merge invariant across a wait `lock_sock()` does not give one writer ownership for the entire call on a vulnerable kernel. If the send buffer is full, `af_alg_wait_for_wmem()` uses `sk_wait_event()`, which releases the socket lock while sleeping and reacquires it on wakeup. Another unfinished `sendmsg()` can therefore change `af_alg_ctx` before the first call resumes.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The published trigger starts with `tail->cur = MAX_SGL_ENTS - 1`, `ctx->merge = false`, and a full send buffer. Both writers block in the wait path. After input is drained, the first writer fills the remaining scatterlist entry with **less than one page** and finishes with `ctx->merge = true` and a full TSG array. The second writer then resumes on the allocation path, appends a new TSG with `cur = 0`, and copies from an invalid userspace address. `memcpy_from_msg()` fails, but the error path leaves the empty TSG at the list tail without clearing `merge`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text Before the wait: tail->cur = MAX_SGL_ENTS - 1, merge = 0 After writer A: tail->cur = MAX_SGL_ENTS, merge = 1 After writer B fails: tail->cur = 0 (new tail), merge = 1 Next sendmsg: sg = tail->sg + 0 - 1 = &tail->sg[-1] ``` The race is not two unsynchronized stores at once: the socket lock still serializes each active segment. The failure is that a wait splits a logical write into segments while shared state and its error path assume a sole writer. KASAN reports a slab out-of-bounds read at `af_alg_sendmsg()` when the final expression uses the forged entry.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: From `sg[-1]` to a write destination (af-alg-concurrent-writer-scatterlist-oob)
text: ## From `sg[-1]` to a write destination On the published x86-64 target, `sg[0]` starts at offset `0x18` in `af_alg_tsgl` and `sizeof(struct scatterlist) == 0x20`; thus `sg[-1]` begins at offset `-0x8`. If a 4096-byte heap object is placed immediately before the TSG, the forged `page_link` comes from its last eight bytes at offset `0xff8`, while the forged entry's `offset` and `length` overlap the current TSG object's list pointer. This layout is **configuration-dependent**: measure the structures and allocator size on the target rather than assuming these offsets elsewhere.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> The exploit sprays same-size objects so controlled bytes occupy the preceding object's last eight bytes. The merge branch computes the destination from the forged entry as shown below. Controlling `page_link` steers `sg_page(sg)`, but the list-pointer-derived `offset` and `length` also affect the final address, so a heap spray alone is not a reliable arbitrary write.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c dest = page_address(sg_page(sg)) + sg->offset + sg->length; err = memcpy_from_msg(dest, msg, len); ``` ### Fault-tolerant usercopy oracle On the demonstrated x86-64 usercopy path, `memcpy_from_msg()` reaches `copy_from_iter_full()` and `raw_copy_from_user()`. `access_ok()` checks the **userspace source**, not this corrupted destination. A fault at an unmapped destination is caught by the usercopy exception path and propagated as `EFAULT`, instead of necessarily crashing the kernel. A one-byte write therefore gives a practical oracle: `sendmsg()` returns `1` for a mapped, writable destination or `-1` with `errno == EFAULT` for an unmapped one. This behavior depends on the target architecture, usercopy implementation, and the destination calculation.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]]

title: HT: Privileged execution and fix (af-alg-concurrent-writer-scatterlist-oob)
text: ## Privileged execution and fix The demonstrated kernel write was used for root execution through `core_pattern`. If a container can access `AF_ALG` on a vulnerable host, this can also cross the container boundary. The [piped-core-handler escalation step](../common-exploiting-problems.md#one-write-privilege-flips-dirtymode-style) is covered separately; the distinctive part here is obtaining the write through an `AF_ALG` state race and usercopy oracle.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The upstream fix, `1b34cbbf4f01`, adds `ctx->write` ownership: a concurrent writer on the same operation socket receives `-EBUSY` even if the first writer temporarily releases the socket lock during its wait. Check for that change or a vendor backport rather than inferring exposure from the kernel version alone.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Futex PI UAF to pipe physical R/W and workqueue execution (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: # Futex PI UAF to pipe physical R/W and workqueue execution {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This page abstracts the **GhostLock** Android chain (CVE-2026-43499): a futex priority-inheritance lifetime bug is converted into a constrained pointer write, CFI-compatible file operations and forged `pipe_buffer` entries provide physical memory R/W, and a forged workqueue item reaches usermode-helper execution when protected credentials cannot be patched.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Primitive ladder (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Primitive ladder The original chain and the Samsung port use the following progression; offsets, syscall frame depth, reclaim objects, physical base, and usable workqueue are build-specific.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```text futex PI lifetime race -> dangling waiter state pselect stack reclaim -> fake rt_mutex_waiter rb-tree erase -> constrained aligned pointer write boot_id ctl_table anchors -> KASLR slide CFI-compatible f_op substitution -> constrained virtual R/W forged pipe_buffer.page -> arbitrary physical R/W forged work_struct/subprocess_info -> privileged usermode helper ``` ### Reclaiming the waiter and obtaining a write After the futex PI race leaves stale `rt_mutex_waiter` state in the blocked task, reclaim the old kernel-stack frame with a syscall that copies controllable data deeply enough into its stack frame. The Android chain uses `pselect()` and its copied `fd_set` bitmaps; other builds may require a different syscall after measuring the freed frame. Forge the waiter's `tree`/`pi_tree` RB nodes plus safe `task` and `lock` pointers so unlinking the node makes RB-tree erase write one chosen pointer to a constrained aligned address.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Treat this as a **single pointer-sized write per successful race**, not arbitrary R/W. Repeat the race for independent targets and validate every dereferenced fake field because a malformed waiter normally crashes before the useful erase operation.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### KASLR oracle and CFI-compatible file operations A useful first target is a readable sysctl's `ctl_table.data`. Repointing the `boot_id` entry can make its normal proc handler disclose a slid kernel pointer. On the Samsung port, accepting a candidate only when the `procname`, `data`, and `proc_handle

title: HT: Workqueue/user-mode-helper endgame (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Workqueue/user-mode-helper endgame Hypervisor-backed data protection can silently discard otherwise valid stores to `cred`, task-slab, or SELinux state. In that situation, avoid a credential-patching endgame and instead make an existing worker execute `call_usermodehelper_exec_work`; the helper inherits privileged kernel/init credentials without modifying the protected credential objects.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> A robust forged-work installation performs these checks before linking anything into a live pool:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. Read the target workqueue pointer and traverse its `pwqs` list (or a validated `dfl_pwq` for an unbound queue) to a `pool_workqueue` and `worker_pool`. 2. Validate pointer ranges and relationships such as `pwq->wq == wq`, then sanity-check `work_color`, `refcnt`, `nr_active`, `max_active`, and the pool work-list links. 3. Place a build-correct `subprocess_info` in kernel-accessible memory. Its embedded `work_struct.func` points to the slid `call_usermodehelper_exec_work`; `path`, `argv`, and `envp` point to stable kernel-accessible strings and arrays. 4. Encode `work_struct.data` with the selected PWQ and color, link `work.entry` into `worker_pool.worklist`, and update the matching PWQ accounting fields consistently. 5. Wake the chosen pool with legitimate work. The demonstrated port creates a `ptmx` allocation/free storm so normal queued work wakes a worker that also consumes the forged entry. The helper can execute a small script such as `/system/bin/sh umh.sh`, create a root marker, and launch a restricted command channel. Start the daemon before slow evidence collection or repeated `sync` calls, and persist its exit status and stderr because helper stdout and rate-limited audit output ar

title: HT: Runtime object discovery without perf leaks (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Runtime object discovery without perf leaks When perf-based object leaks are blocked or too slow, start at `init_task.tasks.prev`, subtract the build's `task_struct.tasks` offset, and walk the global list backward until `tgid` matches the exploit process. From `task_struct.files`, follow `files_struct.fdt -> fdtable.fd`, inspect each `struct file`, and find the ashmem/configfs-backed descriptor used for virtual writes.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Bound every walk, require canonical/direct-map pointers, validate both list directions where possible, and reject unexpected TGIDs or `f_op` values. A corrupt list node should abort the attempt rather than becoming a second uncontrolled kernel write.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Cleaning forged pipe slots without a panic (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Cleaning forged pipe slots without a panic A forged pipe slot can reference a reserved kernel-image page that never received `get_page()`. Pipe teardown then calls `anon_pipe_buf_release -> __folio_put` on a zero-refcount reserved page; with `panic_on_oops=1`, the resulting bad-page warning resets the device.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Use two independent cleanup layers:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Descriptor holder:** an `atexit` handler forks a sleeping child that inherits all exploit FDs. The shared file descriptions never reach zero references, so pipe destruction is deferred until reboot. - **Ring disarm:** before exit, use the surviving virtual-write descriptor to set `pipe_buffer.ops = NULL` for every forged slot. `free_pipe_info()` skips slots without operations instead of calling a release callback. Duplicating a forged slot with `tee()` is not a repair: it only moves the eventual invalid page put to the holder pipe. Keep the descriptor-holder fallback because a partial ring-disarm walk is itself firmware- and corruption-sensitive.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Path-based privileged-exec restrictions (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Path-based privileged-exec restrictions Some Android vendor controls kill UID-0 execution from writable paths while allowing trusted system paths. With `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, a narrowly scoped bypass is to bind-mount the payload over a dormant trusted executable, execute the trusted pathname, and lazily detach the mount after daemonization. The A17 port shadows `/system/bin/lmkd`; this is preferable to overwriting a firmware-specific global DEFEX feature word because it avoids disabling enforcement system-wide.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ```sh if mount --bind "$A/g4d" /system/bin/lmkd 2>"$A/g4d.mnt"; then /system/bin/lmkd >"$A/g4d.out" 2>&1 rc=$? umount -l /system/bin/lmkd else "$A/g4d" >"$A/g4d.out" 2>&1 rc=$? fi echo "G4D-RC=$rc" >"$A/g4d.rc" ``` For a reusable root channel, an abstract Unix socket avoids filesystem socket cleanup, `SO_PEERCRED` can restrict clients to explicitly allowed UIDs, and a fresh PTY per connection preserves interactive shell semantics. This remains per-boot access unless a separate boot-persistent modification is made.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Porting and test checklist (futex-pi-uaf-pipe-buffer-workqueue-usermodehelper)
text: ## Porting and test checklist The public port's workflow is useful beyond this specific bug:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - Extract `boot.img` from the exact stock firmware and recover `vmlinux`/`Image` plus symbols and BTF. - Audit every accessed member and symbol; refuse to run unless the runtime profile matches the expected build. - Parameterize the physical kernel base instead of inheriting another device's value. - Boot the real kernel and the same exploit binary in QEMU with an initramfs, applying only patches required for absent platform components. - Automate success markers and poweroff, and test malformed fake objects, misaligned physical reads, forge-budget exhaustion, and pipe teardown before device deployment. - Treat the race as probabilistic: preserve a healthy boot after ordinary failures and run bounded, observable retries instead of converting every miss into a reboot.

title: HT: ksmbd streams_xattr OOB write → local LPE (CVE-2025-37947) (ksmbd-streams_xattr-oob-write-cve-2025-37947)
text: # ksmbd streams_xattr OOB write → local LPE (CVE-2025-37947) {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This page documents a deterministic out-of-bounds write in ksmbd streams handling that enables a reliable Linux kernel privilege escalation on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (5.15.0-153-generic), bypassing KASLR, SMEP, and SMAP using standard kernel heap primitives (msg_msg + pipe_buffer).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Affected component: fs/ksmbd/vfs.c — ksmbd_vfs_stream_write() - Primitive: page-overflow OOB write past a 0x10000-byte kvmalloc() buffer - Preconditions: ksmbd running with an authenticated, writable share using vfs streams_xattr Example smb.conf ```ini [share] path = /share vfs objects = streams_xattr writeable = yes ``` Root cause (allocation clamped, memcpy at unclamped offset) - The function computes size = *pos + count, clamps size to XATTR_SIZE_MAX (0x10000) when exceeded, and recomputes count = (*pos + count) - 0x10000, but still performs memcpy(&stream_buf[*pos], buf, count) into a 0x10000-byte buffer. If *pos ≥ 0x10000 the destination pointer is already outside the allocation, producing an OOB write of count bytes. - `streams_xattr` stores SMB alternate data streams inside POSIX extended attributes, so the 0x10000 ceiling comes from the Linux single-xattr size limit rather than from an SMB protocol field. That makes the bug practical only when the share explicitly enables `vfs objects = streams_xattr` and the filesystem supports xattrs.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Why the write offset matters - The vulnerable path is not just "write more than 64KiB". The missing check was that `*pos` was not validated against the current stream length (`v_len`) before the append/copy logic ran. - Upstream fixed this by rejecting writes where `*pos >= v_len` with `-E

text: # Example tracer (see reference repo) to log kvmalloc addresses/sizes sudo ./bpf-tracer.sh ``` What to trace while tuning - `kvmalloc_node(0x10000)` confirms when the vulnerable stream write actually consumes an order-4 allocation. - `load_msg`/`kretprobe:load_msg` lets you estimate how many `msg_msgseg` allocations are attached to each sprayed message, which is useful when tuning primary/secondary message sizes for a specific kernel build. - If the exploit is ported to a different distro/kernel, re-check cache names, inline `msg_msg` payload sizes, `anon_pipe_buf_ops` offsets, and gadget addresses rather than assuming the Ubuntu 22.04 LTS `5.15.0-153-generic` constants still match.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Exploitation plan (msg_msg + pipe_buffer), adapted from CVE-2021-22555 1) Spray many System V msg_msg primary/secondary messages (4KiB-sized to fit kmalloc-cg-4k). 2) Trigger ksmbd OOB to corrupt a primary message’s next pointer so that two primaries share one secondary. 3) Detect the corrupted pair by tagging queues and scanning with msgrcv(MSG_COPY) to find mismatched tags. 4) Free the real secondary to create a UAF; reclaim it with controlled data via UNIX sockets (craft a fake msg_msg). 5) Leak kernel heap pointers by abusing m_ts over-read in copy_msg to obtain mlist.next/mlist.prev (SMAP bypass). 6) With an sk_buff spray, rebuild a consistent fake msg_msg with valid links and free it normally to stabilize state. 7) Reclaim the UAF with struct pipe_buffer objects; leak anon_pipe_buf_ops to compute kernel base (defeat KASLR). 8) Spray a fake pipe_buf_operations with release pointing to a stack pivot/ROP gadget; close pipes to execute and gain root.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Bypasses and notes - KASLR: leak anon_pipe_buf_ops, compute base (kbase_addr) and g

title: HT: AF_UNIX MSG_OOB UAF & SKB-based kernel primitives (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: # AF_UNIX MSG_OOB UAF & SKB-based kernel primitives {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: TL;DR (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## TL;DR - A `manage_oob()` regression (`93c99f21db36`, merged for Linux 6.10 and backported to 6.9.8) made the receive path advance past a consumed OOB SKB. The later `5aa57d9f2d53` repair handled one such marker but not two consecutive zero-length SKBs, allowing a normal `recv()` to free the live OOB SKB without clearing `u->oob_skb` and producing CVE-2025-38236.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> - Re-triggering `recv(..., MSG_OOB)` dereferences the dangling `struct sk_buff`. With `MSG_PEEK`, the path `unix_stream_recv_urg() -> __skb_datagram_iter() -> copy_to_user()` becomes a stable 1-byte arbitrary kernel read; without `MSG_PEEK` the primitive increments `UNIXCB(oob_skb).consumed` at offset `0x44`, i.e., adds +4 GiB to the upper dword of any 64-bit value placed at offset `0x40` inside the reallocated object.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - By draining order-0/1 unmovable pages (page-table spray), force-freeing an SKB slab page into the buddy allocator, and reusing the physical page as a pipe buffer, the exploit forges SKB metadata in controlled memory to identify the dangling page and pivot the read primitive into `.data`, vmemmap, per-CPU, and page-table regions despite usercopy hardening.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - The same page can later be recycled as the top kernel-stack page of a freshly cloned thread. `CONFIG_RANDOMIZE_KSTACK_OFFSET` becomes an oracle: by probing the stack layout while `pipe_write()` blocks, the attacker waits until the spilled `copy_page_from_iter()` length (R14) lands at offset `0x40`, then fires the +4 GiB increment to corrupt the stack value.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - A self-looping `skb_shinfo()->frag_list` keeps the UAF syscall spinning in kernel space until a cooperating thread stalls `copy_from_iter()` (via `mpro

title: HT: Version / configuration checklist (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Version / configuration checklist - **Feature lineage:** AF_UNIX `MSG_OOB` support itself was added by `314001f0bf92` ("af_unix: Add OOB support"), merged for Linux 5.15. The last byte of a `send(..., MSG_OOB)` becomes the urgent byte and is tracked through `unix_sock->oob_skb`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Patch lineage matters:** The publicly exploited state starts with `93c99f21db36` (mainline 6.10, stable 6.9.8), not with the original Linux 5.15 AF_UNIX OOB feature. `5aa57d9f2d53` fixes the earlier one-consumed-marker UAF but is **not** evidence that CVE-2025-38236 is fixed. Vendor kernels may carry any subset of this chain, so look for `32ca245464e1` or its stable/vendor equivalent rather than trusting `uname -r`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> - **Build/runtime gates:** The attack path requires `CONFIG_AF_UNIX_OOB=y`. The symbol existed from the feature's introduction and defaulted to `y`, but it had no Kconfig prompt; `5155cbcdbf03` (December 2024) made it possible to select `n` through normal kernel configuration. It did not introduce the symbol or merely make it visible in the generated `.config`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> - **Sandbox reachability:** Any sandbox that exposes AF_UNIX stream sockets and does not filter `MSG_OOB` / `MSG_PEEK` stays interesting even if the application never intentionally uses urgent data. Chrome closed the reachable path by allowlisting socket-call flags in CL `6711812`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ### Non-destructive reachability check On kernels built with `CONFIG_AF_UNIX_OOB=n`, `send(..., MSG_OOB)` returns `EOPNOTSUPP`. The following one-byte round trip only checks whether the feature is reachable; it does **not** build consecutive consumed markers

title: HT: Root cause: `manage_oob()` assumes only one zero-length SKB (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Root cause: `manage_oob()` assumes only one zero-length SKB `unix_stream_read_generic()` expects every SKB returned by `manage_oob()` to have `unix_skb_len() > 0`. After `93c99f21db36`, `manage_oob()` could remove a zero-length SKB left by `recv(MSG_OOB)` and advance to its successor. `5aa57d9f2d53` re-ran the `skb == u->oob_skb` cleanup checks for that successor, fixing the single-marker UAF, but it still did not require the returned SKB to have nonzero remaining length. With two consecutive consumed OOB SKBs, it returned the second empty one; the `SO_PEEK_OFF` skip loop in `unix_stream_read_generic()` then advanced to the live OOB SKB and freed it without clearing `u->oob_skb`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> ### Why the final fix changes the queue invariant `32ca245464e1` does not add another loop to `manage_oob()`. While `unix_stream_recv_urg()` holds the receive-queue lock, it checks whether the SKB immediately before the OOB SKB is already consumed (`unix_skb_len(prev) == 0`), unlinks that previous marker, and frees it after dropping the lock. Therefore the queue can retain the current boundary marker but cannot accumulate two adjacent consumed OOB SKBs; this also removes the ambiguous state that broke `SIOCATMARK`.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ### Minimal trigger sequence ```c char byte; int socks[2]; socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, socks); for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) { send(socks[1], "A", 1, MSG_OOB); recv(socks[0], &byte, 1, MSG_OOB); } send(socks[1], "A", 1, MSG_OOB); // SKB3, u->oob_skb = SKB3 recv(socks[0], &byte, 1, 0); // normal recv frees SKB3 recv(socks[0], &byte, 1, MSG_OOB); // dangling u->oob_skb ```

title: HT: AF_UNIX OOB semantics that matter for exploitation (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## AF_UNIX OOB semantics that matter for exploitation - **Boundary semantics:** AF_UNIX OOB is TCP-like: a normal `recv()` stops at the urgent mark even when the caller's buffer is large enough to consume more (`oob_break` in the upstream kselftest). This is why a consumed OOB SKB can remain relevant after the urgent byte was already read.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> - **Dropping vs. reading urgent data:** With the default `SO_OOBINLINE = 0`, `recv(MSG_OOB)` returns the urgent byte, but the queue still keeps the consumed SKB as a boundary marker. A later plain `recv()` can either stop at that mark or drop the consumed OOB and continue into the following SKB (`oob_break_drop`) — the exact corner that turns stale `u->oob_skb` into a UAF.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **`SO_OOBINLINE` changes the trigger surface:** If `SO_OOBINLINE` is enabled on the receiver, `recv(MSG_OOB)` returns `-EINVAL` and the urgent byte is consumed through plain `recv()` instead. Public reproducers assume the default non-inline mode.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Useful observability:** `EPOLLPRI` tracks whether an urgent mark is still pending, and `ioctl(fd, SIOCATMARK, &atmark)` reveals whether the next unread byte sits at the urgent boundary. When adapting the primitive to another kernel, `tools/testing/selftests/net/af_unix/msg_oob.c` is a good behavioural oracle.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Primitives exposed by `unix_stream_recv_urg()` (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Primitives exposed by `unix_stream_recv_urg()` 1. **1-byte arbitrary read (repeatable):** `state->recv_actor()` ultimately performs `copy_to_user(user, skb_sourced_addr, 1)`. If the dangling SKB is reallocated into attacker-controlled memory (or into a controlled alias such as a pipe page), every `recv(MSG_OOB | MSG_PEEK)` copies a byte from an arbitrary kernel address allowed by `__check_object_size()` to user space without crashing. Keeping `MSG_PEEK` set preserves the dangling pointer for unlimited reads.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 2. **Constrained write:** When `MSG_PEEK` is clear, `UNIXCB(oob_skb).consumed += 1` increments the 32-bit field at offset `0x44`. On 0x100-aligned SKB allocations this sits four bytes above an 8-byte aligned word, converting the primitive into a +4 GiB increment of the word hosted at offset `0x40`. Turning this into a kernel write requires positioning a sensitive 64-bit value at that offset.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reallocating the SKB page for arbitrary read (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Reallocating the SKB page for arbitrary read 1. **Drain order-0/1 unmovable freelists:** Map a huge read-only anonymous VMA and fault every page to force page-table allocation (order-0 unmovable). Filling ~10% of RAM with page tables ensures subsequent `skbuff_head_cache` allocations pull fresh buddy pages once order-0 lists exhaust.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 2. **Spray SKBs and isolate a slab page:** Use dozens of stream socketpairs and queue hundreds of small messages per socket (~0x100 bytes per SKB) to populate `skbuff_head_cache`. Free chosen SKBs to drive a target slab page entirely under attacker control and monitor its `struct page` refcount via the emerging read primitive. 3. **Return the slab page to the buddy allocator:** Free every object on the page, then perform enough additional allocations/frees to push the page out of SLUB per-CPU partial lists and per-CPU page lists so it becomes an order-1 page on the buddy freelist. 4. **Reallocate as pipe buffer:** Create hundreds of pipes; each pipe reserves at least two 0x1000-byte data pages (`PIPE_MIN_DEF_BUFFERS`). When the buddy allocator splits an order-1 page, one half reuses the freed SKB page. To locate which pipe and which offset aliases `oob_skb`, write unique marker bytes into fake SKBs stored throughout pipe pages and issue repeated `recv(MSG_OOB | MSG_PEEK)` calls until the marker is returned. 5. **Forge a stable SKB layout:** Populate the aliased pipe page with a fake `struct sk_buff` whose `data`/`head` pointers and `skb_shared_info` structure point to arbitrary kernel addresses of interest. Because x86_64 disables SMAP inside `copy_to_user()`, user-mode addresses can serve as staging buffers until kernel pointers are known. 6. **Respect usercopy hardening:** The copy succeeds against `.data/.

title: HT: Introspecting allocators with the read primitive (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Introspecting allocators with the read primitive - **Break KASLR:** Read any IDT descriptor from the fixed mapping at `CPU_ENTRY_AREA_RO_IDT_VADDR` (`0xfffffe0000000000`) and subtract the known handler offset to recover the kernel base.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **SLUB/buddy state:** Global `.data` symbols reveal `kmem_cache` bases, while vmemmap entries expose each page's type flags, freelist pointer, and owning cache. Scanning per-CPU vmalloc segments uncovers `struct kmem_cache_cpu` instances so the next allocation address of key caches (e.g., `skbuff_head_cache`, `kmalloc-cg-192`) becomes predictable. - **Page tables:** Instead of reading `mm_struct` (blocked by usercopy), walk the global `pgd_list` (`struct ptdesc`) and match the current `mm_struct` via `cpu_tlbstate.loaded_mm`. Once the root `pgd` is known, the primitive can traverse every page table to map PFNs for pipe buffers, page tables, and kernel stacks.

title: HT: Recycling the SKB page as the top kernel-stack page (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Recycling the SKB page as the top kernel-stack page 1. Free the controlled pipe page again and confirm via vmemmap that its refcount returns to zero.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 2. Immediately allocate four helper pipe pages and then free them in reverse order so the buddy allocator's LIFO behavior is deterministic. 3. Call `clone()` to spawn a helper thread; Linux stacks are four pages on x86_64, so the four most recently freed pages become its stack, with the last freed page (the former SKB page) at the highest addresses. 4. Verify via page-table walk that the helper thread's top stack PFN equals the recycled SKB PFN. 5. Use the arbitrary read to observe the stack layout while steering the thread into `pipe_write()`. `CONFIG_RANDOMIZE_KSTACK_OFFSET` subtracts a random 0x0–0x3f0 (aligned) from `RSP` per syscall; repeated writes combined with `poll()`/`read()` from another thread reveal when the writer blocks with the desired offset. When lucky, the spilled `copy_page_from_iter()` `bytes` argument (R14) sits at offset `0x40` inside the recycled page.

title: HT: Placing fake SKB metadata on the stack (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Placing fake SKB metadata on the stack - Use `sendmsg()` on an AF_UNIX datagram socket: the kernel copies the user `sockaddr_un` into a stack-resident `sockaddr_storage` (up to 108 bytes) and the ancillary data into another on-stack buffer before the syscall blocks waiting for queue space. This allows planting a precise fake SKB structure in stack memory.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Detect when the copy finished by supplying a 1-byte control message located in an unmapped user page; `____sys_sendmsg()` faults it in, so a helper thread polling `mincore()` on that address learns when the destination page is present. - Zero-initialized padding from `CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO` conveniently fills unused fields, completing a valid SKB header without extra writes.

title: HT: Timing the +4 GiB increment with a self-looping frag list (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Timing the +4 GiB increment with a self-looping frag list - Forge `skb_shinfo(fakeskb)->frag_list` to point to a second fake SKB (stored in attacker-controlled user memory) that has `len = 0` and `next = &self`. When `skb_walk_frags()` iterates this list inside `__skb_datagram_iter()`, execution spins indefinitely because the iterator never reaches `NULL` and the copy loop makes no progress.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Keep the recv syscall running inside the kernel by letting the second fake SKB self-loop. When it's time to fire the increment, simply change the second SKB's `next` pointer from user space to `NULL`. The loop exits and `unix_stream_recv_urg()` immediately executes `UNIXCB(oob_skb).consumed += 1` once, affecting whatever object currently occupies the recycled stack page at offset `0x40`.

title: HT: Stalling `copy_from_iter()` without userfaultfd (af-unix-msg-oob-uaf-skb-primitives)
text: ## Stalling `copy_from_iter()` without userfaultfd - Map a giant anonymous RW VMA and fault it in fully.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Punch a single-page hole with `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED, hole, PAGE_SIZE)` and place that address inside the `iov_iter` used for `write(pipefd, user_buf, 0x3000)`. - In parallel, call `mprotect()` on the entire VMA from another thread. The syscall grabs the mmap write lock and walks every PTE. When the pipe writer reaches the hole, the page fault handler blocks on the mmap lock held by `mprotect()`, pausing `copy_from_iter()` at a deterministic point while the spilled `bytes` value resides on the stack segment hosted by the recycled SKB page.

title: HT: Android Binder IPC internals and kernel vulnerability research (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: # Android Binder IPC internals and kernel vulnerability research {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Binder exposes Android's main IPC transport through device nodes such as `/dev/binder`. An ordinary application can reach a large kernel state machine through `ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ)`: transactions may contain Binder endpoints, handles, pointers, file descriptors and file-descriptor arrays. The interesting memory-safety boundary is therefore not only parsing. It is whether every translated object remains alive until all references, queued work, transaction buffers and stack links have been removed.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Object graph and translation boundary (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Object graph and translation boundary Model Binder as a graph rather than as independent allocations. The most important lifetime edges are:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> | Object | Important owners and edges | | --- | --- | | `binder_proc` | Owns the thread and node RB trees, process workqueue and allocator. `tmp_ref` protects temporary kernel pointers. | | `binder_thread` | Belongs to a process, owns a private workqueue and participates in a transaction stack. Its `tmp_ref` is separate from process references. | | `binder_node` | Represents an endpoint owned by one process. It is referenced by remote `binder_ref` objects, buffers, queued node work and temporary kernel pointers. | | `binder_ref` | Gives one process a descriptor/handle for another process's node. It carries independent strong and weak userspace counts. | | `binder_transaction` | Connects sender and receiver threads through `from`, `to_thread`, `from_parent` and `to_parent`. It also owns a transaction buffer. | | `binder_buffer` | Lives in the destination allocator and may retain `target_node` until `BC_FREE_BUFFER` or failure cleanup. | `flat_binder_object` is the main translation boundary. `BINDER_TYPE_BINDER` and `BINDER_TYPE_WEAK_BINDER` identify a sender-owned endpoint. The driver finds or creates its `binder_node`, creates a `binder_ref` in the destination and rewrites the object into `BINDER_TYPE_HANDLE` or `BINDER_TYPE_WEAK_HANDLE`. A forwarded handle is resolved in the source process and translated into a new destination-local handle. Also exercise `BINDER_TYPE_PTR`, `BINDER_TYPE_FD` and `BINDER_TYPE_FDA`, especially in transactions that fail after only some objects were translated.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> For fuzzing, vary object order, offsets, parent

title: HT: Lifetime invariants and UAF auditing (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Lifetime invariants and UAF auditing The node-free decision spans flags, counters and containers. At the kernel revision studied by the researchers, a node should reach the following state before `binder_free_node()`:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c node->proc == NULL node->has_strong_ref == 0 node->has_weak_ref == 0 node->internal_strong_refs == 0 node->local_strong_refs == 0 node->local_weak_refs == 0 node->tmp_refs == 0 hlist_empty(&node->refs) list_empty(&node->work.entry) ``` There is no explicit internal-weak counter. Remote weak ownership is represented by the node's `refs` list, while `tmp_refs` covers transient kernel pointers. `internal_strong_refs` tracks remote references whose per-process strong count crossed from zero to nonzero. Local strong/weak counters cover transactions or embedded Binder objects that refer directly to the local node. This mixed representation makes `binder_dec_node_nilocked()`, `binder_dec_node_tmpref()` and alternative free paths particularly valuable comparison points.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Apply the same reasoning to the surrounding objects: a dead `binder_proc` is freed only after its thread tree and `tmp_ref` are empty; a dead `binder_thread` waits for its own `tmp_ref`; and a `binder_ref` is removed after both its strong and weak counts reach zero. Audit every transition while preserving the relevant node lock and process `inner_lock` assumptions.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Exercise every decrement or detach path, not only the normal RPC flow. High-value paths include `BC_RELEASE`, `BC_DECREFS`, `BC_FREE_BUFFER`, `BINDER_THREAD_EXIT`, descriptor closure, `binder_deferred_release()`, `binder_free_ref()`, failed-transaction unwind, death-notification removal and

title: HT: Concurrency, workqueues and transaction stacks (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Concurrency, workqueues and transaction stacks A synchronous call normally follows `BC_TRANSACTION -> BR_TRANSACTION -> BC_REPLY -> BR_REPLY`. Binder can queue work on `binder_proc->todo`, `binder_thread->todo` or a node's `async_todo`; thread-private work takes priority when a thread reads. Replies target the initiating thread. One-way transactions set `TF_ONE_WAY`, use the target node's asynchronous queue and remain serialized per node until the receiver releases the current buffer with `BC_FREE_BUFFER`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Threads must enter or register the looper protocol with `BC_ENTER_LOOPER` or `BC_REGISTER_LOOPER` before consuming process work. Stress `BR_SPAWN_LOOPER`, `BINDER_SET_MAX_THREADS`, simultaneous looper exit, frozen targets, one-way spam status, death notifications and allocator exhaustion. These transitions move work between different owners and expose assumptions that a queue entry or recipient thread still exists.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Nested synchronous RPC uses two link directions. Sending pushes through `from_parent`; delivery to the receiver pushes through `to_parent`; and replies must pop in LIFO order. Construct a re-entrant chain such as `A -> B -> C -> D -> B`, then kill or close each participant at different points. Verify that failure propagation (`BR_DEAD_REPLY` or `BR_FAILED_REPLY`) clears `from`, `to_thread` and `to_proc` while walking the correct parent link and never revisits a freed transaction or thread.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Transaction allocator and stale-data disclosure (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Transaction allocator and stale-data disclosure Each process has a `binder_alloc` for incoming data. Userspace maps it read-only and the kernel lazily supplies backing pages. Allocation uses a best-fit free-buffer tree; `BC_FREE_BUFFER` releases transaction metadata and coalesces adjacent free buffers. The mapping remains readable after release, but freed bytes are not cleared unless the sender requested `TF_CLEAR_BUF`. This can expose stale transaction contents to the receiving process when allocator space is reused.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> Set `TF_CLEAR_BUF` for transactions containing secrets. AIDL interfaces can request the same behavior for generated proxy/stub transactions with `@SensitiveData`. Keep this information-disclosure condition separate from corruption of an *active* transaction: active object metadata is later trusted during translation and reference cleanup, so corrupting it can instead lead to kernel memory corruption.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Minimal raw Binder research harness (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Minimal raw Binder research harness [`libdevbinder`](https://github.com/androidoffsec/libdevbinder) provides a small C wrapper around Binder ioctls and is useful for deterministic lifetime and ordering tests without first reproducing all of `libbinder`. It supports native Linux, arm64 cross-compilation and Android NDK builds.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash git clone https://github.com/androidoffsec/libdevbinder.git cd libdevbinder make # native x86_64 ARCH=arm64 make # cross-compile NDK_ROOT=/path/to/android-ndk ANDROID=1 make ``` The example server becomes the Binder context manager, so it normally cannot claim Android's existing `/dev/binder`. On a rooted test device, mount a separate binderfs instance, change the examples to `/dev/mybinder/binder`, and run the client and server there. Use this only in an isolated research environment.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```bash mkdir /dev/mybinder mount -t binder binder /dev/mybinder ./server ./client "hello world" ```

title: HT: Audit checklist (android-binder-ipc-internals-kernel-vulnerability-research)
text: ## Audit checklist Use a revision-specific kernel tree because structure layout and locking rules change. For every test case, trace these questions:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> 1. Which operation created each node, reference, buffer, transaction and queued work item? 2. Which lock protects each edge, counter and dead-state transition? 3. Does a zero crossing update both the userspace-facing count and the node-side aggregate state exactly once? 4. Does partial object translation unwind only objects that were successfully installed? 5. Can thread exit, process release, death notification or failed reply race with queue delivery or `BC_FREE_BUFFER`? 6. After free, can an RB tree, list, work item, async queue or transaction-stack link still resolve the old address? 7. Are secret-bearing transactions cleared explicitly rather than assuming allocator reuse erases them?

title: HT: Android Binder transaction cleanup UAF exploitation (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: # Android Binder transaction cleanup UAF exploitation {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Android Binder is reachable through `/dev/binder` from ordinary application sandboxes and from some more restricted processes. A native client opens and maps the device, then exchanges `BC_*` commands and replies with the `BINDER_WRITE_READ` ioctl. This makes transaction parsing, object translation and object lifetime management part of the Android kernel attack surface.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c int fd = open("/dev/binder", O_RDWR); void *map = mmap(NULL, 4096, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0); struct binder_write_read bwr = { .write_size = write_len, .write_buffer = (uintptr_t)write_buf, .read_size = read_len, .read_buffer = (uintptr_t)read_buf, }; ioctl(fd, BINDER_WRITE_READ, &bwr); ``` The following chain abstracts the exploitation of a Binder transaction-cleanup flaw on Android GKI 5.4 and 5.10. Structure sizes, member offsets, cache configuration and allocator behavior are build-specific. Recover them from the exact kernel image instead of copying the example values.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Binder objects and lifetime state (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Binder objects and lifetime state The transaction data buffer can contain Node (`BINDER_TYPE_BINDER`), Ref/handle, pointer, file-descriptor and file-descriptor-array objects. The accompanying offsets array tells the driver where each object starts. A userspace Node is represented internally by `struct binder_node`; when another process receives it, that process gets a `struct binder_ref` handle to the same Node.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Four counters are especially useful while auditing Node lifetime:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `local_strong_refs` and `local_weak_refs` account for Node references held by transactions. - `internal_strong_refs` accounts for Refs held by other Binder clients. - `tmp_refs` protects a Node while kernel code temporarily holds its pointer. - `binder_buffer->target_node` keeps the destination Node reachable while an incoming transaction is pending. Temporary Node access must end at `binder_dec_node_tmpref()`. A pointer used after this decrement is no longer protected from concurrent destruction.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c struct binder_node *node = ...; binder_inc_node_tmpref(node); /* safely access node */ binder_dec_node_tmpref(node); /* node must not be dereferenced here */ ```

title: HT: Cleanup-boundary confusion to `binder_node` UAF (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Cleanup-boundary confusion to `binder_node` UAF Transaction processing walks every entry in the offsets array and translates the corresponding Binder object. On the vulnerable path, an unaligned `offsets_size` jumps to `err_bad_offset` before this loop, leaving `buffer_offset == 0`. Cleanup receives this zero as `failed_at`, but interprets zero as "release the whole object range" rather than "no objects were processed." It therefore reverses side effects that never occurred.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ```c if (!IS_ALIGNED(tr->offsets_size, sizeof(binder_size_t))) goto err_bad_offset; /* translation loop was never entered */ binder_transaction_buffer_release(target_proc, NULL, t->buffer, buffer_offset, true); ``` A useful trigger places multiple `BINDER_TYPE_BINDER` objects for the same Node in the malformed transaction. Cleanup looks up that Node and repeatedly calls `binder_dec_node(..., strong=1, internal=0)`, which decrements `local_strong_refs`. Prepare the Node so the only legitimate strong reference belongs to a pending target transaction: create a Node/Ref pair, send a transaction to that handle, then close the peer Binder FD to drop the Ref. The malformed cleanup can now free the Node while the pending `binder_buffer->target_node` still points to it.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The important root-cause pattern is broader than this CVE: an error-unwind API uses a sentinel value both for "nothing completed" and "process everything." When object translation mutates reference counts, file tables or mapped buffers, every failure edge must carry an unambiguous count or end offset for the successfully processed prefix.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> ### Single-object trigger while retaining the client handle An alternative to clo

title: HT: Primitive ladder (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Primitive ladder The demonstrated exploit develops the dangling `target_node` through this sequence:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text malformed offsets_size -> binder_node UAF binder_thread_read -> 16-byte slab disclosure fake binder_node -> constrained hlist unlink write cross-cache epitem -> struct file leak epoll + FIGETBSZ -> 4-byte arbitrary kernel read seq_file pointer pivot -> arbitrary kernel write cred / policy changes -> sandbox escape and root ``` ### UAF disclosure and victim-address recovery When the receiver reads the pending transaction, `binder_thread_read()` follows the dangling `target_node` and copies `node->ptr` and `node->cookie` into the userspace transaction reply. In the analyzed build, `binder_node` came from `kmalloc-128` and these fields occupied offsets 88 and 96, providing a 16-byte read from the reallocated slot.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The same cache and offset alignment can disclose the freed Node address itself. Reallocate the slot as a `binder_ref`; its `node` pointer was also at offset 88. Reading the dangling transaction then returns that pointer. Verify both layouts on the target kernel with GDB rather than assuming these offsets:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text (gdb) ptype /o struct binder_node (gdb) ptype /o struct binder_ref (gdb) ptype /o struct epitem ``` ### Fake-Node unlink write Reclaim the freed slot with attacker-controlled data, for example with a `sendmsg()` ancillary-data spray, and shape it as a dead `binder_node`. The fake object needs zero `proc`, counters, flags and `refs`, while `work.entry` must be self-referential so `list_empty()` succeeds. The address disclosure supplies the required self-pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text proc = 0 has_strong_ref = has_weak_ref = 0 local_strong_refs =

title: HT: Cross-cache replacement on SLUB (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Cross-cache replacement on SLUB Direct replacement stops working when the victim and target types belong to separate caches. On the analyzed 5.10 kernel, `binder_node` used `kmalloc-128`, while `struct epitem` used the separately accounted `eventpoll_epi` cache. Both caches nevertheless obtained order-0 pages from the buddy allocator, so a fully freed victim slab page could later become an `eventpoll_epi` slab page.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The demonstrated grooming sequence was:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Fill victim slabs with 32 128-byte `binder_node` objects per 4096-byte page. 2. Free all Nodes through the cleanup flaw while retaining dangling transaction pointers. 3. Exceed the `kmalloc-128` partial-list threshold. Because the affected SLUB accounting tracked partial slabs instead of free objects, the exploit used `36 * 32` Nodes to get beyond `cpu_partial == 30`. 4. Allocate more than 32 `epitem` objects to consume existing `eventpoll_epi` partial slots and request returned pages from the buddy allocator. 5. Probe each dangling Node. Kernel-looking values at offsets 88 and 96 indicate that `epitem.fllink` now overlaps the disclosure window; one list pointer leads to the associated `struct file`. This is not a portable allocation formula. Confirm object size, slab order, CPU partial behavior, memcg flags and allocator hardening for the target build.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Keep Binder metadata out of the victim slab Binder also allocates `struct binder_buffer` metadata from `kmalloc-128`, and that object contains the dangling `target_node` required later. Prevent it from contaminating a Node-only slab by shaping Binder's separate best-fit transaction-buffer allocator. Send transactions of different sizes and selectively release them so later r

title: HT: Turning the unlink into reads and unrestricted writes (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Turning the unlink into reads and unrestricted writes ### `epitem` plus `FIGETBSZ` read Use the constrained unlink to replace a controlled file's inode pointer with the known address of an `epitem`. In the demonstrated layout, attacker-controlled `epitem.event.data` at offset 40 overlapped the fake inode's `i_sb` field. Set `event.data` with `epoll_ctl()` to `read_address - offsetof(struct super_block, s_blocksize)`, then invoke `FIGETBSZ`; the VFS path returns the four-byte `inode->i_sb->s_blocksize` value to userspace.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c ev.data.u64 = chosen_super_block_pointer; epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, watched_fd, &ev); ioctl(victim_fd, FIGETBSZ, &value); /* four-byte read */ ``` The UAF disclosure makes this usable without guessing heap addresses: when `epitem` overlays the Node, its `fllink.next` and `fllink.prev` occupy the same 88/96 window and connect to `file->f_ep_links`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### `seq_file->buf` pointer pivot A reusable upgrade from "write NULL or a kernel pointer" to write-what-where uses two `/proc/self/comm` descriptors. Each open allocates a `seq_file`. First use the unlink primitive to make `seq_file_A->buf` point at the address of `seq_file_B->buf`. `comm_show()` copies the current task name to the first buffer, so an eight-byte address encoded with `prctl(PR_SET_NAME)` and a read-position change on descriptor A replace B's buffer pointer. Setting a new task name and triggering B then writes controlled bytes to that address.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c prctl(PR_SET_NAME, encoded_target_address, 0, 0, 0); lseek(comm_fd_a, 1, SEEK_SET); /* target address -> seq_file_B->buf */ prctl(PR_SET_NAME, controlled_bytes, 0, 0, 0); lseek(comm_fd_b, 1, SEEK_SET); /* controlled write to target */ ```

title: HT: Android endgame and patch verification (android-binder-transaction-cleanup-uaf)
text: ## Android endgame and patch verification Once arbitrary reads are stable, Binder provides a short path to the current process: `binder_node->proc->tsk->cred`. The demonstrated chain zeroed the credential ID fields, disabled SELinux enforcement and altered the task's seccomp state to escape the originating application sandbox. Every field and symbol is version-specific, and modern devices may protect these targets with additional mechanisms.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> CVE-2023-20938 was first addressed in the February 2023 bulletin, but the cleanup ambiguity remained reachable through another path and became CVE-2023-21255. The complete fix calculates the cleanup boundary explicitly before calling the release routine instead of overloading a zero `failed_at` value. When auditing vendor kernels, check for commit `1ca1130ec62da7638497478539c0f55ffbbf9a5e` or the corresponding backport; do not rely only on the presence of the earlier transaction-copying patch.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Linux USB Audio Descriptor OOB Reads to KASLR Leaks (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: # Linux USB Audio Descriptor OOB Reads to KASLR Leaks {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} A programmable USB peripheral can exploit a host-side descriptor parser without any userland foothold. The useful pattern is to shape kernel allocations through normal device enumeration, make a malformed descriptor walk into an adjacent object, and turn the host's subsequent USB requests into an information-disclosure channel. NCC Group demonstrated this pattern against a Linux-based vehicle IVI using CVE-2024-53150 and multiple coordinated USB devices.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> This is an **address-disclosure stage**, not a complete compromise: a leaked code pointer can remove KASLR uncertainty for a separate corruption primitive, while a heap pointer only reveals heap layout unless it can be related to the randomized kernel image.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Descriptor-length bug (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: ## Descriptor-length bug The affected ALSA USB-audio traversal in `sound/usb/clock.c` searched UAC2/UAC3 clock source, selector, and multiplier descriptors without first proving that each descriptor's `bLength` covered every field later accessed. Clock selectors are especially important because their variable-length `baCSourceID[]` array contains `bNrInPins` entries followed by protocol-specific tail fields. A short descriptor with a large attacker-controlled pin count therefore made `__uac_clock_find_source()` consume bytes beyond the declared descriptor as additional clock entity IDs.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The demonstrated parser path required a sufficiently valid UAC2/UAC3 topology—audio descriptors including input/output terminals, an AS header, and a format descriptor—before the malformed clock selector was reached.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Turning traversal into a selector-ID oracle (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: ## Turning traversal into a selector-ID oracle The peripheral does not receive an unrestricted raw memory dump. Instead, attacker-supplied clock selectors form a **lookup table**: when an out-of-bounds byte equals the entity ID of one of those selectors, the host finds that entity and emits a USB control request for it. The malicious device observes the requested selector ID in its control-request callback, converting descriptor traversal into a conditional byte-disclosure oracle.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> A practical extraction workflow is:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> 1. Populate the descriptor buffer with clock selectors whose IDs cover the candidate byte values. The number that fits depends on the `kmalloc` cache selected for that descriptor allocation. 2. Put the malformed selector last and set `bNrInPins` to `255`; its position controls how far the source-ID walk extends beyond the valid buffer. 3. Reserve an uninteresting selector ID as padding so the out-of-bounds window stays small. If all candidates do not fit, partition the ID range and repeat against stable adjacent data. 4. Record the IDs observed in host control requests. A selector is not requested more than once in one traversal, so this first pass yields a set and repeated bytes remain ambiguous. 5. Repeat using only the observed IDs. The resulting requests follow traversal order, allowing the bytes in the leak window to be ordered. Infer fixed/aligned bytes where possible to reduce collisions and duplicate-value ambiguity. This oracle is more constrained than an arbitrary read: reliability depends on a stable adjacent object, candidate coverage, non-repeating bytes, and the ability to replay enumeration without changing the target value.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: USB-only kernel heap grooming (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: ## USB-only kernel heap grooming Physical peripheral attacks cannot assume access to local spray interfaces such as `ioctl()`. Instead, enumerate devices whose drivers create many objects in the **same slab cache** as the vulnerable descriptor buffer; the public demonstration targeted `kmalloc-512`. Useful sprayers either allocate repeatedly inside a USB driver path or store attacker-sized descriptor data in a large kernel allocation. For a KASLR leak, seek a sprayed object whose first field is a kernel function pointer so it begins immediately after the vulnerable chunk.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> The physical grooming loop is:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> 1. Attach several sprayer devices through hubs to fill the target cache. 2. Attach one or more malicious USB-audio devices so a vulnerable chunk may land immediately before a sprayed pointer-bearing object. 3. Trigger the selector oracle and validate whether the expected pointer bytes appeared. 4. If adjacency failed, programmatically detach the devices and retry with a different sprayer/leaker ratio. Because connection order, driver lifetime, and hub capacity affect allocation order, separate devices are useful for **spray**, **trigger**, and **exfiltration** roles. NCC Group's DUET design coordinates Raspberry Pi Pico boards using TinyUSB, a Python/C manager, Wi-Fi control, physical hubs, programmable insertion/removal, and a bidirectional channel for control-request results. The published material describes the framework architecture but does not provide a public source repository or directly runnable exploit.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: From pointer disclosure to KASLR bypass (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: ## From pointer disclosure to KASLR bypass Once the reconstructed value is a pointer into a known kernel code object, calculate the runtime base from the corresponding link-time symbol in the **exact target build**: ```text runtime_kernel_base = leaked_pointer - (symbol_link_address - vmlinux_link_base) ``` Validate candidates using expected canonical address bits, alignment, and nearby known bytes before consuming the result in a later exploit stage. A disclosed slab address is still valuable for heap-layout work, but it is not by itself proof of the kernel text base. The demonstrated chain stopped at the information-disclosure/KASLR primitive and did not establish a kernel write, control-flow hijack, or code execution.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Patch and audit points (usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak)
text: ## Patch and audit points The upstream repair adds minimum-length checks to source and multiplier descriptors. For selectors, it also verifies the variable array and tail: `sizeof(selector) + bNrInPins + 4 + 2` for UAC3, or `sizeof(selector) + bNrInPins + 1 + 1` for UAC2. Invalid short descriptors are skipped rather than cast and traversed.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c if (!DESC_LENGTH_CHECK(cs, proto)) return false; if (GET_VAL(cs, proto, bClockID) != id) return false; if (proto == UAC_VERSION_3) return cs->v3.bLength >= sizeof(cs->v3) + cs->v3.bNrInPins + 4 + 2; return cs->v2.bLength >= sizeof(cs->v2) + cs->v2.bNrInPins + 1 + 1; ``` When auditing an embedded image, check whether `CONFIG_SND_USB_AUDIO` is enabled and verify that its vendor kernel contains upstream commit `a3dd4d63eeb4` or an equivalent backport; a nominal kernel version alone is insufficient because embedded trees frequently carry selective fixes.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Overwriting a freed chunk (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: # Overwriting a freed chunk {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Several heap exploitation techniques require being able to **modify metadata that glibc stored inside a chunk after it was freed**. This page summarises the main bug classes that give that primitive and what is usually worth corrupting afterwards.

title: HT: What changes when a chunk becomes free (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: ## What changes when a chunk becomes free After `free()`, the user data of the chunk is often reused by the allocator itself: - **Tcache / fastbin** chunks reuse the first qwords as singly linked list metadata: - `next` / `fd`: next free chunk in the list - `key` in tcache: double-free detection field - **Unsorted / small / large bin** chunks store doubly linked list pointers: - `fd` / `bk` - for large bins, also `fd_nextsize` / `bk_nextsize` - The chunk header (`size`, flags such as `prev_inuse`) also becomes a target if the bug lets you reach it. Therefore, “writing into a freed chunk” is usually not interesting because of its old application data, but because it lets you corrupt the allocator metadata that will be consumed later by `malloc()` / `free()`.

title: HT: High-value targets inside a freed chunk (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: ## High-value targets inside a freed chunk - **Tcache `next` / fastbin `fd`** --> classic [Tcache Bin Attack](tcache-bin-attack.md) / fastbin poisoning primitive. - **Tcache `key`** --> useful to bypass or interfere with tcache double-free checks; on older glibc it was also directly useful to reach `tcache_perthread_struct`. - **Small-bin / unsorted-bin `bk`** --> useful when the exploitation path relies on unlinking or on moving small-bin chunks into tcache (for example, tcache stashing unlink style attacks). - **Large-bin `bk_nextsize` / `fd_nextsize`** --> follow-up primitive for [Large Bin Attack](large-bin-attack.md). - **Chunk `size` / `prev_size` / `prev_inuse`** --> overlap/consolidation primitive that often becomes a second-stage write into a freed chunk.

title: HT: Common bug classes that give this primitive (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: ## Common bug classes that give this primitive ### Simple Use After Free If it's possible for the attacker to **write into a chunk after it has been freed**, the primitive is usually direct: free a chunk, keep the dangling pointer, and edit the allocator metadata now living there. This is especially strong with tcache-sized chunks because the first 16 bytes become the equivalent of: ```c struct tcache_entry { struct tcache_entry *next; uintptr_t key; }; ``` That means a plain edit-after-free can immediately become: - **Arbitrary allocation** by corrupting `next` - **Double-free check bypass / metadata abuse** by corrupting `key` - **Heap leak recovery** by reading back mangled pointers from the freed entry before rewriting them Version notes: - **glibc 2.32+** added **safe-linking**, so a forged `next` / `fd` usually needs a heap leak or another bypass before `malloc()` will accept it. - **glibc 2.29 - 2.33** exposed a particularly strong target in the tcache `key` field because it pointed to `tcache_perthread_struct` (House of IO style abuse). - **glibc 2.34+** changed that behaviour, so modern UAF chains more commonly pivot to **House of Water / metadata control**, leak-and-poison, or application-specific overwrites instead of relying on the old tcache-key trick.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> A very common modern sequence is actually **read-after-free first, write-after-free second**: 1. Free a tcache chunk and read back the first qword. 2. Recover heap bits or fully decode the protected pointer. 3. Re-encode the real target and only then poison the freelist. For a tcache entry, the stored forward pointer is protected with the address where it is stored: ```c stored_next = target ^ (((size_t) &entry->next) >> 12); ``` Therefore, a freed-chunk **read** is often just as

title: HT: Practical modern notes (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: ## Practical modern notes - On **safe-linked** targets, “I can write into a freed tcache chunk” is no longer the same as “I immediately have arbitrary allocation”. First verify whether you can also **leak the heap**, **decode a protected pointer**, or pivot into **tcache metadata** instead of forging a raw `next`. - If the freed chunk is in **small/unsorted/large bins** instead of tcache, the best follow-up is often **not** classic tcache poisoning but abusing the doubly linked metadata on the next allocator transition. - Some recent techniques specifically avoid forging protected freelist pointers and instead aim for **metadata corruption** (`tcache_perthread_struct`, bin counters, stashing paths, large-bin side pointers). - On recent glibc, do not blindly assume that “large chunk == unsorted/small/large bin”: raising `glibc.malloc.tcache_max` can keep much larger frees inside tcache, so always inspect the real runtime state while developing the exploit.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Quick triage on modern glibc (overwriting-a-freed-chunk)
text: ## Quick triage on modern glibc When you confirm that you can overwrite a freed chunk, answer these first: - **Did the free really land in tcache?** On recent glibc, `glibc.malloc.tcache_max` can be raised far beyond the old default ceiling, so a chunk you expected to hit the unsorted path may still be cached.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> - **Can you read the freed bytes before rewriting them?** If yes, leak first; the stored tcache/fastbin pointer is often the cleanest path to a heap base or to a valid safe-linked poison value. - **Do you only control a low byte or two?** Then `size` / `prev_inuse` / `bk` corruption is often a better route than trying to forge a whole protected `next` immediately. - **Can you reach allocator metadata instead of one freelist node?** Recent chains such as **House of Water**, **safe-link double protect**, or **tcache stashing unlink** are frequently stronger than single-entry poisoning because they pivot into `tcache_perthread_struct` or make glibc consume an already-manipulated pointer through a different path.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> For local research, it is often useful to force the allocator down the classic paths to understand what your primitive is really touching: ```bash GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0 ./vuln GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_max=1032 ./vuln ``` That does **not** describe the remote target by itself, but it is a very practical way to distinguish “my bug corrupts a tcache entry” from “my bug is only useful once the chunk reaches unsorted/small/large bins”.

title: HT: Basic Information <sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> (off-by-one-overflow)
text: ## Basic Information <sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> Even a one-byte overflow may let an attacker modify the next chunk's `size` field. This can change which ranges the allocator treats as free and may create an overlapping chunk that contains another legitimate allocation. Exploitation then resembles a [double free](double-free.md) or another overlapping-chunk attack. There are two common types of off-by-one vulnerability: - **Arbitrary byte:** the overflowing byte can take any value. - **Null byte (off-by-null):** the overflowing byte can only be `0x00`. - A common example appears when inconsistent `strlen` and `strcpy` bounds allow a null terminator to overwrite the first byte of the next chunk. - This can be exploited with the [House of Einherjar](house-of-einherjar.md). - If using Tcache, this can be leveraged to a [double free](double-free.md) situation. <details> <summary>Off-by-null</summary> ```c // From https://ctf-wiki.mahaloz.re/pwn/linux/glibc-heap/off_by_one/ int main(void) { char buffer[40]=""; void *chunk1; chunk1 = malloc(24); puts("Get Input"); gets(buffer); if(strlen(buffer)==24) { strcpy(chunk1,buffer); } return 0; } ``` </details> Among other checks, modern glibc compares the recorded previous size with the preceding chunk when consolidating. This makes the classic attack substantially harder starting with glibc 2.28. ### Code example <sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> - [https://github.com/DhavalKapil/heap-exploitation/blob/d778318b6a14edad18b20421f5a06fa1a6e6920e/assets/files/shrinking_free_chunks.c](https://github.com/DhavalKapil/heap-exploitation/blob/d778318b6a14edad18b20421f5a06fa1a6e6920e/assets/files/shrinking_free_chunks.c) - The original shrinking-free-chunks example targets an older allocator and is not directly portable to tcache-era glibc. - M

title: HT: Basic Information (large-bin-attack)
text: ## Basic Information For more information about what is a large bin check this page: {{#ref}} bins-and-memory-allocations.md {{#endref}} The how2heap glibc 2.35 PoC provides a concrete large-bin attack example.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The glibc 2.35 how2heap example demonstrates a remaining write through a corrupted **`p->bk_nextsize`** during sorted large-bin insertion. glibc 2.35 is the version of that PoC, not the current glibc release, and the primitive must be matched to the target allocator.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> In that example you can find the following conditions:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - A large chunk is allocated - A large chunk smaller than the first one but in the same index is allocated - It must be smaller so that sorted insertion places it before the first chunk. - (A chunk to prevent merging with the top chunk is created) - The first large chunk is freed, then a request larger than it moves chunk 1 from the unsorted bin into the large bin. - Then, the second large chunk is freed - Now, the vulnerability: The attacker can modify `chunk1->bk_nextsize` to `[target-0x20]` - Then, a larger chunk than chunk 2 is allocated, so chunk2 is inserted in the large bin overwriting the address `chunk1->bk_nextsize->fd_nextsize` with the address of chunk2 > [!TIP] > Other layouts are possible. The essential condition is insertion of a chunk smaller than an existing chunk `X`, causing it to be linked immediately before `X`, while the attacker controls `X->bk_nextsize` so the insertion write targets a chosen address. title: HT: Basic Information (unlink-attack)
text:
## Basic Information Historically, this attack used to give a very strong WWW (Write-What-Where) primitive. Modern glibc added integrity checks, so the technique is no longer the old "write-anything-anywhere by corrupting `fd`/`bk`" bug class. However, **unsafe unlink is still relevant** as a way to obtain a **relative pointer overwrite**, create **overlapping chunks**, or pivot a pointer table into a more useful primitive. ### Code Example: <details> <summary>Code</summary> ```c #include <unistd.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <string.h> #include <stdio.h> // Altered from https://github.com/DhavalKapil/heap-exploitation/tree/d778318b6a14edad18b20421f5a06fa1a6e6920e/assets/files/unlink_exploit.c to make it work struct chunk_structure { size_t prev_size; size_t size; struct chunk_structure *fd; struct chunk_structure *bk; char buf[10]; // padding }; int main() { unsigned long long *chunk1, *chunk2; struct chunk_structure *fake_chunk, *chunk2_hdr; char data[20]; // First grab two chunks (non fast) chunk1 = malloc(0x8000); chunk2 = malloc(0x8000); printf("Stack pointer to chunk1: %p

title: HT: House of Einherjar (house-of-einherjar)
text: # House of Einherjar {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (house-of-einherjar)
text: ## Basic Information For the generic single-byte overflow background, check [Off-by-one overflow](off-by-one-overflow.md). The important part here is that **House of Einherjar turns an off-by-null into a backward-consolidation primitive**, which then gives **overlapping chunks**. The overlap is usually only the first stage; on modern glibc the follow-up is commonly a [Tcache Bin Attack](tcache-bin-attack.md) or another metadata-corruption primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Code - Updated how2heap PoC (still present in current branches such as `glibc_2.39` / `glibc_2.42`): [https://github.com/shellphish/how2heap/blob/master/glibc_2.42/house_of_einherjar.c](https://github.com/shellphish/how2heap/blob/master/glibc_2.42/house_of_einherjar.c)<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Older but still useful walkthrough: [https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/42-house_of_einherjar/house_einherjar_exp/index.html#house-of-einherjar-explanation](https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/42-house_of_einherjar/house_einherjar_exp/index.html#house-of-einherjar-explanation)<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ### Goal<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> - The practical goal is to make `free()` **consolidate backward into an attacker-controlled fake chunk**, so a later `malloc()` returns memory that **overlaps another still-interesting chunk**. - In old explanations this is often described as “allocate memory in an almost arbitrary address”, but on modern glibc the most common outcome is first **an overlap primitive**, and only then an **arbitrary allocation / write** by corrupting freed-chunk metadata inside that overlap. ### Requirements<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> - A **fake chunk** where we want the new free region to start: - Put it in the **same heap arena**

title: HT: Modern glibc notes (house-of-einherjar)
text: ## Modern glibc notes - The technique is **not just historical**: the how2heap PoC still exists in modern branches such as `glibc_2.39` and `glibc_2.42`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - The classic modern layout is slightly different from older writeups: - instead of relying on the old small-bin style flow, - it is common to **fill tcache first** and make the victim reach the **unsorted-bin consolidation path**. - On **glibc 2.32+**, if you finish with tcache poisoning, remember that **safe-linking** protects the singly linked freelist pointer:<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> ```c encoded_fd = target ^ (address_of_fd_field >> 12) ``` The XOR key uses the address where the protected pointer is stored. For a tcache entry this is normally the freed chunk's user pointer, not its chunk-header address. Using the header address can silently produce the wrong key when the two addresses cross a page boundary. Therefore the overlap by itself is not enough anymore; you usually need a **heap leak** and a **16-byte aligned target** for the next `malloc()` to accept the forged pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> - On **glibc 2.34+**, the old `__malloc_hook` / `__free_hook` finish is no longer the default assumption. A modern House of Einherjar chain usually targets: - an application object, - `tcache_perthread_struct` metadata, - a leak-to-stack path (for example, then pivoting to a return address), or - an FSOP-oriented writable structure. - On **glibc 2.42+**, `tcache` can optionally cache much larger chunks if `glibc.malloc.tcache_max` is raised. If a lab or target unexpectedly keeps your victim in tcache, **fill/disable tcache first** before assuming the unsorted-bin path will be reached.

title: HT: Reliable local reproduction (house-of-einherjar)
text: ## Reliable local reproduction The default tcache count is 7, but it is tunable. Do not hard-code that value when analyzing an unknown target. In a controlled lab, disabling tcache makes it easier to confirm the backward-consolidation stage by itself:<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> ```bash GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0 ./einherjar_overlap_only ``` Use that setting with a harness that stops after creating the overlap. The complete how2heap example later performs tcache poisoning, so disabling tcache for the complete example would break that follow-up stage. This is a debugging aid, not an exploit assumption. For the real target, inspect its glibc build and environment. If tcache is enabled, fill the victim's exact size class up to its configured count before `free(C)`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Practical checks while debugging (house-of-einherjar)
text: ## Practical checks while debugging - `corrupted size vs. prev_size while consolidating` - Your forged `prev_size` does not exactly match `chunksize(A)`, or `C_header - C->prev_size` does not land on the fake chunk.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> - `corrupted double-linked list` - The fake chunk failed the safe-unlink relations. Recheck `A->fd->bk` and `A->bk->fd` at the instant `free(C)` runs.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> - `double free or corruption (!prev)` - The chunk after `C` does not mark `C` as in use. Check the guard chunk and verify that the null byte hit `C->size`, not the following header.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup> - No overlap after `free(C)` - The victim chunk probably stayed in **tcache** instead of reaching consolidation, or it merged with the **top chunk** instead of your fake chunk. - `malloc(): unaligned tcache chunk detected` in the follow-up stage - The House of Einherjar overlap worked, but your later **safe-linked `fd`** is wrong or the target address is not aligned.
