title: HT: Basic Information (heap-overflow)
text: ## Basic Information A heap overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a heap-allocated buffer than the allocation can hold.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> It is analogous to a [**stack overflow**](../stack-overflow/index.html), but the corrupted data is in the heap. In a stack overflow, saved control data such as a return address may be near the vulnerable buffer. A heap buffer has no single equivalent layout: the overflow may corrupt allocator metadata, application data, object pointers, or function pointers. Therefore, the impact depends on **what is adjacent to the vulnerable allocation**, how reliably the attacker can shape that layout, and how the corrupted data is later used.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> > [!TIP] > In order to find overflow offsets you can use the same patterns as in [**stack overflows**](../stack-overflow/index.html#finding-stack-overflows-offsets). ### Stack Overflows vs Heap Overflows In stack overflows, the layout and data present when the vulnerability is triggered are often relatively predictable. A function's stack frame commonly has a repeatable structure containing local variables and saved control data. Heap allocations, by contrast, are placed and reused according to allocator policies such as size classes, bins, zones, and freelists. The object adjacent to a vulnerable allocation can therefore be difficult to predict. Exploitation usually requires a **reliable way to place a useful victim object immediately after the overflowing buffer**. One technique for controlling this layout is **heap grooming**. The cited iOS kernel example explains that when a zone ran out of space for objects of a particular size, it expanded by a kernel page and split that page into suitable chunks. Those chunks were allocated in order on the older vers

title: HT: Large fake chunks with tuned tcache (glibc 2.42+) (house-of-spirit)
text: ## Large fake chunks with tuned tcache (glibc 2.42+) glibc 2.42 added optional large tcache bins, but caching above the traditional small-tcache limit remains disabled by default. Check whether the process raises `glibc.malloc.tcache_max`; a local test can opt in with `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_max=2048 ./binary`.<sup>[[8]](#references)[[9]](#references)</sup> With this setting, a controlled, 16-byte-aligned `0x510`-byte region can carry a `0x511` size header. Passing `region + 0x10` to `free()` then queues it for a later `malloc(0x500)`, provided that bin has a free slot and the region is writable through the tcache `next` and `key` fields. No second fake chunk is needed on this path.<sup>[[9]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> Use the **normalized chunk size**, not just the broad large-tcache bin, to plan the reclaiming request: glibc 2.43 requires an exact size match when allocating from a large tcache bin.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup> If the bin is full, disabled, or the tunable remains at its default, `free()` proceeds to the normal arena checks instead of providing this overlap.<sup>[[9]](#references)[[10]](#references)</sup> See [tcache bin attacks](tcache-bin-attack.md) for the distinct case where a freed entry's `next` pointer is corrupted after insertion.

title: HT: Fixed-address input buffers as fake chunks (house-of-spirit)
text: ## Fixed-address input buffers as fake chunks A House-of-Spirit target does not need to begin as allocator-managed memory. A reusable input buffer at a **predictable writable address** can hold valid fake chunk metadata. If an arbitrary `free()` accepts that address, a later size-matched allocation can turn the buffer into a live application object.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> The important extra primitive is a second write path that continues to use the **same backing address** after the allocator has returned it as an object. In the Canon example, closing and reopening a BJNP session caused new client data to be copied to the fixed BJNP buffer again. The copy could therefore replace a function pointer in the object that had reclaimed that buffer. Earlier research on this printer family also documents BJNP session data at a firmware-specific fixed address.<sup>[[6]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> The complete pattern is:<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> 1. Place allocator-compatible fake metadata in one fixed-address input buffer. If direct code execution is planned, stage the control-flow payload separately and first confirm that its memory permissions allow execution. 2. Redirect a pointer passed to `free()` to the fake chunk. The fake size must match a reliable later allocation. 3. Let that allocation reclaim the input buffer as a legitimate object. An allocation made automatically on the vulnerable path is usually more reliable than trying to force unrelated allocator activity. 4. Reset the input session and confirm that the producer writes to the original address rather than allocating a new buffer. The new input now overwrites fields in the live object, such as a function pointer. For the initial bug-to-primitive analysis, fuzz length fields with recognizable

title: HT: Heap Basics (README)
text: ## Heap Basics The heap is basically the place where a program is going to be able to store data when it requests data calling functions like **`malloc`**, `calloc`... Moreover, when this memory is no longer needed it's made available calling the function **`free`**. As it's shown, its just after where the binary is being loaded in memory (check the `[heap]` section): ### Basic Chunk Allocation When some data is requested to be stored in the heap, some space of the heap is allocated to it. This space will belong to a bin and only the requested data + the space of the bin headers + minimum bin size offset will be reserved for the chunk. The goal is to just reserve as minimum memory as possible without making it complicated to find where each chunk is. For this, the metadata chunk information is used to know where each used/free chunk is. The allocator can reserve space in different ways depending on the bin in use, but the general process is:[[1]](#references) - The program starts by requesting certain amount of memory. - If in the list of chunks there someone available big enough to fulfil the request, it'll be used - This might even mean that part of the available chunk will be used for this request and the rest will be added to the chunks list - If there isn't any available chunk in the list but there is still space in allocated heap memory, the heap manager creates a new chunk - If there is not enough heap space to allocate the new chunk, the heap manager asks the kernel to expand the memory allocated to the heap and then use this memory to generate the new chunk - If everything fails, `malloc` returns null. Note that if the requested **memory passes a threshold**, *

title: HT: Arenas (README)
text: ## Arenas In **multithreaded** applications, the heap manager must prevent **race conditions** that could lead to crashes. Initially, this was done using a **global mutex** to ensure that only one thread could access the heap at a time, but this caused **performance issues** due to the mutex-induced bottleneck.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> To address this, the ptmalloc2 heap allocator introduced "arenas," where **each arena** acts as a **separate heap** with its **own** data **structures** and **mutex**, allowing multiple threads to perform heap operations without interfering with each other, as long as they use different arenas. The default "main" arena handles heap operations for single-threaded applications. When **new threads** are added, the heap manager assigns them **secondary arenas** to reduce contention. It first attempts to attach each new thread to an unused arena, creating new ones if needed, up to a limit of 2 times the number of CPU cores for 32-bit systems and 8 times for 64-bit systems. Once the limit is reached, **threads must share arenas**, leading to potential contention. Unlike the main arena, which expands using the `brk` system call, secondary arenas create "subheaps" using `mmap` and `mprotect` to simulate the heap behaviour, allowing flexibility in managing memory for multithreaded operations. ### Subheaps Subheaps serve as memory reserves for secondary arenas in multithreaded applications, allowing them to grow and manage their own heap regions separately from the main heap. Here's how subheaps differ from the initial heap and how they operate: 1. **Initial Heap vs. Subheaps**:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - The initial heap is located directly after the program's binary in memory, and it expands using the `sbrk` system call. - Subheaps, used

text:
## Examples ### Quick Heap Example Quick heap example from [https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/25-heap/index.html](https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/25-heap/index.html) but in arm64: ```c #include #include #include void main(void) { char *ptr; ptr = malloc(0x10); strcpy(ptr, "panda"); } ``` Set a breakpoint at the end of the main function and lets find out where the information was stored: It's possible to see that the string panda was stored at `0xaaaaaaac12a0` (which was the address given as response by malloc inside `x0`). Checking 0x10 bytes before it's possible to see that the `0x0` represents that the **previous chunk is not used** (length 0) and that the length of this chunk is `0x21`. The extra spaces reserved (0x21-0x10=0x11) comes from the **added headers** (0x10) and 0x1 doesn't mean that it was reserved 0x21B but the last 3 bits of the length of the current headed have the some special meanings. As the length is always 16-byte aligned (in 64bits machines), these bits are actually never going to be used by the length number. ``` 0x1: Previous in Use - Specifies that the chunk before it in memory is in use 0x2: Is MMAPPED - Specifies that the chunk was obtained with mmap() 0x4: Non Main Arena - Specifies that the chunk was obtained from outside of the main arena ``` ### Multithreading Example
Multithread ```c #include #include #include #include #include void* threadFuncMalloc(void* arg) { printf("Hello from thread 1 "); char* addr = (char*) malloc(1000); printf("After malloc and before free in thread 1 "); free(addr); printf("After free in thread 1 "); } voi

title: HT: musl mallocng exploitation notes (Alpine) (README)
text: ## musl mallocng exploitation notes (Alpine) - **Slab group/slot grooming for huge linear copies:** mallocng sizeclasses use mmap()'d groups whose slots are fully `munmap()`'d when empty. For long linear copies (~0x15555555 bytes), keep the span mapped (avoid holes from released groups) and place the victim allocation adjacent to the source slot.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Cycling offset mitigation:** On slot reuse mallocng may advance the user-data start by `UNIT` (0x10) multiples when slack fits an extra 4-byte header.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> This shifts overwrite offsets (e.g., LSB pointer hits) unless you control reuse counts or stick to strides without slack (e.g., Lua `Table` objects at stride 0x50 show offset 0). Inspect offsets with muslheap’s `mchunkinfo`<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup>: ```gdb pwndbg> mchunkinfo 0x7ffff7a94e40 ... stride: 0x140 ... cycling offset : 0x1 (userdata --> 0x7ffff7a94e40) ``` - **Prefer runtime-object corruption over allocator metadata:** mallocng mixes cookies/guarded out-of-band metadata, so target higher-level objects. In Redis’s Lua 5.1, `Table->array` points to an array of `TValue` tagged values; overwriting the LSB of a pointer in `TValue->value` (e.g., with the JSON terminator byte `0x22`) can pivot references without touching malloc metadata.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Debugging stripped/static Lua on Alpine:** Build a matching Lua, list symbols with `readelf -Ws`, strip function symbols via `objcopy --strip-symbol` to expose struct layouts in GDB, then use Lua-aware pretty-printers (GdbLuaExtension for Lua 5.1) plus muslheap to check stride/reserved/cycling-offset values before triggering the overflow.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Unterminated heap strings to command injection (README)
text: ## Unterminated heap strings to command injection A transformation can write entirely inside its allocation and still create a heap out-of-bounds read: if it omits the final `\0`, consumers such as `%s`, `sprintf()` or `strlen()` continue through uninitialized bytes until another zero byte is found. When the resulting string is interpolated into a command passed to `system()`, bytes left by a previous heap occupant—or, less reliably, bytes in a following allocation—can become shell syntax even though the application escaped the original input.<sup>[[7]](#references)[[8]](#references)</sup> CVE-2026-8037 in Kemp LoadMaster is a useful example. Its quote-escaping routine allocated with `malloc()`, expanded every single quote to the four-byte shell sequence `'\''`, but did not terminate the output. The escaped `apiuser` was then formatted into a `validuser ... -u '%s' ...` command and executed. ZDI attributes the original finding to Syed Ibrahim Ahmed of TrendAI Research; authentication was not required and successful exploitation ran code as root.<sup>[[7]](#references)[[8]](#references)</sup> ### Exploitation workflow 1. **Reach the allocating branch.** Choose input that forces the sanitizer to return a new heap buffer rather than the original string. Also calculate the transform's maximum expansion so the allocation lands in the same size class as attacker-populated chunks.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> 2. **Remove early terminators from reused metadata.** On 64-bit glibc, a freed tcache chunk reuses the first `0x10` bytes of user data for `next` and `key`; these words commonly contain zero bytes. title: HT: GNU obstack function-pointer hijack (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: # GNU obstack function-pointer hijack {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Overview (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Overview GNU obstacks embed allocator state together with allocator callbacks. The following offsets are from the cited **x86-64 glibc 2.42 challenge build** and are not ABI-stable:<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - `temp` is at `+0x28`, followed by the 32-bit `alignment_mask` at `+0x30` and ABI padding. - `chunkfun` is at `+0x38` with stored type `struct _obstack_chunk *(*)(void *, long)`. - `freefun` is at `+0x40` with stored type `void (*)(void *, struct _obstack_chunk *)`. - `extra_arg` is at `+0x48`; the bitfield containing `use_extra_arg` begins at `+0x50` on this build. Confirm all offsets from the target's debug symbols or matching `<obstack.h>` instead of treating them as a stable ABI. `use_extra_arg` selects the legacy one-argument callback ABI or the two-argument ABI. In the latter form, glibc calls `chunkfun(extra_arg, new_size)` and `freefun(extra_arg, old_chunk)`.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> If an attacker can corrupt an application-owned `struct obstack *` or its fields, a checked non-empty grow when `next_free == chunk_limit` calls `_obstack_newchunk` and then indirectly calls `chunkfun`. This converts a data-pointer overwrite into a control-flow primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} ../arbitrary-write-2-exec/README.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: Primitive: size_t desync → 0-byte allocation → pointer OOB write (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Primitive: size_t desync → 0-byte allocation → pointer OOB write A common bug pattern is using a **32-bit register** to compute `sizeof(ptr) * count` while storing the logical length in a 64-bit `size_t`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Example: `elements = obstack_alloc(obs, sizeof(void *) * size);` is compiled as `SHL EAX,0x3` for `size << 3`. - With `size = 0x20000000` and `sizeof(void *) = 8`, the multiplication wraps to `0x0` in 32-bit, so the pointer array is **0 bytes**, but the recorded `size` remains `0x20000000`. - Subsequent `elements[curr++] = ptr;` writes perform **8-byte OOB pointer stores** into adjacent heap objects, giving a controlled cross-object overwrite primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Leaking libc via `obstack.chunkfun` (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Leaking libc via `obstack.chunkfun` 1. Place two heap objects adjacent (e.g., two stacks built with separate obstacks). 2. Use the pointer-array OOB write from object A to overwrite object B’s `elements` pointer so that a `pop`/read from B dereferences an address inside object A’s obstack. 3. Read `chunkfun` (`malloc` by default) at offset `0x38` to disclose a libc function pointer, then compute `libc_base = leak - malloc_offset` and derive other symbols (e.g., `system`, `"/bin/sh"`).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Hijacking `chunkfun` with a fake obstack (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Hijacking `chunkfun` with a fake obstack Overwrite a victim’s stored `struct obstack *` to point at attacker-controlled data that mimics the obstack header. Minimal fields needed:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `next_free == chunk_limit` to force `_obstack_newchunk` on next push - `chunkfun = system_addr` - `extra_arg = binsh_addr`, `use_extra_arg = 1` to select the two-argument call form Triggering growth then invokes the forged callback. In the demonstrated System V x86-64 chain, setting `chunkfun=system`, `extra_arg="/bin/sh"`, and `use_extra_arg=1` places the string pointer in the first argument register; the extra size argument is ignored by `system`. Re-evaluate calling conventions and control-flow protections on other targets.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Example fake obstack layout (glibc 2.42 offsets):<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ```python fake = b"" fake += p64(0x1000) # chunk_size fake += p64(heap_leak) # chunk fake += p64(heap_leak) # object_base fake += p64(heap_leak) # next_free == chunk_limit fake += p64(heap_leak) # chunk_limit fake += p64(0) # temp union fake += p32(0xF) # alignment_mask fake += p32(0) # x86-64 ABI padding fake += p64(system_addr) # chunkfun fake += p64(0) # freefun fake += p64(binsh_addr) # extra_arg fake += p64(1) # use_extra_arg flag set ```

title: HT: Alternative trigger: hijacking `freefun` (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Alternative trigger: hijacking `freefun` A reachable obstack reset/destructor can be a simpler trigger than forcing growth. `__obstack_free` walks `h->chunk` backwards and calls `freefun` for every released chunk. Calling `obstack_free(h, NULL)` selects the out-of-line free path and releases the complete chain.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> 1. Overwrite the real obstack fields, or redirect the application's obstack pointer to a fake header. 2. Set `freefun = system`, `extra_arg = binsh_addr`, and `use_extra_arg = 1`. 3. Keep `chunk` pointing to a readable `_obstack_chunk`. For a fake chunk, set `prev = NULL`; if the callback returns, an invalid `prev` makes the subsequent walk crash. 4. Trigger an application path that executes `obstack_free(obs, NULL)`. The first release dispatches `freefun(extra_arg, chunk)`, which places the command pointer in the first SysV x86-64 argument register. The extra chunk argument is ignored by `system`. This variant does not require `next_free == chunk_limit` or a usable `chunkfun`, but it does require a reachable free/reset path and valid chunk-chain memory until the callback executes.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Attack recipe (gnu-obstack-function-pointer-hijack)
text: ## Attack recipe 1. **Trigger size wrap** to create a 0-byte pointer array with a huge logical length. 2. **Groom adjacency** so an OOB pointer store reaches a neighbor object containing an obstack pointer. 3. **Leak libc** by redirecting a victim pointer to the neighbor obstack’s `chunkfun` and reading the function pointer. 4. **Choose a callback trigger**: forge `chunkfun` and force `_obstack_newchunk`, or forge `freefun` and reach an obstack reset/free path.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: House of Roman (house-of-roman)
text: # House of Roman {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (house-of-roman)
text: ## Basic Information House of Roman is a leakless heap-exploitation technique that combines a fake fastbin chain, an unsorted-bin write, and partial pointer overwrites. The original `__malloc_hook` chain targets old glibc versions; later unsorted-bin integrity checks and hook removal break its assumptions.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[6]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> ### Applicability in 2026 - **glibc window:** The how2heap PoC targets glibc 2.23 and reports tests through 2.25. The technique can be adapted to the early-tcache glibc 2.26–2.27 era only when tcache does not consume the relevant sizes. The unlink-time unsorted-bin check present in glibc 2.28 invalidates the classic write, glibc 2.29 adds broader size/link validation, and glibc 2.34 removed the active malloc hooks. Use the original chain only with a verified old libc or a custom/CTF build that preserves its assumptions.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[6]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> - **Tcache era (2.26–2.27):** Set the tunable when launching the process, not with `setenv()` inside `main()`: `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0 ./target`. Tunables are consumed during process startup and a zero count disables tcache. If the target environment cannot be changed, heap grooming must keep the relevant tcache full before frees intended for fastbins and exhaust cached entries before allocations intended to pop the fastbin; merely freeing seven chunks does not “drain” tcache.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - **Safe-Linking:** Safe-Linking protects fastbin/tcache next pointers in glibc 2.32 and later. Although the classic chain is already stopped by earlier unsorted-bin hardening, any attempted port that corrupts a protected fastbin pointer must produce the correct encoded value for the ad

title: HT: Attack Steps (house-of-roman)
text: ## Attack Steps ### Part 1: Fastbin Chunk points to \_\_malloc_hook Create several chunks as described in the original implementations:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> - `fastbin_victim` (0x60, offset 0): UAF chunk later to edit the heap pointer later to point to the LibC value. - `chunk2` (0x80, offset 0x70): For good alignment - `main_arena_use` (0x80, offset 0x100) - `relative_offset_heap` (0x60, offset 0x190): relative offset on the 'main_arena_use' chunk Then `free(main_arena_use)` which will place this chunk in the unsorted list and will get a pointer to `main_arena + 0x68` in both the `fd` and `bk` pointers. Now it's allocated a new chunk `fake_libc_chunk(0x60)` because it'll contain the pointers to `main_arena + 0x68` in `fd` and `bk`. Then `relative_offset_heap` and `fastbin_victim` are freed. ```c /* Current heap layout: 0x0: fastbin_victim - size 0x70 0x70: alignment_filler - size 0x90 0x100: fake_libc_chunk - size 0x70 (contains a fd ptr to main_arena + 0x68) 0x170: leftover_main - size 0x20 0x190: relative_offset_heap - size 0x70 bin layout: fastbin: fastbin_victim -> relative_offset_heap unsorted: leftover_main */ ``` - `fastbin_victim` has a `fd` pointing to `relative_offset_heap` - `relative_offset_heap` is an offset of distance from `fake_libc_chunk`, which contains a pointer to `main_arena + 0x68` - Changing the last byte of `fastbin_victim.fd` makes `fastbin_victim` point to `main_arena + 0x68`. For the previous actions, the attacker needs to be capable of modifying the fd pointer of `fastbin_victim`. Then, `main_arena + 0x68` is not that interesting, so let's modify it so the pointer points to **`__malloc_hook`**. On the demonstrated amd64 libc builds, choosing `__malloc_hook - 0x23` makes a byte from the nearby `__memalign_hook` point

title: HT: Modern Tips and Variants (house-of-roman)
text: ## Modern Tips and Variants - **Unsorted-bin hardening (2.28+):** The classic primitive corrupts only `victim->bk`, but glibc 2.28 checks `victim->bk->fd == victim` before performing `bck->fd = unsorted_chunks(av)`. Therefore the destination must already contain the victim pointer; satisfying that normally needs an additional write plus knowledge of the victim address, defeating the original leakless/UAF-only assumptions. Glibc 2.29 also validates the victim/next sizes, `next->prev_size`, both list directions, and `next->prev_inuse`.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup> - **The 2023 check cleanup is not a bypass:** glibc removed the later duplicate `bck->fd != victim` test, historically associated with the `corrupted unsorted chunks 3` diagnostic. The same invariant is still enforced by the earlier combined unsorted-list check, so the patch did not restore the House of Roman write primitive.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> - **Hook removal (2.34+):** With `__malloc_hook` gone, a different target and usually a different chain are required. A GOT target such as `exit@GOT` is viable only when RELRO leaves that entry writable. Modern techniques such as House of Pie, which corrupts the allocator's `top` pointer, have their own version-specific prerequisites and are not drop-in replacements.<sup>[[4]](#references)[[6]](#references)</sup> For modern leakless tcache designs, follow the House of Water and safe-link double-protect notes in the [tcache-bin attack page](tcache-bin-attack.md) rather than treating them as House of Roman ports. - **Any‑address fastbin alloc (romanking98 writeup):** The second part shows repairing the 0x71 freelist and using the unsorted‑bin write to land a fastbin allocation over `__free_hook`, then placing `system("/bin/sh")` and triggering it via `free()` on l

title: HT: House of Rabbit (house-of-rabbit)
text: # House of Rabbit {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} > [!CAUTION] > House of Rabbit describes historical glibc allocator behavior. The published PoCs target older allocator layouts; tcache, safe-linking, and newer integrity checks mean the examples are not version-independent. Reproduce them with the matching libc before adapting the primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> ### Requirements 1. **Ability to modify fast bin fd pointer or size**: This means you can change the forward pointer of a chunk in the fastbin or its size. 2. **Ability to trigger `malloc_consolidate`**: This can be done by either allocating a large chunk or merging the top chunk, which forces the heap to consolidate chunks. ### Goals 1. **Create overlapping chunks**: To have one chunk overlap with another, allowing for further heap manipulations. 2. **Forge fake chunks**: To trick the allocator into treating a fake chunk as a legitimate chunk during heap operations.

title: HT: Steps of the attack (house-of-rabbit)
text: ## Steps of the attack ### POC 1: Modify the size of a fast bin chunk **Objective**: Create an overlapping chunk by manipulating the size of a fastbin chunk.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Step 1: Allocate Chunks** ```cpp unsigned long* chunk1 = malloc(0x40); // Allocates a chunk of 0x40 bytes at 0x602000 unsigned long* chunk2 = malloc(0x40); // Allocates another chunk of 0x40 bytes at 0x602050 malloc(0x10); // Allocates a small chunk to change the fastbin state ``` We allocate two chunks of 0x40 bytes each. These chunks will be placed in the fast bin list once freed. - **Step 2: Free Chunks** ```cpp free(chunk1); // Frees the chunk at 0x602000 free(chunk2); // Frees the chunk at 0x602050 ``` We free both chunks, adding them to the fastbin list. - **Step 3: Modify Chunk Size** ```cpp chunk1[-1] = 0xa1; // Modify the size of chunk1 to 0xa1 (stored just before the chunk at chunk1[-1]) ``` We change the size metadata of `chunk1` to 0xa1. This is a crucial step to trick the allocator during consolidation. - **Step 4: Trigger `malloc_consolidate`** ```cpp malloc(0x1000); // Allocate a large chunk to trigger heap consolidation ``` Allocating a large chunk triggers the `malloc_consolidate` function, merging small chunks in the fast bin. The manipulated size of `chunk1` causes it to overlap with `chunk2`. After consolidation, `chunk1` overlaps with `chunk2`, allowing for further exploitation. ### POC 2: Modify the `fd` pointer **Objective**: Create a fake chunk by manipulating the fast bin `fd` pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Step 1: Allocate Chunks** ```cpp unsigned long* chunk1 = malloc(0x40); // Allocates a chunk of 0x40 bytes at 0x602000 unsigned long* chunk2 = malloc(0x100); // Allocates a chunk of 0x100 bytes at 0x602050 ```

title: HT: Bins & Memory Allocations (bins-and-memory-allocations)
text: # Bins & Memory Allocations {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (bins-and-memory-allocations)
text: ## Basic Information In order to improve the efficiency on how chunks are stored every chunk is not just in one linked list, but there are several types. These are the bins and there are 5 type of bins: [62](https://sourceware.org/git/gitweb.cgi?p=glibc.git;a=blob;f=malloc/malloc.c;h=6e766d11bc85b6480fa5c9f2a76559f8acf9deb5;hb=HEAD#l1407) small bins, 63 large bins, 1 unsorted bin, 10 fast bins and 64 tcache bins per thread.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> The initial address to each unsorted, small and large bins is inside the same array. The index 0 is unused, 1 is the unsorted bin, bins 2-64 are small bins and bins 65-127 are large bins.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Tcache (Per-Thread Cache) Bins Even though threads try to have their own heap (see [Arenas](bins-and-memory-allocations.md#arenas) and [Subheaps](bins-and-memory-allocations.md#subheaps)), there is the possibility that a process with a lot of threads (like a web server) **will end sharing the heap with another threads**. In this case, the main solution is the use of **lockers**, which might **slow down significantly the threads**.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> Therefore, a tcache is similar to a fast bin per thread in the way that it's a **single linked list** that doesn't merge chunks. Each thread has **64 singly-linked tcache bins**. Each bin can have a maximum of [7 same-size chunks](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=blob;f=malloc/malloc.c;h=2527e2504761744df2bdb1abdc02d936ff907ad2;hb=d5c3fafc4307c9b7a4c7d5cb381fcdbfad340bcc#l323) ranging from [24 to 1032B on 64-bit systems and 12 to 516B on 32-bit systems](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=blob;f=malloc/malloc.c;h=2527e2504761744df2bdb1abdc02d936ff907ad2;hb=d5c3fafc4307c9b7a4c7d5cb381fcdbfad340bcc#l315).<sup>[[3]](#ref

title: HT: Basic Information (unsorted-bin-attack)
text: ## Basic Information For more information about what is an unsorted bin check this page: {{#ref}} bins-and-memory-allocations.md {{#endref}} Unsorted lists are able to write the address to `unsorted_chunks (av)` in the `bk` address of the chunk. Therefore, if an attacker can **modify the address of the `bk` pointer** in a chunk inside the unsorted bin, he could be able to **write that address in an arbitrary address** which could be helpful to leak a Glibc addresses or bypass some defense. In short, this attack can **write a large pointer value to a chosen address**. The value may be a heap or glibc address. A traditional target was **`global_max_fast`**, which enlarged the accepted fastbin sizes and enabled a follow-on fastbin attack.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - Modern note (glibc ≥ 2.39): `global_max_fast` became an 8‑bit global. Blindly writing a pointer there via an unsorted-bin write will clobber adjacent libc data and will not reliably raise the fastbin limit anymore. Prefer other targets or other primitives when running against glibc 2.39+. See "Modern constraints" below and consider combining with other techniques like a [large bin attack](large-bin-attack.md) or a [fast bin attack](fast-bin-attack.md) once you have a stable primitive. > [!TIP] > In the linked example, changing the chunk requests from `0x400`/`0x500` to `0x4000`/`0x5000` avoids tcache but causes current glibc to report **`malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted`**.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> > > Therefore, this unsorted bin attack now (among other checks) also requires to be able to fix the doubled linked list so this is bypassed `victim->bk->fd == victim` or not `victim->fd == av (arena)`, which means that the address where we want to write must have the address of the fake chunk i

title: HT: Modern constraints (glibc ≥ 2.33) (unsorted-bin-attack)
text: ## Modern constraints (glibc ≥ 2.33) To use unsorted‑bin writes reliably on current glibc: - Tcache interference: for sizes that fall into tcache, frees are diverted there and won’t touch the unsorted bin. Either - make requests with sizes > MAX_TCACHE_SIZE (≥ 0x410 on 64‑bit by default), or - fill the corresponding tcache bin (7 entries) so that additional frees reach the global bins, or - if the environment is controllable, disable tcache (e.g., GLIBC_TUNABLES glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0). - Integrity checks on the unsorted list: on the next allocation path that examines the unsorted bin, glibc checks (simplified): - `bck->fd == victim` and `victim->fd == unsorted_chunks(av)`; otherwise it aborts with `malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted`.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> - This means the address you target must tolerate two writes: first `*(TARGET) = victim` at free‑time; later, as the chunk is removed, `*(TARGET) = unsorted_chunks(av)` (the allocator rewrites `bck->fd` back to the bin head). Choose targets where simply forcing a large non‑zero value is useful. - Typical stable targets in modern exploits - Application or global state that treats "large" values as flags/limits. - Indirect primitives (e.g., set up for a subsequent [fast bin attack]({{#ref}}fast-bin-attack.md{{#endref}}) or to pivot a later write‐what‐where).<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> - Avoid `__malloc_hook`/`__free_hook` on new glibc: they were removed in 2.34. Avoid `global_max_fast` on ≥ 2.39 (see next note). - About `global_max_fast` on recent glibc - On glibc 2.39+, `global_max_fast` is an 8‑bit global. The classic trick of writing a heap pointer into it (to enlarge fastbins) no longer works cleanly and is likely to corrupt adjacent allocator state. Prefer other strategies.<sup>[[5]](#re

title: HT: Minimal exploitation recipe (modern glibc) (unsorted-bin-attack)
text: ## Minimal exploitation recipe (modern glibc) Goal: achieve a single arbitrary write of a heap pointer to an arbitrary address using the unsorted‑bin insertion primitive, without crashing. - Layout/grooming - Allocate A, B, C with sizes large enough to bypass tcache (e.g., 0x5000). C prevents consolidation with the top chunk. - Corruption - Overflow from A into B’s chunk header to set `B->bk = (mchunkptr)(TARGET - 0x10)`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Trigger - `free(B)`. At insertion time the allocator executes `bck->fd = B`, therefore `*(TARGET) = B`. - Continuation - If you plan to continue allocating and the program uses the unsorted bin, expect the allocator to later set `*(TARGET) = unsorted_chunks(av)`. Both values are typically large and may be enough to change size/limit semantics in targets that only check for "big". Pseudocode skeleton: ```c // 64-bit glibc 2.35–2.38 style layout (tcache bypass via large sizes) void *A = malloc(0x5000); void *B = malloc(0x5000); void *C = malloc(0x5000); // guard // overflow from A into B’s metadata (prev_size/size/.../bk). You must control B->bk. *(size_t *)((char*)B - 0x8) = (size_t)(TARGET - 0x10); // write fake bk free(B); // triggers *(TARGET) = B (unsorted-bin insertion write) ``` > [!NOTE] > • If you cannot bypass tcache with size, fill the tcache bin for the chosen size (7 frees) before freeing the corrupted chunk so the free goes to unsorted. > • If the program immediately aborts on the next allocation due to unsorted-bin checks, re‑examine that `victim->fd` still equals the bin head and that your `TARGET` holds the exact `victim` pointer after the first write.

title: HT: Unsorted Bin Infoleak Attack (unsorted-bin-attack)
text: ## Unsorted Bin Infoleak Attack This is actually a very basic concept. The chunks in the unsorted bin are going to have pointers. The first chunk in the unsorted bin will actually have the **`fd`** and the **`bk`** links **pointing to a part of the main arena (Glibc)**.\ Therefore, if you can **put a chunk inside a unsorted bin and read it** (use after free) or **allocate it again without overwriting at least 1 of the pointers** to then **read** it, you can have a **Glibc info leak**. A similar [**attack used in this writeup**](https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/33-custom_misc_heap/csaw18_alienVSsamurai/index.html), was to abuse a 4 chunks structure (A, B, C and D - D is only to prevent consolidation with top chunk) so a null byte overflow in B was used to make C indicate that B was unused. Also, in B the `prev_size` data was modified so the size instead of being the size of B was A+B.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup>\ Then C was deallocated, and consolidated with A+B (but B was still in used). A new chunk of size A was allocated and then the libc leaked addresses was written into B from where they were leaked.<sup>[[7]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Basic Information (double-free)
text:
## Basic Information Freeing the same allocation more than once is undefined behavior and may corrupt allocator state. In glibc, the exact checks and exploitation path depend on the release, bin, chunk size, and mitigations. The classic **fastbin dup** pattern is `free(a); free(b); free(a)`: older/local fastbin checks reject an immediate duplicate at the head, while the intervening chunk can make the second `free(a)` pass that particular check. This is not a universal bypass—tcache has separate duplicate detection, and modern glibc also uses safe-linking for singly linked lists.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> Now, when you ask for new memory (using `malloc`), the allocator might give you a **block that's been freed twice**. This can lead to two different pointers pointing to the same memory location. title: HT: Basic Information (tcache-bin-attack)
text: ## Basic Information For more information about what a Tcache bin is, check this page: {{#ref}} bins-and-memory-allocations.md {{#endref}} The **Tcache attack** (also known as **Tcache poisoning**) is the tcache equivalent of a fast-bin attack: the attacker corrupts the `next` pointer stored in a freed tcache entry so that a later `malloc()` returns an **attacker-chosen address**. If instead you control a pointer passed to `free()` and can place a fake header at its destination, use [House of Spirit](house-of-spirit.md) to insert that address into tcache without poisoning a freed entry. This primitive is only useful if the attacker can first **write into a freed chunk**. Common ways of getting that primitive are explained here: {{#ref}} overwriting-a-freed-chunk.md {{#endref}} Historically, this was introduced together with tcache in **glibc 2.26** and was initially very easy to exploit. Modern glibc added several checks, so the attack is still relevant, but it now depends a lot more on the target version and the primitive you start from. ### Modern constraints - **glibc 2.29+** added stronger tcache **double-free detection** using the `key` field stored inside a freed `tcache_entry`. A plain `free(A); free(B); free(A);` usually aborts now unless the `key` check is bypassed or the chunk is reintroduced through another path. - **glibc 2.32+** added **safe-linking** to singly-linked allocator lists (`tcache` and `fastbins`). The stored `next` pointer is no longer raw, but mangled as: ```c stored_next = target ^ (address_of_next_field >> 12) ``` Therefore, a modern tcache poisoning usually needs either: - A **heap leak** to compute the protected pointer correctly, or - A different primitive that bypasses/abuses safe-linking instead of forging the pointer directly.<sup>[[1]

text: # VirtualBox Slirp NAT Packet Heap Exploitation {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: TL;DR (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## TL;DR - VirtualBox ships a heavily modified fork of Slirp whose packet buffers (mbufs) live in a custom zone allocator with inline metadata and function-pointer callbacks (`pfFini`, `pfDtor`). - A guest can rewrite the trusted `m->m_len` with an attacker-controlled IP header length, which destroys all later bounds checks and yields both infoleak and overwrite primitives. - By abusing UDP packets with checksum `0` and oversized `ip_len`, the guest can exfiltrate mbuf tails and the metadata of neighbouring chunks to learn heap and zone addresses. - Providing crafted IP options forces `ip_stripoptions()` to `memcpy()` too much data in-place, so the attacker can overwrite the next mbuf's `struct item` header and point its `zone` field at fully controlled data. - Freeing the corrupted mbuf triggers `zone->pfFini()` with attacker-supplied arguments; pointing it to `memcpy@plt` gives an arbitrary copy/write primitive that can be steered toward GOT entries or other control data inside the non-PIE VirtualBox binary.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Packet allocator anatomy (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## Packet allocator anatomy VirtualBox allocates every ingress Ethernet frame from a per-interface zone named `zone_clust`. Each 0x800-byte data chunk is preceded by an inline header: ```c struct item { uint32_t magic; // 0xdead0001 void *zone; // uma_zone_t pointer with callbacks uint32_t ref_count; LIST_ENTRY(item) list; // freelist / used list links }; ``` When an mbuf is freed the call stack `m_freem -> ... -> slirp_uma_free()` trusts the inline header: 1. `uma_zfree_arg()` recomputes `item = (struct item *)mem - 1` and *should* validate `item->zone`, but `Assert()` is compiled out in release builds. 2. `slirp_uma_free()` loads `zone = item->zone` and unconditionally executes `zone->pfFini(zone->pData, data_ptr, zone->size)` followed by `zone->pfDtor(...)`. Therefore, any write-what-where into the mbuf header translates into a controlled indirect call during `free()`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Infoleak via `m->m_len` override (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## Infoleak via `m->m_len` override At the top of `ip_input()` VirtualBox added: ```c if (m->m_len != RT_N2H_U16(ip->ip_len)) m->m_len = RT_N2H_U16(ip->ip_len); ``` Because the assignment happens **before** verifying the IP header, a guest can advertise any length up to 0xffff. The rest of the stack (ICMP, UDP, fragmentation handlers, etc.) assumes `m->m_len` is trustworthy and uses it to decide how many bytes to copy off the mbuf. Use UDP packets with checksum `0` (meaning "no checksum"). The NAT fast-path forwards `m->m_len` bytes without inspecting payload integrity, so inflating `ip_len` causes Slirp to read past the real buffer and return heap residues to the guest or to a cooperating external helper beyond the NAT. Because the chunk size is 2048 bytes, the leak can include:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - The next mbuf's inline `struct item`, revealing the freelist order and the real `zone` pointer. - Heap cookies such as `magic` fields, helping to craft valid-looking headers when performing corruptions later.

title: HT: Overwriting neighbouring chunk headers with IP options (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## Overwriting neighbouring chunk headers with IP options The same bogus length can be turned into an overwrite primitive by forcing the packet through `ip_stripoptions()` (triggered when the IP header has options and the payload is UDP/TCP). The helper computes a copy length from `m->m_len` and then calls `memcpy()` to slide the transport header over the stripped options: 1. Supply a long `ip_len` so the computed move length extends past the current mbuf. 2. Include a small number of IP options so Slirp enters the stripping path. 3. When `memcpy()` runs, it reads from the following mbuf and writes over the current mbuf's payload and inline header, corrupting `magic`, `zone`, `ref_count`, etc. Because the allocator keeps packets from the same interface contiguous on the freelist, this overflow deterministically hits the next chunk after modest heap grooming.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Forging `uma_zone_t` to hijack `pfFini` (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## Forging `uma_zone_t` to hijack `pfFini` Once the adjacent `struct item` is corruptible, the exploit proceeds as follows:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Use leaked heap addresses to build a fake `uma_zone` structure inside a mbuf fully controlled by the guest. Populate: - `pfFini` with the PLT entry of `memcpy()`. - `pData` with the desired destination pointer (e.g. GOT entry, vtable slot, function pointer array). - `size` with the number of bytes to copy. - Optional: `pfDtor` as a second stage call (e.g. to invoke the newly-written function pointer). 2. Overwrite the target mbuf's `zone` field with the pointer to the fake structure; adjust `list` pointers so freelist bookkeeping remains consistent enough to avoid crashes. 3. Free the mbuf. `slirp_uma_free()` now executes `memcpy(dest=pData, src=item_data, n=size)` while the mbuf still contains guest-controlled data, yielding an arbitrary write. Because the Linux VirtualBox binary is non-PIE, PLT addresses for `memcpy` and `system` are fixed and can be used directly. The guest can also stash strings such as `/bin/sh` inside another mbuf that remains referenced when the hijacked call executes.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Heap grooming via fragmentation (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## Heap grooming via fragmentation Slirp's per-interface zone is 3072 chunks deep and initially carved as a contiguous array whose freelist is traversed from high addresses downward. Deterministic adjacency can be achieved by:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Flooding the NAT with many `IP_MF` fragments of constant size so the reassembly code allocates predictable mbuf sequences. - Recycling specific chunks by sending fragments that time out, forcing frees back into the freelist in LIFO order. - Using knowledge of the freelist walk to place the future victim mbuf right after the mbuf that will carry the IP options overflow. This grooming ensures the overflow hits the targeted `struct item` and that the fake `uma_zone` remains in-bounds of the leak primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: From arbitrary write to host code execution (virtualbox-slirp-nat-packet-heap-exploitation)
text: ## From arbitrary write to host code execution With the memcpy-on-free primitive:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Copy an attacker-controlled `/bin/sh` string and command buffer into a stable mbuf. 2. Use the primitive to overwrite a GOT entry or indirect callsite (e.g. a function pointer inside the NAT device state) with the PLT entry of `system()`. 3. Trigger the overwritten call. Because VirtualBox runs the NAT device inside the host process, the payload executes with the privileges of the user running VirtualBox, allowing a guest-to-host escape. Alternative payloads include planting a miniature ROP chain in heap memory and copying its address into a frequently-invoked callback, or repointing `pfFini`/`pfDtor` themselves to chained gadgets for repeated writes.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Windows RIO registered-buffer UAF to kernel R/W (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: # Windows RIO registered-buffer UAF to kernel R/W {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Winsock Registered I/O (RIO) keeps long-lived user buffers mapped so repeated socket operations can refer to buffer slices instead of submitting a new buffer on every call. A client creates the socket with `WSA_FLAG_REGISTERED_IO`, obtains `RIO_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_TABLE` through `WSAIoctl(..., SIO_GET_MULTIPLE_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_POINTER, ...)`, and then uses `RIORegisterBuffer`, `RIOSend`, `RIOReceive`, and `RIODeregisterBuffer`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> CVE-2024-38193 is a useful example of a general Windows kernel exploitation chain: a non-atomic reference acquisition leaves a cached pointer to a freed object, exact-size non-paged-pool reclamation replaces it with controlled bytes, and a forged MDL converts normal I/O into arbitrary kernel read/write.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Reverse-engineered object model (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: ## Reverse-engineered object model In the analyzed `afd.sys` build, each registered buffer is represented by a `0x20`-byte non-paged-pool allocation tagged `bOIR`. The following layouts are reverse engineered and must not be treated as stable ABI definitions.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c struct RIOBuffer { PMDL AssociatedMDL; uint64_t VirtualAddressBuffer; uint32_t LengthBuffer; uint32_t RefCount; uint32_t IsInvalid; uint32_t Unknown; }; struct CachedBuffer { uint32_t IdBuffer; uint32_t RefCount; RIOBuffer *BufferPtr; }; ``` The socket context stores `RIOBuffer` pointers in an ID-indexed array and also keeps recently used objects in a separate cache. This separation matters because the array entry can be cleared while a stale `BufferPtr` remains reachable through the cache.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Lifetime-acquisition race (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: ## Lifetime-acquisition race `AfdRioGetAndCacheBuffer()` validates the array entry and `IsInvalid`, then calls `_InterlockedIncrement(&buffer->RefCount)` before placing the pointer in the cache. The increment itself is atomic, but the preceding pointer/state checks and the acquisition of a live reference are not one indivisible lifetime operation. An `_mm_lfence()` before loading the pointer orders memory operations but does not close this race.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> `AfdRioDereferenceBuffer()` can decide that `RefCount == 1` before it acquires the write lock used to clear the array entry. A competing lookup can increment and cache the object after that decision. The deregistration path can then obtain the lock, remove the array entry, and free the object based on its stale last-reference decision. The cache consequently retains a dangling pointer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text lookup thread deregistration thread ------------- --------------------- observe RefCount == 1 validate array pointer validate IsInvalid == 0 InterlockedIncrement(RefCount) cache BufferPtr clear array slot free RIOBuffer use cached BufferPtr --------------> freed non-paged-pool chunk ``` To exercise this class of bug, keep one worker issuing RIO send/receive requests so lookups and cache fills occur while another worker repeatedly deregisters the same population of buffer IDs. The important audit pattern is **validate pointer -> later increment reference**, racing with **decide last reference -> later unlink and free**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Exact-size non-paged-pool reclamation (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: ## Exact-size non-paged-pool reclamation The demonstrated reclamation uses controlled unbuffered named-pipe entries. Unlike buffered entries, these entries do not add a data header, so their allocation can match the vulnerable `0x20`-byte object exactly.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Fill the relevant non-paged-pool size class with controlled pipe entries. 2. Close selected pipes to create holes. 3. Register RIO buffers so `bOIR` objects occupy those holes. 4. Win the lookup/deregistration race, leaving cached pointers to freed chunks. 5. Allocate more controlled pipe entries of the same size to reclaim the freed addresses. 6. Trigger an operation through each cached buffer and identify which stale entry now interprets pipe data as a `RIOBuffer`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This layout is build- and allocator-dependent. Confirm the target allocation size, pool type, tag, named-pipe entry layout, and cache behavior on the exact Windows build instead of assuming that the analyzed `0x20` layout is portable.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Fake MDL to arbitrary kernel read/write (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: ## Fake MDL to arbitrary kernel read/write Once the reclaimed bytes control `AssociatedMDL`, point it to a forged MDL in user memory and set the fake MDL's `MappedSystemVa` to the chosen kernel address. The stale `RIOBuffer` makes `afd.sys` consume the forged descriptor as though it described the original registered buffer.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The direction of the legitimate socket copy determines the primitive:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `RIOSend()` reads from `MappedSystemVa` and places those bytes in an outgoing packet, producing a kernel-read primitive. - `RIOReceive()` copies incoming packet bytes to `MappedSystemVa`, producing a kernel-write primitive. A data-only privilege-escalation endgame is to aim the write at the exploit process's `_SEP_TOKEN_PRIVILEGES` and enable the required privilege state. Structure locations and offsets vary by Windows build, so resolve them for the target rather than embedding values from another release.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Patch status (afd-rio-buffer-uaf)
text: ## Patch status Microsoft fixed CVE-2024-38193 in the August 2024 security updates. The published exploit strategy was tested on Windows 11 21H2; that test result does not establish exploitability on other builds because the internal structures and allocator behavior are not API contracts.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Windows UAS REPORT LUNS cached-table OOB write (uasp-report-luns-cache-size-oob-write)
text: # Windows UAS REPORT LUNS cached-table OOB write {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} A programmable USB Attached SCSI (UAS) device can make Windows `uaspstor.sys` reuse a small non-paged-pool LUN table during a later, larger `REPORT LUNS` response. The device controls the response length and LUN values; Storport issues the discovery requests without a userland trigger. The published research demonstrates kernel corruption and a Special Pool crash, **not** a completed privilege-escalation or code-execution chain. This is a device-side write primitive, unlike the [Linux USB-audio descriptor read oracle](../linux-kernel-exploitation/usb-audio-descriptor-oob-kaslr-leak.md).<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Cached size versus updated count (uasp-report-luns-cache-size-oob-write)
text: ## Cached size versus updated count `UaspPostProcessSrb` handles completed SCSI `REPORT LUNS` commands (`CDB[0] = 0xA0`). It interprets the first four response bytes as a big-endian `LUN LIST LENGTH` and calculates `count = length >> 3`. In the analyzed build, the per-device table pointer is at `devext+0x468` and its count at `devext+0x3E8`. A response with a nonzero count allocates `32 * count` bytes only if the pointer is null. Every later response replaces the count, but a non-null pointer skips allocation, so the new count can exceed the table's original capacity. These offsets describe the analyzed binary, not a stable Windows ABI.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The fill loop reads eight-byte LUN values from the device response and stores them at `table + 32 * index`. Its `DataTransferLength` test checks whether the source entry is present; it does **not** check `32 * index + 8` against the cached table size. A larger advertised length alone therefore does not guarantee every store: the host-supplied transfer length must also cover each source entry. In the decompiled loop, entry `index` is copied only when `DataTransferLength >= 8 * (index + 2)`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text count = be32(response[0:4]) >> 3 if table == NULL: table = pool_alloc(32 * count) for index in 0 .. count-1: if 8 * (index + 2) <= DataTransferLength: table[32 * index : 32 * index + 8] = response[8 + 8 * index : 16 + 8 * index] ```

title: HT: Rescan while preserving the undersized table (uasp-report-luns-cache-size-oob-write)
text: ## Rescan while preserving the undersized table The attack depends on a protocol status that **repeats discovery without freeing cached state**, not just on sending a large first response. NCC Group's sequence is:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. On the first bus-scan `REPORT LUNS`, report `LUN LIST LENGTH = 8`: one entry gives `count = 1` and a 32-byte table. 2. On a later command, return SCSI unit attention `06/3F/0E` (`REPORTED LUNS DATA HAS CHANGED`). Storport reissues `REPORT LUNS`; the device remains attached, and the small table survives. The analyzed `BulkResetDeviceWorkItem` path does not release it. 3. Respond with `LUN LIST LENGTH = 0x7F8`, giving `count = 255`. The existing pointer causes allocation to be skipped while the count is updated to 255. Supply corresponding device-controlled LUN entries within the actual transfer length. 4. At `index = 1`, the eight-byte store targets `table + 0x20`, just beyond the 32-byte allocation. Later qualifying entries write at 32-byte intervals; the loop can issue up to `max(0, min(255, floor(DataTransferLength / 8) - 1))` stores, of which all but the first are out of bounds for this initial allocation. `UaspFreeResources(a1, 1)` frees or nulls the table on teardown, device removal, or initialization failure. Reattaching between the two responses loses the stale-allocation condition; the unit-attention rescan is the useful state-preserving trigger.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Validating the write primitive (uasp-report-luns-cache-size-oob-write)
text: ## Validating the write primitive With Driver Verifier Special Pool enabled for `uaspstor.sys`, the published crash occurs in `uaspstor!UaspPostProcessSrb+0x98` at `mov qword ptr [rdx+rcx],rax`: the table ends at a guard page, `rdx = 0x20` is the second-entry stride, and `rax` holds a device-supplied LUN value. This confirms the first out-of-bounds write, but a guard-page crash does not establish reliable pool grooming, an arbitrary-address write, or code execution. Check the exact target build and the response transfer length before treating the full 255-entry count as reachable.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Windows USB MIDI packet-size pool overflow (usb-midi-packet-size-pool-overflow)
text: # Windows USB MIDI packet-size pool overflow {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} A programmable USB MIDI peripheral can choose a legal OUT endpoint size that is incompatible with a host driver's fixed-width buffering. In the analyzed Windows `USBMIDI2.sys` USB-MIDI-1.0 path, `wMaxPacketSize` becomes the `NonPagedPoolNx` allocation size, but the driver appends four-byte UMP words and flushes only when the accumulated byte count **equals** that size. A local MIDI client is also needed to keep the output stream active. This is a different device-controlled pool-write primitive from the [UAS cached-table size mismatch](uasp-report-luns-cache-size-oob-write.md), and is separate from the [MIDI service shared-memory ring position bug](../array-indexing.md#client-controlled-shared-memory-ring-positions).<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Select a size that the flush check cannot reach (usb-midi-packet-size-pool-overflow)
text: ## Select a size that the flush check cannot reach The OUT-pipe setup copies `pipeInfo.MaximumPacketSize` into `MidiOutMaxSize` without checking its alignment or transfer type. A full-speed interrupt OUT endpoint can advertise a non-multiple of four, such as 13 bytes; the full-speed bulk sizes listed in the advisory are multiples of four. This makes the interrupt endpoint the relevant descriptor shape, not simply any MIDI device.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> In `USBMIDI2DriverIoWrite`, the USB-MIDI-1.0 branch allocates `MidiOutMaxSize` bytes and performs the indexed store **before** its flush test (simplified below):<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c ((PUINT32)DeviceWriteBuffer)[DeviceWriteBufferIndex++] = umpWord; if (DeviceWriteBufferIndex * sizeof(UINT32) == MidiOutMaxSize) flush_and_reset(); ``` For `MidiOutMaxSize = 13`, the test observes 4, 8, 12, 16, ... bytes and can never equal 13. The fourth word already crosses the 13-byte requested capacity at offsets 12–15; if the usable pool slot is 16 bytes, the fifth word at offsets 16–19 is wholly beyond it. `DeviceWriteBufferIndex` lives in the device context and the USB-MIDI-1.0 allocation path does not reset it. The sibling USB-MIDI-2.0 path does reset its index on allocation and checks that the proposed transfer **fits** with `<=`, rather than relying on equality after a store.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Keep the fallback flush from resetting the index (usb-midi-packet-size-pool-overflow)
text: ## Keep the fallback flush from resetting the index The remaining USB-MIDI-1.0 flush runs only when `DeviceWriteBufferIndex != 0 && !isMoreData`. The MIDI-Out worker passes `isMoreData = (finalReadPosition != midiOutWritePosition)` while consuming packets from the client-mapped cyclic buffer. Keep the producer's write position ahead of the consumer during a sustained drain: intermediate calls then receive `isMoreData = TRUE`, so the end-of-call flush is skipped while the impossible exact-size check also fails. If the queue drains completely, the fallback can send and reset the buffer, so a single short write is not equivalent to the sustained-stream trigger.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Resulting write primitive and limits (usb-midi-packet-size-pool-overflow)
text: ## Resulting write primitive and limits The incrementing index produces sequential four-byte stores into adjacent non-executable kernel pool memory, not an arbitrary-address write. For the channel-voice conversion case, three bytes of each written word come from the client's UMP data; the first byte combines a chosen cable/group nibble with a constrained code-index nibble. Thus the stream controls about 24 bits of each word fully while the remaining byte is format-constrained. The advisory reports a working privilege-escalation exploit but does **not** publish its pool target, grooming sequence, or final payload. Validate the actual allocator slot size and target build before inferring which store first hits another object.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Windows File Handle-Table Object Redirection (file-handle-table-object-redirection)
text: # Windows File Handle-Table Object Redirection {{#include ../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} An arbitrary kernel read/write primitive can repoint a process-owned File handle at an existing `_FILE_OBJECT`. This is not a user-mode sharing-mode bypass: the target must already be open somewhere, and the attacker must already be able to modify kernel memory. The [DumpNTDS proof of concept](https://github.com/S12cybersecurity/HandleRedirect/tree/main/DumpNTDS) uses a vulnerable GIO driver to copy locked credential files on a domain controller without opening those target paths, taking a shadow copy, or reading LSASS memory.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Find an existing File object (file-handle-table-object-redirection)
text: ## Find an existing File object Open an ordinary reference file, then request `NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemHandleInformation)` (`0x10`). Grow the snapshot buffer on `STATUS_INFO_LENGTH_MISMATCH`. Match the reference handle and current PID to learn the runtime File `ObjectTypeIndex`; do not hardcode the type number. Scan File-typed system handles and use the kernel-read primitive to inspect each candidate `_FILE_OBJECT.FileName`. The PoC reads `UNICODE_STRING.Length` at `+0x58` and `Buffer` at `+0x60` on its x64 Windows 10/11 layout, then compares the path suffix. These offsets are build-dependent, and a snapshot object pointer must still be live when used.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> This can locate an object held by another process even when `CreateFileW` on the same path returns `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`. It does **not** grant a new file handle through the normal object-manager path.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Redirect the caller's handle-table entry (file-handle-table-object-redirection)
text: ## Redirect the caller's handle-table entry The PoC first opens a benign file with `GENERIC_READ` and `FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED`. It locates its own `_EPROCESS`, follows `ObjectTable` to `_HANDLE_TABLE.TableCode`, and computes the victim entry as `tableBase + (handleValue / 4) * 16` after masking the low two `TableCode` bits. That flat calculation is the PoC's assumed table layout; resolve offsets and table levels for the target build rather than treating them as a stable Windows ABI.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> For the demonstrated x64 layout, replace only `_HANDLE_TABLE_ENTRY.LowQword`. The entry encodes an `OBJECT_HEADER` pointer, not the `_FILE_OBJECT` body address. Keep its low 20 metadata bits and leave `HighQword` unchanged. Because this does not add access rights, the benign handle must already permit reading:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```c uint64_t header = fileObject - 0x30; uint64_t redirected = (((header >> 4) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFULL) << 20) | (originalLowQword & 0xFFFFFULL); WritePrimitive(driver, (void *)entryAddress, &redirected, sizeof redirected); ``` A raw body pointer or wrong encoding can crash the kernel when the object manager references the handle. Check `GetFinalPathNameByHandleW` on the original handle after patching, and restore the saved `LowQword` before closing that handle or exiting. The published copy routine restores after normal completion and destination-creation failure, but its `VirtualAlloc`-failure branch returns **without restoring**; repair every error path before reuse.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Read through the redirected handle (file-handle-table-object-redirection)
text: ## Read through the redirected handle Read from the same handle into an attacker-controlled destination. The PoC uses a page-aligned `VirtualAlloc` buffer, 4096-byte sectors, 64-KiB chunks, `OVERLAPPED` offsets/events, and `GetOverlappedResult` because the borrowed file object can require unbuffered I/O. Alignment and chunk sizes must satisfy the target device rather than being assumed universal. Restore the original entry after **each** target copy.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[5]](#references)</sup> On a domain controller, the demonstrated targets are `SYSTEM` (boot key), `ntds.dit` (directory database), and `SECURITY` (LSA secrets). The published offline extraction shows boot-key and LSA material, but its NTDS stage fails; that transcript does not establish a completed domain-hash dump. See [Stealing Windows Credentials](../../windows-hardening/stealing-credentials/) for offline extraction and other NTDS acquisition paths.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **First Fit** (first-fit)
text: ## **First Fit** When a program frees memory through glibc, the allocator may place chunks in several caches or bins. The following unsorted-bin and fastbin behavior describes the classic allocator model; on glibc 2.26 and later, the per-thread tcache usually intercepts eligible chunks first.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> ### Unsorted Bins With tcache bypassed or disabled, a freed arena chunk that is not kept in a fastbin is commonly coalesced and placed in the unsorted bin. New entries are linked at the front, while allocation scans from the back. A sufficiently large chunk can be split, returning its front portion and leaving a remainder for subsequent processing. Top-chunk consolidation and other bins are important exceptions.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> Example: - In a legacy/no-tcache setup, allocate 300 bytes (`a`), then 250 bytes (`b`), free `a`, and request 250 bytes (`c`). - When you free `a`, it goes to the unsorted bin. - If you then request 250 bytes again, the allocator finds `a` at the tail and splits it, returning the part that fits your request and keeping the rest in the bin. - `c` can point into the previous `a` region and retain any bytes that allocation did not overwrite. ```c char *a = malloc(300); char *b = malloc(250); free(a); char *c = malloc(250); ``` On default modern glibc, `a` is normally cached in its own tcache size class, while the 250-byte request belongs to another size class; this exact example therefore does **not** demonstrate unsorted-bin splitting unless tcache is disabled/bypassed or the sizes are adjusted. ### Fastbins Fastbins cache selected small chunks in last-in-first-out (LIFO) singly linked lists. title: HT: Basic Information (README)
text: ## Basic Information A use-after-free (UAF) occurs when a program continues to use a pointer or reference after the referenced allocation has been freed. The stale reference is often called a _dangling pointer_. If the allocator later reuses that region, the stale pointer may refer to data owned by a different object.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Accessing freed memory is invalid, but it does not necessarily fail immediately. Depending on the operation and the allocator state, a UAF may cause a crash, disclose memory, corrupt a live object, or enable code execution. Exploitation commonly involves reclaiming the freed region with attacker-influenced data before the program dereferences the stale pointer; overwriting a function pointer or another control-sensitive field can then redirect execution.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: First-Fit Attack (README)
text: ## First-Fit Attack A first-fit attack uses predictable allocation selection to reclaim a freed chunk with a chosen allocation. In a UAF scenario, heap grooming can place attacker-controlled contents where the dangling pointer will later read or write. In glibc, some same-size free lists—notably tcache bins and fastbins—are last-in, first-out, so a matching allocation may return the most recently freed chunk. Other bins and allocators use different selection rules, so the exact result depends on the glibc version, size class, cache/bin state, and allocation sequence.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> See the dedicated page for details: {{#ref}} first-fit.md {{#endref}} For Windows NT-heap targets, [BEA guards and LFH reuse](../../windows-userland-heap-grooming.md) have different allocation-selection rules from glibc.

title: HT: Allocation Order Summary [[1]](#references) (malloc-and-sysmalloc)
text: ## Allocation Order Summary [[1]](#references) (Security checks are not described in this summary, and some cases are omitted for brevity.) 1. `__libc_malloc` tries to get a chunk from the tcache, if not it calls `_int_malloc` 2. `_int_malloc` : 1. Tries to generate the arena if there isn't any 2. If any fast bin chunk of the correct size, use it 1. Fill tcache with other fast chunks 3. If any small bin chunk of the correct size, use it 1. Fill tcache with other chunks of that size 4. If the requested size isn't for small bins, consolidate fast bin into unsorted bin 5. Check the unsorted bin, use the first chunk with enough space 1. If the selected chunk is larger, split it, return the requested part, and add the remainder to the unsorted bin 2. If a chunk is of the same size as the size requested, use to to fill the tcache instead of returning it (until the tcache is full, then return the next one) 3. For each chunk of smaller size checked, put it in its respective small or large bin 6. Check the large bin in the index of the requested size 1. Starting with the first chunk larger than the requested size, return a suitable chunk and place any remainder in the unsorted bin 7. Check the large bins from the next indexes until the end 1. Starting with the next larger index, split the first suitable chunk and add the remainder to the unsorted bin 8. If nothing is found in the previous bins, get a chunk from the top chunk 9. If the top chunk wasn't big enough enlarge it with `sysmalloc`

title: HT: Free Order Summary (free)
text: ## Free Order Summary (No checks are explained in this summary and some case have been omitted for brevity) 1. If the address is null don't do anything 2. If the chunk was mmapped, unmap it and finish 3. Call `_int_free`: 1. If possible, add the chunk to the tcache 2. If possible, add the chunk to the fast bin 3. title: HT: Attacker notes and recent changes (2023–2025) (free)
text: ## Attacker notes and recent changes (2023–2025) - Safe-Linking in tcache/fastbins: `free()` stores the `fd` pointer of singly-linked lists using the macro `PROTECT_PTR(pos, ptr) = ((size_t)pos >> 12) ^ (size_t)ptr`. This means crafting a fake next pointer for tcache poisoning requires the attacker to know a heap address (e.g., leak `chunk_addr`, then use `chunk_addr >> 12` as the XOR key). See more details and PoCs in the tcache page below. - Tcache double-free detection: Before pushing a chunk into tcache, `free()` checks the per-entry `e->key` against the per-thread `tcache_key` and walks the bin up to `mp_.tcache_count` looking for duplicates, aborting with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` when found. - Recent glibc change (2.42): `free()` can now keep **much larger arena chunks** inside tcache when `glibc.malloc.tcache_max` is raised above the historical ceiling (up to **4 MiB**). Therefore, assumptions such as “large free => unsorted bin” are no longer reliable on modern tuned targets. **Mmapped chunks are still not cached in tcache.**<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Heap-grooming gotcha (glibc 2.42+): if your first heap activity uses **large chunks that never touch tcache**, the `tcache_perthread_struct` may be initialized **later** than in older labs. This can place tcache metadata **after attacker-controlled large chunks**, which is useful when an overflow/UAF can later target that metadata.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> ### Quick crafting of a safe-linked fd (for tcache poisoning) ```py

title: HT: Heap Memory Functions (README)
text: # Heap Memory Functions {{#include ../../../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} The C allocation interface centers on `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, and `free`: `malloc` reserves an uninitialized block, `calloc` allocates and clears an array, `realloc` changes an existing allocation's size, and `free` releases an allocation. In glibc, these calls are backed by allocator internals whose metadata and consistency checks are important when studying heap corruption.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The pages in this section describe the relevant allocation and release paths, the `unlink` operation, and security checks performed by heap-management functions. Allocator behavior changes across glibc versions, so verify the target's exact library build before relying on a particular data structure or exploitation technique.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>
